items.title: TILE: Bridging LLMs and Table Foundation Models for Tabular Learning with Strings
items.content: arXiv:2610.17065v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Real-world tables are often heterogeneous, combining numerical features with free-form string columns. Table foundation models (TFMs) excel on numerical tables but require strings to be encoded numerically, while large language models (LLMs) hold semantic knowledge but are not designed for tabular predictions. Most existing bridges use LLMs as plug-in encoders for cell strings, yet how to extract representations effectively for tabular learning remains underexplored. We show that the interface between LLMs and tables matter as much as the LLM itself. Applied cell-wise, larger LLMs do not give better features. With our interface, the same LLMs improve steadily with size. TILE (Table-Interfaced LLM Embeddings) combines four ingredients: row serialization to provide cross-column context, intermediate-layer extraction to avoid layers specialized for next-token prediction, columnar pooling to remove mean pooling's length bias, and by-pass features to route numbers and categories past the LLM. Paired with TFMs, TILE sets a new state of the art for tables with strings. Across 100 datasets, it beats the strongest baseline on 89% of splits, with gains across 7 LLMs and 10 tabular learners, and ranks first on the 108-dataset STRABLE benchmark.
items.author: F\'elix Lefebvre, David Holzm\"uller, Gioia Blayer, Myung Jun Kim, Marine Le Morvan, Ga\"el Varoquaux
items.summary: TILE introduces a table-interfaced way to extract LLM embeddings for heterogeneous tables containing both numeric and free-form string columns, showing that the LLM-table interface matters as much as the LLM itself: with the right interface, larger LLMs consistently help, unlike naive cell-wise encodings. It combines row selection and other ingredients to feed LLM representations into table foundation models.
items.reasoning: Practical and well-designed contribution from an experienced tabular-ML group (Varoquaux and colleagues), with a counterintuitive finding about scaling behavior under different interfaces. Relevant to the large industrial niche of tabular prediction, though incremental in overall scope.

items.title: CodeLift: Your Test Suite Is Secretly a Dense SWE Curriculum
items.content: arXiv:2610.17224v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The pass-all-test binary reward has become a standard recipe for training software engineering agents, but its sparsity eliminates difference of partially correct patches. The test pass-rate is a natural alternative. However, we find that it is not a reliable indicator of patch quality. A functionality being tested can be covered by either one challenging test or one hundred trivial tests, where the majority might be already satisfied pass-to-pass tests. We introduce CodeLift, a reinforcement learning method that dynamically calibrates pass-rate rewards, turning the test suite into an adaptive curriculum. At each iteration, CodeLift groups tests that kill the same patches and patches that pass the same tests, then gives more weight to test groups that fewer patch groups pass. This reduces the impact of majority simple tests and focuses more on what is still challenging. Within each rollout, CodeLift applies the same scoring rule to repository snapshots, assigning credit to useful actions even when later ones introduce regressions. Experiments on SWE benchmarks show that CodeLift consistently improves pass@1/2/4/8 over binary and pass-rate baselines. Analyses show that CodeLift provides dense, stable learning signals and unlocks the inherent curriculum in the test suite.

This attacks the sparse binary reward problem in SWE-agent training.

items.title: Two For The Price Of One: Curvature-Aware Pruning Preserves Influence Functions Too
items.content: arXiv:2610.18516v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Post-training pruning enables efficient deployment, but conventional methods do not explicitly preserve internal-gradient alignment between sparse and dense models. We study novel connections between downstream performance of compressed models and the ability to retain gradient information via influence-function preservation. Central to this connection is a curvature-aware objective that accounts for both layer activations and backpropagated gradients. Despite its promise, this objective remains underexplored in pruning due to a lack of efficient solvers. We introduce $\texttt{CACTUS}$, a novel ADMM-based optimizer supporting both pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank decompositions of pre-trained weights. Compared to LLM-Surgeon which targets the same objective, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ can achieve over an order-of-magnitude speedup. At $50\%$ pruning of Qwen3-4B, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ reduces the C4 perplexity gap to the dense model by $45\%$, improves compressed-to-dense per-sample gradient cosine similarity on WikiText-2 from $0.670$ to $0.755$, and runs over $28\times$ faster than LLM-Surgeon on substantially weaker hardware. By preserving influence functions, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ supports effective data selection. On Llama-3.2-3B, fine-tuning a fresh dense model on the $5\%$ of data selected by $\texttt{CACTUS}$ achieves $49.44\%$ accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard, compared with $47.22\%$ using ALPS and $49.54\%$ using dense-model selection. Finally, integrating $\texttt{CACTUS}$ with LoGRA, a recent gradient-projection strategy, on Qwen3-4B with MLP layers pruned to 2:4 sparsity and a rank-64 correction retains a $0.711$ cosine alignment with dense LoGRA-projected C4 gradients.

items.summary: The paper introduces CACTUS, an ADMM-based pruning optimizer with a curvature-aware objective that preserves both layer activations and backpropagated gradients, connecting compression quality to influence-function fidelity. It shows that pruning can simultaneously preserve downstream performance and gradient-information retention, compared against methods like LLM-Surgeon.
items.reasoning: Novel linkage between pruning and influence-function preservation is conceptually interesting and relevant to efficient LLM deployment and interpretability, though it builds on an established pruning literature and the empirical scope is unclear from the abstract.

items.title: TartanMatch: Towards Universal Dense Correspondence Across Modalities
items.content: arXiv:2610.14513v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Robotic platforms combine multi-modal sensors to operate across diverse conditions, but most dense correspondence methods are limited to RGB-RGB or a small set of modality pairs. Training a model for each modality pair scales poorly with the number of sensors and forgoes potential positive transfer across modality pairs. We introduce TartanMatch, a unified model for dense correspondence across all 25 ordered pairs among RGB, event, thermal, depth, and projected LiDAR. TartanMatch adapts an RGB-pretrained correspondence model to all modality pairs within one shared network using lightweight modality adaptation and a mixture of real and synthetic data. On zero-shot real-world benchmarks, TartanMatch reduces Endpoint Error (EPE) over the strongest baselines by 61.9% for cross-modal matching and 49.6% for same-modal matching. We further show that joint training across all modality pairs improves average matching accuracy over pair-specific training, especially on challenging cross-modal pairs. These results demonstrate that a single model achieves broad multi-modal coverage and state-of-the-art matching accuracy.

It reduces endpoint error on zero-shot real-world benchmarks versus strong baselines. This is significant for multi-sensor robotics where training per-pair models scales poorly.

items.title: CoLA: Multi-VLA Coordination via Learned Adapters
items.content: arXiv:2610.15337v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically deployed as isolated single-agent policies. When several such agents share a workspace, they can coordinate implicitly, by observing one another, or explicitly, by exchanging messages, but it remains unclear when explicit communication becomes necessary. We introduce CoLA (Coordination via Learned Adapters), which keeps each agent's VLA backbone frozen and trains a lightweight message channel and a per-arm diffusion action head on top, with fully decentralised execution. Across three tasks that differ in how much each agent can observe, the channel matters only when information is private. On an occluded tray handover, where the box's colour marker is visible to one agent only, CoLA reaches 76.0% success versus 1.3% with messages zeroed throughout training. On two-arm and three-arm handover tasks, removing messages has no measurable effect with a shared overhead camera (90.6% vs. 88.3% at two arms; 63.5% vs. 60.0% at three), but lowers success on the two-arm task's wrist-only variant (74.8% vs. 64.3%). This architecture generalises across different VLA backbones as well. With a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone on the same occluded tray task, CoLA matches the overall success rate of a LoRA-fine-tuned baseline (37.3% vs. 34.7%) using a fraction of the trainable parameters. When CoLA places the box, it selects the correct tray 71.8% of the time, whereas the independently fine-tuned baseline, whose placing arm never sees the marker, selects it at chance level (34.7% against 33.3%).
items.author: Ahaskar Kashyap, Jiawen Zong, Boyu Ma, Chuhao Zhou, Jingliang Li, Stefano V. Albrecht, Jianfei Yang

items.title: Inference on the Value of Policy Improvement in Adaptive Experiments
items.content: arXiv:2610.15789v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In this paper, we develop an asymptotically normal estimator for the value of policy improvement (VPI) under adaptively collected data. This value, which is defined as the gap between the value of the best treatment policy in a class and that of a baseline policy, gauges whether or not it is worth deploying a personalized treatment policy. Building an estimator for the VPI is naturally more difficult than estimating the value of a fixed policy. This is because, in addition to contending with the correlated data and decaying propensities associated with adaptive experiments, any estimator must also handle the non-regularity, or lack of pathwise differentiability, of the underlying estimand when the optimal policy is non-unique. Our proposed estimator works by sequentially fitting a weighted empirical welfare maximizing policy on historical data and then evaluating it using inverse propensity weighting on future samples. We neither assume that the optimal policy is unique nor make a margin assumption on the underlying heterogeneous treatment effects. A key difficulty in analyzing our estimator is showing that the regret incurred through policy learning is asymptotically smaller than the standard error of the estimator. We accomplish this by showing faster regret rates for policy learning under decaying propensities, which may be of independent interest. We not only evaluate the coverage of our estimator on a mix of synthetic and semi-synthetic data, but also employ it to estimate the VPI in an adaptive experiment evaluating the efficacy of job assistance programs in Jordan due to Caria et al. Although our estimates are generally more conservative than their hierarchical Bayesian analysis, which assumes that the optimal policy is unique, we still corroborate the benefits of personalization amongst Syrian refugees.
items.author: Justin Whitehouse, Emma Brunskill, Vasilis Syrgkanis
items.summary: The authors develop an asymptotically normal estimator for the value of policy improvement (VPI) under adaptively collected data, handling correlated samples, decaying propensities, and non-regularity when the optimal policy is non-unique. This enables principled inference on whether deploying a personalized treatment policy is worthwhile.
items.reasoning: Technically demanding and practically relevant contribution to off-policy evaluation and adaptive experimentation from credible researchers (Whitehouse, Brunskill, Syrgkanis); addresses the difficult non-regular estimand problem.

We not only evaluate the coverage of our estimator on a mix of synthetic and semi-synthetic data, but also employ it to estimate the VPI in an adaptive experiment evaluating the efficacy of job assistance programs in Jordan due to Caria et al. Although our estimates are generally more conservative than their hierarchical Bayesian analysis, which assumes that the optimal policy is unique, we still corroborate the benefits of personalization amongst Syrian refugees.

items.title: Gluing Local Contexts into Global Meaning: A Sheaf-Theoretic Decomposition of Transformer Representations
items.content: arXiv:2610.17117v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Existing interpretability tools do not test whether a representation keeps the same content when only the phrasing changes. We treat each paraphrase pair as a local witness that two activations should agree and build a cellular sheaf over the paraphrase graph; its Laplacian $L_\mathcal{F}$ answers the question on a frozen model with no training. The kernel $H^0$ is a content subspace: at 20 dimensions it beats the preserved subspace of the concept eraser LEACE on held-out CounterFact fact retrieval across eight architectures by a mean $+17.1$\,pp, and constraining all paraphrases of a fact jointly adds a further $+6.5$\,pp. The spectral complement concentrates causal influence: ablating the most paraphrase-variable coordinates, a coordinate-wise proxy for it, changes model outputs $5.6$ to $26.5\times$ more than ablating coordinates of matched per-coordinate variability, across nine models from 124M to 13B parameters. Stacking layers into a grid creates $b_1 = N(L-1)$ algebraic 1-cycles, and the resulting model-derived harmonic mass varies by nearly three orders of magnitude across six architectures and ranks them as their steering fragility does (Spearman $\rho = 0.90$, exact one-sided permutation $p = 0.014$). The same paraphrase graph yields the content subspace, the influence directions, and the fragility measure. Project page: https://cwru-aism.github.io/gluing-lc-page/

items.title: Monitoring for Shifts at Unknown Times: Parameter-Free Conditional Conformal Martingales
items.content: arXiv:2610.17343v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Conditional conformal test martingales provide sequential tests for detecting distribution shifts, using a fixed reference dataset to avoid contamination from test-time samples. Prior work used a penalized betting function via online optimization with smoothing, clipping, and other hyperparameters, which can adapt slowly when a shift occurs after a long stationary period. In this work, we introduce an approach that requires no hyperparameters and provably adapts quickly to shifts occurring at unknown times. Our key idea is to frame the penalized betting problem as portfolio selection in a three-asset market. Then, we use a restarting universal portfolio, with a heavy-tailed wealth allocation over time. We establish anytime false-alarm control and derive optimal finite-sample bounds on detection delay under detectable alternatives. We also develop an FFT-based implementation that computes the portfolio sequence over $T$ rounds in $\mathcal{O}(T^2\ln T)$ time, instead of $\mathcal{O}(T^3)$ of the naive implementation. Synthetic and real-world experiments suggest that the proposed approach adapts rapidly after long periods of null samples, with detection delays depending substantially less on shift time than prior baselines.

items.title: Encoding Context into LLM Weights: What Makes It Context?
items.content: arXiv:2610.17686v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Longer contexts allow large language models (LLMs) to condition their predictions on more information, but inference costs grow prohibitively with context length. An emerging alternative uses test-time updates to encode context as temporary changes to model weights. However, encoding this information into weights that already represent general knowledge obscures its role as context, so the LLM may fail to use it properly to condition subsequent inference. To restore this contextual role, we first associate each context with an identifier during encoding, thereby distinguishing the newly encoded information from pre-existing knowledge. Invoking the identifier at inference then enables the LLM to recite the encoded context. Nevertheless, successful recitation does not ensure that the LLM will use the recalled information as context. We therefore further introduce a prompting framework that explicitly guides the LLM to use this information as context. Across diverse controlled tasks and practical benchmarks, our method outperformed the baseline using only off-the-shelf LLMs, showing its advances in context encoding.

items.summary: The paper studies test-time updates that encode context into LLM weights as an alternative to long in-context prompts, noting that encoding into knowledge-bearing weights obscures the information's contextual role. The authors associate encoded context with an identifier so it can be invoked and recited at inference, and analyze what distinguishes genuine context from baked-in knowledge. This touches a fundamental question about the boundary between parametric knowledge and context in LLMs.

items.title: Simplifying and Improving On-Policy Distillation for Few-Step Diffusion
items.content: arXiv:2610.18472v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Few-step distillation reduces the sampling cost of diffusion and flow models, but existing approaches often require auxiliary score models or specialized architectures. We show that simple on-policy velocity regression already provides a strong foundation for 4-NFE generation. To represent teacher velocity variation within each coarse transition, we introduce Pivot, a training-only residual proxy that separates local corrections from the student's interval-mean prediction. We further repel the student from weaker teacher predictions, providing a lightweight mechanism for avoiding undesirable modes. The resulting framework, Simplified Matching Distillation (SMD), remains entirely regression-based, requires neither online score estimation nor adversarial training, and leaves the deployed generator unchanged. We evaluate SMD on image generation and editing, 3D generation, video synthesis, and joint audio--video generation, scaling to 33 billion parameters. At 4-NFE, SMD outperforms strong few-step baselines and surpasses multi-step teachers on several benchmarks. It also supports cross-model, multi-teacher, and causal-video distillation.

items.title: TL;QR: Querying Temporal Discursive Patterns in Textual Corpora
items.content: arXiv:2610.15712v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Many questions about large textual corpora concern patterns that unfold over time, such as a political group whose stance on a topic drifts from support to criticism over several years of debates. We present TL;QR (Too Long; Query with logical temporal Reasoning), a declarative query language and open-source engine for finding such temporal discursive patterns. In TL;QR, a single query combines natural-language predicates, whose truth is judged by a Large Language Model (LLM), with regular expressions and the operators of a temporal logic. The LLM answers only local questions about individual text passages; a symbolic engine then aggregates these judgments over time and links every match to the recorded passages and predicate decisions behind it. With this division of labor, the temporal and relational reasoning stays exact and auditable even over long time horizons. In addition, when a query includes a regular-expression pre-filter, only a small fraction of the corpus ever reaches the LLM. On a suite of controlled synthetic benchmarks with temporally and semantically complex patterns, TL;QR is substantially more accurate than LLM-only baselines. In a case study on ten years of European Parliament debates (442,593 multilingual speeches), TL;QR identifies candidate shifts in the political groups' stances on the GDPR privacy regulation.

items.title: More Reasoning Is Not Always Better: Executing Clinical Guidelines with LLMs and Rules
items.content: arXiv:2610.15912v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in clinical decision support. However, existing approaches often rely on multi-step reasoning or multi-agent collaboration to execute clinical guidelines, introducing substantial computational overhead without reliably preventing decision errors. To address these limitations, we propose a framework for Medical Decision Execution (MedDEx) that integrates structured patient states with deterministic rule execution to support guideline-based treatment planning. MedDEx separates clinical record interpretation from guideline execution, leveraging LLMs to extract patient information and generate treatment plans while assigning guideline-defined decision logic to a rule executor. Experiments across multiple clinical guideline benchmarks demonstrate that MedDEx improves decision accuracy while reducing inference costs. Further analyses highlight the critical roles of structured patient representations and deterministic rule execution, suggesting that additional LLM reasoning does not necessarily translate into better guideline adherence.
items.author: Xiaoqian Lu, Guangfu Guo, Long Cheng, Kunpeng Liu
items.summary: MedDEx separates clinical record interpretation (handled by LLMs) from guideline execution (handled by a deterministic rule executor), arguing that heavy multi-step reasoning or multi-agent setups add overhead without reliably preventing errors. Experiments show the hybrid achieves better guideline-based treatment planning with less computation.
items.reasoning: Counterintuitive and safety-relevant result in clinical decision support: deterministic rules beat elaborate LLM reasoning chains for guideline execution. Clean architecture with clear applicability, though clinical validation depth is unclear from the abstract.

items.title: Strong yet Controllable LLM Abstention without Learning to Abstain
items.content: arXiv:2610.16318v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can reduce hallucination by abstaining from questions they would likely get wrong. Abstention can be implemented outside the model (selective answering) using a confidence threshold that controls the answer rate (coverage), or learned inside it (abstention training), which can perform better but fixes coverage once trained. To compare the two, we match their coverage and decompose risk (error rate) into answering ability and distinguishing ability, i.e., how well the model answers and how accurately it abstains, respectively. The decomposition shows that abstention training performs better mainly by answering better: with strong confidence estimators, the two have nearly equal distinguishing ability. This motivates Train for Accuracy, then Post-hoc Select (TAPS), a modular approach that keeps coverage controllable, needs only standard post-training and an off-the-shelf confidence estimator, and benefits from advances in either component. Across three LLMs and three factual QA benchmarks, TAPS with a probing-based confidence estimator attains 1.5--9.4 percentage points lower mean risk than three representative abstention training methods at matched coverage. Within TAPS, accuracy training often weakens the model's own confidence signals, yet refitting the estimator largely preserves distinguishing ability. Together, these results establish TAPS as a strong yet controllable baseline and raise the bar for future abstention training: sacrificing control over coverage should yield gains beyond what can be achieved by optimizing answering and abstaining separately.

This motivates selective answering with strong confidence estimators, which retains the flexible coverage control that fixed-coverage abstention training lacks.

items.title: PIG: Parallel Inconsistency Guidance for Accelerating Diffusion Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.17375v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Diffusion language models accelerate generation by decoding multiple masked positions per forward pass. However, accuracy is known to drop when parallel decoding trajectories deviate from their sequential counterparts, which are slow and expensive "oracles" that adhere to the joint distribution of language. In this paper, we propose Parallel Inconsistency Guidance (PIG), a new paradigm that uses a trained auxiliary model to directly estimate the inconsistency between parallel and sequential generation from a single model forward pass. During inference, masked positions are traversed by decreasing confidence, and tokens are added to the parallel decode set one-at-a-time until the total estimated inconsistency between the parallel and sequential generation exceeds a threshold. Surprisingly, it suffices to train a lightweight ~2M parameter auxiliary model on a small mixture drawn from OpenCoder, GSM8K-train, MATH-train, and MBPP-train. For LLaDA-8B Instruct and NemotronDiffusion-3B Instruct, PIG extends the accuracy-TPF frontier on GSM8K, MATH500, MBPP, HumanEval, and MMLU, when compared to the industry standard Fast-dLLM and measures favorably on LLaDA-8B Instruct against DAPD, KLASS, EB-sampler, and other learned unmasking policies.
items.author: Quentin Fruytier, Anton Xue, Sanjay Shakkottai, Sujay Sanghavi
items.summary: PIG uses an auxiliary trained model to estimate, in a single forward pass, the inconsistency between parallel and sequential decoding trajectories in diffusion language models, adding tokens to the parallel decode set until estimated inconsistency stays acceptable. This mitigates the accuracy degradation of parallel decoding while retaining its speed benefits.
items.reasoning: Novel inference-time technique for a promising architecture family (diffusion LMs), addressing a well-known quality-speed trade-off; authors from a strong research group though empirical gains need broader validation.

items.title: Attacking Only Half the Data: Two-Sided Evaluation of AI-Text Detector Robustness
items.content: arXiv:2610.18151v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We investigate the robustness of widely used AI text detectors under attacks applied to both human and machine text. Prior evaluations typically attack only machine text, overlooking that human text is routinely modified through grammar correction, formatting, or invisible character insertion. We introduce a two-sided protocol that applies attacks to both classes. Across two corpora and nine detectors, reported AUROC gains vanish under two-sided evaluation, with attacked human text misclassified at rates up to 100%. While simple preprocessing reverses character-level attacks, word-level synonym substitution remains effective meaning-preserving, and irreversible.

This substantially weakens confidence in current AI-text detection.

items.title: Retrieval Disagreement as a Signal: Diagnosing and Steering Multilingual Dense Embedders
items.content: arXiv:2610.18526v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multilingual dense retrievers place all languages in one shared space so that a question finds relevant documents, regardless of which language they are written in. We show that the same question, asked in different languages, retrieves substantially different documents, and this disagreement is not because of weak language understanding. Each language performs well on its own and ranks candidates consistently with the other languages; divergence appears only when languages share an index. We trace the mechanism: each language keeps its own ranking, but in the shared index, its correct answers are pushed far down, buried under non-relevant documents that are either in the query's own language or in English, depending on the model. We introduce disagreement-guided steering: for each language, we contrast the documents that other languages agree on for a question against those that language retrieves idiosyncratically, and take the difference of their representations as a language-specific direction, added to that language's queries at inference. Against baselines of language-mean removal, subspace removal, and per-language rotation, it most strongly reduces same-language crowding while remaining competitive on recall, trading off against mean removal, which better preserves ranking quality.
items.author: Faeze Ghorbanpour, Shaghayegh Kolli, Jana Diesner, Alexander Fraser
items.summary: The authors show that multilingual dense retrievers return substantially different documents for the same question in different languages, and trace this to shared-index interference rather than weak per-language understanding. They diagnose the mechanism in the shared embedding space and use retrieval disagreement as a signal for steering. This is a useful contribution to making multilingual retrieval more reliable.
items.reasoning: Well-motivated diagnosis with mechanistic insight into a practical failure mode of shared multilingual embedding spaces; the steering application adds applied value. Score limited by being an incremental analysis rather than a new architecture or SOTA result.

Against baselines of language-mean removal, subspace removal, and per-language rotation, it most strongly reduces same-language crowding while remaining competitive on recall, trading off against mean removal, which better preserves ranking quality.

items.title: StateHarness: Maintaining Evolving Project State for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.17616v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Long-horizon coding requires agents to maintain an evolving view of the project they are changing: what problem is currently being solved, what has already been learned or modified, which other artifacts may be affected, and what work remains unresolved. When this information is scattered across a growing interaction history, local edits can become disconnected from their later consequences and progress can be difficult to carry forward. We introduce StateHarness, a runtime framework that maintains evolving project state without updating model parameters. The working agent records its current problem and hypothesis, important findings and decisions, discovered repository relationships, and unfinished work. Runtime support prompts record updates, searches for callers, tests, and documentation that may be affected by a change, and maintains a compact working brief for subsequent decisions. When behavioral signals accumulate, a separate diagnostic session revisits the recorded history and surfaces overlooked evidence. Across three repository-level evaluations, StateHarness improves task completion and several measures of change consistency. On RefactorBench, full-chain completion increases from 29.4% to 35.3% and cleanup-check accuracy from 87.0% to 95.4%. On five LHTB software-engineering tasks, mean reward improves from 0.427 to 0.576, exceeding LongHorizon-Harness at substantially lower recorded execution cost. On ChainSWE, bug-fix rate increases from 35.1% to 39.5% and residual debt decreases from 60 to 43 items, although pass-to-pass regressions increase. These results show that maintaining project state can improve long-horizon coding while introducing measurable execution and regression trade-offs.

items.title: Learning Transferable World-Action Models from Task-Paired Human Videos
items.content: arXiv:2610.14351v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: World-action models inherit broad visual and physical priors from video pre-training. However, standard within-video next-frame prediction allows them to rely on appearance shared between the context and future, rather than learning interactions that transfer across scenes and embodiments. We introduce WATCH, a cross-video pre-training that learns from task-paired human demonstrations collected across diverse environments. Conditioned on the video and actions of one demonstration, the model jointly predicts another demonstration's actions and future frames from its current observation. Predicting one demonstration from another encourages the model to learn task-relevant interactions that transfer across scenes and demonstrators. Our pre-training shows that these capabilities can be learned from readily scalable human-human pairs alone, without requiring matched human-robot demonstrations. Analyses before robot post-training show improved motion alignment across embodiments and better action and video prediction on unseen robots, with representations closer to those learned from robot pairs. After robot post-training, WATCH improves MimicDroid in-context success from 40.9% to 68.3% with Cosmos Policy and from 59.8% to 77.7% with Cosmos3, with the largest gains on the unseen levels. Gains persist under context-free post-training across robot embodiments. WATCH outperforms within-video pre-training and co-training baselines, supporting cross-video prediction as a scalable approach to learning transferable world-action representations.

items.title: Adversarial Gradient Forcing for Robust Few-Step Autoregressive Video Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.14553v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Autoregressive video generation models generate videos sequentially, with each new block conditioned on previously generated blocks. By training on the model's own rollouts, Self Forcing and its follow-up methods substantially mitigate exposure bias caused by the mismatch between training- and inference-time history distributions. However, these models still suffer from error accumulation during long-horizon generation. We identify a key underlying limitation: the model remains highly sensitive to errors in its generated history, allowing small deviations to be amplified through subsequent generations. We refer to this underexplored problem as the local history robustness gap. To address this gap, we introduce Adversarial Gradient Forcing (AGF), a framework designed to improve the robustness of few-step autoregressive video models to perturbations and accumulated errors in their own generated histories. AGF uses distribution matching gradients from future block predictions to select adversarial perturbations of self-generated histories. It then jointly trains the generator on the original and perturbed histories to improve the robustness of future generation. Extensive experiments show that AGF achieves the highest VBench Total score on 60-second video generation and the best visual quality on four-minute video generation. Notably, AGF achieves such long-horizon robustness while requiring only 5-second rollouts for training.

items.reasoning: Clean problem identification with a principled adversarial training fix for a real limitation of autoregressive video diffusion; relevant to a very active research direction, though built on an established training paradigm.

items.title: VideoEvoHarness: Self Evolving Agent Harness from Unlabeled Videos for Video Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2610.15389v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video understanding agents rely on a harness to acquire evidence, use tools, and reason, but improving it requires substantial effort. Recent self evolution methods seek to optimize harnesses through execution feedback to reduce human intervention. However, existing methods often rely on annotated video questions and answers or focus on updating model parameters, leaving harness evolution from unlabeled videos underexplored. VideoEvoHarness jointly evolves a Questioner and a Solver harness from unlabeled videos with frozen model parameters. The Questioner constructs questions and computes reference answers directly from video memory records. Question quality assessments and Solver execution trajectories guide question generation policy revisions. The Solver supports evolving skills, strategies, hyperparameters, and tools using execution feedback. Executable strategies define workflows in code, reducing repeated interpretation of natural language instructions. Each round, candidate harnesses are compared on identical validation questions, with validated improvements retained for later use. Experiments on benchmarks and a dedicated benchmark question set, using videos disjoint from evolution videos, show higher overall accuracy than initially and transfer gains across backbones. Overall accuracy on this set also improves progressively across rounds. This supports our foundational framework for harness evolution from unlabeled videos, opening a promising direction for self evolving video agents. Code is available at https://github.com/Wei-Xin-Xu/VideoEvoHarness.

items.reasoning: Novel direction in self-improving agents: evolving the harness rather than model weights using only unlabeled video. Removes a key annotation bottleneck and connects agentic workflows to self-supervised evolution, though evaluation robustness of self-generated questions is a risk.

items.title: PhySimCode: A Benchmark and Evaluation Method for Physics Video to Code Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.15722v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are good at video understanding and code generation, but it remains unclear whether they can recover the physical laws underlying videos, a capability essential for converting videos into executable simulations and for providing structured physical supervision in robotics. Captioning motion video does not imply that a model has inferred its governing dynamics, estimated quantitative parameters, or can regenerate the observed scene from code. Existing video-physics benchmarks evaluate plausibility, property estimation, or future-state prediction, but offer limited insight into whether models can translate visual dynamics into runnable simulation code. We introduce PhySimCode, a benchmark for physics video-to-code generation: given only a raw video, a model must infer the relevant physics, recover parameter values, and generate runnable Python that reproduces the input video. The dataset contains 160.6K procedurally generated samples spanning 162 physics phenomena across analytic SciPy simulations and PyBullet-rendered rigid-body, articulated, fluid, and contact-rich scenes; each sample bundles the simulation code, physical parameters, rendered video, and a structured chain-of-thought covering observations, laws, ODEs, numerical methods, and validation checks. We evaluate ten state-of-the-art closed- and open-source MLLMs along physical-law correctness, simulation equivalence, code executability, and parameter recovery. Models reliably state physics laws (4.27-4.93/5) yet score only 1.51-2.47/5 on inferring them from video, and the best system (Claude Sonnet 4.6) recovers just 7.7% of ground-truth parameters within $\pm 20\%$, exposing a substantial video-to-simulation gap. The 2,430-video evaluation set is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/SourajaKundu123/PhySimCode and the evaluation code at https://github.com/SourajaKundu/PhySimCode

It tests dynamics inference, quantitative parameter estimation, and scene regeneration from code.

items.title: Data-Centric Recursive Self-Improvement for Navigation via Policy-Synchronized Language-Action Dual Bootstrapping
items.content: arXiv:2610.15782v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-language navigation requires agents to follow natural-language instructions to reach target locations, making high-quality language supervision essential. Since human annotation is costly, prior work has explored scalable data synthesis methods. However, existing methods typically either use separate models for navigation and instruction generation or couple the two tasks through task-specific components; most also annotate the full trajectory corpus with a fixed model before updating, which can cause generated supervision to lag behind the evolving policy. Therefore, we introduce RSI-Nav, a data-centric recursive self-improvement framework for navigation via policy-synchronized language-action dual bootstrapping, which unifies vision-language-to-action instruction following and vision-action-to-language instruction generation within a shared model. Specifically, after supervised fine-tuning establishes fundamental capabilities, RSI-Nav progressively processes unlabeled trajectories in small shards. The current model generates instructions for these trajectories, executes them to evaluate goal completion and path efficiency, retains qualified samples, and immediately updates itself before processing the next shard. This shard-wise update keeps newly generated supervision aligned with the evolving policy. We also incorporate spatial understanding data, since stronger spatial reasoning benefits navigation. Extensive experiments show that RSI-Nav reaches 68.6% SR on R2R-CE and 72.4% SR on RxR-CE, while providing stronger instruction-generation utility and modestly improved spatial understanding after recursive evolution.

items.summary: RSI-Nav is a recursive self-improvement framework for vision-language navigation that unifies policy and instruction generation, synchronizing supervision data with the evolving policy instead of annotating trajectories with a fixed model. This dual bootstrapping reduces supervision lag and the cost of human annotation for navigation agents.

items.title: Geometric Parrots: Rule Absence vs. Rule Fragility in Spatial and Physical Reasoning for Vision-Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.16170v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer many geometric and physical reasoning questions correctly, yet still behave inconsistently in interaction, for example, abandoning a correct answer when confronted with a confident but incorrect user assertion. Standard single-turn accuracy cannot distinguish such capitulations from beneficial corrections because it scores each response in isolation. We introduce GRIP, a controlled benchmark with 34 procedurally generated reasoning domains, 100,000 images, and 600,000 questions spanning geometric, spatial, visual, and physical reasoning. Each scene is generated by deterministic code, and every answer is derived directly from the underlying scene state, providing exact ground truth without human annotation. On GRIP, we propose Dual-Loop Evaluation. A closed loop probes each image with a five-step compositional question ladder to localize where reasoning fails. An open loop then re-elicits the model's answer under controlled challenges, including peer-model responses and unsupported user assertions. Because ground truth is known exactly, answer changes can be signed as corrections (wrong-to-right) or capitulations (right-to-wrong), separating two failure modes: rule absence and rule fragility. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/bilaljawaid980/GRIP-Benchmark, with further details at https://bilaljawaid980.github.io/grip-benchmark/.

items.title: ClothAtlas: Joint Garment Identification and State Estimation under Self-Occlusion
items.content: arXiv:2610.16293v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Garment manipulation requires inferring both garment identity and complete configuration from partial, self-occluded observations. This creates a chicken-and-egg problem: completing a partial observation requires a garment-specific deformation prior, while identifying the garment requires a configuration that explains the observation. We introduce ClothAtlas, which jointly identifies garments and estimates their complete configurations from partial point clouds and a library of canonical meshes. A shared graph-conditioned flow-matching model samples configurations for each candidate mesh and ranks candidates by observation fit. The model accommodates different mesh shapes, vertex counts, and connectivities, allowing new garments to be added from canonical meshes alone without retraining. On held-out DexGarmentLab garments, ClothAtlas ranks the correct mesh first among 221 candidates for all 22 test garments from a single flat observation. From a single self-occluded observation, it identifies 15/22 garments, compared with 8/22 for a deterministic graph estimator. Persistent vertex identities support grasp-target localization on real garments, reducing mean error from 15.4 to 6.4 cm overall and from 17.0 to 8.3 cm on occluded targets compared with dense descriptor matching. Project page: https://clothatlas.github.io/

The approach handles varying mesh shapes and topologies so new garments can be added without retraining.

Robotics garment manipulation is a hard, underexplored area, so this is a valuable contribution even if still lab-conditioned.

items.title: Teaching Vision-Language Models to Decline: Support Completion Against Mirage
items.content: arXiv:2610.16465v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-language models answer questions about images they were never shown, a failure called mirage. Such an answer can be correct without being justified by the evidence, and the difference matters wherever a model's output is checked by someone who did not see its input. We locate the failure in the training objective: cross-entropy separates a model that reads the image from one that ignores it by only the conditional mutual information between answer and image, and no training example rewards declining. We formalise support completion, TIDE, which also shows each training question with a blank image, a same-domain wrong image and an out-of-domain image, with targets that decline, and prove that under TIDE every image-blind predictor is suboptimal by at least 1.04 nats per example, that the optimum declines exactly on the counterfactual kinds while keeping its behaviour on valid images, and that for any finite model the error of its answer-or-decline decision, declining on valid input plus answering on invalid input, is bounded below by how well its representation separates valid from invalid evidence. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B under a frozen held-out protocol with two judges, the three-condition predecessor of TIDE reduced the invalid-evidence mirage rate from 0.759 to 0.097 and the blank-image rate from 0.700 to 0.003 at a false-abstention cost of 0.126; label-free grounding raised the rate to 0.859, a likelihood-advantage contrast moved it only to 0.718 because its empty-image term carries no gradient, and grounding applied after support completion re-opened the mirage. items.title: Image Tokenizers Should Be Trained Between Images
items.content: arXiv:2610.16759v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Latent diffusion models generate images as codes of an image tokenizer, whose decoder turns them into the pixel image. Recent tokenizers improve how well these codes reconstruct an image and how easily a generator learns them. Yet a generator does not reproduce the codes of training images, and when a generated code lands outside what the decoder expects, the decoded image contains imperfections. Current methods make the decoder more robust to generated codes by adding noise during training. However, generated codes lie between the training codes and resemble their mixture more than one of them plus noise. To improve generated images, decoders should therefore be trained on codes in the space between training samples. We propose InterpTok, which fine-tunes MAETok to decode mixtures of image codes into natural images. Since no target image exists between two training samples, a discriminator judges whether each decoded mixture looks as natural as its two sources. A mixing ratio loss requires the decoded mixture to keep the mixing ratio of the two codes. Together, they prevent collapse to a trivial solution and yield a sharp and natural composition of both images. InterpTok keeps MAETok's reconstruction quality and improves interpolation quality more than threefold, the best of all tokenizers in a recent benchmark. Beyond interpolation, InterpTok improves the generation FID of a matched diffusion transformer from 11.61 to 8.48 without guidance, and even reaches 8.11 at an eighth of the sampling steps, where the generator on MAETok's codes worsens. The generator trained on our tokenizer also reaches the final result of the one trained on MAETok at half the training steps. Our findings show that the space between image codes can and should be explicitly supervised rather than ignored.

items.summary: InterpTok argues that latent diffusion decoders should be robust not to noise but to codes lying between training codes, since generators produce interpolated mixture-like codes. The paper proposes training tokenizers on codes sampled in the space between training samples, improving generated image quality over noise-augmentation approaches.
items.reasoning: A clean conceptual insight about the mismatch between generator-produced codes and decoder training distributions, directly relevant to latent diffusion image generation quality. The framing is elegant and testable, though the tokenizer space is highly active and competitive.

items.title: UniMetric: Universal Metric Scale Recovery for Visual Geometry Foundation Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.16945v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models, exemplified by GPT-6 Astra, raise the prospect of general-purpose embodied reasoning and planning. Using Internet videos for embodied pretraining calls for reliable physical-scale annotations. Yet visual geometry foundation models often recover scene structure and camera motion without reliable metric scale. We show that uncertain size priors of familiar objects can jointly constrain a reconstruction's shared scale. Building on this insight, we present UniMetric, a universal and training-free metric scale recovery framework for geometry foundation models, without additional sensors or task-specific metric supervision. Specifically, Metric Prior Acquisition elicits object height intervals from a vision-language model. Semantic-Geometric Alignment measures reconstructed object heights along the estimated support-surface normal in each frame and converts the priors into scale intervals. Global Scale Recovery reconciles these intervals through a convex objective, yielding a jointly feasible scale when they overlap and a unique compromise otherwise. The estimated sequence-level scale is applied uniformly to reconstructed points and camera translations. Controlled experiments with real VLM priors show that combining observations improves scale accuracy with exact relative object heights. To evaluate metric accuracy on GFM reconstructions without ground-truth scale alignment, we introduce MetricBench, covering twelve embodied, driving, and roadside subsets with sensor-derived ground truth. Across nine geometry foundation models, UniMetric reduces mean depth Abs Rel, reconstruction Chamfer distance, and trajectory error by 54.2%, 83.8%, and 65.6%, respectively, improving every model on all three tasks at the suite level. We release the UniMetric code and MetricBench data.

items.title: EgoProbe: Benchmarking Long-Range and Exact Memory in Streaming Egocentric Videos
items.content: arXiv:2610.17128v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Egocentric video provides a continuous first-person record of everyday activities, making it a natural foundation for wearable AI assistants. Unlike offline video understanding, streaming systems must process observations as they arrive, while queries may refer to experiences from the distant past. Recent work has begun to explore whether information can be recalled across long temporal gaps. Yet remembering how far is only part of the challenge: recurring objects, actions, and locations also require models to remember exactly which detail belongs to which event. We introduce EgoProbe, a benchmark that evaluates streaming egocentric memory along these two complementary dimensions: long-range retention, i.e., how far, and event-specific recall under interference, i.e., how exact. Built on long-form egocentric videos, EgoProbe uses an event-grounded data engine to extend recall intervals, identify related events, and construct event-grounded distractors, followed by human verification. It contains two subsets: EgoProbe-Base, which evaluates long-range recall without intervening related events, and EgoProbe-Echo, which challenges models with similar intervening events and event-grounded distractors. EgoProbe-Echo adopts coarse-to-fine multi-turn probing: the first turn evaluates coarse-grained event recall, while the second tests whether the model can retrieve the target-specific detail associated with the designated event. Extensive evaluation across diverse models reveals substantial limitations in long-range recall, with further challenges in recovering target-event details among related experiences. Even when models correctly answer coarse-grained questions, they often fail to recall the specific details of the designated event. EgoProbe exposes this underexplored failure mode and provides a testbed for advancing long-range and exact memory in streaming egocentric video understanding.

items.title: PLEDGE: Progressive Lossy Error-Bounded Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting
items.content: arXiv:2610.17605v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) codecs report reconstruction quality after compression, and give users little control over the distortion of individual primitives. We present PLEDGE, a training-free, progressive, error-bounded codec that translates four user-declared tolerances into per-primitive quantization bounds: screen-space position, footprint deformation due to rotation and scale, view-dependent color, and opacity. The bounds apply throughout a declared camera domain, including previously unseen viewpoints. Position and opacity are bounded directly; footprint deformation is bounded under the rasterizer's affine projection model, and color is bounded over all viewing directions. PLEDGE organizes quantized residuals into a progressive bitstream with explicit error bounds for every valid prefix. Experiments across thirteen scenes verify all declared per-mechanism bounds and demonstrate competitive rate-distortion performance. The four tolerances incur substantially different rate costs, so users can spend rate where their application needs it.

items.title: Web Scale on a Budget: Tail-Aware Retrieval Evaluation
items.content: arXiv:2610.17986v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A common practice in instance retrieval is to grow the gallery size to improve a benchmark's discrimination capability. One prominent example is ILIAS, which adds up to 100 million distractor images. The prevailing assumption is that faithful evaluation demands web scale, and that indexing all 100M images through the backbone is the unavoidable price of a comparable number. That price is steep: hundreds of GPU-hours and ~200 GB of descriptors per model, paid again for every method or ablation. We show the web-scale indexing price is largely avoidable: evaluation itself obeys a scaling law. The number of distractors that outrank a positive is Binomial in the gallery size. We define the per-query retrieval hardness, a gallery-scale agnostic quantity that yields a retrieval metric at any scale, and demonstrate it can be derived from a small random sample. The underlying sampled-rank machinery is long established in recommender-system and biometric evaluation, but to our knowledge has never been adapted to visual retrieval. We make the law per-query and estimable, and validate it at true 100M scale on ILIAS and INSTRE, and on the full 759k-distractor Google Landmarks v2 pool. Concretely, within a 5% sample (a flat 20x less indexing), every backbone's tail-aware (EVT) estimate has converged onto the large-scale mAP, to within ~0.01 (mean absolute error 0.005), across five backbones, three benchmarks, and two distractor pools (mAP@1000 at 100M on ILIAS/INSTRE; the official mAP@100 at the full 759k pool on GLDv2); the recommender-systems count baseline over-predicts everywhere (+0.037 to +0.068). This is an order of magnitude better than naively reporting the metric on the same subset (+0.08 to +0.13). We release code and the per-query hardness to facilitate faster, cheaper, and greener retrieval evaluation.

This avoids the expensive full indexing of web-scale distractor sets like ILIAS's 100M images, saving hundreds of GPU-hours per model.

items.title: VARI: Robust Text-to-Video Generation via Group-Structured Intent Alignment
items.content: arXiv:2610.18189v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Modern text-to-video (T2V) models generate visually compelling videos, yet meaning-preserving changes in prompt wording can substantially alter semantic realization and overall quality. Existing prompt rewriting modifies the inference input, whereas conventional post-training constructs supervision from one prompt formulation at a time; neither explicitly optimizes reliability across equivalent forms. We introduce VARI (Verified Alignment over Representations of Intent), a group-structured framework that treats automatically verified formulations of the same visual intent as a shared supervision unit. VARI builds matched form-seed rollout pools, cross-scores each video against all forms, and applies a wording-independent structured intent audit to identify valid realizations and hard semantic failures. Group-Consistent Distillation (GCD) aligns every verified form with interchangeable valid realizations, while Form-Contrastive Flow-DPO (FC-DPO) learns group-level preferences from audited positive-negative pairs, prioritizing same-seed, different-form contrasts. On HunyuanVideo-1.5, VARI attains the highest T2V-CompBench, VBench, and StoryEval scores among the evaluated methods. On prompt-form extensions of T2V-CompBench and VBench, it improves weakest-form alignment over the strongest prompt-level baselines by 2.45 and 3.55 points and reduces cross-form drop by 30.5% and 32.2%, respectively, while preserving visual quality. Human evaluation, natural-caption controls, prompt-enhancement experiments, diversity analyses, and transfer to LTX-2.3 further support the robustness and transferability of these gains, while VARI requires no additional inference-time module.

items.title: Physics-Aware Deepfake Detection via Distance-Speech Consistency
items.content: arXiv:2610.18485v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent progress in generative models has made talking-head deepfakes highly realistic and easy to create, jeopardizing public trust. However, most audio-visual deepfake detectors rely on lip-speech synchronization and are designed for static, frontal videos, limiting their reliability in dynamic, in-the-wild recordings where the speaker moves and lip cues are degraded or missing. As an alternative, we propose a physics-aware detector for dynamic speaking videos that leverages an acoustic constraint: in real recordings, speech energy varies predictably with speaker-to-camera distance, whereas deepfake generation can break this coupling. Our method combines distance estimates from video with distance-dependent acoustic measures from speech to detect deepfakes. Experiments on in-the-wild benchmarks show that the proposed physical cue is effective in dynamic scenarios, and that it complements lip-sync-based detectors, with a simple ensemble achieving consistent gains across datasets. Codes are available at https://byulharang.github.io/PADD/.

items.summary: Proposes a physics-aware talking-head deepfake detector that exploits the acoustic constraint that speech energy varies predictably with speaker-to-camera distance in real recordings, a coupling that generative fakes typically break. Unlike lip-sync detectors, it remains robust in dynamic, in-the-wild videos where lip cues are degraded or missing. A novel physical signal for media forensics with safety relevance.

Deepfake detection has high societal importance; the approach may be circumventable as generators adapt, tempering long-term impact.

items.title: Segment Where You Look: Attention as the Interface Between Language Models and Segmenters
items.content: arXiv:2610.18729v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) that segment from language must pass the location of the referent to a pixel decoder. The dominant interface compresses it into the hidden state of a single [SEG] token, a d-dimensional vector with no spatial index, and leaves the decoder, which never sees the expression, to recover the referent's extent. We show that the VLM already computes a better signal: the [SEG] token's attention over the image tokens, which is defined on the patch grid by construction. items.title: ClothCode: Generative Modeling for Garment State Estimation and Dynamics Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2610.14200v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We introduce ClothCode, a unified generative framework for garment state estimation and action-conditioned dynamics prediction in a shared discrete configuration space. A material-aligned tokenizer encodes garment configuration as residual vector-quantized patch tokens, while task-specific Masked Generative Transformers predict these tokens through parallel confidence-guided refinement. Across three garment templates, ClothCode reduces mean displacement error by 26.6% for state estimation and 37.0% for dynamics prediction relative to the strongest baselines. Dynamics prediction requires only 16.7 ms per window, compared with 556.2 ms for diffusion. Integrated into the same model-predictive controller, ClothCode improves real-world folding and flattening success from 56.7% to 78.9%. Further results and videos are available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ClothCode-DE32

items.title: Uncertainty-Aware Cortical Surface Reconstruction and Spherical Registration for Heterogeneous Brain MRI
items.content: arXiv:2610.16595v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Surface-based cortical analysis is useful in many applications as it is a natural way to model the highly folded structure of the cerebral cortex, allowing quantities such as curvature and thickness to be easily calculated. Existing deep learning (DL) methods have focused on 1x1x1 mm3 T1-weighted (T1w) scans, thus replicating classical pipelines. Here we present a neural network that is trained exclusively on synthetic scans with random contrast and resolution. Consequently, it can be applied to almost any kind of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan. In addition, our model provides vertex-wise uncertainty estimates of the predicted surface as well as a spherical registration to fsaverage space. Our model performs on par with other state-of-the-art DL methods on 1x1x1 mm3 T1w scans and outperforms the only other method capable of estimating cortical surfaces from low resolution, non-T1w scans. The predicted uncertainty, moreover, correlates with overall scan quality on low resolution scans and highlights areas of poor surface reconstruction on 1x1x1 mm3 T1w scans, suggesting that it can be used for quality control. Finally, the predicted spherical registrations prove comparable to other DL and classical registration methods. These qualities, when combined with the fast inference time, will provide the ability to analyze large, existing databases of clinical MRI scans, with the potential for finding disease-specific patterns that would otherwise be infeasible in a research setting.

items.title: Code2Worlds-2: Physically Plausible Agent Harness for Embodied World Simulation
items.content: arXiv:2610.17651v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recent coding large language models (LLMs) can synthesize dynamic 4D worlds from natural language, but the resulting content remains a visual artifact. It lacks physical semantics such as the collision geometry, mass, friction, inertia, and joint structure, required to enable it to simulate the physical world, and its dynamics are scripted to look plausible rather than designed to execute. What is needed is an executable world: one that a physics engine can load and step, resolving contact physically. We present Code2Worlds-2, an extension of Code2Worlds that turns 4D world generation into an embodied world simulation. We keep the original dual-stream generation pipeline intact and append two modules. First, a SimReady Scene Compiler that turns a generated visual scene into a simulator-compatible representation: it assigns collision meshes via convex decomposition, estimates physical attributes with a vision-language model, infers a lightweight support graph, instantiates the engine's contact, friction, and dynamics constraints, and applies a gravity settling pass, before exporting the scene as MuJoCo MJCF. Second, a Simulator-in-the-Loop 4D Refiner that implements an automated agent harness-a compile, simulate, critique and refine loop-that converts visual dynamics into executable rigid and articulated dynamics and evolves the physical settings rather than only the code, replacing the purely visual motion critic with a simulator critic that inspects penetration depth, collision pairs, stability, contact forces, joint limits, and robot reachability. We further propose SimCode4D, a state-based benchmark with five task templates for evaluating embodied simulation. Experiments on SimCode4D and across natural, indoor, industrial, urban, and service scenes show that Code2Worlds-2 produces physically plausible, simulator-compatible, and robot-interactable scenes.

The result is a world that a physics engine can load and step rather than a merely visually plausible scripted artifact. This bridges the gap between generative world synthesis and usable simulation environments.

items.title: DexStitch: Learning and Composing Dexterous Skills from Human Videos via Contact-Aware Robotic Inpainting
items.content: arXiv:2610.17789v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A long-horizon manipulation task consists of primitive skills and the transitions connecting them. Learning skills that can be executed in sequence requires supervision for both, which is costly to collect on a robot. Human videos offer a scalable source of demonstrations, but transferring them to robots requires extracting robot-compatible observations and actions together with their skill structure. We present DexStitch, a framework that cuts long-horizon human videos into skills and transitions, converts them into aligned robot observation-action-skill data, and stitches the learned skills into a requested sequence. A skill classifier first segments the videos into manipulation skills and transitions. DexStitch then converts the human demonstrations into robot observations and actions while retaining their corresponding skill labels. During conversion, per-finger human-object contacts guide dexterous hand retargeting and robotic inpainting, preserving contact geometry and finger-object occlusion ordering. To stitch the learned skills into a sequence, a shared skill-conditioned policy is pretrained on the resulting synthetic data and finetuned on a mixture of synthetic data and a small set of single-skill teleoperation episodes. Conditioning on the current and next skills guides each transition toward the following skill, while predicted skill progression enables closed-loop switching. On a held-out session, the classifier agrees with manual annotations on 92.4% of frames. Across four household skills, DexStitch achieves 80.0% single-skill success and 77.5% sequence success.

items.title: FidLIF: Parallel Training of High-Fidelity Spiking Neurons with Exact BPTT
items.content: arXiv:2610.16924v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) show promise in energy-efficient computing through event-driven computation and stateful temporal processing, their recurrent membrane dynamics render their training inherently sequential and inefficient for long sequences. Existing methods achieve full-sequence parallelism in SNNs through two main strategies: redesigning or approximating spiking dynamics to avoid reset-coupled temporal dependencies, or relying on iterative relaxed fixed-point solvers that suffer from excessive memory costs and iteration-dependent backward overhead. To address these limitations, we present FidLIF, a novel framework that reconciles the incremental update and hard-reset behavior of standard spiking LIF neurons with parallel forward propagation and BPTT-equivalent backward propagation. FidLIF iteratively recovers the full-sequence membrane-potential trajectory in parallel. By exploiting the lower bidiagonal structure induced by the local recurrence of LIF neurons, FidLIF formulates each forward trajectory correction and backward adjoint propagation as associative scans with an $O(\log T)$ temporal depth. This formulation also supports input-dependent neuronal parameters and allows the same neuron to perform full-sequence parallel training and incremental step-by-step inference at deployment. In our numerical convergence evaluation, FidLIF achieves a mean absolute error below $10^{-7}$ relative to the matched serial relaxed LIF dynamics, while yielding gradients numerically equivalent to exact BPTT. Our Triton implementation delivers favorable long-sequence latency and memory scaling, while achieving competitive performance on four sequential classification benchmarks. By reconciling parallel training with step-by-step execution, FidLIF enables high-fidelity spiking dynamics to benefit from parallel hardware without compromising incremental inference at deployment.

This advances energy-efficient neuromorphic training on long sequences.

items.title: In View or Out of View? A Vision-Aware Filter that Infers and Reacts to the Human's Field of View
items.content: arXiv:2610.14577v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: During human-robot interaction, sight plays an important role. When the human sees a robot, they can observe the robot's actions and better predict the robot's future behaviors. Conversely, when the human cannot see the robot, they become uncertain about the robot's intent and plans. In this paper, we focus on the human's field of view. Existing human-aware planners either ignore this field of view and assume the human can observe the entire scene, or intentionally design their interactions so the robot is always visible to the human. By contrast, we enable robots to infer what the human has and has not seen during interaction, i.e., the human's field of view. We then apply this estimate as a vision-aware filter on the robot's actions. Given a nominal robot policy and a model of the interaction, we roll out the policy over a short horizon to see how the robot's state updates. We then reweight the actions based on how those actions impact the robot's predicted visibility: higher weights are assigned to actions that bring the robot into (or away from) the human's line of sight. In practice, our framework provides an online estimation and filtering process that repeatedly updates its understanding of the human's field of view and then locally perturbs robot actions based on the human's vision. We evaluate our vision-aware filter on robots that assist humans in collaborative cooking and coordinate with them in driving environments. Across simulations and a 12-participant user study, we find that our vision-aware filter changes both performance and preference: participants completed over three times as many subtasks with in-view assistance while cooking, and had fewer collisions with cars that purposely stayed out of their view while driving.

items.title: StreamingWAM: Streaming World Action Modeling via Chunk-Wise Staircase Flow Matching
items.content: arXiv:2610.15585v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs), often built upon pretrained video-generation world models, have emerged as a promising framework for general-purpose and open-ended robot control. However, their real-world deployment often suffers from discontinuous and jerky execution. Existing methods typically address this issue by either improving inference efficiency or enhancing action continuity across prediction chunks, without jointly addressing both challenges. To bridge this gap, we propose StreamingWAM, a streaming-diffusion framework for WAM-based robot control. StreamingWAM combines a noise ladder for chunk-wise action prediction, a prefix rollout module for cross-chunk continuity, and dense video-history memory for temporally consistent conditioning. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world robotic tasks demonstrate that StreamingWAM improves action continuity across static and dynamic settings, achieving competitive performance while reducing steady-state replanning latency to 72.9 ms in simulation and 57.3 ms on the real robot. The method also produces smoother action transitions, while the streaming staircase reduces sensitivity to the execution horizon K.

It targets real-time, temporally consistent control built on pretrained video-generation world models.

items.title: P-BFM: Perceptive Behavioral Foundation Models for Humanoid Control via Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.15833v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Behavioral foundation models (BFMs) provide humanoids with reusable repertoires of whole-body behaviors; in real-world humanoid control, the same behavioral intent may require fundamentally different motions under different terrain constraints. Covering such variation with terrain-matched demonstrations requires enumerating a combinatorial space of behaviors and terrain geometries. We introduce P-BFM, a perceptive behavioral foundation model that factorizes humanoid control into terrain-invariant intent and terrain-conditioned realization. A forward-backward representation maps motion references, target states, and reward functions into a shared intent space without terrain information, while a perceptive policy learns how to realize each intent under the surrounding terrain geometry. We further identify a complementary limitation of purely latent control: behavioral latents can preserve local motion patterns while losing precise global progress. We therefore introduce Explicit Root Instructions (ERI), which separates global transport (e.g., heading and planar velocity) from behavioral intent, while leaving local whole-body adaptation to the perceptive policy. This decomposition leads to a characteristic capability absent from conventional BFMs: one fixed intent induces different, terrain-appropriate behaviors, including changes in step height, stride, posture, foothold placement, and contacts, without terrain-specific demonstrations. Across challenging terrains, P-BFM improves motion fidelity, root-control precision, and perturbation recovery over strong baselines. A single frozen policy further supports motion tracking, goal reaching, reward inference, teleoperation, and terrain-aware recovery, and transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 using onboard depth sensing.

items.title: Declarative Reactive Robot Behaviors from Imperative Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.17083v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are predominantly trained on imperative programming languages, and existing work on LLM-based robot programming reflects this: it focuses on goal-directed tasks expressed as plans. However, many robotic applications require not tasks but behaviors--open-ended, continuous patterns of sensory-motor engagement with no termination condition (e.g., greeting visitors, patrolling an area). Such behaviors are better served by declarative and reactive programming, on which LLMs have virtually no training. We investigate whether this gap can be bridged. Using Playful, a reactive scripting language, we show that an LLM-based coding agent can generate correct declarative and reactive programs for robotic behaviors. These programs are produced from under-specified natural language descriptions, given suitable context and a set of reusable programming guidelines. The guidelines encode design principles that redirect the agent from imperative defaults toward proper reactive patterns. Developed once by an expert, they generalize across robots and behaviors. Starting from only the generic robot operating system API, the agent jointly designs both the imperative component (Python modules for sensing, acting, and evaluating) and the declarative component (the reactive script that composes them into behavior logic). The declarative nature of reactive programming supports both incremental refinement through conversational turns and one-shot generation of complete behaviors.

Using Playful, a reactive scripting language, the authors show an LLM agent can produce correct declarative/reactive programs, bridging a fundamental mismatch between LLM training distribution and behavior-oriented robot programming. This complements the dominant plan/task-centric uses of LLMs in robotics.
items.reasoning: A conceptually sharp observation — LLMs are imperative, robot behaviors want declarative/reactive code — with a concrete demonstration of a bridge via a purpose-built language. The MPI-affiliated authorship (Berenz, Schoelkopf) lends credibility. The reliance on a niche custom language somewhat limits immediate applicability, but the direction is important for behavior-layer robot software.
