items.title: PotentialEP: Backprop-Free Training of CIFAR-Scale Generative Models via Equilibrium Propagation
items.content: arXiv:2610.14409v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generating an image with a diffusion or flow-matching model typically involves integrating a velocity field for hundreds of sequential steps. That computation suits a GPU poorly and an analog neuromorphic substrate well, where one fast, low-power physical relaxation could replace the whole sequence. Two things are needed: a generative algorithm whose computation is a relaxation, and a way to train it without backpropagation, whose global gradient transport is hard to realise in analog. Energy Matching supplies the first, sampling by gradient-descent relaxation on a time-independent potential - but obtaining the gradient that descent follows is itself a backward pass, once per integration step. We prove that a predictive coding network with a single linear injection term added to its energy relaxes to a state whose visible layer carries that gradient inherently, with an error that vanishes for small injection strengths. An Energy Matching model trained by backpropagation can therefore be loaded into this network unchanged and sampled by relaxation alone, matching the original model's FID to within 0.04 at CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 scale. The network can also be trained without backpropagation: Equilibrium Propagation reproduces backpropagation's parameter updates to a cosine similarity of 0.9998, and training end to end with those updates reaches an FID of 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10 against 3.54 for backpropagation. To our knowledge this is the first CIFAR-10 generative model trained with Equilibrium Propagation, and the first at competitive quality by any backpropagation-free rule. This quality does not require group normalisation or attention: an architecture of only convolutions and pointwise nonlinearities, both native to an analog crossbar, reaches an FID of 3.51 when trained by backpropagation.

items.title: Characterizing the Separability Gap in Prior-Data Fitted Networks
items.content: arXiv:2610.14989v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) are transformers pretrained on simulated datasets to approximate Bayesian posterior predictive distributions. Standard PFN theory assumes a separable task prior, under which the feature distribution and the mechanism generating labels from features are independent. We show that common PFN priors are non-separable, even in simple settings. Consequently, standard pretraining targets a predictive distribution based on a task posterior updated using both the labeled context and the query features. We characterize its difference from the predictive based on the context posterior alone and show that this difference vanishes under posterior concentration. Under misspecification (i.e., when the true joint distribution lies outside the prior's support), however, prior non-separability can favor better feature fit at the expense of conditional label fit. We illustrate the consequences for feature attribution, Bayesian optimization, and martingale checks of Bayesian behavior. The same dependence also enables PFNs to learn from additional unlabeled observations. We demonstrate this with SemiTabICL, a PFN explicitly pretrained to use these observations, which improves accuracy over a matched supervised baseline. Our findings highlight the need for explicit rules on unlabeled data use in PFN evaluation and establish the dependence between feature and label distributions as a consequential prior design choice.

items.summary: This theory paper shows that common priors used in prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) are non-separable, contradicting standard PFN theory assumptions that feature distributions and label mechanisms are independent. The authors characterize the gap between predictions based on the full task posterior versus context-only posterior, showing the gap vanishes under posterior concentration but can persist under misspecification. This sharpens the theoretical foundations of in-context learning via PFNs.

items.title: Beyond Adjacent Layers: Graph-Guided Layer Fusion for Compressing Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.15159v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Existing depth-compression methods for large language models (LLMs) score layers individually or group only adjacent or contiguous layers, implicitly assuming that functional redundancy is local. We test this assumption by computing full pairwise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity matrices for thirteen LLMs from six architecture families (1.6B-14B parameters). Non-adjacent layers have 3.6-15.9x more high-similarity pairs than adjacent ones, a structure that prior similarity-based layer merging has not systematically exploited. We propose Fusion via Community Mining (FCM), which builds the full L x L similarity graph, uses spectral community detection to find clusters of functionally equivalent layers, keeps the highest-Block-Influence layer in each cluster, and applies LoRA recovery; a pre-specified rule computed only on calibration data chooses between cosine and CKA similarity. At 2x compression, FCM lowers mean perplexity below ShortGPT on twelve of thirteen models, significantly on ten (Welch's t-test with Holm-Bonferroni correction; up to 50% on Qwen3-4B), with Mistral-7B the only loss (+13.4%). Against FlattenGPT, SWM, and DeltaLLM under matched calibration and recovery, FCM gives the best perplexity on ten of thirteen models (mean rank 1.15), and it also outperforms MKA on three anchor models. FCM matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning cells and also improves MMLU, LAMBADA, HumanEval pass@1, and free-form generation quality. The 2x-compressed Qwen2.5-7B has 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on a single A100. Spectral grouping outperforms Fisher contiguous segmentation by 41% and uniform partitioning by 51%, and FCM's advantage grows beyond a 2x crossover up to 3x and persists at the 14B scale. Code: https://github.com/Usama1002/fcm-layer-fusion

items.title: Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.15662v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generative policies offer expressive action distributions for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion- and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling. We propose DriftSpread, a one-step generative policy based on Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL. To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density, we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the negative MaxEnt objective. Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same actor, using action regression for value improvement and distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy. The actor updates require neither direct samples from the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density or score estimation. Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step limit followed by the long-time limit. On MuJoCo, DriftSpread achieves the highest aggregate normalized return among all evaluated methods, while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

items.title: Dissipative Lagrangian Neural Networks for the Interpretable Modelling of Passive Mechanical Systems
items.content: arXiv:2610.15996v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In this paper, we propose the Dissipative Lagrangian Neural Network (dLNN), a continuous-time system identification technique that separately learns the conservative and dissipative dynamics of a mechanical system directly from data. A key contribution is a novel parametrisation of dissipative forces that (i) is structurally constrained to be dissipative, enforcing passivity of the learned model, (ii) cannot absorb conservative mechanics, and (iii) retains sufficient expressivity to represent a broad family of state-dependent damping and regularised friction forces. The model is validated on prediction tasks on two real-world mechanical systems: trajectory prediction of a chaotic double pendulum and inverse-dynamics modelling of a six-degree-of-freedom industrial robot. Across these tasks, the dLNN demonstrates improved predictive performance over existing Lagrangian architectures while remaining competitive with a black-box neural model. The imposed physical structure also improves generalisation to unseen states, with the benefits becoming particularly pronounced when training data is limited. Finally, we introduce a symbolic distillation procedure that extracts closed-form expressions from the learned physical components. Applied to the industrial robot, this produces interpretable symbolic models that retain high predictive accuracy while reducing the computational overhead associated with evaluating neural Lagrangian models.

The model is validated on prediction tasks on two real-world mechanical systems: trajectory prediction of a chaotic double pendulum and inverse-dynamics modelling of a six-degree-of-freedom industrial robot. Across these tasks, the dLNN demonstrates improved predictive performance over existing Lagrangian architectures while remaining competitive with a black-box neural model. The imposed physical structure also improves generalisation to unseen states, with the benefits becoming particularly pronounced when training data is limited. Finally, we introduce a symbolic distillation procedure that extracts closed-form expressions from the learned physical components. Applied to the industrial robot, this produces interpretable symbolic models that retain high predictive accuracy while reducing the computational overhead associated with evaluating neural Lagrangian models.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning with Hawkes-Structured Networks for Market Making
items.content: arXiv:2610.16524v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Market making under realistic order-flow dynamics is challenging due to the clustered, self-exciting nature of order arrivals, which are naturally modeled by non-Markovian Hawkes processes. We propose a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) framework for market making with general Hawkes order-flow dynamics. We first establish non-asymptotic performance bounds that quantify the loss incurred by approximating the infinite-dimensional Hawkes state using a finite collection of exponentially weighted features. Guided by this analysis, we introduce the Hawkes-Structured Network (HSN), a novel neural architecture that encodes historical order flow through a learnable mixture-of-exponentials filter. HSN is trained end-to-end using model-free RL, jointly optimizing the feature representation and quoting policy directly from reward feedback. Experiments on single- and multi-asset market-making problems with mixture-of-exponentials, power-law, and regime-switching kernels demonstrate that HSN outperforms general-purpose neural architectures, achieving higher trading rewards while implicitly recovering the underlying order-flow intensities.

items.title: Optimal Transport PAC-Bayes Bounds
items.content: arXiv:2610.16560v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds are among the strongest distribution-dependent guarantees in statistical learning and are typically expressed in terms of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between a prior and posterior distribution. While analytically convenient, the KL divergence requires the posterior to be absolutely continuous w.r.t. the prior, imposing support constraints that can substantially restrict the choice of posterior. Moreover, the KL divergence does not account for the underlying geometry of the probability space. In this work, we derive new PAC-Bayesian bounds replacing the KL divergence with general optimal transport (OT) distances, including the total variation and Wasserstein-$p$ distances.
items.author: Armin Beck, Peter Ochs, Jalal Fadili
items.summary: The authors derive new PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds that replace the standard KL divergence between prior and posterior with optimal transport distances, including total variation and Wasserstein-p distances. This removes absolute continuity requirements on the posterior and incorporates the geometry of the probability space.
items.reasoning: A meaningful theoretical advance in generalization bounds: OT-based PAC-Bayes bounds relax restrictive support constraints and are geometry-aware, a direction of active interest. However, the practical impact on deep learning remains to be demonstrated.

items.title: Radial Tail Repair: Post-Training Correction for Diffusion and Flow Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.16851v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Diffusion and flow-matching models may struggle to accurately represent distributional tails, especially for heavy-tailed data. Existing approaches often use heavy-tailed noise or modify the generative dynamics, requiring dedicated retraining and more difficult estimation. We take a simpler approach: rather than relearning the full distribution, we correct only the model's behavior in the extreme regime. Our method builds on the radial-angular decomposition of multivariate heavy tails, where radius and direction become asymptotically independent. This allows us to preserve the directional structure learned by the pretrained model and correct only its radial tail. We estimate the tail onset from reference and generated samples, then rescale generated extremes so that their radial survival matches the target distribution. The resulting method is a lightweight post-training correction applied to a frozen diffusion or flow-matching model, requiring neither retraining nor changes to its sampling dynamics. Experiments on challenging synthetic heavy-tailed distributions and real weather and wildfire datasets show that this simple correction substantially improves extreme-tail coverage using only a small number of fitting samples.

items.reasoning: Addresses a real, underexplored failure mode of diffusion models (heavy tails) with an elegant, theoretically grounded and cheap fix that requires no retraining. Practical relevance for scientific and financial applications, though it targets a specialized distributional regime.

items.title: Constant-Depth Rational-Weight GNNs and their Connection to Schanuel's Conjecture
items.content: arXiv:2610.16993v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A landmark result states that the expressive power of graph neural networks (GNNs) is bounded from above by the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (1-WL) test. We ask whether a constant-depth GNN can match the expressive power of 1-WL while using only rational weights. We prove that this is the case when Schanuel's conjecture, a famous open problem from transcendental number theory, is taken to be true. Our GNN construction works even with integer weights, and more generally with a broad range of rational weights. As the activation function, it may use logistic sigmoid, hyperbolic tangent, or related functions. It is uniform across all graph sizes. We also prove a partial converse: if a GNN with exponentiation, hyperbolic sine or hyperbolic cosine as activation matches the expressive power of the 1-WL test in a slightly more expressive setting where graphs may contain certain auxiliary vertices, then this implies Schanuel's conjecture restricted to the numbers that arise in computations of the GNN. We also conduct experiments showing that the constructed GNNs indeed match the 1-WL test.
items.author: Daumantas Kojelis, Carsten Lutz
items.summary: This theoretical paper proves that constant-depth graph neural networks with only rational (even integer) weights can match the expressive power of the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman test, provided Schanuel's conjecture from transcendental number theory holds. It also establishes a partial converse connecting the impossibility direction to the same conjecture, using standard activation functions like logistic sigmoid and tanh. The result is notable for linking GNN expressivity theory to deep open problems in number theory.
items.reasoning: The connection between GNN expressivity and Schanuel's conjecture is a striking and original theoretical contribution, and the rational/integer weight construction is practically relevant since real-world models use such weights. However, it is pure theory with conditional results hinging on an unproven conjecture, which limits immediate practical impact.

items.title: Online LLM Personalization from Pairwise Preferences Across Users
items.content: arXiv:2610.17203v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models can answer the same question in different styles, but users' preferred styles are hidden and vary across users and questions. We study inference-time personalization through online selection from a fixed set of prompts, each representing a persona. Users arrive sequentially, each asks a short sequence of questions, and the system displays two responses per question and observes one pairwise choice. We formulate this interaction as a variant of the contextual dueling bandit problem in which the learner starts without preference data, adapts within each session, and exploits information shared across users. The objective is to minimize cumulative strong regret, summing the utility gaps of both displayed responses relative to the user's best response among the available options. We make two contributions. First, we introduce the problem and release a reproducible preference benchmark and dataset built around a tutoring case study, containing educational questions, LLM-generated answers in six teaching styles, and pairwise judgments from LLM-simulated students with hidden preference profiles. We fit Bradley-Terry models to these judgments to obtain reference utilities for regret evaluation. Second, we propose a baseline that learns a mixture prior over users from completed sessions and adapts to each new user within the session. On students and topics never used in development, it removes 44-48% of random pairs' excess regret and achieves over half the performance of a per-user linear oracle fitted in hindsight. We release code, prompts, and the benchmark.

items.title: Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics
items.content: arXiv:2610.17885v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Microscopic simulations resolve spatial patterns but are feasible only over small domains and short timescales, whereas bulk descriptions erase those patterns through spatial averaging. Mesoscopic fields preserve this spatial organisation, but their effective equations are known only for selected microscopic systems and scaling limits. We introduce Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics (DeepMesoD), which uses neural networks to learn an effective mesoscopic field equation from microscopic trajectories at a prescribed coarse-graining scale. For the nonconserved dissipative dynamics studied here, DeepMesoD learns the free-energy functional with a spatial interaction kernel and a state-dependent dissipation operator constrained by the fluctuation-dissipation relation. We first validate the construction in the Ising-Kac model, where the learned mesoscopic equation recovers the known hydrodynamic limit and rollouts remain stable far beyond the training horizon. We then treat two systems without closed-form mesoscopic descriptions. For a two-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnet governed by atomistic spin dynamics, DeepMesoD learns a mesoscopic model whose predictions match atomistic references up to 1 ns, and a rollout with an unseen initial condition remains bounded up to 25 ns. For layered CrBr$_3$, the learned kernel captures the suppression and sign reversal of interlayer coupling at a stacking fault whose location and strength are not supplied as inputs. Controlled changes to the learned interaction show how fault number and placement shape multistep magnetic responses, complementing our magneto-photoluminescence measurements. Across the two atomistic systems, DeepMesoD achieves a three-to-four-order-of-magnitude reduction in wall-clock time compared with atomistic spin dynamics.

Co-authors include Kostya Novoselov (Nobel laureate), indicating strong physics credibility.

items.title: Graph Metanetworks for Transformer Based Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.18471v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Weight-space learning treats the weights of neural networks as data, processed by other models called metanetworks. A key challenge is that different weights can realize the same function, related by a group of symmetries the metanetwork should respect. While symmetry-aware metanetworks for simple architectures such as MLPs are well developed, a comprehensive treatment of transformers, and in particular transformer-based language models, is still missing. Importantly, their weight space has a richer symmetry group: beyond neuron permutations, attention introduces continuous general-linear symmetries of the attention matrices and permutations of entire heads. Existing methods for transformer weights either capture only part of these symmetries or are restricted to a single, fixed architecture, and none accounts for language-model-specific components such as the token embeddings. Building on graph metanetworks, we propose a graph-based approach that is both symmetry-aware and applicable across depths and widths. We formalize a weight-space symmetry group of complete decoder-only language models and provide a graph construction that is invariant to it. We further introduce two new transformer-population datasets with novel tasks, such as training-corpus prediction and fine-tuning detection, on which our approach notably outperforms existing baselines.
items.author: Yonathan Wolanowsky, Guy Bar-Shalom, Fabrizio Frasca, Haggai Maron
items.summary: This paper develops symmetry-aware graph metanetworks for processing Transformer weights as data, fully accounting for the richer weight-space symmetry group that includes continuous general-linear symmetries of attention matrices and head permutations beyond neuron permutations. This fills a gap where prior metanetwork work covered only MLPs or partial Transformer symmetries.

items.title: MultiAlloc: Budget-Aware Precision Allocation for KV Cache Quantization
items.content: arXiv:2610.18642v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The Key-Value (KV) cache constitutes a dominant source of memory consumption during large language model (LLM) inference, particularly in long-context and complex reasoning scenarios. Existing KV cache quantization methods have explored different compression granularities, including layer-wise precision adjustment and token-level information preservation. In practical deployment, however, the key challenge is not merely compression, but how to allocate limited quantization resources among heterogeneous precision preservation strategies under a fixed KV cache memory budget. We propose MultiAlloc, a profiling-guided precision allocation framework for KV cache quantization that adaptively distributes limited quantization resources between layer-wise precision enhancement and token-wise preservation. MultiAlloc employs lightweight offline profiling to characterize layer sensitivity and token importance, enabling adaptive precision allocation under a fixed memory constraint. Guided by the profiled memory--accuracy trade-off, it automatically derives an effective precision allocation strategy without online allocation search, and applies the resulting policy during inference. Extensive experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks demonstrate that MultiAlloc consistently improves over layer-wise, token-wise, and recent multi-granularity KV cache quantization methods under matched memory budgets across diverse models, including Mistral, Llama, DeepSeek-Qwen, and QwQ.

It targets long-context and reasoning-heavy inference where KV cache memory is the dominant cost.

items.title: SlideDP: Scaling Host-Resident LLM Fine-Tuning Across Multiple GPUs
items.content: arXiv:2609.34162v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Host-resident layer streaming enables full-parameter LLM fine-tuning beyond GPU memory, but data-parallel ranks compete for shared host resources. Replicated transfers amplify traffic, while strong scaling can expose host work as computation windows shrink. We present SlideDP, a synchronous data-parallel runtime for shared-host multi-GPU systems. It maintains one authoritative host state, decouples communication routes from state layout, and pipelines parameter delivery, gradient aggregation, and CPU updates across ranks and chunks. An analytical step-time model characterizes resource bottlenecks and pipeline exposure; runtime measurements guide communication, chunking, and activation policies under a GPU memory budget. In matched-batch sweeps, SlideDP achieves geometric-mean throughput ratios of 1.46-2.64$\times$ over SlideFormer, MegaTrain, and ZeRO-Offload. On four H100s, SlideDP approaches GPU-resident FSDP2 throughput for Qwen3-14B at a smaller batch size. With a larger batch, it processes over 1M tokens per step and exceeds FSDP2's measured peak throughput by 11.2%. Separately, it supports 256K-token sequences for the same model and fine-tunes Qwen2.5-72B on four RTX 4090 GPUs. Project page: https://github.com/RegiaYoung/SlideDP.

items.title: ByteMark: A Unified Byte-Level Watermark for Detection Across Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.14427v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: As watermarking of LLM-generated text enters deployment, users increasingly need to check text whose source is unknown. Existing detectors read the watermark through a specific tokenizer or embedding pipeline, and even if all providers adopted the same watermarking method, differences in these representations would leave their watermarks incompatible, and the text alone does not reveal which representation produced it. We propose ByteMark, a unified watermarking scheme that defines its signal on the UTF-8 bytes of published text. Models with different tokenizers embed this signal under one public specification and key, and a single detector verifies the text from the text and key alone. When the tokenizer or embedding model of a baseline detector is replaced, its detection degrades sharply, whereas ByteMark, which uses neither, retains its detection rate; ByteMark also remains detectable when participating models continue or rewrite the text.

items.title: Physics Foundation Models for Efficient Control of Fluid Flows
items.content: arXiv:2610.15173v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We investigate whether a physics foundation model (PFM) pretrained for PDE forecasting can be repurposed for closed-loop fluid-flow control. We construct a PFM-based controller by attaching lightweight Gaussian actor and critic heads to frozen pretrained representations and train the policy using proximal policy optimization (PPO). We evaluate the approach on HydroGym's two-dimensional Kolmogorov-flow environment using vorticity observations at \(64\times64\) and \(128\times128\) resolutions and Reynolds numbers \(\mathrm{Re}=100\) and \(200\). Across these settings, we compare the frozen PFM controller against a baseline MLP policy trained with the same PPO framework. The PFM controller achieves consistently higher reward while requiring smaller executed action magnitudes over training, indicating improved control performance with reduced control effort. These results provide initial evidence that representations learned through self-supervised next-frame prediction can be transferred directly to closed-loop fluid flow control. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/morph.

items.title: Poisoned into Action: Context Attacks on Typed Decision Workflows
items.content: arXiv:2610.15537v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Typed decision interfaces restrict models to predefined actions, yet schema-valid choices can still trigger policy-violating state changes. Evaluating context poisoning thus requires connecting model decisions to execution outcomes while accounting for legitimate automation retained by defenses. We introduce an execution-aware protocol tracing poisoned evidence through retrieval, model choice, automated action, and persisted state. We evaluate it with 1,659 fresh calls to Jev-1.13.0 across 20 development tasks in two synthetic workflows, using three repetitions per condition. Under natural retrieval, a standalone payload reaches all 60 trials and produces five security-violating executions, while a carrier-payload pair exposes the payload in 57 trials and produces one violation. An initial source-exclusion gate blocks the pair's observed violation but also withholds ten otherwise correct attacked decisions and sixteen correct clean decisions. Correcting its empty-scope behavior restores twelve clean decisions without additional model calls. Factorial controls show that adding correct evidence reduces wrong executions from 119/120 to 55/120 in the semantic arm and from 60/120 to zero in the neutral arm, suggesting that much of the improvement reflects general evidence value rather than attack-specific protection. Three prespecified contrasts are not statistically supported after Holm correction, so the findings remain exploratory. The protocol provides an auditable framework for studying which poisoning-induced errors reach execution and how much correct automation defenses preserve. Code is available at https://github.com/WuXixiong/jev-poisoning-bench.

items.title: How the Classical Baseline Shapes Machine-Learning Speed Claims in Topology Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2610.16051v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Topology optimization places material so that a structure resists deformation under given loads. Machine-learning methods often report large speed-ups over classical, non-learned optimization, but a slow classical code or a less stiff learned design can exaggerate them. We re-ran released code for eight methods on one workstation and studied two in depth: Optimize Any Topology (OAT), a diffusion model that generates designs, and a graph-based neural optimizer. Speeding up only the classical code's finite-element solver cut these two methods' speed-ups by up to 20-fold. We then timed the classical code until its design was at least as stiff as the learned one; for OAT, we read this point off the completed runs. Published timings imply a 134x speed-up for OAT on a 256 x 256 grid; our matched single-design comparisons gave 1.5x to 3.5x. At matched stiffness, the graph-based optimizer was slower than the classical code in all six two-dimensional problems. Of the six other methods, two kept their advantage, one shrank, one reversed and two were not comparable. In an exploratory audit of published claims, language models judged that 8 of 28 speed comparisons in randomly sampled, openly accessible articles lacked evidence of equal design quality; our own review counted 11, so the count depends on who judges. We provide a comparison procedure and a minimum report: classical code, hardware, design quality, what each timing includes, and data-generation and training costs.

items.title: Think Before You Speak: Enabling Training-Free Latent Communication Between Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.16165v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks in coding, mathematical logic, and iterative reasoning, especially by coordinating effectively within multi-agent systems (MAS). However, language agents traditionally communicate via text exchange, which introduces a bottleneck in information transfer and adds prefill latency for downstream agents. Recent work proposes that directly sharing the key-value (KV) cache between language models can enable efficient latent collaboration, entirely bypassing standard text-based communication. To enable latent communication between heterogeneous models of different sizes, prior work introduces trained fusion adapters for each model pair, which limits practical deployment. We introduce CacheFuse, a training-free method which demonstrates that augmenting a downstream model with an upstream model's KV cache using linear interpolation consistently enables superior performance than the standalone downstream model can achieve. We systematically analyze CacheFuse across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks and demonstrate up to 8.6 percentage points higher accuracy compared to single-model baselines and up to 12.2x TTFT speedup compared to text-based communication in multi-model inference.
items.author: Rishi Khare
items.summary: This work removes the need for trained fusion adapters in KV-cache-based latent communication between heterogeneous LLMs, enabling training-free latent collaboration in multi-agent systems. By bypassing text-based exchange, it reduces information bottlenecks and prefill latency for downstream agents.
items.reasoning: Training-free KV-cache sharing across heterogeneous models is a practical and timely multi-agent efficiency contribution with clear latency benefits; novelty is moderate since it builds on prior trained-adapter latent communication work, and single-author credibility is harder to gauge.

items.title: Prorsa: Unleashing the Potential of Prefill-Decode Disaggregation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.16592v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly used to enhance the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in solving complex multi-turn tasks. During rollout, agentic RL exhibits a workload pattern distinct from that of traditional RL: multi-turn interactions repeatedly introduce prefill requests, causing prefill and decode workloads to coexist throughout rollout. This workload makes prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation, a design widely used for online LLM serving, promising for speeding up agentic RL rollout. This paper shows that PD disaggregation can improve rollout efficiency by (a) mitigating interference among data-parallel attention modules, (b) enabling stage-specific parallelism, and (c) reducing end-to-end trajectory completion time. However, a fixed prefill-decode allocation may fail to sustain these benefits as workload composition varies across tasks and over time. We therefore present Prorsa, an agentic RL framework for prediction-guided prefill-decode resource allocation. Prorsa observes the lifecycle of every trajectory to forecast short-horizon prefill and decode demand. These forecasts then guide worker allocation decisions and trigger role switching of rollout engines, aligning prefill and decode capacity with anticipated workload demand. Across synchronous and asynchronous agentic RL settings, Prorsa achieves end-to-end rollout speedups of 1.11x-4.05x over prefill-decode colocation.

It improves rollout efficiency by reducing interference among data-parallel attention modules, enabling stage-specific parallelism, and cutting end-to-end trajectory completion time.
items.reasoning: Systems work targeting a genuinely important bottleneck: rollout cost dominates agentic RL training, and tailoring serving-system ideas to RL workloads is timely and likely to influence RL infrastructure. Novelty is moderate since it adapts known serving concepts, but practical impact is high.

items.title: MENTOR: Procedural Shielding of Tool-Using LLM Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.17039v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Tool-using LLM agents are increasingly used to automate workflows governed by procedural manuals, such as company rules for booking travel or procuring hardware. These manuals are written in natural language for humans and describe general requirements over such complex workflows. Ensuring compliance of LLM agents with these manuals is difficult, and state-of-the-art techniques use either LLM judges or manually written rules to forbid problematic tool-calls locally at runtime. This is insufficient because (i) only blocking tool calls keeps the agent clueless about how to make correct progress towards fulfilling its task, and (ii) can lead to overly conservative behavior of the agent, as tool calls might only be problematic in certain contexts. To overcome these challenges, we introduce MENTOR, which (i) additionally provides guidance for the agent to make procedural-compliant progress on the task, and (ii) ensures that this compliance is context-aware. We achieve these goals by building a novel history-dependent runtime shield that is obtained from the procedural manual via a multi-step autoformalization pipeline. At its core, MENTOR utilizes a game-based technique to ensure robustness against runtime uncertainty without over-resticting agents' behavior. This yields a formally assisted framework for procedural shielding of LLM agents that improves compliance well beyond existing methods. In particular, MENTOR lifts the compliance of shielded light-weight open-source LLMs above that of non-shielded proprietary models. Since a shield is synthesized once per manual and then serves every task, a MENTOR-shielded agent becomes a viable choice for repeatedly executed workflows, potentially reducing deployment costs when the offline construction cost is amortized over repeated tasks.

The approach aims to give agents constructive guidance toward correct progress while avoiding overly conservative behavior.

The shielding framing (moving from blocking to constructive guidance) is a meaningful advance for agent reliability, though results shown are early-stage.

items.title: GPU Goldmines: Tunable WebGPU Kernels for Edge LLM Inference
items.content: arXiv:2610.17321v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: As demand for LLM inference grows and consumer GPUs grow more capable, edge deployment is becoming increasingly attractive. WebGPU is compelling in this setting because it offers cross-platform portability and browser accessibility. However, these same strengths also make high performance difficult to achieve, as an implementation that performs well in one context may not perform well in another. To address this, we present GPU Goldmines, a framework for specifying, executing, and tuning WebGPU kernels. We instantiate GPU Goldmines with kernels for key LLM building blocks: matrix multiplication, matrix-vector multiplication, and flash attention. We characterize performance across diverse devices, shapes, and browsers, and use the resulting database to accelerate subsequent autotuning and configuration selection. On shapes drawn from Llama and Qwen models, our matrix multiplication kernels outperform ONNX Runtime and llama.cpp WebGPU kernels by 7.0x and 1.41x geometric mean, respectively, and deliver end-to-end improvements of 1.48x in the prefill stage of llama.cpp for chat workloads.

items.summary: This paper presents GPU Goldmines, a framework for specifying, executing, and auto-tuning WebGPU compute kernels for key LLM building blocks such as matrix multiplication and flash attention. Because WebGPU is portable and browser-accessible but hard to optimize per-device, the authors characterize kernel performance across devices, shapes, and browsers to select the best implementation per context. It matters for making edge LLM inference practical without native code.

items.title: FastEEP: Fast Intra-Instance Elastic Scaling for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving
items.content: arXiv:2610.18451v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large-scale expert parallelism (EP) has become the standard deployment configuration for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models in production. Meanwhile, the highly dynamic nature of LLM workloads requires providers to continuously adjust serving capacity to match fluctuating demand. Scaling MoE serving cannot be efficiently achieved by simply adding or removing serving instances; instead, it often requires resizing the EP group within an existing instance, which we refer to as intra-instance scaling.Existing inference engines primarily rely on instance-level scaling, which destroys and reconstructs entire serving instances, incurring substantial scaling overhead.   We present FastEEP (Fast Elastic Expert Parallel), a fast intra-instance scaling system for MoE serving based on the principle of Partial Reuse. FastEEP reuses existing runtime state across worker execution, GPU memory, and communication by separating reusable execution structures from the resources activated by the current EP configuration. This separation enables coordinated resource reclamation and reconfiguration while preserving costly-to-reconstruct state, allowing fast EP scaling without full instance teardown and reconstruction. Our evaluation shows that FastEEP achieves 4.5x--11.7x faster scaling than the existing vLLM-based approach across different models, enabling efficient, fine-grained scaling of MoE serving.
items.author: Yunfei Feng, Jingkai He, Shiqi Liu, Cheng Zhang, Dong Du, Erhu Feng
items.summary: FastEEP enables fast intra-instance elastic scaling of expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts serving, avoiding the costly destroy-and-reconstruct cycle of instance-level scaling when workloads fluctuate. The system resizes the expert-parallel group within a live instance, reducing scaling overhead for production MoE deployments.
items.reasoning: Addresses a real and growing infrastructure problem given that expert parallelism is standard for production MoE LLM serving; practical systems work with clear value, though it is applied engineering rather than new modeling insight.

items.title: MajorTOM:Elliot Pretrain, A Multi-Sensor, Multi-Temporal Pretraining Dataset for Earth Observation
items.content: arXiv:2610.18624v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Pretraining generalist Earth observation foundation models requires data that combine several sensors, varied temporal sampling and, increasingly, text, yet open datasets rarely provide all three in one consistent, easily accessible form. We introduce MajorTOM:Elliot Pretrain, a collection of 279,166 tiles of 10 km drawn from the Major-TOM grid by clustering AlphaEarth embeddings. Each tile stacks Sentinel-2 L1C, Landsat-8/9, Sentinel-1 RTC, Copernicus DEM and ESA WorldCover on a shared 1056x1056-pixel, 10 m grid, complemented by cloud masks, OpenStreetMap entities and ERA5 weather. The tiles are partitioned into three temporal regimes, Monotemporal (250,000 tiles, one acquisition), Monthly (12,500 tiles, twelve acquisitions spread over the annual cycle) and Burst (16,666 tiles, six acquisitions within 30 days), and are released as 6.3 TB of Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs indexed by TACO v3 Parquet metadata, a standard that allows cloud streaming, efficient data access, and filtering before any pixel is read. A companion library derives sensor-tagged fact sheets, captions and 16 families of vision-language tasks from these layers at load time. We test our design choices in short pretraining runs of OlmoEarth-Base. First, a 25% subset of Major-TOM Core-S2L2A curated with AlphaEarth embeddings matches or exceeds the full corpus on 8 of 9 benchmarks. Second, on Elliot-Pretrain, adding Landsat-8/9 improves or matches Sentinel-2 only pretraining on every benchmark. Third, using DEM and WorldCover as prediction targets during pretraining further improves 8 of 9 benchmarks, while giving the same maps to the encoder as inputs degrades 5 of 9. Fourth, Sentinel-1 helps on 7 of 9 benchmarks, particularly on benchmarks with radar inputs. Fifth, rule-based captions match a small language model at no cost. The dataset is openly available at https://source.coop/major-tom/elliot-pretrain.

We introduce MajorTOM:Elliot Pretrain, a collection of 279,166 tiles of 10 km drawn from the Major-TOM grid by clustering AlphaEarth embeddings. Each tile stacks Sentinel-2 L1C, Landsat-8/9, Sentinel-1 RTC, Copernicus DEM and ESA WorldCover on a shared 1056x1056-pixel, 10 m grid, complemented by cloud masks, OpenStreetMap entities and ERA5 weather. We test our design choices in short pretraining runs of OlmoEarth-Base. First, a 25% subset of Major-TOM Core-S2L2A curated with AlphaEarth embeddings matches or exceeds the full corpus on 8 of 9 benchmarks. Second, on Elliot-Pretrain, adding Landsat-8/9 improves or matches Sentinel-2 only pretraining on every benchmark. Third, using DEM and WorldCover as prediction targets during pretraining further improves 8 of 9 benchmarks, while giving the same maps to the encoder as inputs degrades 5 of 9. Fourth, Sentinel-1 helps on 7 of 9 benchmarks, particularly on benchmarks with radar inputs. Fifth, rule-based captions match a small language model at no cost. items.title: Uniform Information Density-Based Preference Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2610.14578v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: To enable large language models to generate outputs that align with human preferences, optimization algorithms based on the comparison between chosen and rejected output pairs have been developed and been proven effective. Some recent endeavors have utilized certain linguistically-derived assumptions about the preference pairs to guide the design of more precise optimization directions. However, human preferences are complex and hard to measure by simplistic criteria, and it is important to incorporate broader and more sophisticated insights about preferred vs. not-preferred language. In this study, we adopt a well-established psycholinguistic theory, Uniform Information Density, to develop a novel preference optimization algorithm, UIDPO. The basic assumption is that humans prefer to produce language in which information is uniformly distributed, because uniformity induces less cognitive processing effort. To implement this idea into the algorithm, we derive a compound metric for information uniformity by combining the global standard deviation and the local second-order difference, and integrate it to the objective of preference optimization. We compare UIDPO with SimPO, a previous state-of-the-art method, obtaining comparable and sometimes better performance on AlpacaEval2, ArenaHard, and MT-Bench. Additional linguistic analysis on complement clauses also shows that UIDPO can better reflect the tendencies of keeping information uniform in natural language than baselines. Our results show that the subtle human preference over the information rate in language is a helpful source for achieving better human alignment for LLMs. The code repository is published here: https://github.com/CLCS-SUSTech/UIDPO.

items.title: Rate-Resolved Text Evaluation with Masked Diffusion Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.15667v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A single evaluation score can rank generation systems but rarely reveals what failed. We propose rate-resolved text evaluation, which turns the masking rate of masked diffusion language models into a diagnostic axis. By reconstructing text under different fractions of masked tokens, one diffusion score becomes a vector of band-conditioned scores that reflect reconstruction difficulty at varying levels of visible context. On SummEval, preserving this rate structure yields complementary signal: the best masking-rate band improves fusion with autoregressive likelihood over a collapsed diffusion scalar, survives a sample-shuffle control that breaks rate ordering, and adds residual signal to a fixed prompted judge. A second diffusion model reproduces the effect more weakly. On WMT MQM zh-en, roundtrip mask-and-reconstruct probing produces a tunable localization curve in which ranking-oriented AUROC and span-detection F1 peak at different masking rates. Factuality benchmarks bound the interpretation: band semantics are model- and task-dependent, so each application requires empirical validation.

items.title: CivWorldBench: Evaluating Language World Models in Structured Multi-Agent Sandbox Worlds
items.content: arXiv:2610.16450v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The growing use of language models for forecasting motivates a broader evaluation of their world-model capabilities. Such evaluation must go beyond predictive accuracy to assess hidden-state inference and intervention prediction. Real-world forecasting benchmarks offer limited access to hidden-state ground truth and controlled experiments. We introduce CivWorldBench, a benchmark built on a multi-agent strategy game engine with recorded internal states, controlled observations, and paired intervention rollouts. Its 1,900 decision points from 475 worlds support three task levels: association forecasting, belief inference, and intervention prediction. Reference predictors support attributable evaluation of capability gaps, with an expert harness and empirical ceiling estimates contextualizing scores. Stored trajectories make intermediate predictions verifiable, while agent-play experiments test whether world-model capabilities support decision-making. The main panel comprises eleven frontier language models. Composite benchmark scores correlate with real-world forecasting leaderboards on matched model panels, more closely than with a general-capability index, supporting its use as a proxy for real-world forecasting capability. Strong association forecasts do not consistently extend to belief inference or intervention prediction, and effect magnitudes remain poorly calibrated despite informative direction predictions. Process verification reveals errors missed by final-answer evaluation, and structured reasoning improves intervention prediction for the strongest model in the process study. Agent-play experiments identify useful assisted plans and motivate evaluating decision-relevant capabilities beyond association forecasting. These findings identify hidden-state inference, intermediate-state prediction, and effect calibration as priorities for world-model training.

items.title: Ontology-Based Post-Coordinated Expression Assembly: from Clinical Narrative to Queryable Knowledge Graphs
items.content: arXiv:2610.16474v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Clinical oncology documentation records decisive information in free text, where it remains readable but not retrievable at scale, leaving cohort identification dependent on incomplete diagnostic codes or manual review. The current standard, coding individual terms, captures what a document mentions, not what it asserts: meaning lies in how those terms relate to one another. We present a method for deriving queryable knowledge graphs from clinical narratives, conforming to the Extended Grammar of SNOMED CT across multiple ontologies. The method specifies how entities should be annotated and related. It defines five relation classes, each bound to a construction rule that assembles the entities and relations into post-coordinated expressions. A deterministic implementation, UNIGRAPHE, applies those rules to construct knowledge graphs from annotated text. Applied to expert-annotated real-world oncology documentation, UNIGRAPHE reconstructed 5,299 annotations into 2,196 post-coordinated expressions and shows that relation structure is the missing piece to make clinical narrative formally queryable.

items.summary: This paper presents a method for converting free-text clinical oncology narratives into queryable knowledge graphs that conform to the SNOMED CT Extended Grammar across multiple ontologies. The approach defines five relation classes, each with construction rules that assemble annotated entities and relations into post-coordinated expressions, enabling large-scale cohort identification beyond what diagnostic codes or manual review can achieve.
items.reasoning: The work addresses a genuine and persistent pain point in clinical informatics: unstructured narrative captures asserted meaning that simple term coding loses. Its grounding in SNOMED CT post-coordination is technically rigorous and the multi-author team from established academic clinical informatics groups lends credibility. However, the contribution is domain-specific rather than a general AI advance, the abstract alone suggests a methodology paper without demonstrated large-scale clinical validation, and real-world adoption of post-coordinated SNOMED CT expressions has historically been limited, tempering the potential impact.

items.title: Distilling Text LMs into Speech-to-Speech LMs by Matching Internal Text Predictions
items.content: arXiv:2610.17461v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Text language models (LMs) acquire broad linguistic and factual capabilities through large-scale pretraining, while comparable capabilities remain difficult to learn from speech alone. Recent work has shown that knowledge distillation from pretrained text LMs offers a promising way to transfer their linguistic and factual capabilities to speech models. However, existing distillation approaches have largely focused on speech-input, text-output models. This idea has yet to be explored for {\it speech-to-speech} models, which operate on both speech input and speech output. In this work we introduce a speech-to-speech pretraining method that creates an internal text interface for knowledge transfer while preserving the speech-only input and output. The model first consumes speech context without its transcription, switches to text prediction, and then uses the predicted text to lead future speech generation word by word. It also provides an interface for knowledge distillation: the internal text predictions can be directly distilled from the base text LM. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of text LM distillation to a speech-to-speech LM. Under matched training conditions, the proposed sequence construction substantially improves the generative perplexity of spoken continuations over speech-only and interleaved speech-text models, approaching the performance of a text-leading inner-monologue model with external ASR prompt transcription. More importantly, distillation improves factual performance under both text and speech evaluation, indicating better retention of knowledge from the base text language model.

items.title: Agent-Reflex: Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively
items.content: arXiv:2610.17953v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models have evolved from single-turn chatbots into interactive agents capable of long-horizon reasoning. In real deployments, MCP tool services can return noisy feedback and users may intervene to correct the agent, but existing methods provide limited supervision for reflection learning and failure recovery. To bridge this gap, we propose Agent-Reflex, a general training framework for incentivizing proactive reflection in agents. Specifically, Agent-Reflex comprises three stages. First, Environment Reflection Skill Discovery (RSD) injects grounded tool-feedback perturbations into environment scaling, samples a capability-diverse LLM pool, mines matched success-failure pairs, and summarizes reusable reflection meta-skills. Building on this skill library, we then apply Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning (ReSFT) that converts each skill into supervision for self-reflection, skill recovery, and user-centric correction, strengthening complementary reflective behaviors. Finally, we propose On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) to combine agentic reinforcement learning under noisy interactions with reflection-guided on-policy distillation to further elicit proactive reflection. Built on Qwen3-8B, Agent-Reflex reaches 58.6 overall on five long-horizon tool-use benchmarks and 29.1 on AgentNoiseBench, surpassing strong environment-scaling and reflection baselines. Experiments on six challenging agent benchmark suites demonstrate the effectiveness of Agent-Reflex. Further analyses show that Agent-Reflex improves agents' robustness to noise while maintaining stable training dynamics, supporting scalable agent training. Our code is available at https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/Agent-Reflex.

items.title: CREATE: Creativity Evaluation of VLMs using the Visual Remote Associates Test
items.content: arXiv:2610.18569v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) are used in creative tasks such as visual storytelling, design ideation, art interpretation, and advertising. Yet we lack principled ways to measure the lateral reasoning of these models compared to human potential. We introduce CREATE, a semi-automatically constructed benchmark containing 155 visual Remote Associates Test problems. These problems require a solver to find an underlying connection among three seemingly dissimilar images. We conduct a human study (N=25) to validate and ground the quality of our benchmark, and evaluate 11 VLMs. Our findings show that most VLMs underperform humans on this task. Our experiments indicate that the associative ability of VLMs depends on the cue concepts provided in the text and does not universally extend to visual puzzles.

items.title: Legal-R1: Agentic Retrieval for Evidence-Based Legal Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.18611v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Legal question answering requires answers that are not only plausible, but also grounded in legally valid and citable evidence. Standard retrieval-augmented generation often relies on one-shot semantic matching, which is insufficient when legal evidence must be selected according to authority, applicability, and diversity across heterogeneous sources. We introduce Legal-R1, an agentic retrieval framework for evidence-based legal reasoning. Legal-R1 decomposes legal reasoning into a multi-agent workflow, where a Lawyer agent learns when to retrieve, which legal source to query, what evidence to seek, and when the collected evidence is sufficient. A Legal Assistant agent retrieves from normative legal sources and precedent cases with authority-aware and diversity-aware selection, while a Judge agent generates the final answer from the complete evidence trajectory. We post-train only the Lawyer agent with masked supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-aware reinforcement learning. Experiments on multiple Chinese legal benchmarks show that Legal-R1 improves over general-purpose, legal-specific, and retrieval-augmented baselines.

It addresses the limits of one-shot retrieval-augmented generation for legally citable evidence. This targets a concrete gap in grounded legal AI.

items.title: Hashrope: A Persistent Data Structure for Mechanisms of LLM Context Management
items.content: arXiv:2610.16144v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Serving stacks for large language models manage context through four recurring mechanisms: incremental edits to a growing context, branching and snapshotting for tree search, identification of reusable prefixes for KV-cache reuse, and encoding of repeated segments. Each mechanism is served today by a different specialist structure. We show that all four reduce to a single persistent weight-balanced rope whose every node carries a polynomial hash of its subtree over a Mersenne prime, so that the structure supports logarithmic edits and logarithmic verified content-identity queries at the same time. We validate each mechanism with pre-registered, replicated experiments, then compare against a deployed specialist per mechanism: the Ropey editing library, a faithful PagedAttention copy-on-write block table, and the vendored SGLang radix matcher. On workloads that interleave edits with identity queries, Hashrope is net-superior to Ropey by a factor that grows without bound (369.7x at one million characters). items.title: RoboFake: Are Deepfake Detectors Ready for Humanoid Face Robots?
items.content: arXiv:2610.14269v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Humanoid face robots can now move their lips in sync with speech and show detailed facial expressions. Give such a robot the face of a real person and drive it with generated speech, and you get a face forgery that happens in front of the camera: the camera records a real object, and no pixel is edited. We call this a RoboFake. In this paper we ask what current deepfake detectors do when they see a robot face. We test six public detectors trained on FaceForensics++ on video of a physical lip-syncing face robot, on a synthesized video of the same robot, and on rendered robot faces. All thresholds are fixed on FaceForensics++, and every result is compared with real human faces that went through the same processing as the robot videos. At a threshold that flags 5% of real faces, three detectors flag almost every physical robot frame, while two flag fewer than 7%. A matched human control and masking show that the response comes from the face, not from the processing or the background. However, it does not track synthesis: with only the face visible, three of the six detectors give the physical robot a higher fake score than its synthesized video. The response is also fragile, and light JPEG compression is enough to push most robot frames below the threshold for some detectors. Our results suggest that current detectors flag today's robots because their faces do not look human, not because they recognize a forgery. We release our evaluation protocol and code, and state three testable hypotheses about realistic, interactive RoboFakes.

items.title: FreeCHROMA: Generative Chroma Keying from Unaligned Background References
items.content: arXiv:2610.14445v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In film production, chroma keying composites an approved foreground performance into a new environment, but conventional workflows require coordinated background plates and dedicated harmonization. Recent generative methods often require pre-aligned backgrounds, focus on background-conditioned foreground relighting, or represent the environment only through an edited first frame. These restrictions limit background selection, scene composition, and camera motion while adding preparation or editing effort. We present FreeCHROMA, which adapts a pretrained video diffusion model in a parameter-efficient manner for generative video compositing from one to three unaligned background references. The model integrates the foreground into the referenced environment, preserving foreground identity, motion, and fine visual details while generating a spatiotemporally coherent background. Foreground-background harmonization occurs within the same generation process, without a separate relighting stage. Optional text instructions help disambiguate complex spatial relationships and camera behavior. To train the model, we construct pseudo-paired data from readily available real monocular videos through foreground-background separation and augmentation with existing foundation models. The original videos serve as training targets, while automated processing and quality verification enable scalable data construction. Across reference fidelity, foreground preservation, scene integration, harmonization, and overall video quality, FreeCHROMA consistently outperforms recent compositing and conditional video-generation baselines, with particularly clear gains under camera motion. FreeCHROMA relaxes the constraints of existing tools to enable end-to-end generative chroma keying from unaligned inputs, with exploratory experiments demonstrating its potential in robotics.

items.title: What Really Works for Universal Multimodal Embeddings? A Controlled Study of Contrastive Training Strategies
items.content: arXiv:2610.15035v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Contrastive learning has become the standard paradigm for multimodal representation learning, aligning semantically matched pairs while separating mismatched ones in a shared embedding space. Although various contrastive training strategies have been proposed across negative selection, batch construction, and gradient modulation, their actual effectiveness under controlled, reproducible conditions remains poorly understood. This motivates a fundamental question: Do sophisticated contrastive strategies consistently bring meaningful downstream gains in multimodal embedding learning? To address this, we systematically evaluate representative strategies under a unified benchmarking framework on MMEB. Surprisingly, direct evaluations reveal that most existing strategies offer marginal gains over a standard aligned baseline, with several even degrading overall performance. To uncover the underlying failure modes, we introduce an MLLM-as-a-Judge diagnostic framework that dissects top-1 retrieval behaviors into labeled positives, false negatives (unlabeled valid matches), and hard/easy negative errors. Our systematic analysis yields three key insights: (1) Gradient distortion: Upweighting gradients from high-similarity negatives consistently hurts downstream generalization; (2) Distribution illusion: Wider separation between positive and negative similarity distributions does not necessarily translate to better retrieval performance; and (3) Synergistic training: While false-negative mitigation or hard-batch construction yields limited gains in isolation, integrating hard-negative mining, false-negative mitigation, and hard-batch construction achieves optimal performance, delivering an average improvement of 6.0% on MMEB with Qwen2-VL-2B. Overall, our findings demystify popular contrastive strategies and provide actionable recipes for training universal multimodal embedding models.

items.title: Semantically Steerable Image Tokenization
items.content: arXiv:2610.15515v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Adaptive image tokenizers compress an image into a variable number of tokens matched to its complexity, and recent work makes this allocation controllable: conditioned on a target reconstruction error, the tokenizer itself decides how many tokens an image needs. However, the fidelity measure guiding this allocation shapes which aspects of the image are preserved under compression. The pixel-wise error used in prior work is blind to the spatial structure that carries an image's meaning, and under heavy compression such tokenizers are prone to abruptly discarding tokens that encode essential content. We introduce GIST (Guided Image Semantic Tokenizer), an adaptive tokenizer that can be steered toward a requested semantic fidelity. Its token allocation is jointly controlled by pixel-level and semantic target errors, with semantic error measured in the feature space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder. This joint control enables semantic protection: with the semantic target fixed at zero, the reconstruction target can be relaxed to discard pixel detail while preserving what the image depicts. In a controlled comparison on ImageNet-100, GIST outperforms its pixel-controlled counterpart KARL at every token count, with up to $30\%$ lower LPIPS and $37\%$ lower DreamSim. On average, lowering its semantic target reduces LPIPS $2\times$ faster per token than lowering the reconstruction target, and up to $5\times$ in the low-token regime. Semantic fidelity is thus an effective control signal for adaptive tokenization: it lets a tokenizer see, and so preserve, what an image depicts.

items.title: PIGEONS: Incremental Long-Video Captioning with Persistent Identity Gallery and Evolving Overarching Narrative Summary
items.content: arXiv:2610.16066v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Detailed video captioning has become an essential semantic interface for multi-modal understanding and generation. While existing methods mainly target short videos, extending them to long videos remains challenging, primarily due to limited context windows of current video understanding models. A naive solution is to adopt segment-wise captioning followed by concatenation, yet this paradigm often suffers from inconsistent subject references and fragmented long-range narratives. To mitigate these issues, we introduce PIGEONS, an incremental long-video captioning model built upon a Persistent Identity Gallery and an Evolving Overarching Narrative Summary. Before caption generation, PIGEONS scans the entire video to construct an identity gallery that captures key subjects along with their visual references, thereby providing a stable referential anchor. The model then performs clip-by-clip captioning conditioned on the persistent gallery and an evolving overarching narrative summary, which compactly maintains and updates essential long-range contextual information after each captioning step. To enable these capabilities, we develop a three-stage training strategy that integrates supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PIGEONS markedly improves long-video captioning performance, achieving superior accuracy, completeness, and subject referential consistency over existing methods, while maintaining competitive performance on short-video captioning.

items.title: EgoWholeView: Camera-Only Head-Mounted Capture of Body and Bimanual Hand Motion for Embodied Demonstrations
items.content: arXiv:2610.16256v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Head-mounted body and bimanual motion capture supports self-avatars, teleoperation, and embodied demonstrations. However, a single egocentric camera is vulnerable to a limited field of view, scale ambiguity, and hand-object occlusion. We present EgoWholeView, a wearable capture system of six synchronized wide-angle RGB cameras with a role-specialized pipeline. The outward views localize the rig in a world frame, while an overlapping downward pair independently predicts SMPL-X body and MANO hand parameters. Both predictors are adapted to egocentric fisheye data. To combine the two, reliability cues measured from the predictions themselves weight the fusion of body and hand joint rotations, while shape is aggregated across views and frames. The pair's baseline fixes metric scale, and triangulation recovers root translation. Relative to monocular prediction, fusion reduces PA-MPJPE by 3.7% for the body and 11.2% for the hands, and temporal refinement lowers angular-acceleration magnitude by 32.2% and 31.0%, respectively. On our six-camera recording, the pipeline produces body and hand states in a shared world frame using benchmark-fitted gates without retuning, and temporal refinement lowers hand acceleration magnitude by 41.08%. Using only RGB cameras and no third-person view, EgoWholeView offers a low-cost, portable route to egocentric interaction data.

items.title: PathPilot: An Adaptive Question-Conditioned Multi-Magnification Navigation Agent for Whole-Slide Image Analysis
items.content: arXiv:2610.16734v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The diagnostic capability of WSI agents relies on effective slide navigation to identify diagnostically relevant regions and efficiently integrate evidence across the slide. While in clinical practice, pathologists dynamically examine slides across multiple scales, integrating global and cellular evidence in a sequential manner, existing AI navigation approaches mostly operate at a single fixed magnification or rely on predefined magnification traversal. This mismatch prevents existing methods from modeling cross-magnification interactions and adaptive magnification selection inherent to real diagnostic workflows. We propose PathPilot, a clinically consistent multi-magnification WSI navigation agent that explicitly models cross-magnification localization and evidence-adaptive exploration. Specifically, we introduce a CrossMagLoc that learns magnification-specific diagnostic localization from pathologist viewing behavior and integrates information from adjacent magnifications to identify the diagnostically most relevant region within the current ROI, thereby providing a diagnostically informed starting point for subsequent question-conditioned exploration. We further introduce an EviRegionSearch that starts question-conditioned exploration from this region, progressively accumulating question-relevant evidence and adaptively determining the next navigation action according to the remaining evidence requirement. Their iterative interaction enables PathPilot to sequentially explore across ROIs and magnifications until sufficient evidence is acquired. Extensive QA evaluations across five cohorts demonstrate consistent superiority over competing SOTA methods on inter/external cohorts, respectively, validating question-conditioned evidence acquisition across regions and magnifications that mirrors the sequential, knowledge-driven navigation of pathologists.

items.title: Self-Supervised Learning of Semantically Consistent Visual Features via a Simple 3D Prior
items.content: arXiv:2610.16988v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Visual features extracted from vision models like DINOv2 or Stable Diffusion enable high quality semantic correspondence between images. However, such features exhibit documented limitations that hinder accurate correspondence estimation such as the inability to disambiguate the left from right for categories exhibiting symmetries or repeated parts. Previous attempts to improve these features rely on using supervised data such as annotated keypoint pairs or camera pose information, or make restrictive topological assumptions, such as modelling the object of interest as a 3D sphere. We introduce a new self-supervised approach that allows us to learn features for topologically complex object categories using a simple prior. Instead of relying on an expensive instance-level analysis by synthesis pipeline, our approach makes use of contrastive learning and distribution matching at the global dataset-level to learn the coarse shape and appearance of a category. Combined with additional geometric losses, this enables us to replicate the global and local statistics of visual features which match those that are extracted from real images. Quantitative results are presented across several challenging object categories, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

items.summary: This paper proposes a self-supervised method for learning visual features that support accurate semantic correspondence, addressing known failure modes of features from models like DINOv2 such as confusing left/right on symmetric objects. Unlike prior work requiring supervised keypoint annotations, camera poses, or restrictive sphere-like topology assumptions, it uses a simple 3D prior to handle topologically complex object categories.

Combined with additional geometric losses, this enables us to replicate the global and local statistics of visual features which match those that are extracted from real images. Quantitative results are presented across several challenging object categories, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

items.title: Hallucination-aware Faithful Reasoning in Remote Sensing
items.content: arXiv:2610.18369v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities for remote sensing reasoning, yet they frequently generate visually unsupported reasoning that contradicts the visual evidence. Existing post-training methods optimize primarily for final-answer correctness, providing limited supervision for identifying and correcting hallucinations that arise during the reasoning process. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{FaithRS}, a hallucination-aware self-reflection framework for faithful reasoning in remote sensing. We first construct \textbf{SFHD-43K}, a dataset of 43K structured, fine-grained hallucination annotations, and train a detector to identify hallucination types, underlying causes, and supporting visual evidence. FaithRS then incorporates this diagnostic feedback into a Safe Detector-Guided Corrective Rollout framework, where a safety-aware gate selectively determines whether and how to revise the response. Training is driven by a composite reward that jointly optimizes answer accuracy, reasoning faithfulness, hallucination reduction, format compliance, and revision safety. Experiments with Qwen3.5 backbones (0.8B, 4B, and 9B) show consistent improvements across four remote sensing benchmarks, with gains of up to 11.64 points.

items.title: CoTL: Compact Token Learning for 3D Scene Representation
items.content: arXiv:2610.18446v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present CoTL, a framework that learns a compact set of tokens that preserves scene geometry and appearance from unposed multi-view images. Our encoder compresses the input images into small per-view sets of latent tokens that aggregate information across views to form a view-consistent scene representation. Each additional view expands the representation with only a small, resolution-independent set of tokens, allowing its capacity to grow with the available observations. To force this compact bottleneck to retain sufficient scene information, a query-based Gaussian decoder uses scene-independent queries to attend to the learned tokens and recover an explicit, renderable set of 3D Gaussian primitives. Novel-view rendering supervision trains the compact representation end to end through the reconstructed Gaussian scene. Experiments on \retenk{} and ACID show that the resulting compact, unstructured token set supports competitive novel-view synthesis and can serve as the latent space of a generative model for 3D Gaussian scene generation. Together, these results show that 3D Gaussian reconstruction is an effective objective for compact scene representation learning and the learned token space provides a basis for broader downstream tasks in 3D vision.

items.title: GAD: Geometry Attention Distillation for Consistent Video Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.18779v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video diffusion models generate visually compelling short-term sequences but often struggle to preserve scene geometry and object structure over time. In this paper, we first demonstrate that current video attention cannot identify reliable correspondences across frames, with responses dispersed across multiple regions even after recognizable scene structure has emerged. We argue that reliable cross-frame associations are essential for information exchange as scene structure forms in video generation. Thus, we introduce Geometry Attention Distillation (GAD), which transfers correspondences from a frozen geometry model's attention to video attention. Extracted from clean videos, these correspondences link the same static surface or moving object across frames. Since structure formation begins in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise, we apply attention distillation at a student layer selected according to the noise timestep. After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding locations. Experiments across all three video backbones demonstrate improved long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency, with geometric gains across generation lengths. On Wan2.2 5B, GAD improves cross-frame matching accuracy by at least 30% over the Wan baseline on both long-range benchmarks. Notably, GAD achieves these gains without additional inference modules, offering a promising approach to efficient and consistent video-based world simulation. Project page: https://fantasy-amap.github.io/GAD/.

items.reasoning: A well-motivated method with a clear diagnostic insight about attention dispersion in video diffusion, from a strong team including BIGAI and related researchers. Geometry-guided distillation is a compelling mechanism for long-horizon consistency, an active frontier in video generation, though evaluation scope in the abstract suggests room for broader validation.
