items.title: On the Theoretical Limits of Learning Unconstrained Interatomic Potentials
items.content: arXiv:2610.15078v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) accelerate molecular dynamics (MD) simulations by learning the energies and forces that govern atomic motion. Recent work has shown that relaxing physical inductive biases can improve computational efficiency and predictive accuracy, raising the question of whether energy-and-force matching alone is sufficient to ensure accurate sampling. We show that, for unconstrained hypothesis classes, the relationship between prediction error and sampling accuracy is exponentially ill-conditioned in dimension. In particular, prediction errors that decay exponentially with dimension can coexist with nearly maximal total variation distance between the learned and target distributions. We identify two failure mechanisms. The first is kinetic trapping, where relaxation to an accurate learned equilibrium requires exponentially long times, even when simulations are initialized from training configurations at which energies and forces are matched exactly. The second is equilibrium mismatch, where the learned stationary distribution itself remains far from the target. Under explicit assumptions, we show that equilibrium mismatch can persist even in local, symmetry-preserving models, where small per-atom errors coexist with a distributional discrepancy that approaches its maximum as system size increases. Finally, we establish global energy-control conditions that guarantee equilibrium accuracy and identify additional conditions required for rapid relaxation.

items.title: Heterogeneous Structured Pruning Under Resource Constraints for Hardware-Efficient Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.15781v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Training-free pruning removes weights from pretrained large language models to reduce their deployment cost. However, existing approaches typically consider only the total number of retained weights. Consequently, their pruning decisions do not account for how target hardware stores and processes those weights. These methods select a sparsity structure in advance and apply it uniformly to all projections, rather than accounting for how each structure trades pruning error against latency and memory across sublayers. We propose Heterogeneous Structured Pruning (HSP), a hardware-aware pruning framework that combines two components: (i) a heterogeneous search space of dense, unstructured, 2:4, block-sparse, and head / channel (H/C) pruning options and (ii) structure-regularising constraints based on latency and memory models. Our contribution generalises existing importance-based methods: a global solver selects one option per sublayer to minimise proxy pruning loss under a resource budget, thereby assigning each projection a structure and density. We evaluate HSP on OPT and LLaMA models for an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super edge device, where it improves the quality-resource frontiers over training-free baselines.   A project page and updated links for the related code is maintained at: cameronbarker.me/publications/hsp.

items.title: Sampling from Neural Operator Priors to Solve Partial Differential Equations
items.content: arXiv:2610.16396v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Guided sampling with sparse observations and PDE residuals has recently been combined with neural operator priors to solve partial differential equations in function space, their natural setting. We pair such a prior with pseudo-bootstrap sequential Monte Carlo (pBS SMC), a guided sampling framework that accommodates proposals without tractable densities, and introduce a new proposal by adapting the DPM++ algorithm to the guidance setting. Across five benchmark PDE systems this proposal attains the best error--time trade-off at every step count tested, and wrapping it in pBS gives the lowest error on most inverse-problem settings, with the largest gains when few sampling steps are used.

It introduces a new proposal by adapting the DPM++ algorithm to the guidance setting, achieving the best error-time trade-off across five benchmark PDE systems. items.title: Intrinsic Geometry Matching: learning observation-equivariant process geometry
items.content: arXiv:2610.16995v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Real data are often arbitrary, indirect observations of an unknown underlying process, and those observations can distort its geometry. Existing geometric methods equip data with the induced geometry of the ambient space, but this entangles the true geometry of the process with the distortion of the observation. To address this, we introduce Intrinsic Geometry Matching (IGM): a scalable approach to learn the intrinsic geometry of the underlying process. Specifically, we learn the carr\'e du champ operator of the process, allowing us to recover its diffusion geometry. Our method uses the fact that data often come with natural perturbations, like steps in a time series, to recover the intrinsic carr\'e du champ while transforming naturally with changes in observation: it is observation-equivariant. Furthermore, since this equivariance relates the geometry of different spaces, we can train a model using additional sources of data, even when that data lies in another space. We evaluate IGM on molecular dynamics, image, and video data and find better performance and scaling than existing neural and graph-based geometric tools.

items.title: Robustly Reliable Learning for Regression
items.content: arXiv:2610.17381v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We introduce the problem of robustly reliable learning for the regression setting in adversarial environments. Given a test point $x_{test}$, a training dataset $S$ of $n$ data points, a corruption budget $b \ll n$, and a real-valued hypothesis class $\mathcal H$, our goal is to output the optimal prediction range $I^*_{x_{test}}(S, b)$, such that any $L$-Lipschitz predictor consistent with all but at most $b$ points in $S$ must predict a value $h(x_{test}) \in I$. We then instantiate the analysis for $L$-Lipschitz hypothesis classes, a natural and widely studied class in the regression setting, focusing on two key scenarios. First, for the restricted case where the corrupted dataset is guaranteed to be $L$-Lipschitz consistent, we propose a simple and efficient $b^{th}$-best heuristic algorithm and prove its correctness in computing the tightest possible range $I^*_{x_{test}}(S, b)$. We then establish its computational complexity of $O(n)$ and show that it is computationally optimal in this scenario. Building on this foundation, we address the general scenario where the dataset $S$ is no longer $L$-Lipschitz consistent. We demonstrate that computing the optimal range in this setting reduces to analyzing a violation graph, which models the pairwise $L$-Lipschitz violations among data points. By leveraging the structural properties of this graph's kernel, we propose a Fixed-Parameter Tractable (FPT) algorithm that computes the exact optimal range in $O(n^2 + b^4)$ time. Furthermore, under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), we establish a computational lower bound of $\Omega(n^{2 - o(1)})$, proving that our algorithm is computationally optimal. Finally, we discuss open directions for the problem of robustly reliable learning for regression.

It extends reliable learning theory from classification to the regression setting with concrete algorithms.

items.title: Learning Source Structure: Bayesian Prediction with Transformers
items.content: arXiv:2610.18725v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A transformer trained on sequences whose source parameters are drawn afresh each time can learn only what the sequences share: the source family and its prior. The Bayesian predictor that knows both, which we call informed Bayes, is the unique minimizer of the training loss and is computable from the family alone; we use it as a quantitative, falsifiable reference. Where earlier work compared transformers with Bayes on sources whose contexts can be learned independently, we build Markov sources with up to 64 symbols in which observations in one context inform prediction in another: product sources with known or hidden encodings, transition rows sharing an unknown base law and depth, and a mixture of three families. Our main result is that informed Bayes predicts, from the family and prior alone, how a trained transformer behaves in four tests that go beyond the learning curve: the loss that remains under a source outside the training family (predicted 2.237 bits, measured 2.309), the doubling of the extra loss when two independent components change rather than one (0.345 predicted, 0.350 measured), the benefit of other contexts when a token appears for the first time, and the depth at which copying an earlier continuation starts to pay. On the learning curves themselves, small transformers match informed Bayes when the shared structure is visible in the tokens, and hidden structure needs more layers and training, with gaps below 0.01 bits per token for the largest models. We explain why the imitation is possible and where it must fail: informed Bayes decomposes into sufficient statistics that attention selects and accumulates and an estimator, fixed by the prior, that the feed-forward network learns; training pays the complexity of informed Bayes under the architecture's prior, and finite-memory universal prediction bounds how closely a bounded network can reach it.

items.title: Screening Collapse under Recursive Synthetic Data
items.content: arXiv:2610.15617v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recursive synthetic-data training can degrade a fitted model, but its effects on the variable-screening stage that precedes model fitting are less understood. When each generation labels data for the next, a marginal screener ranks variables against the current pseudo-label target rather than the original response. Across generations, this target drift can erode or reverse the active--inactive score margin and cause screening to discard variables that clean-label screening would retain. We call this process \emph{screening collapse}. In a Gaussian linear model with minimum-norm recursive generators, we establish finite-sample screening bounds, characterize a late-generation information-loss limit, and derive a minimax impossibility result. Screening collapse can precede and compound ordinary model collapse: omitted variables incur a covariance-weighted loss that no refit restricted to the selected variables can eliminate, while recursive labels further degrade estimation on the retained variables. We also examine two approaches to mitigating screening collapse. Fixed-fraction real-label retention preserves a clean-label component but leaves resolution fixed, whereas data accumulation can avoid screening collapse if the pooled target preserves a positive margin and the growing sample resolves it. Numerical experiments on gene-expression data support the theoretical findings.

items.title: Efficient Fr\'echet Distributional Decoder Alignment for Latent Generative Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.17466v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Fr\'echet Distributional (FD) objectives provide an effective distribution-level signal for post-training generative models. For latent generative models, however, existing FD-based post-training methods optimize only the latent generator while keeping the decoder frozen: the decoder is trained on reconstruction latents obtained from real images but deployed on generator-produced latents at generation time. When these latent distributions differ, this \textbf{decoder train-generation mismatch} means that the decoder is deployed on inputs drawn from a distribution it was not directly trained on. We introduce \textbf{Fr\'echet Distributional Decoder Alignment (FDDA)}, an efficient post-training method that freezes the latent generator and directly optimizes the decoder on generation-time latents using an FD objective. A single epoch of FDDA consistently improves gFID and gFDr$^6$ across diverse flow-based and autoregressive latent generative models. Across all 11 evaluated models, FDDA reduces gFDr$^6$ by 34.0-59.6\% from the original pretrained models and provides a further 10.2-57.2\% reduction after generator-side FD post-training. FDDA also reduces total wall-clock time by factors of $3.6\times$-$328.7\times$ relative to generator-side FD post-training across these models. These results show that generator-side post-training alone does not exhaust the benefits of FD optimization, and that further gains can be obtained by adapting the decoder at substantially lower cost.

This should improve output fidelity for latent diffusion and similar models with minimal cost.

items.title: Self-Distillation with Verbal Regularization
items.content: arXiv:2610.16354v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a large language model using supervision from a teacher instantiated from the same model as the student. The teacher is conditioned on privileged information (PI), such as verified solutions. The student, which does not observe PI, learns from the teacher's next-token distributions along its own sampled responses. However, PI can bias supervision toward shortcut reasoning with limited verification or reconsideration, accompanied by a sharp drop in the entropy of the output distribution. To address this challenge, we introduce self-distillation with verbal regularization (VRSD), which uses system prompts to regulate how the teacher uses PI, thereby encouraging rethinking and exploration to counteract premature commitment. Theoretically, we model prompting as attenuating the influence of PI on the teacher distribution and derive conditions for entropy preservation. Across three models and four tasks, VRSD improves Pass@1 over OPSD in 11 of 12 model-task settings, by 3.9 percentage points on average, while generally maintaining higher token entropy.

It uses system prompts as verbal regularization on the teacher, encouraging rethinking and exploration to counteract the entropy collapse.

items.title: TETRIS-4DGS: Efficient Post-Training Compression of 4D Gaussian Splatting
items.content: arXiv:2610.14663v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) has emerged as a powerful dynamic scene representation, supporting real-time high quality rendering but suffers from prohibitive storage overhead. Existing methods typically attempt to solve this by treating compression as a per-scene optimization problem, limiting generalizability and applicability where low-latency compression is required. In this work, we leverage existing image and video codecs and propose a generalized post-training compression framework for 4DGS to address these issues. Specifically, we apply importance-based adaptive quantization to Gaussians according to their importance levels, effectively refining bitrate allocation while remaining fully compatible with existing codecs. To further improve compression efficiency, we utilize the statistical properties of 4DGS and propose motion- and importance-aware packing to reorganize attributes into codec-friendly 2D maps. Our approach can achieve over 40x compression rate in seconds while maintaining high quality, facilitating the practical deployment of 4DGS.

This avoids per-scene optimization, enabling low-latency compression and better generalization for dynamic scene representation.

items.title: Visually Legible but Adversarial: Watermark-Constrained Attacks on End-to-End VLMs for Document Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2610.15728v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Visible watermarks convey document ownership, confidentiality, and status, but can also carry adversarial signals. We introduce Auto-Regional Adversarial Watermarking (AR-AWM), a model-aware white-box attack on end-to-end visual language models (VLMs) for document understanding. AR-AWM constructs a small, spatially distributed watermark-text support and optimizes only its pixels to disrupt visual representations. The attack is untargeted and question-agnostic: generation uses no questions, answers, parsing prompts, language-model gradients, or language-model outputs. Each attacked page is reused across downstream queries. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, a watermark support covering 7.98% of page pixels under the reporting threshold reduces DocVQA exact match from 0.899 to 0.150 and average normalized Levenshtein similarity (ANLS) from 0.939 to 0.212. Selected qualitative cases retain visually legible source fields. The same support without optimization and with matched random perturbations retains ANLS of 0.932 and 0.933, respectively, identifying adversarial optimization as the primary cause of degradation. Layout-matched optimized rectangles yield ANLS of 0.276, showing an incremental benefit from text-shaped geometry. AR-AWM also degrades all reported text, formula, reading-order, and table metrics on OmniDocBench. Separate white-box optimization on InternVL2.5-8B reduces ANLS from 0.922 to 0.046, while weak cross-model transfer reveals strong encoder specificity. These results identify conventional watermark-shaped supports as an adversarial surface for document VLMs in the evaluated white-box setting.luated white-box setting.

items.title: VGGA: Geometry-Grounded Autoencoder for Video Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.16204v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Autoencoders are the core component of latent video generative models, compressing high-dimensional videos into compact latent spaces for downstream generation. However, existing video autoencoders are primarily optimized for pixel-level reconstruction, providing limited supervision for learning structured latent representations. We argue that videos should not be treated merely as signals to be reconstructed, but rather as 2D projections of dynamic 3D worlds that exhibit explicit and well-structured geometric properties. Building on this insight, we propose \textbf{V}ideo \textbf{G}eometry \textbf{G}rounded \textbf{A}utoencoder (\textbf{VGGA}), a geometry-aware video autoencoder that explicitly incorporates geometric constraints into the reconstruction process. Specifically, VGGA grounds the learned representations along three complementary geometric dimensions: \emph{Structural Depth}, \emph{Motion Correspondence}, and \emph{Projective Warping}. These objectives are unified within a Video Geometry Decoder, which employs a shared spatio-temporal upsampling trunk to jointly optimize geometric learning and RGB reconstruction. Through these geometry-grounded objectives, VGGA encourages the latent representations to capture the underlying 3D structure and motion of dynamic scenes. VGGA consistently improves video generation across both geometry-centric and human-motion domains, reducing gFVD by 28.1\% on RealEstate10K and 37.7\% on Taichi-HD. Notably, these substantial generation improvements are achieved while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality, demonstrating that geometry-grounded representation learning yields a more effective latent space for video generation.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.16204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autoencoders are the core component of latent video generative models, compressing high-dimensional videos into compact latent spaces for downstream generation. However, existing video autoencoders are primarily optimized for pixel-level reconstruction, providing limited supervision for learning structured latent representations. We argue that videos should not be treated merely as signals to be reconstructed, but rather as 2D projections of dynamic 3D worlds that exhibit explicit and well-structured geometric properties. Building on this insight, we propose \textbf{V}ideo \textbf{G}eometry \textbf{G}rounded \textbf{A}utoencoder (\textbf{VGGA}), a geometry-aware video autoencoder that explicitly incorporates geometric constraints into the reconstruction process. Specifically, VGGA grounds the learned representations along three complementary geometric dimensions: \emph{Structural Depth}, \emph{Motion Correspondence}, and \emph{Projective Warping}. These objectives are unified within a Video Geometry Decoder, which employs a shared spatio-temporal upsampling trunk to jointly optimize geometric learning and RGB reconstruction. Through these geometry-grounded objectives, VGGA encourages the latent representations to capture the underlying 3D structure and motion of dynamic scenes. VGGA consistently improves video generation across both geometry-centric and human-motion domains, reducing gFVD by 28.1\% on RealEstate10K and 37.7\% on Taichi-HD. Notably, these substantial generation improvements are achieved while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality, demonstrating that geometry-grounded representation learning yields a more effective latent space for video generation.

items.title: Auditing Observation-Quality Shortcuts in the Evaluation of Person-Centered Motion for Video Anomaly Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.16471v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video anomaly detection (VAD) identifies deviations from normal patterns, but such deviations do not necessarily correspond to safety-critical events. We focus on human-centered emergencies and violence and investigate whether motion-based anomaly discrimination reflects task-relevant motion information or observation-quality differences arising from person detection, pose estimation, and tracking. We introduce an observation-quality-aware evaluation framework that combines quality diagnostics, quality balancing, motion orthogonalization, and robustness analyses. On human-centered categories of UCF-Crime, quality-only features match or exceed the discrimination of multi-cue motion in the original cohort, revealing a strong observation-quality shortcut. After cardinality matching brings all 11 measured quality variables below a prespecified marginal balance threshold, multi-cue motion consistently outperforms quality-only features across Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and RBF-SVM, yielding ROC-AUC gains of 0.046-0.141. Because nonlinear quality-only prediction remains above chance after matching, we interpret this result as additional discrimination beyond measured marginal quality rather than as evidence of quality-free or causal motion understanding. These findings show that high VAD performance should not be interpreted as evidence of abnormal-motion modeling without auditing the reliability of the person-observation pipeline. Our study provides a systematic protocol for evaluating observation-quality shortcuts and for assessing whether motion-based discrimination survives explicit control of detection, pose-estimation, and tracking reliability.

items.title: FoveaTree: Information-Density Trees for Query-Guided Visual Token Pruning in Video Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.16744v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) encode each frame into hundreds of visual tokens, making video inference expensive. Existing methods reduce this cost through similarity-based merging or attention-based selection but face two challenges: Hierarchy-blind Pruning, which overlooks regional compressibility and can discard critical evidence, and Attention Drift, where positional effects and attention sinks shift text-to-vision attention away from task relevance. We propose FoveaTree, a two-stage, training-free visual-token pruning framework. First, Merge-Gain Density Estimation measures the feature distortion caused by regional merging and constructs a quadtree-derived density map to guide token dropping, merging, and retention. Second, Attention Tree Pruning uses the surviving units and inherited tree topology to refine text-to-vision attention in intermediate LLM layers, preserving relevant regional evidence while removing low-relevance content. We evaluate FoveaTree on InternVL3.5-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B across five video question-answering benchmarks and one captioning benchmark at 50%, 30%, and 10% visual-token retention. FoveaTree consistently achieves overall state-of-the-art performance across the evaluated settings, offering a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

items.title: Physical-Field-Bridged Material Parameter Inference from Multi-View Deformation Videos
items.content: arXiv:2610.17591v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Estimating simulation-ready material parameters from visual observations is crucial for deformable-object manipulation but challenging because material properties are only indirectly revealed through physical responses. We introduce physical-field-bridged material inference, a single-pass framework that uses dense physical responses to connect multi-view RGB deformation videos with constitutive-type classification and continuous parameter regression. Unlike inverse-physics methods requiring per-scene reconstruction, online tuning, or simulation-in-the-loop optimization, our model predicts force/contact masks, projected motion-flow fields, and projected stress-response maps, then conditions material inference on these fields to reduce reliance on appearance or category shortcuts. We construct DeformFieldBench, a 3DGS MPM learning environment comprising 5,000 simulations across 100 object shapes and five mechanically informative loading modes, with dense pixel-aligned physical supervision. Our method achieves the best median errors on all four continuous parameters, improves stress-hotspot recall from 0.0762 to 0.5121, and attains 0.8676 SSIM/36.82 dB PSNR in same-simulator replay on unseen objects. Under a protocol-matched GSO evaluation, inference and future-state prediction take approximately 30 seconds, compared with 15-120 minutes for per-scene optimization. The method also yields measurable replay agreement on five real-world sequences. These results support dense physical fields as an effective bridge for fast material inference, while cross-simulator and real-world tests reveal remaining domain and identifiability gaps.

items.title: Multimodal Fusion of RGB and Complementary Modalities for Semantic Segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2610.17800v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-modal semantic segmentation adds an auxiliary sensing stream to RGB images (RGB-X), such as thermal, LiDAR, depth, event, polarization, or light field. This can improve robustness in poor lighting and under motion blur. But different sensors often produce features that do not match well, and fusion can become unstable. To alleviate these issues, we propose a bidirectional polarity-aware cross-modality fusion (BPCF) module that effectively captures complementary cues while enhancing feature alignment. We evaluate the framework on six modality pairings: RGB-Thermal, RGB-LiDAR, RGB-Depth, RGB-Event, RGB-Polarization, and RGB-Light Field. Our model achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on eight public datasets, including MFNet, KITTI-360, DELIVER, DDD17, DSEC, MCubeS, ZJU, and UrbanLF. The codes and trained models will be released upon acceptance.

items.title: Efficient Scene-Text Refinement via Pixel-Space Grouped Image Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.18284v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generated images often have coherent layouts and visual content, yet local errors in small text and complex characters still limit their readability and practical use. Scene-text refinement requires accuracy, preservation, and efficiency. Existing methods based on variational autoencoders (VAEs) can lose fine strokes during reconstruction, while full-image editing can shift background colors. In this work, we introduce PixText, a model that formulates local text refinement as grouped image generation in pixel space. Conditioned on the original image, PixText generates only the target regions, preserves unedited content, and uses MeanFlow for four-step generation. We further introduce Text Refinement Bench to evaluate text correction and image preservation in generated images. On this benchmark, PixText achieves 83.06% glyph pass and 94.66% exact target-character OCR accuracy, versus 36.77% and 52.31% for the strongest baseline. Its four-step MeanFlow variant retains an 81.84% pass rate with less than one GPU-second of amortized generation cost per image.

It also releases Text Refinement Bench for evaluating text correction in generated images. Addresses the persistent weakness of generative models at rendering small, legible text.

items.title: Refine Where It Matters: Contact-Adaptive Meshing for Deformable Object Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2610.14142v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Deformable-object manipulation requires accurate modeling of highly localized contact while maintaining simulation speeds suitable for interactive use. Uniformly fine tetrahedral meshes can resolve these interactions, but they introduce unnecessary degrees of freedom throughout the object. Coarse meshes are more efficient, yet they may under-resolve contact-induced deformation. We present a contact-adaptive mesh refinement framework that introduces spatial resolution only where it is most useful. The method uses geometric, elastic, and contact quantities already available from the deformable-body solver to score candidate edges. A fully GPU-parallel procedure then selects a conflict-free subset and updates both mesh topology and physical state directly within the simulation loop. We evaluate the approach on real deformable-object manipulation sequences. Adaptive refinement reduces simulation-to-real error, improves agreement with a fine-mesh reference, and remains substantially more efficient than uniformly fine simulation. These results show that local refinement can improve physical fidelity without incurring the cost of a globally fine discretization. The framework provides a practical basis for contact-rich simulation in interactive manipulation, sim-to-real modeling, and online physical digital twins.

items.title: FoundationVIO: Enforcing Metric Scale in Feed-forward Visual-Inertial Odometry
items.content: arXiv:2610.14951v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Feed-forward geometric foundation models (GFMs) directly predict dense geometry and camera poses from batches of images. Emerging visual SLAM methods chain together consecutive GFM batches to form dense point cloud maps. A core challenge is how to address the ambiguous geometric scale of GFM predictions: independent predictions are locally consistent up-to-scale but not constrained by any direct physical measurements. Models trained on data with known scale improve the consistency of GFM reconstructions but again do not directly measure it. Consequently, trajectories and 3D reconstructions from GFM-enabled SLAM methods inherit this issue. Motivated by parallels with classical visual-inertial odometry, we introduce FoundationVIO which integrates inertial sensing with GFM predictions to recover metric scale reconstruction using a factor-graph based approach. We demonstrate odometry estimates competitive with classical state-of-the-art VIO methods and accurate dense reconstructions that outperform GFM-enabled SLAM methods. We also add a minimal GFM-based loop-closure mechanism to create a full Visual-Inertial SLAM system capable of creating globally accurate reconstructions and pose estimates. We evaluate our method on three datasets with well known sensor systems and demonstrate its compatibility on ubiquitous camera and IMU sensors. The method runs at approximately real-time on a consumer-grade laptop GPU. Code: https://github.com/ori-drs/FoundationVIO.

GFM predictions are locally consistent up-to-scale but unanchored to physical measurement, which propagates into trajectories and reconstructions. The method enforces metric scale in GFM-enabled odometry pipelines.

items.title: MIRROR: Reflecting Hidden Symmetries from Offline Robot Interaction Data
items.content: arXiv:2610.17422v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Symmetry-aware robot policy learning requires coupled observation-action transformations. For pixel observations, even simple physical symmetries can induce complex, viewpoint-dependent image transformations that are difficult to specify by hand. Existing symmetry-aware methods often rely on representations with predefined transformations, requiring preprocessing tailored to the sensing setup and task. We introduce MIRROR, a framework that learns how a known symmetry group operates jointly on observations and actions in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) from offline interaction data. MIRROR couples these transformations through adversarial tuple matching over one-step transition tuples, while explicit group-consistency regularization penalizes violations of the group-operation axioms. On four Robosuite tabletop manipulation tasks, MIRROR achieves the lowest aggregate error on three of four symmetry-quality metrics, including a 61% reduction in compatibility error (which measures consistency under transformation composition) relative to an adapted LaLiGAN baseline. Using the learned transformations in frame-averaged behavior cloning (BC) yields higher mean success rates than vanilla BC on all four tasks, increasing average success from 80.48% to 85.12%, with per-task gains up to 9.66 percentage points. We also repeat symmetry discovery and policy training in simulation with heightmap and segmentation-mask observations, then deploy the resulting policy zero-shot on a real Kinova GEN3 arm. Project page: https://pomdp-mirror.github.io.
items.author: Shiqi Liu, Yihang Yao, Peide Huang, Mengdi Xu, Ding Zhao
items.summary: MIRROR learns how a known symmetry group operates jointly on observations and actions in POMDPs directly from offline interaction data, using adversarial tuple matching over one-step transitions plus explicit group-consistency constraints. This removes the need for hand-specified, viewpoint-dependent pixel transformations that prior symmetry-aware policy learning requires. The learned coupled transformations can then be used for symmetry-aware policy learning and data augmentation.

Learning the transformations from offline data is a clean idea with theory-backed structure (adversarial matching, group consistency). CMU-affiliated authorship and a principled framing support the score, though downstream empirical gains matter for full impact.

items.title: TRACE: Efficient Transfer Learning for Neural Whole-Body Control Across Humanoid Embodiments
items.content: arXiv:2610.17999v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) enable diverse whole-body control, but adapting a pretrained controller to a new embodiment remains challenging because of kinematic and dynamic mismatch. We present TRACE, a framework for efficient cross-embodiment adaptation that preserves pretrained motion representations while specializing feedback control to the target robot.TRACE first injects kinematic priors into input and output projection layers and aligns nominal joint dynamics to reduce embodiment mismatch and support stable fine-tuning. It then combines encoder distillation with low-rank reinforcement learning on a compact, quality-screened motion set, using a two-phase curriculum to establish stable tracking before refining difficult motions. We apply TRACE to transfer SONIC from Unitree G1 to Unitree H2 using 10 million motion frames and approximately eight hours of training on a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU, at less than 0.1% of the GPU-hour cost of training SONIC from scratch. The adapted controller achieves 96.08\% success on 67,953 evaluation motions under a height-scaled tracking criterion. Real-robot demonstrations span dynamic motion tracking and whole-body teleoperation, with collected demonstrations supporting downstream vision-language-action policy post-training. These results demonstrate practical reuse of a pretrained humanoid controller across robots with different body scales and dynamics.

It preserves pretrained motion representations while specializing feedback control to the target robot.

Novelty is moderate (parameter-efficient transfer techniques adapted to a new domain), but practical significance is high.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.17999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) enable diverse whole-body control, but adapting a pretrained controller to a new embodiment remains challenging because of kinematic and dynamic mismatch. We present TRACE, a framework for efficient cross-embodiment adaptation that preserves pretrained motion representations while specializing feedback control to the target robot.TRACE first injects kinematic priors into input and output projection layers and aligns nominal joint dynamics to reduce embodiment mismatch and support stable fine-tuning. It then combines encoder distillation with low-rank reinforcement learning on a compact, quality-screened motion set, using a two-phase curriculum to establish stable tracking before refining difficult motions. We apply TRACE to transfer SONIC from Unitree G1 to Unitree H2 using 10 million motion frames and approximately eight hours of training on a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU, at less than 0.1% of the GPU-hour cost of training SONIC from scratch. The adapted controller achieves 96.08\% success on 67,953 evaluation motions under a height-scaled tracking criterion. Real-robot demonstrations span dynamic motion tracking and whole-body teleoperation, with collected demonstrations supporting downstream vision-language-action policy post-training. These results demonstrate practical reuse of a pretrained humanoid controller across robots with different body scales and dynamics.

items.title: Unconstrained CTI-REALM with Open-Weights
items.content: arXiv:2610.14180v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Organisations that want language-model agents for security work face a choice between open-weight models, which they can run and audit themselves, and far more expensive closed frontier models. We study that choice on CTI-REALM (arXiv:2603.13517), a benchmark in which an agent turns a threat-intelligence report into a working detection by querying a live telemetry store. We evaluate twenty-six models, nineteen open-weight and seven closed, under a common harness, scorer and panel of LLM judges. Our main finding is that an open-weight model can match the strongest closed models at less than a tenth of their cost, provided it is given enough turns. The benchmark's published limit on agent messages is a confound: a task that exhausts the limit scores zero on every checkpoint, including those it had already passed, so results at that limit partly measure which models finish in time. At the published limit the leading open-weight and closed models cannot be distinguished. With the limit relaxed, the models it was truncating recover, and the highest rewards belong to open-weight models. Among the leading models, price is a poor guide to capability: models with similar rewards differ in cost by more than an order of magnitude. Because the benchmark's checkpoint scores largely record what an agent did or mentioned, we also introduce stage-level metrics that score what the agent submits, by executing its detection queries in the telemetry store and judging its outputs against the answer key. Rather than combining them into one more overall reward, we show that different models lead different stages, which suggests routing each stage of the workflow to the model that performs it best rather than choosing a single model by its overall score. We also report how many tokens each model generates, and find that the share of output spent on thinking does not track the reward.

items.title: ConicFlow: constrained Inference-time optimal control for flow matching models
items.content: arXiv:2610.14307v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We propose ConicFlow, which frames constrained sampling from a flow matching model at inference time as an optimal control problem that balances deviation from the pretrained trajectory against reward, subject to hard terminal constraints. We discretize this problem and adapt receding-horizon control, optimizing only a short window of the trajectory at each step for computational tractability. We address the resulting sequence of receding-horizon subproblems with a receding-horizon primal-dual algorithm. Its dual multipliers capture the difficulty of satisfying each constraint and are refined throughout sampling, steering generation toward feasible final samples. We further propose a terminal-estimate variant that avoids accumulating local truncation errors by evaluating the reward and constraints at the predicted terminal point rather than at the end of the current horizon. Under standard regularity assumptions, we establish finite-horizon guarantees on suboptimality. Under convex-affine structure, we derive a sharper bound that scales linearly with omitted horizon length, and we show that the terminal-estimate variant is provably tighter when the flow dynamics change slowly. Experiments in both low- and high-dimensional settings with a recent large-scale flow matching model show that ConicFlow achieves high reward and strong constraint satisfaction while deviating less from the pretrained flow than recent baselines.

items.title: Decoupling Knowledge Forgetting and Refusal Learning in MLLM Unlearning
items.content: arXiv:2610.14605v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Current evaluations of multimodal unlearning typically focus on whether a model stops outputting target information. This surface-level criterion, however, masks two critical failure modes. First, knowledge suppression techniques often induce confabulation, leading the model to hallucinate facts about the unlearned subject. Second, refusal training merely alters observable behavior without erasing the underlying knowledge; such models might decline open queries but still identify correct answers under multiple-choice probing. To overcome these limitations, we propose Forget-Aware Self-Distillation (FASD). This method is designed to achieve honest ignorance, a state where the model genuinely loses the target knowledge and learns to acknowledge its absence. FASD separates these goals into two complementary channels. The behavior channel distills appropriate refusals from an ignorance-prompted copy of the model itself. Crucially, target tokens are masked from the teacher distribution to avoid accidentally reteaching the forgotten concepts. Simultaneously, the knowledge channel directly suppresses ground-truth answer spans independently of the model's generated responses. Experiments demonstrate that FASD successfully unlearns target knowledge, prevents information leakage in open-ended tasks, and preserves performance on retained data. The resulting model not only forgets the specified information but accurately recognizes the boundaries of its own knowledge. Code and data will be released upon publication.

items.title: EvoCowork: A Benchmark for Real-World Office Tasks
items.content: arXiv:2610.14828v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Office workflows are a demanding testbed for self-improving agents because their deliverables must be correct, natively editable, and mutually consistent. A central question is whether gains on feedback tasks reflect reusable procedures rather than task-specific fixes. We introduce EvoCowork, a 240-task benchmark for evaluating harness-level recursive self-improvement across four office modalities, with model weights held fixed. The benchmark covers presentations, documents, spreadsheets, and cross-office workflows, and scores submitted artifacts for content, native structure, formulas, cross-file consistency, and visual quality where needed. Its protocol separates feedback, revision selection, and final testing: methods learn from single-modality tasks, then are evaluated on unseen single-modality tasks and cross-office workflows under a shared initial harness and explicit budgets. In static evaluations of two models and four harnesses, the best configuration scores 42.25 overall and 30.62 on cross-office tasks. Starting from the same MSA harness with GLM 5.3, ACE and AHE improve in-domain scores by 4.90 and 2.64 points, respectively, but change cross-office scores by only +0.03 and -1.72. Thus, gains on the file types that provide feedback do not necessarily transfer to coordinated workflows. EvoCowork makes this distinction explicit while recording the capability, transfer, and cost of harness evolution. Code and task packages: https://github.com/DeepThinkingZhouLiu/cowork-evolution-benchmark.

items.title: Certify the Decision, Not Every Score: Exact Top-k Selection from Few Evaluations
items.content: arXiv:2610.14996v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Choosing a few robust algorithms or schedules can require evaluating every candidate under many adverse scenarios, even though an agent only needs to identify the winners. A predictor may suggest those winners, but cannot rule out a surprise in an unevaluated scenario. We introduce Certified Adaptive Selection (CAS), which returns the exact top-$k$ set as soon as remaining uncertainty cannot change it. CAS keeps guaranteed lower and upper bounds on Expected Shortfall (ES), the average loss in the worst scenarios. Its stopping test compares the worst admissible selected candidate with the best admissible excluded one; for information-disjoint Cartesian intervals this one-cut test is necessary and sufficient. Prediction has a separate role: selecting the next outcome to evaluate, never authorizing the decision. For empirical ES with exact unit-cost queries, we compute in polynomial time the fewest evaluations that could have proved the realized decision in hindsight. Our prediction-guided agent CAS-PG is exact for every predictor, including adversarial ones. On two public algorithm-selection matrices, CAS-PG certifies the exact top three after 630 of 3150 and 981 of 2200 replayed queries, or $1.14$ and $1.18$ times that hindsight minimum. Without historical outcomes, its transcript-only variant requires $1.28$ and $1.37$ times the minimum, outperforming the tested non-predictive certified policies. Separately, a prediction-free CAS policy avoids $93.0\%$ of exact recourse solves in synthetic energy scheduling. One certificate thus supports several acquisition policies and separately proved risk/cost extensions: prediction changes the work, not the justified choice.

items.title: Words to World: Benchmarking LLMs in Interactive Physical Environments
items.content: arXiv:2610.15228v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Words are increasingly becoming an interface for action: large language models (LLMs) can now invoke tools, operate devices, and make decisions that affect the physical world. However, current benchmarks largely evaluate LLMs through static text responses, offline tool calls, or simulated tasks, leaving open the question of how well they can act in real physical environments. We present a benchmark for measuring LLMs in closed-loop physical interaction, where models control a harness system connected to real-world components including robotic arms, cameras, and sensors. In each task, the model must issue instructions, receive physical feedback from the environment, interpret the resulting state, and adapt its next action accordingly. This setting evaluates capabilities beyond language understanding, including grounded perception, action planning, tool selection, spatial reasoning, feedback-driven correction, and robustness to execution uncertainty. Through experiments with representative LLMs, we characterize their ability to translate linguistic reasoning into physical actions and identify common failure modes such as hallucinated state changes, poor recovery from unexpected outcomes, and unstable long-horizon plans. Our benchmark aims to provide a systematic foundation for evaluating LLMs as interactive agents that connect words, tools, and the physical world.

items.reasoning: Fills a genuine gap between text-centric agent benchmarks and real physical environments, which is increasingly important as LLMs interface with the physical world. Real-hardware benchmarking is costly and relatively rare, adding value, though adoption depends on infrastructure availability.

items.title: Large Decision Models: Repurposing Large Language Models as Single-Pass Decision Makers
items.content: arXiv:2610.15501v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models make decisions through parallel prefill and sequential decoding. Although effective, this approach incurs decoding costs and does not explicitly expose decision probabilities. Existing task-specific classifiers require per-task training and offer limited generalization to unseen decision schemas. We propose Large Decision Models (LDMs), repurposing language models to return explicit probabilities over labels specified at run time using one prefill forward pass. We first adapt models to this interface through Diverse Decision Supervision (DDS), covering varied domains, rules and labels. To further narrow the performance gap to a reasoning model, Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation (SPRD) adds tasks generated by a frozen teacher, filters them for answer consistency, and trains on label distributions obtained from repeated teacher reasoning. We evaluate on DecisionVista, pairing new-schema tests with held-out human-labelled sources. Across three base models, the recipe improves accuracy over a step-matched baseline by 1.8 and 1.5 percentage points, respectively, achieving a 182-fold speedup in latency over reasoning rollout on Gemma-4-31B. Reasoning remains stronger on the new-schema test, motivating a confidence router for uncertain decisions. On development sets, routing recovers a median 92% of reasoning's accuracy advantage while generating 27-58% of its tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/LDM.
items.author: Ziyi Chen, Yan Zhang, Jianhui Wei, Jianing Yin, Daoan Zhang
items.summary: Large Decision Models repurpose LLMs to output explicit probabilities over run-time-specified labels in a single prefill pass, avoiding sequential decoding costs. Diverse Decision Supervision adapts models to this interface and Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation narrows the gap to reasoning models via teacher-generated tasks.
items.reasoning: A clever efficiency-oriented reframing that exposes calibrated decision probabilities without per-task classifier training, with potential for cheap, schema-general decision making. Novelty is moderate since it builds on classification and distillation, and single-pass prediction may sacrifice the accuracy of deliberative reasoning.

items.title: From Stages to States: Unified Iterative Reasoning for MLLMs
items.content: arXiv:2610.15620v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (MCoT) substantially enhances the complex reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by explicitly modeling intermediate reasoning processes. However, most learning-based MCoT methods follow a stage-centric paradigm, where different reasoning behaviors are assigned to predefined stages and optimized separately. This results in fragmented reasoning and a training-inference reasoning-state gap. To address these limitations, we propose ReState, a unified iterative reasoning framework that reformulates multimodal reasoning from a stage-driven pipeline into a state-driven dynamic process. It comprises two complementary components: Unified Reasoning State Modeling (URSM) and Closed-Loop Reasoning-State Learning (CRSL). URSM unifies reasoning construction, correct reasoning preservation, and erroneous reasoning correction as reasoning-state transitions within a shared state space, enabling these heterogeneous reasoning behaviors to be learned jointly. CRSL further incorporates self-generated historical reasoning states during training and recursively updates the current state during inference, thereby mitigating the reasoning-state gap and enabling iterative self-refinement without requiring an additional reflection module, critic, or independent correction stage. Furthermore, we construct VersaCoT-10K, a high-quality CoT dataset spanning eight visual reasoning domains, which provides diverse supervision for multi-domain reasoning and reasoning-state refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReState exhibits strong adaptability across different MLLM backbones and achieves strong performance on multiple public reasoning benchmarks, supporting the shift from stage-centric reasoning toward state-centric reasoning. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/YuChuang1205/ReState

items.title: Knowledge Interaction in Hypernetwork-based Continual Learning: Conflict and Composition
items.content: arXiv:2610.15677v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Continual learning aims to adapt pretrained large language models (LLMs) to evolving data while preserving their pretrained capabilities. A central challenge is catastrophic forgetting: adaptation to new data can impair performance on previously learned knowledge. Since continual learning commonly changes model parameters, the model's predictions may draw on knowledge from the base model, the parameter update, and the input context. Understanding how these sources interact is essential: conflicts reveal whether new knowledge can override outdated knowledge, while multi-hop reasoning tests whether new knowledge can be composed with existing knowledge to support generalization. We study these interactions in a hypernetwork-based adaptation framework, where a shared network generates adapters from context, allowing a frozen base model to adapt without task-specific updates. We find that, under knowledge conflict, models preferentially follow the context, and their choices depend more on where knowledge is presented than on its content. We also show that context and adapter knowledge perturb the base model's representations along directions orthogonal to its clean hidden states, enabling us to derive steering vectors that control which source the model follows. In multi-hop reasoning, we find that models fail to reliably compose knowledge across the three sources, with the key breakdown arising from the interaction of the hypernetwork with both the base model and the context. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/missswiftie/Knowledge-Interaction-in-CL

items.title: Uncovering Robustness Weaknesses in LLM Agents via Persona Evolution with Task-Integrity Constraints
items.content: arXiv:2610.16155v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Interactive-agent evaluations commonly rely on standardized LLM-based user simulators that exhibit broadly cooperative behavior, potentially overlooking failures that arise under diverse but realistic user interactions. This can lead to overly optimistic estimates of agent robustness and provide limited failure signals for training agents that generalize across users. Existing approaches largely rely on predefined user behaviors, which may miss agent- or domain-specific weaknesses, while failure-oriented search can reduce task success by invalidating the underlying task rather than exposing genuine robustness failures. To fill this gap, we introduce TIPER, a task-integrity-preserving persona evolution method that automatically discovers agent-specific user policies exposing robustness weaknesses while keeping the underlying task valid and solvable. TIPER evolves persistent user personas through reflection-guided behavioral mutations and task-wise Pareto selection under a task-integrity constraint. Across four interactive-agent benchmarks, TIPER yields lower held-out avg@3 scores in all 12 GPT-5.4 settings, with observed reductions of 5.8 to 33.7 percentage points, and in all 28 agent-domain pairs spanning seven agents, with a median observed reduction of 22.9 points. Further analysis yields a behavior-to-failure taxonomy that connects discovered user behaviors to recurring agent failure modes. Together, these results show that TIPER enables more diagnostic robustness evaluation of interactive agents and provides informative failure analysis for future agent robustness improvement. Code repository: https://github.com/UCSB-NLP-Chang/TIPER.

items.title: RetroPlanner: Multi-Route Expansion and Multi-Objective Reasoning for LLM-Based Retrosynthesis Planning
items.content: arXiv:2610.16391v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning is often considered solved once a route to purchasable starting materials is found, but such a route should also be practical in real-world chemistry. Recent LLM-based planners formulate this process as sequential decision-making over an AND-OR graph, yet typically expand a single molecule per turn and are optimized for solvability alone, leaving alternative routes uncompared across the multiple objectives that determine practicality before the search budget is committed. We introduce RetroPlanner, an LLM-based planner that jointly compares multiple routes to steer the search toward higher synthesizability, as measured by reaction plausibility, round-trip consistency, and starting-material price. RetroPlanner is trained to reason over chemical evidence: structural progress from the target molecule, bond changes and reaction classes, where candidate routes diverge from one another, and how they rank across multiple objectives. Experiments on multi-step retrosynthesis benchmarks demonstrate that RetroPlanner recovers more alternative routes than prior LLM-based planners while improving synthetic route quality and maintaining a high success rate.

items.title: When 1+1 Backfires: Rethinking Relevance-Diversity Balancing for Sample-Aware Visual Token Reduction
items.content: arXiv:2610.16615v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Visual token compression has emerged as a critical technique for reducing the inference cost of Vision-Language Models. Existing methods select tokens based on text relevance, visual diversity, or a fixed combination of both---treating the relevance-diversity balance as a universal constant independent of the input. We conduct a systematic analysis to challenge this assumption. At the dataset level, grid-searching the optimal relevance-diversity weight per benchmark reveals substantial cross-task variation. More critically, we further maximize per-sample answer likelihood to recover sample-level oracle weights, finding that their distributions not only differ markedly across benchmarks but also exhibit high within-benchmark variance. Based on these observations, we propose SAVER, a framework for Sample-Aware relevance-diversity balanced Visual tokEn Reduction. We first derive a Geometric Intent Prior (GIP) from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens to infer a sample-specific relevance-diversity weight, and then apply this weight to jointly select tokens via a Weighted Text Centroid (WTC) for relevance scoring and a Visual Marginal Coverage Gain (VMCG) for diversity. SAVER requires no additional training and achieves sample-aware balancing entirely at inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAVER consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, retaining 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B with only 11.1% of the original visual tokens, and further generalizing to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.
items.author: Yihang Huang, Peisong Wen, Chenhao Zhou, Difu Feng, Qianqian Xu
items.summary: Systematically challenges the assumption of a universal relevance-diversity balance in visual token compression for vision-language models, showing via dataset-level grid search and per-sample oracle-weight recovery that optimal weights vary across benchmarks and even within a single benchmark. The work motivates sample-aware token reduction strategies rather than fixed relevance-plus-diversity combinations.
items.reasoning: A careful analysis paper on an efficiency-critical component of VLMs, with a clear empirical refutation of a common design assumption. The insight is useful but incremental in scope, focused on one design hyperparameter of token pruning.

items.title: Neural Bayesian Networks for Modular and Scalable Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
items.content: arXiv:2610.16902v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Bayesian Networks (BNs) are established tools for letting agents reason under uncertainty in sequential decision-making. They split a joint distribution into local conditional mechanisms arranged on a directed acyclic graph, which makes them modular, interpretable, and ready to perform probabilistic inference. Their classical formulation, however, has limitations in both expressiveness and scale: each conditional is usually stored as a table or a linear-Gaussian form, and inference evaluates the graph one node and one query at a time.   In this paper we introduce Neural Bayesian Networks (NBNs), in which each conditional is a differentiable, tensor-valued mechanism, while the graph and its factorization are unchanged. NBNs retain the modularity and local mechanisms of BNs, can represent any learnable conditional distribution, and run natively on GPUs. We also release NBN, a PyTorch-based library for learning and inference in NBNs, together with a public benchmark. Our evaluation shows gains in both expressiveness and scale: NBNs fit distributions that classical BN libraries struggle to represent, and on large networks and large batches of queries they run two orders of magnitude faster thanks to GPU parallelization. NBN is available at https://github.com/Giovannibriglia/NeuralBayesianNetworks.

The idea is elegant and useful for decision-making under uncertainty, though similar neural-CPT hybrids have been explored, tempering novelty.

items.title: When LLM Agents See a Conflict but Still Proceed: Cross-Domain Dependencies in Network Slicing
items.content: arXiv:2610.17118v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Future AI-native networks are being designed to apply autonomous agents built on large language models (LLMs) in network management through intents. When intents from different domains meet on the same resource, an agent must recognize the cross-domain dependency before taking an irreversible action. We investigate this problem through a smart-grid use case, in which a power utility holds an active intent on a backup slice for protection traffic. This slice appears idle by design, which is precisely the profile targeted by a cost-reduction intent. We built a tool-based environment in which the dependency must be either queried by the agent or read from an inventory annotation, together with a negative control, and evaluated ten models from four different providers in 600 runs. Most models acted against the dependency they had observed: seven of the ten models removed the protection slice at least once after receiving the cross-domain dependency, and in the high-harm tier the slice was removed in 76% of the exposed runs, while four models practically never did. Only one of ten models never removed the slice. We identify two failure modes, not querying the dependency and querying it but proceeding anyway, and show that agents often reported no conflict after observing it. These results indicate that, in AI-native networks, visibility of cross-domain dependencies is not a sufficient safeguard, and that dependency verification should be enforced by the management architecture before irreversible actions rather than delegated to the LLM's judgment.

items.summary: Evaluates ten LLM models in a smart-grid network-slicing scenario where an agent must detect a cross-domain dependency before an irreversible action, such as decommissioning an intentionally idle protection slice. The study measures whether agents query or read dependency information before acting, with a negative control.

items.title: REA: From Correct LLM Judgments to Safe Decision Delivery
items.content: arXiv:2610.17473v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generative safety guards must classify requests correctly and return outputs that applications can parse. Reasoning guards can improve classification accuracy while producing outputs that applications cannot parse. When applications cannot extract a correct prediction, fallback handling can allow harmful requests or block safe ones. We introduce Resolve--Express--Act (REA), a framework that traces judgments through parsing and fallback to application actions. Experiments on classifiers and safety guards show that correct predictions can appear in incorrectly formatted outputs. Parsing the safety verdict preserves the reasoning guard's accuracy advantage, while stricter explanation requirements reject additional correct predictions. Accepting formatting variations recovers most rejected correct predictions. Held-out tests confirm that output requirements and generation limits affect whether correct predictions can be parsed. In our fail-open replay, matching the parser to the output and fixing formatting reduced the fraction of harmful requests allowed despite correct guard judgments from 95.5% to 0%. A fixed-output comparison shows that model-based extraction can preserve guard verdicts, but is not automatically reliable; deterministic normalization already repairs the observed native-format failures. Fallback replay shows that the same correct prediction can lead to different safety actions depending on the parser and fallback policy, including allowing requests the guard correctly identifies as harmful.

items.summary: REA (Resolve-Express-Act) is a framework that traces safety-guard judgments through output parsing and fallback handling to the final application action, showing that correct classifications can be lost through formatting and parsing failures. Experiments show parsing the safety verdict preserves reasoning guards' accuracy advantages, while stricter explanation requirements can reject additional correct predictions. The work highlights an overlooked gap between a guard being correct and its decision being safely delivered.

items.title: RoTA-Bench: Evaluating 3D Spatial Reasoning through Interactive Projection Alignment
items.content: arXiv:2610.17665v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Can vision-language models turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action? This requires inferring object geometry, anticipating the effects of rotation, and refining actions through visual feedback. We introduce RoTA-Bench to evaluate these abilities through interactive 3D-to-2D projection alignment. Given a target silhouette, a model observes a rotated object and chooses successive rotations to recover the target projection within a limited action budget. Our automated pipeline constructs silhouette-preserving 3D objects from 2D icons and uses reversible initialization to guarantee solvability, yielding 674 tasks and a stratified 100-task test set. Empirically, we find that (i) a substantial human-model gap persists: GPT-5.6-Sol succeeds on only 17% of tasks, whereas 20 undergraduate participants collectively complete the test set four times with a 100% success rate; (ii) image-space and pose-space progress can diverge: at matched states, the model more often improves silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment than humans (19.4% vs. 10.9%); and (iii) fine-grained control is sensitive to interaction history: removing it leaves 96.8% of the model's actions at a coarse 30-degree step size and sharply reduces observed task success. These findings highlight the challenge of converting visual evidence into precise 3D control, beyond recognizing or matching individual images.

A substantial human-model gap persists, exposing weaknesses in embodied spatial reasoning.

items.title: Adaptive-Group Process Rewards for GUI Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.17710v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Training graphical user interface (GUI) agents with reinforcement learning suffers from sparse outcome rewards, leading to inefficient learning. Process rewards offer a promising direction for credit assignment to intermediate actions; however, accurately evaluating an action requires identifying evidence across long-horizon GUI trajectories, as its value may depend on information beyond its immediate state and observation. In this paper, we propose an adaptive-group process reward framework that dynamically partitions a GUI trajectory into semantically coherent subgoal groups, enabling process reward estimation at both the action and group levels. At the action level, a critic evaluates each action based on the visual changes and subsequent actions within the group for action correctness and contribution to the subgoal. At the group level, the framework aggregates action-level evaluations to assess subgoal completion and contribution to the overall task, and further refines these assessments by leveraging the context of all groups in the trajectory. The process reward of each action is obtained by combining its action-level evaluation with the refined group-level evaluation. We further augment GRPO's outcome advantage with the proposed process rewards to provide finer-grained guidance for GUI agent training. Experiments on process reward benchmarks and downstream RL training demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

items.summary: This paper tackles sparse outcome rewards in RL training of GUI agents by proposing an adaptive-group process reward framework that dynamically segments trajectories into semantically coherent subgoal groups. It estimates process rewards at both action and group levels, with a critic evaluating actions based on visual changes and downstream evidence across long-horizon trajectories.
items.reasoning: Process reward design for GUI agents is an active and practical area, and the adaptive grouping idea addresses the real credit-assignment challenge of long-horizon computer-use tasks. Strong relevance to agentic RL, though similar process-reward approaches are emerging concurrently.

Experiments on process reward benchmarks and downstream RL training demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

items.title: Socratic Skill Learning: Interleaving Teaching and Practice for Transferable Agent Skills
items.content: arXiv:2610.17860v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Agent Skills improve LLM agents by making task knowledge reusable across sessions. Learning transferable Skills requires evidence about a procedure and its conditions of use, which a successful task attempt can leave untested. We introduce Socratic Skill Learning (SSL), which interleaves expert teaching with Student practice. An Educator guides investigation while the Student remains the sole environment operator and Skill author, able to question, test, and adapt advice. To test reuse beyond the learning task, we construct SkillTransferBench, with 35 task families and 408 executable cases, pairing public variation specifications with held-out evaluation in fresh solver sessions. On the main 22-family, 155-case cohort, Fixed-Window SSL reaches 0.801 utility, versus 0.723 without a Skill, 0.761 for adapted Trace2Skill (trajectory distillation), and 0.751 for adapted SKILL-KD (contrastive distillation). Across three model pairs on shared families, interleaved guidance outperforms expert authoring and post-hoc teaching. Process analysis links guidance to Student writing and package revision; a case study shows the Student testing and refining a proposed procedure for later reuse. As demand for new lessons falls, the cost of fixed-window review grows. Issue-Guided SSL tracks unresolved questions across Skill revisions to select and focus review, reaching 0.805 utility with 61.7% fewer Educator tokens and 16.9% fewer total acquisition tokens than Fixed-Window SSL on the main cohort.

items.title: LifeSearch: Benchmarking Deep Research Agents for Real-World Life and Productivity
items.content: arXiv:2610.18092v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Deep research (DR) agents address open-ended information needs through multi-step reasoning, long-horizon web search, and evidence synthesis. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on academic research or synthetic tasks, leaving DR agents' capabilities in real-world life and professional productivity settings insufficiently evaluated. To bridge this gap, we introduce LifeSearch, a challenging benchmark comprising 203 Chinese and English tasks derived from real-user query seeds across 7 concrete life and productivity domains. With more than 4,500 hours of human annotation, we construct over 4,000 expert-written, fine-grained rubrics, covering both report-content criteria for coverage and accuracy and concrete criteria specifying values, units, dates, and URLs. We conduct extensive experiments on 12 advanced DR agents under a unified evaluation harness, systematically analyzing their performance patterns and failure modes. We find that even the best-performing frontier agent, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves a score of only 63.4%, leaving substantial room for improvement on realistic life and professional DR tasks. We select the grading configuration by comparing candidate LLM judges against human rubric labels, and a human ranking study shows strong alignment between aggregate benchmark scores and human judgments (Spearman's $\rho = 0.89$, Kendall's $\tau = 0.81$). LifeSearch provides a rigorous evaluation framework and foundation for advancing DR agents toward real-world life and productivity.

items.title: Judges Follow the Reference: The Derivation Gap in Verifying Tool-Call Arguments
items.content: arXiv:2610.18497v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Tool-call judges evaluate argument values proposed by LLM agents. We find that they accept a correct value less often when their input holds no reference for it, that is, no text that says what the value should be. This happens when the value is a default value from the function schema that the user did not mention, when it has to be inferred, or when the text it comes from was cut from the judge input. We call this drop in acceptance the derivation gap. It appears across all seven judges we evaluate, including System One models CLM and Jev. The gap is not only a truncation artifact: correct default values have the largest gap on a benchmark with no truncation. A controlled source-relocation test shows that judges follow the reference in their input: they favor a visible incorrect value over a correct value whose source is hidden. We introduce DeRef (Derived Reference): a separate model reads the full history without seeing the candidate and writes a reference for the judge. Across three benchmarks, DeRef improves overall argument AUROC for all judges tested. On the controlled test, it raises AUROC from chance or below to between 98.40 and 99.59.

items.reasoning: A well-designed diagnostic study exposing a systematic blind spot in LLM-as-judge verification for agent tool calls, with controlled experiments and broad model coverage; findings are immediately actionable for anyone building agent verifiers, though the scope is narrow.

items.title: Can an Agent Learn to Predict Its Own Failure? Outcome-Grounded Confidence Calibration in LLM Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.18614v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Controlling an acting LLM agent means deciding, at each step of a long-horizon task, whether to trust its next action, abstain, or hand off to a human. That decision needs a per-step confidence signal predicting whether the current rollout will eventually succeed. The agent's own self-reported verbalized confidence is the natural candidate, but existing reinforcement learning methods calibrate it against the correctness of a decision at the current step. We propose a method to calibrate it against the eventual outcome of a multi-step episode: under GRPO, the group of rollouts for a task supplies success labels, and a proper scoring rule scores each step's confidence against the realized outcome. In offline RL on recorded trajectories of a Qwen2.5-7B agent in ALFWorld, TextWorld, and WebShop environments, the AUROC of step confidence against episode outcome rises from near chance to 0.68-0.85, and the top-10% of steps the agent is most confident about succeed ~4.3x more often than average. In online RL on the live ALFWorld agent, four calibration rewards improve early-step AUROC, expected calibration error goes from 0.42 to below 0.12, and selective execution improves over both the untrained agent and a format-only RL control, without degrading task success. We also introduce an evaluation protocol that separates episode depth, task difficulty, and attempt-level foresight, which shows where the gain lies: the trained agent recognizes from its first step which tasks it will fail, while telling a succeeding attempt from a failing one at the same task is harder, with some early-window signal emerging on TextWorld.

items.title: Pack Light, CarryOn: Building Object-Oriented Context for Long-Horizon Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.18784v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Long-horizon agents accumulate progress in persistent task state, yet repeatedly process interaction histories describing how that progress was achieved. This raises a natural question: can long-horizon context instead be organized around reusable progress rather than the history that produced it? In this paper, we introduce CarryOn, an object-oriented context runtime that organizes continuation around reusable task objects. Rather than treating compressed histories or reconstructed accounts of progress as the primary basis for continuation, CarryOn builds a context view from continuation carriers, complementary execution context, and a live tail of recent interactions. A core challenge is keeping this reusable basis valid after its surrounding history is retired: how can CarryOn update the basis without reconstructing the full representation at every fold? CarryOn maintains carrier records across folds, revising affected records against bound evidence and applicable environment checks while carrying forward unaffected records and jointly updating execution context. Experiments on OSWorld 2.0 and BrowseComp-Plus show improved gains of 5.8% and 7.0% while reducing total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9%, respectively. Project page: https://ethannju.github.io/carryon

items.reasoning: A timely contribution to agent memory and context management, an area of intense practical interest; the object-oriented framing is fresh, though the work appears to be a system design with limited theoretical grounding.
