items.content_html: arXiv:2610.16825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A release decision about a fine-tuned model is an operational commitment about the \emph{next} rerun of its training recipe. Yet standard benchmark reporting gives only the mean accuracy of past seeds. These target fundamentally different questions: release decisions depend on catastrophic tail risk, whereas standard evaluation reports only central tendency. Because fine-tuning induces bimodal mode collapse, high average accuracy frequently conceals severe failure rates. Auditing $2\,124$ fine-tuned models across eleven language models, we show that shipping models based on mean accuracy violates a $10\%$ deployment failure budget $48.0\%$ of the time. Common heuristics like $\bar b - 2\sigma$ prove equally dangerous: by underestimating variance on small samples, they become most permissive when evidence is weakest. We introduce \textbf{recipe cards}, an evaluation framework that directly certifies rerun tail failure rates using exact finite-sample binomial bounds. Recipe cards reduce held-out budget violations to $0.6\%$, enforce a mathematical sample floor ($N \ge 22$) that prevents certification on thin evidence, and explicitly refuse unverified claims under domain and task shifts.

items.title: Towards Universal Calibration for In-Context Classification
items.content: arXiv:2610.17096v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) has received a lot of interest recently due to its ability to improve classification accuracy for new tasks without having to fine-tune the model over these tasks. However, the impact of ICL on calibration has been far less studied. Recent work has shown that ICL can have a negative impact on calibration due to biased selection of in-context examples. The existing methods for improving ICL calibration require additional task and model-specific training, detracting from the no-fine-tuning convenience of ICL. In this work, we introduce CALIBFORMER, a universal ICL calibrator for classification tasks, that generalizes to new models and tasks without further fine-tuning on these tasks. Specifically, we design a transformer-based calibrator which uses the model predictions on in-context examples to predict a confidence score for the test input. We show that the calibrator trained on three models and ten tasks, is able to generalize/calibrate ICL predictions on several new tasks and four LLMs unseen during training. Even for frontier models like Gemini, CALIBFORMER is able to obtain over 50% reduction in calibration error.
items.author: Awik Dhar, Sunita Sarawagi, Arpit Agarwal
items.summary: CALIBFORMER is a transformer-based universal calibrator for in-context classification that generalizes to new models and tasks without task-specific fine-tuning, addressing calibration degradation caused by biased in-context example selection. This preserves the core no-fine-tuning convenience of ICL while improving reliability.
items.reasoning: Addresses an important, underexplored problem, calibration of in-context learning, with a genuinely generalizable approach rather than per-task training. Solid novelty in the LLM reliability space, though evaluation breadth across frontier-scale models will determine ultimate impact.

items.title: COMPASS: Membership Inference Attack Against Vision Large Language Models via Adaptive Noise Calibration
items.content: arXiv:2610.17332v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision large language models (VLLMs) are deployed in privacy-sensitive domains, raising training-data exposure concerns. Existing gray-box membership inference attacks (MIAs) commonly rely on entropy statistics or generated descriptions, requiring costly generation with limited membership separation. Perturbation-based methods instead measure response changes but focus on large perturbations, leaving VLLM membership behavior under smaller perturbations poorly understood. We systematically characterize VLLM membership behavior under controlled Gaussian perturbations across noise levels at fine resolution. We find that optimal perturbation magnitude and membership-signal direction vary across model-dataset pairs. In many settings, a previously unstudied low-noise regime yields stronger separation than large perturbations, with members exhibiting lower divergence than non-members, reversing the conventional score direction. Other settings retain the conventional direction, demonstrating that neither a fixed perturbation magnitude nor a predetermined score orientation is universally reliable. We propose COMPASS, an adaptive gray-box MIA that calibrates both the perturbation magnitude and membership-score direction using a loosely distribution-matched, known non-member reference set. We instantiate COMPASS using Renyi-normalized KL divergence and Renyi divergence, with max-k aggregation over the most informative image-logit positions. Across LLaVA v1.5-7B, MiniGPT-4, and HuluMed-32B, spanning pretraining, instruction-tuning, and medical-image datasets, COMPASS outperforms baselines. On general-domain data, COMPASS achieves AUCs up to 0.88. On the distribution-matched medical evaluation, it reaches 0.64 AUC, while the strongest baseline remains at chance level. These results establish full-range adaptive perturbation analysis as an effective approach to VLLM membership inference.

items.title: Structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics for partial differential equations
items.content: arXiv:2610.17483v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Machine learning surrogates of partial differential equations (PDEs) are commonly trained on data generated by numerical solvers. Therefore, the training data obey not the PDE but the modified equation of the numerical scheme, and the test loss, computed on data from the same solver, cannot distinguish a model that learned the physics from one that learned the discretization error. Here, we show that the difference is nevertheless visible in the trained model. We propose a suite of structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics, simple scores that measure whether a learned model respects one known property of the physics, such as a conserved quantity, a symmetry or a Hamiltonian structure, without access to the training data or the governing equation. Over five systems, the diagnostics track the error with respect to the true dynamics with a rank correlation of up to $0.94$, while the test loss is uncorrelated or anti-correlated with it. For the Burgers, Korteweg-de Vries and Navier-Stokes equations, the diagnostics separate numerical schemes that the test loss ranks as equivalent, including schemes of the same order. order.

This addresses a real evaluation blind spot in neural PDE surrogates.

items.title: Follow the Perturbed Leader for Linear Bandits: $\sqrt{T}$ Regret over General Convex Sets
items.content: arXiv:2610.17818v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We give the first adversarial linear bandit algorithm based on Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL) that achieves $\sqrt{T}$ regret over general convex action sets. Our algorithm attains $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^{5/4}\sqrt{T})$ regret using only linear optimization oracles, and the near-optimal $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{T})$ regret when an optimal-design exploration distribution is further available. This improves on the $T^{2/3}$ regret of the FTPL algorithm of Dani and Hayes (2006) for general convex sets, and generalizes the $\sqrt{T}$ regret of L\'evy et al. (2026) over two special action sets (hypercube and Euclidean ball). Compared to previous oracle-efficient linear bandit algorithms based on continuous exponential weights, the FTPL approach generally has better computational efficiency, and is much simpler to implement.   The key algorithmic element is a perturbation distribution that adapts to the estimated rewards. Its simplest form, an adaptive Gaussian perturbation, is straightforward to implement and already attains the regret bound above. We further extend it to two general constructions, random-weighting and elliptical perturbations, each covering distributions from light tails (Gaussian) to heavy tails (Student-$t_2$). On the technical side, we develop a systematic way to analyze the stability term in the FTPL regret through the Fisher information of the perturbation distribution. This builds a general framework for FTPL beyond existing ones such as the hazard rate and the FTRL-FTPL duality.

This improves the T^{2/3} regret of prior FTPL algorithms and generalizes recent results over special action sets. It is a clean theoretical advance in oracle-efficient bandit optimization.

items.title: Causal Discovery Under Hard Selection Bias: A New Robust Score-Matching Approach
items.content: arXiv:2610.18075v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Selection bias is a difficult yet widespread problem in causal discovery, occurring whenever non-random selection processes lead to data that is not representative of the underlying populations. Due to its practical importance, related works have been proposed to address the problem under local [Versteeg et al., 2022] or interventional settings [Dai et al., 2025a], but general algorithms for observational data remain elusive. In this paper, we focus on truncated data (hard selection), and provide a general result for Additive Noise Models (ANM). We show that score-based methods are a surprisingly suitable candidate due to a special property of the score function ($\nabla \log p(x)$): deterministic truncation preserves both the score of the joint distribution as well as the Jacobian of the score. While established score-matching algorithms still fail in most settings, we actively leverage this observation to propose a new method for causal discovery that is robust under truncated data with ANMs. Overall, our approach offers a general, robust solution that is agnostic to external information about the selection process and still achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art approaches when selection is not present.
items.author: Yiwen Qiu, Francesco Montagna, Shimeng Huang, Francesco Locatello
items.summary: This work provides a general method for causal discovery from truncated (hard-selected) observational data using Additive Noise Models, showing score-based methods are well-suited because deterministic truncation preserves key score function properties. This fills a gap where prior selection-bias results were limited to local or interventional settings.
items.reasoning: Selection bias is a genuine and widespread obstacle for causal discovery on observational data, and a general score-matching result is a meaningful theoretical contribution. Strong author team with causal representation learning expertise.

items.title: How Vision Transformers Represent Position: A Mechanistic Comparison of Absolute and Rotary Positional Encodings
items.content: arXiv:2610.13992v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Positional embeddings encode the spatial position of each image patch in a Vision Transformer (ViT), allowing the model to distinguish different spatial arrangements of visual content. However, we know little about how the choice of embedding shapes a vision transformer's internal representation. In this work, we show that Absolute Positional Embeddings (APE) and Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) encode spatial position through different internal mechanisms: APE stores position in explicit features, while RoPE builds it inside attention and rebuilds it when it is withheld. Specifically, in APE models, sparse autoencoders recover causal row- and column-specific features, whereas interventions on RoPE reveal distinct rotary components that separately encode row and column information. Additionally, causal interventions selectively disabling RoPE's row or column rotations show that decodable row and column information can be independently removed and, once rotations are restored, partly reconstructed, in part by axis-specialized attention heads. Both mechanisms are causally important for classification: permuting APE's positional features across patches reduces top-1 accuracy by 24--31 points, and ablating the rotations of RoPE's primary rebuilding head reduces it more than ablating those of any other head. Our findings show that the choice of positional encoding fundamentally changes how spatial information is organized and processed inside Vision Transformers. More broadly, our work demonstrates how mechanistic analysis can reveal how models construct, reconstruct, and maintain structured representations, providing a basis for targeted interventions in vision models.

items.title: KedgeFlow: A Programmable Control Plane for Enterprise AI Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.14810v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Enterprise AI agents can execute altered versions of approved actions, concurrently reuse the same permission, or retry operations whose responses were lost. These failures arise when approval and resource execution lack a shared contract. KedgeFlow specifies language-independent contracts for trusted controllers to authorize state-changing operations and privileged gateways to enforce that authority independently of agent reasoning. Inspired by OpenFlow, it connects policy checks supported by evidence, signed permission for an exact action, a shared allowance that can be consumed only once, target-side conditions for applying the change, and retained outcome records. Under trusted issuance of exact-action authority, two conditional properties establish at most one successful claim per allowance and link every governed dispatch to a matching grant, claim, and subsequent dispatch authorization, even when the agent is compromised. A reference implementation exposes this execution path to agent systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In the single-resource evaluation, 6,560 concurrent ledger claim attempts yielded exactly one successful claim for each of 82 allowances. Boundary tests rejected unauthorized and altered requests before consumption. A 32-call gateway race produced one committed mock effect, and a retry after a lost response produced no additional dispatch. Deliberately permissive policy nevertheless authorized an undesirable effect, exposing the limits of execution authorization. Evaluation uses three members of the etcd coordinated key-value store on one host, synthetic authentication and authorization inputs, and a mock target that rejects stale requests. Distributed reservations, enforcement of every production access route, native crash recovery, exactly-once effects at real targets, and interoperability between independent implementations remain untested.
items.author: Jun He, Deying Yu
items.summary: KedgeFlow proposes language-independent contracts separating trusted controllers that authorize state-changing operations from privileged gateways that enforce authority independently of agent reasoning, addressing failures like altered actions, permission reuse, and lost-response retries in enterprise AI agents. Inspired by OpenFlow, it ties evidence-backed policy checks, signed exact-action permissions, single-use allowances, and outcome records. Conditional correctness properties are proven under trusted issuance.

items.title: From Acoustic Sensing to Physical Actions: A Comprehensive Survey of Security Risks in Edge-Deployed Audio LLM-Based Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.15390v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) are embedded in agents for smart homes, vehicles, wearables, and embodied systems, where acoustic inputs can propagate from perception into persistent state and consequential execution. This setting extends security analysis beyond model behavior to the system conditions that determine how acoustic inputs can influence agent behavior and external actions. Existing surveys examine acoustic security, LLM-based agents, and edge deployment in isolation, leaving their security interactions in deployed Audio LLM-based agents insufficiently characterized. This survey introduces an Acoustic Sensing-to-Action (S2A) system model that traces these security implications along the path from acoustic sensing to external execution, while accounting for edge-cloud runtime and lifecycle transformation. We use the model to synthesize attacks, defenses, and evaluation methods across the acoustic, agent, and edge-system literature. The synthesis shows that security gaps can emerge within components and at the transitions between stages, where protections developed for one stage do not necessarily provide end-to-end assurance in the deployed system. These findings motivate security evaluation that follows acoustic influence from sensing to action across persistent state, system boundaries, and changing deployment conditions in real-world agents.

items.summary: A survey introducing an Acoustic Sensing-to-Action (S2A) system model that traces security risks in deployed audio-LLM agents from acoustic input through model behavior to persistent state and physical execution across smart homes, vehicles, wearables, and embodied systems. It unifies previously siloed literatures on acoustic security, LLM agents, and edge deployment.
items.reasoning: Fills a genuine gap by connecting acoustic attack surfaces to consequential physical actions in deployed audio agents, a safety-relevant and increasingly realistic scenario. As a survey it synthesizes rather than produces new results, but the framing is original.

items.title: Latent Taxonomies: How Property Induction Develops in Language Model Pre-training
items.content: arXiv:2610.15836v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: When told that robins have sesamoid bones, people are far more prone to extend the property to sparrows than to whales. This behavior, called category-based property induction, is well documented in humans, but whether and how it develops in language models trained only to predict the next token is unclear. To shed light on this, we construct a hierarchical taxonomy of synthetic entities grouped by the properties they share. We then inject facts from this latent taxonomy into the continued pre-training of Pythia and OLMo 2 models from 70M to 7B parameters, and track the development of inductive behaviors. We find that taxonomically aligned induction emerges from next-token prediction alone: a property learned for one entity transfers more strongly within its taxonomic category than across categories. Internally, entities that share a deeper category become more similar in activation space, and clustering recovers the full taxonomic tree from entity representations. Contrary to the usual expectation that scale helps, we find that induction weakens with model size when the data budget is fixed, suggesting that larger models memorize individual facts rather than compress them into shared structure. Induction also strengthens with more pre-training before the taxonomy injection, transfers to novel in-context properties, and can be overridden by a latent taxonomy implied by the prompt. Together, these results show that a model's inductive generalization reflects the latent organization of its training data, with implications for data curation and for predicting how far a learned fact will spread.
items.author: Jan Sobotka, Ekaterina Goliakova, Marcin Detyniecki, Antoine Bosselut, Xavier Renard

They find taxonomically aligned induction emerges, with properties learned for one entity transferring more to taxonomically close entities.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.15836v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When told that robins have sesamoid bones, people are far more prone to extend the property to sparrows than to whales. This behavior, called category-based property induction, is well documented in humans, but whether and how it develops in language models trained only to predict the next token is unclear. To shed light on this, we construct a hierarchical taxonomy of synthetic entities grouped by the properties they share. We then inject facts from this latent taxonomy into the continued pre-training of Pythia and OLMo 2 models from 70M to 7B parameters, and track the development of inductive behaviors. We find that taxonomically aligned induction emerges from next-token prediction alone: a property learned for one entity transfers more strongly within its taxonomic category than across categories. Internally, entities that share a deeper category become more similar in activation space, and clustering recovers the full taxonomic tree from entity representations. Contrary to the usual expectation that scale helps, we find that induction weakens with model size when the data budget is fixed, suggesting that larger models memorize individual facts rather than compress them into shared structure. Induction also strengthens with more pre-training before the taxonomy injection, transfers to novel in-context properties, and can be overridden by a latent taxonomy implied by the prompt. Together, these results show that a model's inductive generalization reflects the latent organization of its training data, with implications for data curation and for predicting how far a learned fact will spread.

items.title: CloneOT: predicting clone-specific perturbation responses with lineage-supervised neural inverse optimal transport
items.content: arXiv:2610.16093v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Predicting single-cell perturbation responses requires mapping between two unpaired populations of cells measured before and after the perturbation. Optimal transport (OT) provides a principled framework for constructing such mappings by minimizing the transport cost, and neural OT methods (\textit{e.g.}, CellOT) have been employed for this prediction task. However, these methods rely on a fixed transport cost, typically the squared Euclidean distance. This cost may connect cells with the wrong responses. Lineage tracing provides the information needed to learn the cost, as heritable barcodes link the cells of the same clone before and after the perturbation. Here, we propose \CloneOT, a neural inverse OT method that learns both the transport cost and the transport map from partially lineage-traced single-cell datasets. \CloneOT\ represents the cost as a neural network. It learns the cost by minimizing the extra cost that the lineage adds to the optimal transport, so that the cheapest transport keeps the cells of each clone together. Our experiments demonstrate that \CloneOT\ recovers the correct transport on 2D datasets, while the squared Euclidean cost fails. Moreover, \CloneOT\ outperforms five baselines on 14 lineage-tracing perturbation scenarios of cancer cells, for both seen and unseen clones. Furthermore, we show that \CloneOT\ reveals the clone-specific transcriptional programs of drug-tolerant persister cells and forecasts the fate of each clone from its cells before treatment. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/poseidonchan/CloneOT.

items.title: SSM-Attack: Learning Where to Perturb for Black-Box Face Privacy
items.content: arXiv:2610.17323v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Face recognition systems are deployed widely enough that a photograph shared online can be matched without its subject's consent. Generator-based protection methods rely on heavy pretrained backbones, multi-stage inference or visible semantic edits. We introduce SSM-Attack, a black-box face privacy framework built on Selective State Space Models. Rather than synthesizing the perturbation, the state-space model predicts in one linear-time pass a spatial allocation of the perturbation budget, marking which facial locations carry identity evidence; a short projected refinement then sets the values within this per-pixel budget. Against published benchmark results, SSM-Attack attains the highest average black-box attack success rate on all three evaluation sets: 87.10 percent on CelebA-HQ, 86.90 on LADN and 81.15 on FFHQ, the last from a network that never saw that dataset. The allocation network holds 5.73 million parameters, or 16.13 million with the frozen networks used by its quality terms. Under the same cap of 0.10 on the maximum per-pixel change, allocation improves structural similarity by 0.044, peak signal-to-noise ratio by 1.62 decibels and Frechet Inception Distance by 11.2 points over a uniform map while spending 37 percent of its capacity. Strong facial privacy protection therefore does not require a large generative prior; it requires knowing where to spend a small one.

It is notable both as an application of SSMs and for privacy-protection tooling against ubiquitous face recognition.

items.title: Learning Distributions from Samples and Qualities
items.content: arXiv:2610.17956v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study parameter estimation when each sample from a continuous parametric distribution is accompanied by a binary quality label governed by the same unknown parameter. By imposing hard feasibility constraints, deterministic labels can accelerate estimation from the classical $n^{-1/2}$ rate of smooth quality-aware M-estimators to $n^{-1}$. Combining PAC guarantees with local error-to-parameter conversions, we establish this rate for both identifiable and finitely ambiguous quality classifiers, with likelihood information resolving the latter ambiguity. When the quality model is known only up to an additive constant, we construct threshold-free pairwise preferences from oppositely labeled samples and retain the accelerated rate despite the unknown threshold. We further show that pointwise qualities and pairwise preferences are incomparable: either can be strictly more informative than the other. Our assumptions hold for Gaussian, Laplace, and exponential families under thresholded log-likelihood rewards. Finally, a minimax lower bound establishes the optimal $n^{-1}$ dependence on sample size, up to logarithmic and dimension-dependent factors, while experiments confirm the benefits of constraint-based estimation.

items.title: LADDER: A Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation Benchmark
items.content: arXiv:2610.18053v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: General-purpose robot manipulation policies learn short-horizon skills effectively, but degrade rapidly on long-horizon tasks. Existing benchmarks cannot isolate failures because task horizon is either too short or entangled with scene and object variations. We propose LADDER, a long-horizon robot manipulation benchmark scaling from 1 to 10 subgoals within the same environment over three suites (SimplerEnv-Long, RobotArena-$\infty$-Long, and RoboLab-Long), 145 tasks, eight categories, two embodiments, and 2,024 simulated episodes per system. We evaluate two orchestration paradigms: text subgoals for learned low-level policies (VoLo) and tool selection orchestration (CaP-X, GPT-Policy, PSP-Agent, TiPToP). Given the full instruction directly, low-level policies achieve 85.4% on single-subgoal tasks, but drop to near zero on extended tasks. While orchestration remedies this, it remains bounded by physical execution errors of the low-level policy rather than high-level planning and achieves only ~25%. Tool selection orchestration with GPT-Policy on GPT-6 Astra significantly outperforms learned-policy methods, but incurs significant time and cost budget and succeeds only ~62%. Real-world experiments across two embodiments confirm the collapse of the low-level policy and the gain from orchestration. Project website: https://ladder.insait.ai

items.title: Data Free Training of Diffusion Models for Lattice Field Theories
items.content: arXiv:2610.18863v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Sampling equilibrium field configurations remains a major computational bottleneck in lattice field theory, motivating the development of generative samplers that can produce independent configurations. Diffusion models are promising for this purpose, but their standard denoising score matching objective requires samples from the target distribution, seemingly reintroducing the original sampling problem. Here, we show that diffusion models can instead be trained from their own generated samples using the target score identity, provided access to the unnormalized probability density. Importance-weighted formulations of this identity yield a consistent target throughout training, while unweighted variants define a self-consistent fixed-point training scheme. We benchmark the different approaches in two-dimensional \(\phi^4\) theory and identify effective choices that enable efficient training and sampling across the symmetric, critical, and broken phases. Ultimately, our data-free training approach achieves comparable performance to training on HMC reference data.
items.author: Dennis Grinwald, Ankur Singha, Khaled Kahouli, Karl Jansen, Shinichi Nakajima
items.summary: The authors show that diffusion models for sampling lattice field theory configurations can be trained without target samples by exploiting the target score identity with the unnormalized density, using importance-weighted or self-consistent fixed-point variants. This removes the circular dependency that normally reintroduces the sampling bottleneck.
items.reasoning: A technically clever resolution to a fundamental circularity in applying diffusion models to scientific sampling, with potential to accelerate lattice computations; niche application area but methodologically significant.

items.title: FidelityQ: Preserving Predictive Fidelity in Ultra-Low-Bit Language Model Quantization
items.content: arXiv:2610.14934v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Ultra-low-bit scalar quantization offers a regular arithmetic structure for efficient deployment of large language models, but preserving predictive behavior at extreme precision remains challenging: with only a few reconstruction levels, accurate weight representation must translate into consistent predictions from a small calibration set. We propose FidelityQ, a scalar quantization framework that preserves predictive fidelity at weight precisions down to 2 bits. For accurate quantization, we introduce Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC), which shapes each weight row toward a centered symmetric source via randomized Hadamard mixing and fits a mirrored four-level minimum-distortion quantizer to its empirical weights. Every level set in this family decomposes exactly into two sign-valued bases with associated scales, combining source-adaptive reconstruction with lookup-free decoding compatible with scaled integer arithmetic. Our analysis further shows that residual predictive discrepancies are heavy-tailed and concentrate on tokens the teacher predicts confidently, motivating Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC) for consistent quantization. KIC ranks sequences by the tail of token-wise teacher-student divergence, allocates a limited calibration budget to the highest-scoring samples, and restores predictive agreement by updating only quantization levels and scales under teacher supervision, keeping pretrained weights frozen. Experiments on the LLaMA and Qwen families demonstrate the effectiveness of FidelityQ in weight-only and joint quantization settings. On LLaMA-2-7B, FidelityQ achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 6.62 at W2A16 and improves the prior state-of-the-art W2A4KV4 result from 8.31 to 6.96, while reducing linear-layer weight memory by 8.0x relative to FP16.

It addresses the practical deployment challenge of extreme compression with regular arithmetic structure.

items.title: Do LLM Tutors Actually Teach? A Process-Centered Synthesis of the Tutoring Loop
items.content: arXiv:2610.15692v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models can produce fluent tu- toring dialogue, but whether they actually help students learn remains unclear. We present a process-centered synthesis of LLM tutoring that follows the path from learner-state infer- ence to pedagogical action, tutor training, eval- uation, and student simulation. This view ex- poses a central gap: implementing a tutoring component does not establish that it works or that its outputs meaningfully affect later stages. A structured study-level audit shows that peda- gogical evaluation is common, while evidence becomes much thinner for learner-conditioned intervention, human learning gains, and espe- cially transfer or delayed retention. Human studies nevertheless provide a conditional posi- tive result: LLM tutors can improve learning, but benefits depend on pedagogical structure, learner engagement, and how learning is mea- sured. We argue that progress requires validat- ing the interfaces between tutoring stages, not only improving individual components.

The audit finds strong evidence for pedagogical evaluation but thin evidence for learner-conditioned intervention, human learning gains, and especially transfer or delayed retention.

items.title: PAIR: Memory-Efficient and Fast Inference with Reading--Reasoning Fusion
items.content: arXiv:2610.16003v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: For context-based question answering, using one large model for both evidence extraction and answer reasoning requires substantial memory and computation. Existing approaches trade accuracy for efficiency within a single model only. We propose a multi-model approach for efficient inference: our method, PAIR, employs two differently sized models for evidence extraction and answer reasoning, respectively. A smaller Reader model processes and retains the full context, while a larger Reasoner model sees only the question and generated sequence without directly attending to the context. These capabilities are fused at the logit level: at each token, both Reader and Reasoner produce a prediction, and their logits are combined into one, behaving as a single next-token-prediction model. Fine-tuning further boosts their performance. On HotpotQA, PAIR with a 32B Reasoner retains 96% of that same 32B model's full-context accuracy while using roughly one quarter of its KV memory. At 45.7K-token contexts, PAIR achieves up to 3.2$\times$ higher end-to-end throughput than the full-context 32B model on the same GPU. PAIR also improves the accuracy-memory and accuracy-throughput trade-offs over evaluated token-reduction baselines. Its accuracy-preserving behavior generalizes across Qwen2.5, OLMo-3, and Gemma-3 model families.

This reduces memory and computation compared to running one large model over the context.

items.title: SpecGuardBench: Can Coding Agents Construct Reliable Validation Harnesses from Natural Language Specifications?
items.content: arXiv:2610.16870v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As coding agents become more capable, tests remain the primary evidence for judging whether their code is correct. Yet passing available tests does not establish that an implementation satisfies its natural language specification. Reliable validation requires checks that faithfully capture the specification and scenarios that thoroughly exercise the code, but current benchmarks provide limited insight into whether agents can construct such evidence themselves. We introduce SpecGuardBench, a benchmark of 291 tasks from 13 real-world repositories, covering 8 types of verification logic such as functional postconditions and interaction protocols. Given a natural language specification, repository context, and a reference implementation, an agent constructs a validation harness comprising executable checks and test scenarios. The checks should reject implementations that violate the specification while accepting those that satisfy it, and the scenarios should thoroughly exercise the code. Across four proprietary and open-weight coding agents, none constructs a harness scored as faithful on the benchmark's implementations for more than 63% of the tasks. The bottleneck lies less in exploring test scenarios than in constructing checks that faithfully reflect the specification. Specifically, the agents show a clear tendency to write checks that mirror the reference implementation rather than the specification, and therefore reject implementations that the specification permits.
items.author: Zhiqing Zhong, Mingyu Chen, Aoyang Fang, Yuzhong Zhang, Haoye Tian, Lionel Briand, Boxi Yu, Pinjia He
items.summary: SpecGuardBench tests whether coding agents can construct reliable validation harnesses that faithfully capture natural language specifications, using 291 tasks from 13 real-world repositories covering eight types of verification logic such as functional postconditions and interaction protocols. It goes beyond whether agent code passes available tests to whether agents can generate their own trustworthy evidence. This targets a key trust question for autonomous coding.
items.reasoning: A well-motivated benchmark addressing verification of agent-generated code, from a credible software engineering group; the focus on constructing validation evidence is novel and practically important. Real-world impact depends on adoption, and abstract lacks headline results.

It goes beyond whether agent code passes available tests to whether agents can generate their own trustworthy evidence. This targets a key trust question for autonomous coding.
items.content_html: arXiv:2610.16870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As coding agents become more capable, tests remain the primary evidence for judging whether their code is correct. Yet passing available tests does not establish that an implementation satisfies its natural language specification. Reliable validation requires checks that faithfully capture the specification and scenarios that thoroughly exercise the code, but current benchmarks provide limited insight into whether agents can construct such evidence themselves. We introduce SpecGuardBench, a benchmark of 291 tasks from 13 real-world repositories, covering 8 types of verification logic such as functional postconditions and interaction protocols. Given a natural language specification, repository context, and a reference implementation, an agent constructs a validation harness comprising executable checks and test scenarios. The checks should reject implementations that violate the specification while accepting those that satisfy it, and the scenarios should thoroughly exercise the code. Across four proprietary and open-weight coding agents, none constructs a harness scored as faithful on the benchmark's implementations for more than 63% of the tasks. The bottleneck lies less in exploring test scenarios than in constructing checks that faithfully reflect the specification. Specifically, the agents show a clear tendency to write checks that mirror the reference implementation rather than the specification, and therefore reject implementations that the specification permits.

items.title: Machine--human agreement in marking undergraduate assignments is specific to model, prompt and institution
items.content: arXiv:2610.18019v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) promise to automate one of higher education's most resource-intensive activities: assessing student writing. Existing evaluations are typically limited to a single model, a single prompt and a single institution. Using 761 undergraduate psychology assignments from three UK universities, we evaluated three frontier LLMs, individually and in ensemble, on accuracy, prompt sensitivity, error independence, generalisability and evidential basis. Agreement between human and machine marks varied widely, with no model or prompt optimal across institutions. All models compressed marks towards a common central tendency, overvaluing the weakest assignments and undervaluing the strongest. Because this error was shared, ensembling failed to remove it. Machine marks also rewarded linguistic features more strongly than human marks. Since human-machine agreement was a joint product of model, prompt and institution, we conclude that current LLMs lack evaluative capacity transferable across contexts, and that single-context validation overstates readiness for deployment.

items.title: Estimating Surprisal from the Speech Signal
items.content: arXiv:2610.18439v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Although language is predominantly spoken, empirical tests of surprisal theory rely almost entirely on written text. In practice, surprisal is estimated using language models (LMs) trained on text and applied to transcriptions, creating a text bottleneck that limits evaluation of the theory in the spoken modality. We remove this bottleneck by estimating surprisal directly from the speech signal using a speech LM. This raises a key question: should surprisal be defined over realization-specific acoustic inputs or over abstract linguistic units? Since a single unit can have many distinct acoustic realizations, each assigned a different probability by the model, defining surprisal over abstract units is difficult. To address this, we introduce an importance sampling estimator that approximates the probability of an abstract unit by marginalizing over realizations generated by a text-to-speech model. Using pupillometry data from a listening study, we evaluate surprisal theory in this text-free setting at multiple levels of granularity. Obtaining surprisal from several speech LMs, we consistently find that surprisal estimated via importance sampling better predicts pupil dilation than realization-specific surprisal for words. We also find that surprisal values for sub-lexical units are predictive of pupil dilation. While we find that surprisal can be estimated without recourse to text, and that marginalizing over distinct realizations of words is more predictive of lexical processing effort, surprisal as a whole is not a strong predictor of change in pupil size, regardless of its source.

This enables empirical tests of surprisal theory in the spoken modality, where language predominantly lives.

items.title: Re-executing Coding-Agent Evaluations: Unchanged Decisions and Unresolved Policy Risk
items.content: arXiv:2610.14460v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Executable tests grade large language model (LLM) coding-agent patches for leaderboards, rewards and self-improvement. Two preregistered re-execution studies returned negative results. SWE-bench Pro v1's offline option rejected none of 59 accepted Go patches whose grading configuration changed. Their exploratory, unweighted upper confidence limit is 4.95% under candidate independence, leaving a 3% exposed-patch risk unresolved; the preregistered estimator uses inverse sampling-probability weights. An extension was inconclusive. In a selected stratum, a reconstructed module cache built from the reference solution's dependencies rejected accepted alternatives from four models that passed with their own dependencies. Re-executing 1,929 selected agent-version/task evaluations from the Darwin G\"odel Machine's archive preserved best-agent selection and system-variant ranking, with search history and scores of evaluations not rerun fixed. Exploratory host, image and adapted-grader comparisons also preserved them. Seven of 23 disagreements with archived verdicts did not recur on a second host; rebuilt images changed 16 three-run majority verdicts (0.83%) under four-CPU execution. We provide an evidence-to-claim summary, lessons for grader audits and an anonymous replication package. These results concern accepted patches and fixed-history decisions; general policy safety and adaptive-learning robustness require broader evaluations.

items.title: Thinking with Images without Coordinates
items.content: arXiv:2610.14265v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent advances in multi-modal large language models have shifted toward the "thinking with images" paradigm to improve reasoning faithfulness, yet existing methods rely heavily on explicit coordinate- based grounding. We identify two fundamental limitations in this approach, i.e., a semantic gap where sparse regressions miss high-dimensional latent structures, and a resolution gap due to the granularity mismatch between patch-level tokens and pixel-level coordinates. To address these, we propose TiCO (Thinking with images without COordinates). It reformulates visual reasoning as a semantic evidence discovery process within the latent space, and evidence is injected as token-level regions without pixel coordinates. Specifically, TiCO utilizes a dedicated probe token to estimate similarity distributions and performs importance sampling over spatially connected components to generate diverse, semantically dominant evidence rollouts. Extensive experiments across multiple high-resolution and general visual reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our TiCO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art coordinate-based methods with significantly improved inference efficiency.

items.title: TAG: Calibrating SAM3 for Universal Image Segmentation without Dense Supervision
items.content: arXiv:2610.14651v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The recent Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3) extends powerful promptable segmentation from spatial cues to concepts, raising the prospect of a single foundation model for universal image segmentation. However, this promise often fails to translate into reliable performance on downstream segmentation tasks. In this work, we empirically identify concept recognition, rather than mask quality, as the primary bottleneck: SAM3 accurately delineates the objects it recognizes yet struggles to robustly determine which concepts are present. Driven by this, we present \textit{\underline{T}ext \underline{A}nchor re-\underline{G}rounding (\TAG{})}, a simple yet effective framework that rectifies the concept recognition of SAM3 on the target domain without dense annotations. Specifically, \TAG{} introduces an \textit{Anchor Residual Pathway} comprising image-conditioned, low-rank adapters to re-ground text anchors in the target distribution and modulate subsequent text-conditioned interactions. Guided solely by image-level category labels, \TAG{} jointly optimizes binary cross-entropy with \textit{Soft Boundary Ranking} objectives to calibrate presence confidence and distinguish present concepts from confusable negatives. Building upon this, we devise \textit{Confidence-Weighted Distillation} to couple rich semantic context of a multimodal large language model with fine-grained spatial priors of SAM3, thereby achieving effective calibration in the absence of manual annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that \TAG{} unlocks SAM3's segmentation potential with only 3.1M trainable parameters, achieving impressive performance across diverse scenarios, and notably, even surpassing leading mask-supervised methods on several metrics. \href{https://github.com/MiSsU-HH/TAG_SAM3}{Our code will be publicly available at GitHub \faGithub}.

items.title: SPARE: Shared Perception and Adaptive Retrieval of Evidence for Streaming Video Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2610.14671v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Streaming video understanding requires answering questions from the observed video, with evidence drawn from recent observations or earlier events. Historical context can improve recall but may interfere with judgments based on recent frames. Its usefulness depends on both when it is introduced and which clips are selected, while relevance alone does not guarantee sufficient evidence for an answer. We propose SPARE, a framework that combines adaptive historical retrieval with visual encoder sharing. A lightweight gate predicts whether recent observations provide sufficient evidence to answer the question. When additional evidence is predicted to be necessary, a multimodal embedding model retrieves relevant historical clips to supplement the current context. LoRA instruction tuning trains the understanding model to use recent observations and retrieved history jointly and abstain when the evidence remains insufficient. To reduce redundant visual parameters, the understanding and retrieval branches share a visual encoder while retaining separate language backbones. Four linear adapters align the shared features with the retrieval model through distillation at the visual token and final retrieval embedding levels. With visual-only inputs, SPARE achieves 77.78% on the evaluated Real-time and Backward task groups of OVO-Bench and 73.31% on StreamingBench. Compared with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluated at 2 fps, SPARE improves accuracy by 20.68 percentage points on OVO-Bench and 14.15 percentage points on StreamingBench.

items.title: MORE: Learning Motion-Oriented Registers for Driving World Models and Planning
items.content: arXiv:2610.14871v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: By predicting future states, latent world models provide rich self-supervision for end-to-end driving, but often inherit dense features from pretrained visual encoders as their world-state interface. This creates a mismatch: visual pretraining produces information-rich, spatially dense features, but their adaptation for motion-conditioned world modeling and planning is deferred to downstream training. The dense grid also makes future prediction more computationally expensive as visual resolution increases. We therefore argue that video pretraining should directly learn state representations suited to downstream world modeling and planning, rather than relying on downstream training to adapt inherited visual features. We propose ***MORE***, a V-JEPA framework that learns **M**otion-**O**riented **RE**gisters during video pretraining as a shared state interface for driving world models and planning. MORE injects temporally aligned ego motion into a small set of registers and uses them as the sole context for masked patch prediction, channeling dense patch-level supervision through a compact state bottleneck. A complementary blockwise register-masking objective further shapes predictive structure in the register space. During downstream training, the same register space defines the future states predicted by the world model and provides shared scene memory for trajectory generation and scoring. On NAVSIM-v2, MORE outperforms the state of the art by 1.6 in EPDMS, while achieving superior efficiency with only 1/10 the inference latency of DriveLaW. These results support learning the state interface for world modeling and planning directly during video pretraining.

Strong relevance to a competitive industrial research direction, though the abstract does not reveal decisive benchmark wins.

items.title: Semantic Saliency from Multi-Modal Large Language Model Scene Understanding Maps
items.content: arXiv:2610.15467v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Image-computable low-level image saliency has shaped perceptual psychology and computer science, but is limited by its inability to capture human high-level cognitive factors that influence attention and eye movements. Here, we propose a new fully automated method to compute semantic saliency by quantifying each object's contribution to scene comprehension without fitting any parameters to human data: the Automated Scene Understanding Map (AUTO-SUM). AUTO-SUM automatically segments and removes individual objects from a scene, uses multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to describe the original and modified scenes, and measures the semantic similarity between these descriptions using text embeddings. We show that AUTO-SUM can predict which object is most important in a human-measured scene understanding map (H-SUM) estimated using human scene descriptions. We also show that AUTO-SUM can predict the object most fixated by human observers during free viewing and scene description tasks better than a low-level saliency model (GBVS, Itti-Koch), a saliency model trained based on human meaning ratings (Meaning Map), and comparable to DeepGaze, which is trained on human fixation data. We contend that AUTO-SUM can be used as a semantic saliency model that complements lower-level saliency models. Code are available at https://github.com/starsky77/AUTO-SUM-Source-Code .

It predicts which objects draw human attention beyond what low-level saliency models capture.

items.title: SlotAVS: Object-Centric Audio-Visual Segmentation via Bi-Modal Slot Attention
items.content: arXiv:2610.15764v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Audio-Visual Segmentation (AVS) requires predicting pixel-wise masks of sounding objects by grounding acoustic signals in visual space. In multi-source scenes, concurrent sound sources often remain entangled within shared visual representations, leading to merged masks or unstable specialization when using standard alignment-focused transformer architectures. To address this, we present SlotAVS, an object-centric framework driven by competitive bi-modal slot attention. While robust foundation models provide rich semantic priors, SlotAVS shifts the paradigm from global cross-modal fusion to explicit competitive binding. By initializing discrete object slots from temporal audio sequences and enforcing strict slot-wise competition over spatial visual tokens, our method structurally mitigates the blending of distinct acoustic entities. Further, to stabilize instance-level learning, we introduce a Hungarian matching strategy that optimally aligns slots with ground-truth objects using spatial and boundary overlap. Coupled with a numerically stable, confidence-aware mask fusion mechanism, SlotAVS robustly aggregates multi-source predictions. Extensive experiments on the AVSBench dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, achieving 88.6% mIoU on the Single-Source (S4) split and 71.7% mIoU on the Multi-Source (MS3) split. These results show that explicit competitive binding is critical for complex audio-visual scene understanding and effectively leveraging foundation-model priors without relying solely on their capacity.
items.author: Arnav Sharma, Anand Mishra, Renu Rameshan
items.summary: SlotAVS tackles audio-visual segmentation of multiple sounding objects using competitive bi-modal slot attention, shifting from global cross-modal fusion to explicit competitive binding of sound sources to object slots. Slots are initialized from temporal audio sequences and compete over spatial locations, reducing merged masks and unstable specialization in multi-source scenes.
items.reasoning: Object-centric slot attention applied to audio-visual segmentation is a sensible and relatively novel combination, addressing a real failure mode of transformer alignment approaches. Moderate impact given the task's niche but growing relevance.

Slots are initialized from temporal audio sequences and compete over spatial locations, reducing merged masks and unstable specialization in multi-source scenes.
items.content_html: arXiv:2610.15764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Audio-Visual Segmentation (AVS) requires predicting pixel-wise masks of sounding objects by grounding acoustic signals in visual space. In multi-source scenes, concurrent sound sources often remain entangled within shared visual representations, leading to merged masks or unstable specialization when using standard alignment-focused transformer architectures. To address this, we present SlotAVS, an object-centric framework driven by competitive bi-modal slot attention. While robust foundation models provide rich semantic priors, SlotAVS shifts the paradigm from global cross-modal fusion to explicit competitive binding. By initializing discrete object slots from temporal audio sequences and enforcing strict slot-wise competition over spatial visual tokens, our method structurally mitigates the blending of distinct acoustic entities. Further, to stabilize instance-level learning, we introduce a Hungarian matching strategy that optimally aligns slots with ground-truth objects using spatial and boundary overlap. Coupled with a numerically stable, confidence-aware mask fusion mechanism, SlotAVS robustly aggregates multi-source predictions. Extensive experiments on the AVSBench dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, achieving 88.6% mIoU on the Single-Source (S4) split and 71.7% mIoU on the Multi-Source (MS3) split. These results show that explicit competitive binding is critical for complex audio-visual scene understanding and effectively leveraging foundation-model priors without relying solely on their capacity.

items.title: Not All Challenges Are Equal: Evaluating Interactive Liveness Detection Against Real-Time Face Swaps
items.content: arXiv:2610.16417v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Remote identity verification assumes that a camera stream shows a live person, yet public real-time face-swap tools can replace that person before the stream reaches the verifier. Passive deepfake detectors generalize poorly to new generators, while interactive challenges are often selected without evidence of which gestures expose current attacks. We evaluate randomized gesture challenges in 108 live sessions with six subjects, 24 impersonated identities, and two face-swap tools, DeepFaceLive and FaceFusion, injected through a virtual camera. The static calibration segment reaches a session-level AUC of 0.878 with a frozen UCF spatial detector, while the mean across the active-gesture windows reaches 0.988. Pose and combined gestures have the highest point estimates, whereas expressions show no clear improvement. Hand occlusion against FaceFusion, configured with an occlusion mask, scores below the static baseline. The end-to-end time required to satisfy the validator also distinguishes attacks from genuine sessions, achieving a session-level AUC of 0.732, although this signal includes synthesis and transport delays. These results show that challenge sets should be tested against current attack configurations and that response time can provide an additional, deployment-specific signal.

items.title: EvoSpatial: Experience-Driven Skill and Tool Evolution for Spatial Reasoning Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.16679v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Tool-augmented vision-language agents compose perception and measurement to reason about spatial relationships, but effective execution also requires tracking geometric assumptions and checking intermediate evidence. Preserving this experience across tasks requires retaining procedural knowledge together with the computations it governs. We introduce EvoSpatial, an experience-driven framework that evolves a library of linked skills and tools. Our key insight is that successful and failed spatial trajectories reveal both how to compute and when to trust the result. EvoSpatial retrieves skills, reuses tools, and synthesizes reusable computational functions (generated helpers) during reasoning. After answer submission, supervised outcome feedback guides skill refinement and tool consolidation for subsequent tasks. Across 20 benchmarks, EvoSpatial attains the highest average score among the compared spatial agents, exceeding SpatialClaw by 4.0 percentage points. Further experiments show cross-benchmark transfer and improved reasoning through skill-guided distillation without external skills at evaluation. These results support accumulating spatial experience for both inference-time reuse and trajectory-based training.

items.title: X-Ragent: Tool-Augmented Reinforcement Learning for Evidence-Grounded Chest X-Ray Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.16811v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation often requires integrating visual findings with task-specific evidence rather than relying on direct visual recognition alone. While tool-augmented medical agents can supply such evidence via external modules, they often lack explicit mechanisms for learning when auxiliary evidence is needed and for preventing inapplicable quantitative evidence from entering diagnostic reasoning. To address this, we propose X-Ragent, a post-training framework for tool-augmented reinforcement learning that decouples learned auxiliary-evidence seeking from validity-gated quantitative measurement acquisition for evidence-grounded CXR reasoning. We construct Rad-CoT, a 7.7K-sample corpus combining causally ordered tool-augmented trajectories with report-style diagnostic reasoning, and use it to initialize Qwen3-VL-8B via agentic supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We then optimize the policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using an accuracy-gated reward that applies process-level terms for measurement consistency and auxiliary-tool cost only to correct trajectories, preventing plausible process behavior from compensating for an incorrect diagnosis. Across three CXR benchmarks, X-Ragent achieves the strongest results, including an 8.6-point improvement on the fully held-out ChestAgentBench. By seeking evidence selectively and admitting only valid measurements, X-Ragent supports more faithful and evidence-grounded CXR reasoning.

items.title: When Left Is Right? Camera-Motion Understanding beyond Screen
items.content: arXiv:2610.17242v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Can a vision-language model tell left from right? Modern VLMs solve visual puzzles and follow hour-long videos, yet when asked whether the camera moved left or right, most do no better than a coin flip. Adding camera-motion data or geometric representations has been tried, separately, and neither closes the gap. We argue that camera-motion understanding needs two conditions at once: the representation must couple off-screen camera motion with on-screen flow dynamics, and it must be interpreted by the language model rather than trained as a standalone pose or depth estimator. We propose CameraVLM, which pairs a motion-state representation with state-language alignment. Camera tokens capture how the camera moves off screen, flow tokens capture how the subject and background move on screen, and a two-stage training strategy keeps language in the loop so that both are learned together with camera-motion semantics. With only 9B parameters, CameraVLM outperforms all open-source and camera-motion-specific models by a wide margin across three benchmarks and more than 20 baselines, and matches or surpasses GPT-6 Astra as well as human viewers in a 48-participant study. Project page: https://3dagentworld.github.io/CameraVLM/
items.author: Chong Cheng, Ran Zhang, Xinyuan Li, Alan Zhao, Hao Wang, Xi Wang
items.summary: The paper shows that modern VLMs perform near chance on questions about camera motion direction (e.g., did the camera move left or right), and argues that solving this requires jointly coupling off-screen camera motion with on-screen flow dynamics and interpreting that representation through language rather than training a standalone pose estimator. CameraVLM pairs a motion-state representation with state-language alignment to close this gap.
items.reasoning: Identifies a genuine, underappreciated blind spot in VLM spatial reasoning with a clear diagnosis and targeted fix; valuable for video understanding and embodied applications, though the scope is a narrow capability.

items.title: SWORD: Scene-Grounded Wasserstein Object-Relation Distance for 3D Scene Graph Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2610.17692v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: 3D scene graph prediction is commonly optimized with object-node and relation-edge classification losses. These objectives encourage exact object and relation label recovery, but they do not directly optimize semantic proximity to the ground-truth scene graph: two wrong graphs can receive comparable penalties even when one is much closer in object roles and relation contexts. A direct graph-distance loss is difficult in general, since graph matching and graph edit distance require correspondence search and edit-cost design. Our key observation is that prior supervised 3D scene graph prediction protocols are conducted on fixed object-node indices and supervised edge slots. This can turn a scene graph comparison into a well-defined aligned graph-distance problem. To this end, we propose SWORD, a Scene-Grounded Wasserstein Object-Relation Distance that builds block-normalized object and relation ground distance metrics from training scene graph annotations through a deterministic base-to-context order, without external semantic priors. SWORD lifts these metrics to Wasserstein distances over aligned node and null-augmented edge marginals, providing semantic graph-distance supervision beyond exact-label penalties while preserving the ground-truth graph as the unique zero-distance solution in aligned marginal probability space. We prove that SWORD is a strict metric on aligned marginal probabilistic scene graphs, preserves scene-graph-grounded substitution ordering, controls additive graph-grounded semantic observables, and yields a surrogate upper-bounding decoded semantic error.

items.title: COMPASS: Contextual Moment Prior Alignment for Generalizable AIGI Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.18034v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generalizable AI-generated image (AIGI) and deepfake detection remain challenging due to the asymmetry phenomenon, where adaptation to limited training distributions can degrade the transferable representations of Vision Foundation Models (VFMs). Recent subspace adaptation methods mitigate this issue by freezing high-magnitude principal components while adapting the residual subspace. However, such magnitude-based decomposition is data-agnostic and does not explicitly account for target-relevant semantics, potentially leading to semantic misalignment. We propose COMPASS (COntextual Moment Prior Alignment for Subspace Separation), a data-aware subspace adaptation framework that uses a small unlabeled Semantic Proxy Set to estimate target activation statistics. COMPASS incorporates activation covariance into the decomposition of pre-trained weights, preserving target-relevant representations as a stable semantic reference while the residual adapter learns forgery-related variations. The proxy calibration requires no gradient-based optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong generalization across cross-dataset, cross-method, joint cross-dataset-method, and open-world cross-generator evaluations, achieving state-of-the-art performance on both Deepfake and AIGI detection benchmarks.

items.title: Closing the Estimation Gap: Training-Free Transductive Inference for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Action Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2610.18209v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Cross-domain few-shot action recognition (CD-FSAR) aims to recognise unseen action classes in a target domain from a handful of labelled videos. Despite advances in representation learning, CD-FSAR inference still relies on prototypes estimated from extremely limited support examples. To assess this bottleneck, we perform an oracle analysis with the representation fixed. Constructing oracle prototypes and decision boundaries from ground-truth query labels improves 5-way 1-shot accuracy by 7--20 percentage points across five target datasets. This reveals a substantial estimation gap: the representation contains useful discriminative information, but prototypes and boundaries estimated from scarce supports fail to capture each episode's true class structure. Motivated by this, we propose TRACE, a training-free transductive inference framework that improves episode-level estimation without modifying the backbone. TRACE comprises two complementary stages. Confidence-Thresholded Transductive Prototype Refinement (CTPR) refines support-based prototypes using confidently predicted queries. The refined prototypes initialise a lightweight per-episode classifier, which Transductive Classifier Refinement (TCR) further adapts by encouraging confident, class-balanced predictions over all queries. Together, the two stages improve prototype and boundary estimation, enabling better use of information in the unlabelled queries. Across five target datasets (HMDB51, UCF101, SSv2, Diving48, and RareAct) in both 1-shot and 5-shot settings, TRACE consistently improves a strong CD-FSAR baseline, including gains of more than six percentage points on HMDB51 1-shot, while recovering much of the oracle-estimated gap. These results suggest that improving test-time estimation is a powerful, broadly applicable complement to representation learning for CD-FSAR under extreme support scarcity.

items.title: VideoJev: System One Model for Video Understanding and Interaction
items.content: arXiv:2610.18615v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Visual agents must turn video observations into timely decisions to track progress and choose what to do next. Building on the emerging System One paradigm, we introduce VideoJev, a family of models that cast video understanding and interaction as structured decision tasks. We adapt pretrained multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by replacing autoregressive answer decoding with a shared head that scores temporal intervals and textual options against video evidence. These scores yield event spans or answer choices, unifying temporal grounding and multiple-choice video question answering. This combines the semantic flexibility of MLLMs with efficient decisions that agents can use directly. As an interaction unfolds, new goals and intermediate results prompt further queries about the same visual history. VideoJev therefore reuses visual computation through Cached inference for queries as they arrive and Joint inference for multiple queries in a single forward pass. Across three temporal grounding benchmarks, VideoJev-4B and VideoJev-35B-A3B improve mean mIoU over their backbones by 6.7 and 10.8 points, respectively, with measured inference speedups of $2.8$-$3.1\times$. On four video QA benchmarks, both achieve performance comparable to their backbones in Thinking mode, with measured inference speedups exceeding $100\times$. These results offer a unified, reusable decision interface for composing structured visual judgments into complex, open-ended workflows.

items.title: RootSLAM: Square Root Bundle Adjustment for Visual-Inertial SLAM
items.content: arXiv:2610.15157v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Efficient perception is a prerequisite for the small, low-power devices targeted by robotics, mixed reality, autonomous driving, and drone applications, all of which rely on Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) to estimate their motion within their surroundings. Learning-based SLAM systems achieve state-of-the-art accuracy but are demanding in compute, whereas classical geometry-based methods retain a strong efficiency advantage with little to no loss in accuracy. In this work we present RootSLAM, a fully-featured visual-inertial SLAM system for multi-camera setups built on Basalt. RootSLAM achieves accuracy competitive with the state of the art while running up to 20 times faster, facilitating the deployment of perception systems in resource constrained environments. We adapt the square-root bundle adjustment formulation from structure from motion into the multi-camera visual-inertial SLAM setting through a novel reformulation that leverages the system's pose-graph, letting the global optimizer run in single-precision floating point, thus doubling its performance. We provide a thorough benchmark against the state of the art together with an ablation study of our contributions. Our new implementation, including its map management and loop detection module, pose-graph optimizer, and global mapping components, will be open-sourced.
items.author: Tom\'as Santucci, Mateo de Mayo, Daniel Cremers, Taih\'u Pire
items.summary: RootSLAM is a fully-featured multi-camera visual-inertial SLAM system built on Basalt that achieves accuracy competitive with learning-based state of the art while running up to 20 times faster. It demonstrates that classical geometry-based methods retain a decisive efficiency advantage for low-power devices in robotics, mixed reality, and drones. The strong efficiency-accuracy trade-off makes it practically important for real-world deployment.

items.title: Do My Samples Help? Compute Budget Allocation for Real-World Sampling-Based MPC in Contact-Rich Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2610.14064v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Sampling-based model predictive control (SMPC) is increasingly practical for contact-rich manipulation because GPU-based physics simulators enable real-time evaluation of large numbers of non-differentiable contact rollouts. However, this computation budget is finite and can be spent in competing ways, including denser control exploration, representing dynamics or state uncertainty, replanning more frequently, or aligning the simulation better with the physical state. Yet, the resulting trade-offs are not well understood in real-world sim-to-real control. In this work, we address this question through a systematic study of how to allocate a fixed computation budget for SMPC in contact-rich manipulation. To enable controlled comparisons, we develop a GPU-based framework named Budget-Allocating Model Predictive Control (BAMPC), which runs on MuJoCo Warp and exposes dynamics uncertainty, state uncertainty, and temporal alignment as independent dimensions of the computation budget while using the same control stack in simulation and on a real robot. Across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, we find that the best budget allocation depends on the dominant sim-to-real error, with dynamics randomization not universally the most effective one.

items.title: Safety-Critical Quadrotor Navigation Using Fourth-Order Control Barrier Functions with Full Nonlinear Quadrotor Dynamics
items.content: arXiv:2610.14522v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Safety-critical quadrotor navigation in cluttered environments typically relies on hierarchical architectures in which a high-level safety filter modifies position references that are then tracked by a separate attitude controller. However, this separation can create a mismatch between translational safety objectives and attitude evolution. To address this gap, we propose a safety controller based on fourth-order control barrier functions (CBFs) that explicitly incorporates the full nonlinear quadrotor dynamics, including attitude dynamics and torque-level actuation. Furthermore, we apply the integral high-order CBF technique to resolve the mixed-relative degree issue in the derived constraint formulation. The resulting formulation enforces obstacle-avoidance constraints while optimizing control torques, granting the safety layer direct authority over attitude behavior and eliminating the hierarchical disconnect inherent in reference-tracking safety filters. We validate the approaches in both high-fidelity simulation and real-world flight experiments, demonstrating reliable constraint satisfaction and successful obstacle avoidance. These results suggest that torque-level high-order CBFs provide a practical pathway to provably safer quadrotor navigation under full rigid-body dynamics.

items.title: Verify, Act, Distill: Turning Test-Time Compute into Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.14885v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Test-time compute (TTC), which scores multiple candidate actions at inference time, is a powerful way to improve the execution performance of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but existing methods keep the policy frozen, so the gain must be recomputed at every execution. We propose Verify, Act, Distill, a framework that consolidates the gains of TTC into the VLA itself. A fixed verifier scores candidates generated by a flow-matching VLA, the weighted aggregate is executed, and the observations and aggregated chunks from successful adaptation episodes are distilled directly into LoRA parameters with the standard flow-matching loss. This reuses supervision that TTC has already produced during execution, without additional reinforcement learning or rollouts dedicated to teacher generation. On the 40 LIBERO tasks with a SmolVLA 5k checkpoint, distilling from only 10 episodes per task raises the mean success rate of verifier-free single-candidate generation from 54.1% to 70.6%, retaining about 74% of the improvement obtained by aggregating eight candidates. Applying the same aggregation to the distilled policy further raises the success rate from 76.4% to 82.3%, with a particularly large gain on LIBERO-Long (44.0% to 57.8%), and the single-candidate policy also improves on LIBERO-plus, which contains distribution shifts. These results show that using verification as a learning signal, rather than only as an execution-time selector, both retains the improvements of TTC and re-amplifies the effect of subsequent TTC.

items.title: PointWalker: Mapless Quadruped Locomotion Directly From Raw LiDAR Point Clouds
items.content: arXiv:2610.15548v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Quadruped robots deployed for inspection and field missions must cross heterogeneous terrain, from stairs, slopes, and gaps to high platforms, stepping stones, and balance beams, where safe support is sparse or see-through. Existing methods interpose a terrain map or a depth image between sensing and control. Maps are costly to maintain, corrupted by odometry drift and outliers, and misled by see-through gratings, while depth cameras degrade with lighting and surface material. In this paper, we present PointWalker, a mapless framework whose single reinforcement learning policy directly consumes raw point clouds from four light detection and ranging (LiDAR) sensors. Voxelized points are encoded by linear self-attention and fused with proprioception through cross-attention, so terrain geometry reaches the policy without maps or foothold estimation. One proximal policy optimization (PPO) run, with terrain-aware rewards and dual-channel simulation of see-through gratings, yields one policy for all seven terrain classes with a 90.1% mean success rate in simulation. Deployed zero-shot on a Deep Robotics X30 at 50 Hz onboard, it crosses 0.8-m gaps, climbs 0.8-m platforms and 45{\deg} steel-grating stairs, carries a 50-kg payload, and completes a 2.5-km mountain route.

items.title: ReTrace: Cross-Stage Failure Attribution for Self-Improving Robotic Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2610.15814v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: General-purpose multimodal foundation models are increasingly capable of directly controlling robots, yet improving their manipulation capabilities through autonomous interaction remains challenging. A key challenge to such self-improvement is learning from failures in complex manipulation tasks involving cross-stage dependencies, where an action may succeed locally but cause a later stage to fail. To address this challenge, we introduce ReTrace, a self-improvement framework for robotic manipulation through autonomous physical interaction and retrospective reasoning, without provided demonstrations or model-parameter updates. ReTrace retrospectively traces downstream failures to earlier decisions, proposes targeted corrections, and evaluates them through subsequent interactions. Across attempts, ReTrace progressively consolidates validated corrections into a reusable manipulation skill that guide subsequent execution. We evaluate ReTrace on four real-world manipulation tasks using a Franka Research 3 robot. On the two tasks with strong cross-stage dependencies, GPT-6 Astra-low improves from 0% to 80% success on plug insertion and from 0% to 100% on ball pouring, while GPT-6 Sol-xhigh improves from 0% to 10% and 0% to 90%, respectively. The learned skills also transfer across model and reasoning configurations and reduce inference-time decision cost in most evaluated settings.
