items.title: Mobility Helps Learning: Unsupervised Model Adaptation for Object Recognition via Movement
items.content: arXiv:2610.15846v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Movable agents, such as autonomous vehicles and robots, should be able to autonomously adapt their pre-trained object recognition models to new environments without human annotations. While existing test-time adaptation (TTA) methods address label-free model adaptation, they typically treat test data as independent snapshots, without constructively exploiting a rich, unique source of supervision: the significant variance in prediction quality as an agent observes the same object from different distances and viewpoints. To capitalize on this, we propose \texttt{MoCaFe}, a model-agnostic and hyperparameter-insensitive paradigm that leverages motion-induced prediction variance for unsupervised adaptation. Specifically, we first develop mobility-calibrated filtering of pseudo-labels, which constructs reliable pseudo-labels by fusing cross-view predictions using inverse-variance weights. The filtered pseudo-labels then guide the selection of ``hard samples'' for effective learning. To further suppress pseudo-label corruption, we introduce \texttt{p-MoCaFe}, an optional extension that uses a public dataset to assign weighting factors to data samples, yielding an estimator of the clean loss with bounded bias. Extensive experiments on autonomous driving (nuScenes, KITTI) and embodied-agent datasets show that \texttt{MoCaFe} significantly outperforms state-of-the-art TTA schemes, achieving up to approximately 20% accuracy gain.

items.reasoning: Novel angle on test-time adaptation by leveraging embodiment and motion as a supervision source; relevant to embodied AI, though evaluation breadth and real-world robustness remain to be fully verified.

items.title: Deep Speech Representations Track Word Timing along a Low-Dimensional Circular Trajectory
items.content: arXiv:2610.16273v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Speech timing is fundamental for speech models to recognize words accurately, but how word-timing information is represented in speech models remains underexplored. We study this question using the framework of representational geometry, which investigates whether and how concepts are represented in low-dimensional subspaces of the representation space. Prior work in cognitive neuroscience has shown that when HuBERT feature sequences are averaged across words of the same duration, they form near-circular trajectories from word onset to word offset in a two-dimensional "temporal subspace." Here we show that this circular structure of word timing is a general property of deep speech representations, by demonstrating its emergence in nine additional speech models covering both supervised and self-supervised. We then move beyond averaged word segments and show that in HuBERT, the circular trajectories are consistent enough at the level of individual words to perform word segmentation. Our approach, Rotary Segmentation (RoSeg), achieves 64.3% boundary F-score on Librispeech by detecting word boundaries when cycles complete in the temporal subspace. Although supervision is needed to identify a good subspace, nevertheless this result demonstrates much stronger implicit word knowledge in HuBERT than has previously been shown.

This representational-geometry finding illuminates how speech models internally track word onsets and offsets.
items.reasoning: A clean, well-executed interpretability finding demonstrating a universal geometric structure for timing across many speech models; scientifically interesting, though the practical impact on model development is indirect.

items.title: From a Large-Scale Teacher to Efficient Multimodal Students for Search Relevance Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2610.16569v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Relevance prediction between user queries and items is a fundamental component of e-commerce search systems. Traditionally, high-quality relevance labels are obtained through human judgment, which is reliable but expensive, slow, and difficult to scale. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) enable automated relevance judgment at scale, achieving performance comparable to human annotators. However, such systems often rely on large commercial LLMs with complex prompts, resulting in high inference costs and limited throughput.   In this work, we propose a framework that bridges this gap by distilling a high-performing LLM-based relevance judgment system into efficient multimodal student models. We first curate a small, high-quality human-annotated dataset to serve as ground truth. Using this dataset, we develop a reliable LLM-as-a-judge pipeline through careful prompt engineering and iterative refinement. This pipeline is then used to generate large-scale relevance labels, which serve as training data for compact multimodal models. Our distilled models achieve performance close to the teacher system while significantly improving latency, cost, and scalability. This approach enables practical deployment of high-quality relevance prediction systems in production environments.

items.title: JtT: Rethinking Point Trajectory Diffusion for Diverse and Rigid Motion from an Image
items.content: arXiv:2610.16591v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study forecasting rigid-body motion from a single image: generating diverse and physically plausible future trajectories for arbitrary points in a scene, without building rigidity into the architecture or relying on geometric inputs such as depth. Like video generators, recent trajectory generators fail at this task, even in simple synthetic Kubric scenes, despite scaling up model size and training on real data.   We show how to solve this with the right architecture and parameterization. Our model, JtT, is a simple diffusion transformer that operates directly in coordinate space and decodes arbitrary and dense query patterns, without the trajectory VAEs or fixed grids assumed in prior work. Through a systematic study of the design space of point trajectory diffusion, we find that diffusing per-frame velocities is the only parameterization that captures rigidity, that it must be paired with the right timestep schedule, and that adding full-resolution RGB at the query points resolves the boundary failures of prior methods.   However, evaluating such 2D models rigorously is itself non-trivial. To our knowledge, we are the first to observe that physical plausibility and diversity do not improve together during training: larger models, as used in prior work, memorize the single ground-truth future per training image, becoming more rigid while covering fewer possible futures.   Yet prior work has paid little attention to this, so we show how model rankings depend on model size, metric, and stopping time, and adopt a stricter, checkpoint-averaged evaluation protocol. Under this protocol, JtT improves over prior methods on both distributional and rigidity metrics and approaches ground-truth rigidity, with only about 50M parameters.

items.title: On the Calibration of Crowdsourcing Aggregators
items.content: arXiv:2610.16815v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Calibration has been extensively studied for classifiers, but remains largely unexplored for crowdsourcing aggregation methods, which are increasingly used for making probabilistic decisions. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first theoretical and empirical study of calibration in label aggregation. To our great surprise, we find that widely used aggregation methods can be severely miscalibrated, and in opposite directions: Majority Vote is underconfident while model-based aggregators are overconfident. We prove that the Bayesian aggregator is perfectly calibrated under its data-generating model. We also show that exact calibration of weighted majority votes requires highly restrictive conditions, which helps explain why Majority Vote is generally miscalibrated in realistic crowds. Empirically, we study calibration across $39$ human crowdsourcing datasets and LLM-based crowds. In both cases, we observe systematic miscalibration for aggregation models such as Majority Vote, Dawid--Skene, GLAD, and CrowdFM. Finally, we propose a post-hoc calibration procedure that \emph{aggregates the aggregators}: for any aggregation function $\phi$, we introduce a transformation that first combines its predictive distribution with those of complementary aggregators, before applying temperature scaling. This simple and interpretable transformation makes temperature scaling more effective than when applied directly to $\phi$. It improves calibration, especially in the high-redundancy regime where there are many annotations per item, while generally preserving or even improving accuracy.

items.title: ML Engineering Agents - A Data Management Perspective
items.content: arXiv:2610.16919v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Machine learning engineering (MLE) agents are emerging as a new paradigm for automating end-to-end ML pipeline development. Using large language models for code generation and predictive performance as a machine-gradable feedback signal, these agents iteratively synthesize, execute, and refine pipeline code. Yet current systems are largely evaluated on pre-built, single-table benchmarks that abstract away key data management challenges. This tutorial introduces the foundations of MLE agents and highlights research opportunities for the database community. We cover how agents combine program synthesis with iterative and evolutionary optimization, and discuss open challenges in efficient pipeline execution, data discovery and augmentation over heterogeneous sources, reliability and debugging, as well as fairness and compliance. We connect these challenges to existing data management techniques and conclude with a hands-on session using contemporary MLE agents.

It critiques current benchmarks for abstracting away data management challenges and outlines open research problems for the database community, including efficient pipeline execution and data discovery.
items.reasoning: Timely framing of an emerging agentic-ML paradigm from a data-management angle, with credible authors in the data systems space. As a tutorial rather than novel research, impact is in agenda-setting rather than new results.

items.title: Accounting for model error in ensemble variational data assimilation through learned generative dynamics
items.content: arXiv:2610.17333v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Many approaches have recently been proposed to combine data assimilation with machine learning for improved forecasts with geophysical models. Here, we focus on combining advanced sequential data assimilation schemes with a generative forecasting model which accounts for complex model errors. This generative model provides a stochastic approximation of the conditional distribution of the successor state given the current state. The proposed variational formulation is a novel one-step weak-constraint 4D-Var scheme in which a learned conditional stochastic forecast replaces the prescribed additive Gaussian model error representation. We derive and implement this formulation as an ensemble variational algorithm, the generative iterative ensemble Kalman filter (IEnKF-G), which generalises the iterative ensemble Kalman filter with additive Gaussian model error (IEnKF-Q). We extend the method to a smoother with an assimilation window spanning multiple time steps and propose a simplified variant.   The IEnKF-G is evaluated on a stochastic variant of the Lorenz 1963 model to assess its robustness. It is then tested on a multi-scale variant of the one-dimensional Lorenz 1996 model, in which the resolved variables are affected by model error originating from the hidden small-scale variables. The algorithm is then compared to an ensemble Kalman filter that adaptively mitigates model and sampling errors, and to the IEnKF-Q. The IEnKF-G is generally more accurate in the tested configurations, with substantial gains under partial observations and significant model error. This demonstrates the potential of generative data-driven models when paired with classical data assimilation methods, particularly when model error is substantial.

They derive an ensemble variational algorithm, the generative iterative ensemble scheme, to make forecasts with geophysical models more robust to model error. This advances the growing intersection of machine learning and weather/geoscience data assimilation.

items.title: Privacy-Preserving GNN Inference on Financial Transaction Graphs via Homomorphic Encryption
items.content: arXiv:2610.18054v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) in financial networks requires modeling transaction patterns that span multiple institutions. In practice, however, banks cannot share account and transaction features due to strict privacy regulations. We propose a privacy-preserving graph neural network (GNN) inference framework tailored to this multi-bank setting. A central server holds the graph connectivity and pretrained model weights in plaintext, while each bank keeps its transaction features encrypted. Inference is then carried out entirely on encrypted features under the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme, so that no plaintext transaction features or predictions are exposed to the server. The key to making this practical is an edge-centric GNN architecture, wherein message passing is expressed through operations on node--edge incidence matrices. This formulation not only preserves the edge-attributed multigraph structure of transaction networks but also reduces every aggregation step to plaintext--ciphertext matrix products. Since CKKS can evaluate only polynomial circuits, we also approximate each nonlinearity with a composite polynomial of the sign function, which we calibrate per activation site. On the IBM AML benchmark, our model achieves performance competitive with plaintext baselines, and with a consumer-grade GPU, classifies each queried transaction end-to-end in as little as \textbf{5.31} seconds, while per-transaction latency can be amortized to \textbf{1.65} seconds when optimized for throughput.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.18054v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) in financial networks requires modeling transaction patterns that span multiple institutions. In practice, however, banks cannot share account and transaction features due to strict privacy regulations. We propose a privacy-preserving graph neural network (GNN) inference framework tailored to this multi-bank setting. A central server holds the graph connectivity and pretrained model weights in plaintext, while each bank keeps its transaction features encrypted. Inference is then carried out entirely on encrypted features under the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme, so that no plaintext transaction features or predictions are exposed to the server. The key to making this practical is an edge-centric GNN architecture, wherein message passing is expressed through operations on node--edge incidence matrices. This formulation not only preserves the edge-attributed multigraph structure of transaction networks but also reduces every aggregation step to plaintext--ciphertext matrix products. Since CKKS can evaluate only polynomial circuits, we also approximate each nonlinearity with a composite polynomial of the sign function, which we calibrate per activation site. On the IBM AML benchmark, our model achieves performance competitive with plaintext baselines, and with a consumer-grade GPU, classifies each queried transaction end-to-end in as little as \textbf{5.31} seconds, while per-transaction latency can be amortized to \textbf{1.65} seconds when optimized for throughput.

items.title: Linear Last-Iterate Convergence Rates for Optimistic Learning in Harmonic Games
items.content: arXiv:2610.18560v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We prove that the last iterate of Optimistic Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (OFTRL) converges at a linear rate to a Nash equilibrium in multiplayer harmonic games. Our result holds under a mild game-regularity condition and for a large family of regularizers, including entropy, Tsallis, and log-barrier. Our analysis is based on a dual perspective of OFTRL: we prove that the interaction between optimism and the global structure of harmonic games leads to the dissipation of an energy function along the dual iterates, for which we establish tight quantitative bounds. Our result also holds for the Extragradient FTRL variant.

items.title: LongHisDoc: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Chinese Long Historical Document Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2610.14531v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Chinese historical documents are invaluable cultural treasures, but their complexity poses significant comprehension challenges for non-specialists. Despite the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) in modern document tasks, their capabilities in Long (full-book) Historical Document understanding remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce LongHisDoc, the first benchmark tailored for long historical document understanding. LongHisDoc comprises 1,012 expert-annotated QA pairs derived from 101 PDF documents, with an average of 85.1 pages and 42,776.4 tokens per document. It spans 10 categories and features four QA types: single-page, cross-page, multi-hop, and unanswerable. Answering these questions requires integrating multimodal evidence from text, layout, and visual elements. Our evaluation reveals that the top-performing LVLM and LLM achieve only 62.9% and 69.9% accuracy, respectively, highlighting a substantial performance gap. Furthermore, we assess various modal retrievers and the end-to-end RAG performance to provide references for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. We believe that LongHisDoc serves as a comprehensive benchmark to catalyze future research in full-book historical document understanding. The benchmark and evaluation code are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/qweq12433454/LongHisDoc and https://github.com/SCUT-DLVCLab/LongHisDoc.

items.title: From Candidate Tokens to Final Outcomes: Decoding Relative Long-Horizon Candidate Value from Reasoning Model Representations
items.content: arXiv:2610.15412v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large reasoning models generate reasoning trajectories token by token. At a given prefix, multiple next-token candidates may be plausible, yet shape subsequent reasoning and differ in their chances of leading to the correct answer. Whether these differences are reflected in internal representations remains unclear. To study this question, we define relative long-horizon candidate value to quantify within-prefix differences and construct the Reasoning Candidate-Token Value (RCTV) dataset, pairing mathematical reasoning prefixes with plausible next-token candidates and their empirical long-horizon candidate values. Using RCTV, we examine hidden states, multilayer perceptron outputs, and attention outputs at candidate positions with sparse linear probes. Experimental results provide evidence that relative long-horizon candidate value is linearly decodable from these representations at multiple layers. Candidate-value probes can also outperform probability- and embedding-based baselines. Furthermore, a controlled online intervention experiment shows that using the decoded signals to guide token selection during generation can improve the chances of eventual success. Our findings provide evidence that internal representations encode information about relative long-horizon candidate value, offering insights into how local candidate-level representations relate to long-horizon reasoning outcomes.

The work connects token-level representation analysis with outcome-level reasoning quality.

items.title: RIVO: Lightweight Adaptive Rerouting for Deep Research Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.15910v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Deep Research agents rely on long-horizon reasoning and iterative tool use to solve complex information-seeking tasks. However, adaptive decision-making over these trajectories remains challenging, as agents may stop prematurely when further evidence is needed, continue unnecessarily after sufficient evidence has been gathered, or fail to redirect unproductive trajectories. Existing solutions either require costly model retraining and dense turn-level supervision, or rely on heuristic control rules that are not directly optimized for downstream research utility. This motivates a lightweight, utility-aware alternative for Deep Research control. We formulate adaptive rerouting in long-horizon Deep Research as a state-conditioned trajectory correction problem. Based on this view, we introduce RIVO, a lightweight plug-in framework for adaptive trajectory correction. The agent estimates its research state from lightweight signals and determines whether trajectory redirection is needed. Once triggered, the plug-in modifies the Host token logits to steer generation toward a more promising research direction. Theoretical analysis shows that, under a value-alignment condition and bounded local curvature, a sufficiently small logit intervention can locally improve expected downstream research utility. We further construct BrowseCore, a curated dataset with a paired local corpus, for efficient and controlled Deep Research experimentation. Building on this resource, the plug-in is trained from downstream outcomes, enabling it to learn corrections that improve subsequent research and final task performance. Extensive experiments across multiple Deep Research benchmarks and control settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, showing that lightweight logit intervention can improve long-horizon research without retraining the underlying Host model.

items.title: PersonaFactor: Preference Factors with Dynamic Selection for LLM Personalization
items.content: arXiv:2610.16372v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Although users may express different personalization needs across tasks, these task-specific behaviors can reflect shared underlying preference mechanisms. Existing LLM personalization methods often focus on surface-level interactions or undifferentiated histories, overlooking the shared mechanisms underlying these behaviors. We introduce PersonaFactors, a framework that distills reusable and interpretable personalization factors from heterogeneous user interactions. We construct a library of thirteen PersonaFactors by extracting evidence-grounded rationales and clustering recurring patterns across tasks, and develop a dynamic factor-guided generation framework that selects factors relevant to each user's history and current request. Across four personalization benchmarks and four backbone models, Dynamic PersonaFactor achieves the best score on every reported metric. Representation analyses further show that PersonaFactors and user history induce partially overlapping low-dimensional representations, and that their joint use yields complementary shifts. Taken together, these findings suggest that factor-based and history-based personalization can mutually reinforce each other.

items.title: Nufo: A Benchmark for Ewe Automatic Speech Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2610.17278v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) remains challenging for low-resource languages, where the scarcity of transcribed speech limits the development of accurate systems. This challenge is particularly acute for African languages such as Ewe, which has millions of speakers but remains underrepresented in publicly available ASR resources and benchmarks. In this work, we consolidate, normalize, and partition existing Ewe speech resources into a standardized 174-hour Ewe ASR benchmark, the largest to date to our knowledge. We fine-tune and evaluate pretrained speech models, including Whisper and AfriHuBERT, to establish strong baselines on our benchmark. Whisper-medium achieves a word error rate (WER) of 37.98%, while AfriHuBERT achieves 39.70% on the test set. We further provide a qualitative analysis of common recognition errors. We release the benchmark under the name Nufo, derived from the Ewe word for "talk", accompanied by models and evaluation resources, to facilitate future research on Ewe and other underrepresented African languages.

items.title: Cheap, Consistent, Calibrated, but Biased? Typed Decision Models as Judges
items.content: arXiv:2610.18122v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) return a probability for each allowed answer instead of generating text, which makes them candidates for cheaply replacing LLM judges that compare two answers. Whether they share the biases of LLM judges is untested. We run the CALM benchmark's bias tests on eight TDMs and seven LLM judges of 2024 and 2026. Every TDM is biased, in three to eight of twelve tests. Emotional tone affects them most, and rewriting the better answer in such a tone lowers the accuracy of a typical TDM from 99% to 42%. TDMs are more biased than 2026 LLM judges. All eight change verdicts when the answers swap places, which the 2026 LLM judges hardly do, and several side with an answer that most people allegedly prefer or that a famous model allegedly wrote. Yet both kinds of judge are tripped up by the same prompts. The TDMs' probabilities show that most tests mainly flip verdicts the TDM was unsure of, and that good calibration does not protect against bias. As TDMs are more consistent and 37 times cheaper than 2026 LLM judges, our results suggest they can be attractive judges if their biases are tested for the task.

items.title: The Last Mile of Coding Agents for Long-Document Tasks: An Empirical Study on Clinical Trial Protocol Digitization
items.content: arXiv:2610.18507v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Clinical trial protocols serve as the source of truth for study design, but are mostly written and used as unstructured PDF documents. Digitizing protocols turns static content into structured, machine-readable data that clinical software can analyze, validate, and execute. Coding agents, which select tools, execute code, and revise their approach as they work, are increasingly applied to such long-document tasks, yet it remains unclear how reliably they turn complete documents into accurate structured outputs. We study this question using protocol digitization as a testbed. We introduce TrialPD-Bench, an expert-annotated benchmark of 150 publicly available protocol PDFs spanning four task categories. Beyond final-answer performance, our evaluation measures evidence recall from agent traces, agent behavior, and cost. Across nine proprietary and open-weight models in five coding-agent harnesses, even the strongest agents do not fully solve protocol digitization. Our analysis further shows that agents usually locate the required evidence but fail in the last mile of transcribing and structuring it. We further develop TrialScribe, a domain-specific harness that equips coding agents with task skills and a verification loop. TrialScribe improves a locally served open-weight model by 6.2-59.4 points across eight metrics, enabling it to match or surpass proprietary models such as GPT-5.6-Sol.

Beyond final-answer accuracy, the evaluation examines process-level behaviors of agents on these long-document workflows. The study probes the gap between coding-agent competence on code tasks and reliable document-to-structure transformation in a high-stakes domain.

items.title: Decomposing and Predicting Annotation Disagreement in Harmful Content Across Languages
items.content: arXiv:2610.18588v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Annotator disagreement is increasingly recognized as a meaningful property of subjective tasks, rather than merely noise to be removed. Predicting which items are likely to be contested could help allocate annotation effort and route difficult cases to human review. We propose predicting disagreement from interpretable semantic properties of the text. An LLM answers a set of binary questions covering harmful-content characteristics, disagreement-related cues such as borderline severity and missing context, and language-sensitive cues such as local slurs. A classifier predicts disagreement from these answers, and we analyze which questions contribute most to the predictions. Across four datasets in English, German, and Turkish and three open-weight LLMs, our structured question features outperform direct prompting by 10.5 ROC-AUC points and the strongest text-based baselines by 5.0 points. A compact subset of eight questions performs within 1.5 ROC-AUC points of the full twenty-question set. In leave-one-dataset-out evaluation, models retain roughly 90-95% of their in-domain ROC-AUC. Across models and datasets, questions about derogation, missing context, and decision boundaries serve as the strongest predictors, suggesting that what makes harmful content contested is partly observable in the text.

Experiments span four datasets in English, German, and Turkish. This treats disagreement as signal for routing difficult cases rather than noise to discard.

A classifier predicts disagreement from these answers, and we analyze which questions contribute most to the predictions. Across four datasets in English, German, and Turkish and three open-weight LLMs, our structured question features outperform direct prompting by 10.5 ROC-AUC points and the strongest text-based baselines by 5.0 points. A compact subset of eight questions performs within 1.5 ROC-AUC points of the full twenty-question set. In leave-one-dataset-out evaluation, models retain roughly 90-95% of their in-domain ROC-AUC. Across models and datasets, questions about derogation, missing context, and decision boundaries serve as the strongest predictors, suggesting that what makes harmful content contested is partly observable in the text.

items.title: RelLedger: Relational Information Governance for LLM Agent Organizations
items.content: arXiv:2610.16281v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In LLM agent organizations, shared records determine which facts are available for later decisions. A sender consults interaction histories before deciding whether to report an event. A delivery gap across histories does not show whose relationship drove the choice or whether the resulting record matters downstream. We introduce RelLedger to audit these links. It holds the event, evidence, risk, and message fixed while crossing the sender's histories with the event target and an unrelated actor. Role reassignment and history rewrites locate the controlling cue. Message and cost interventions show when the effect appears. An attribution ledger maps each claim to its required response cells and separates missing interventions from sampling uncertainty. Recipient replay follows delivered information into downstream decisions. Executable workflows for a simulated one-person company extend the audit to retrieved histories, tool calls, and shared ledger updates. Across GPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, and Qwen, the audit reveals model-specific control paths and smaller relation gaps under explicit loss rules. Claude sends the same factual notice 62.22 percentage points more often with conflict histories than with friendly histories. In executable workflows, strained histories reduce recipient review rates by 45.83 points relative to warm histories for Claude.

items.title: Image Diffusion Models Are Good 3D Human Motion Generators
items.content: arXiv:2610.14254v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Text-to-motion generation typically relies on dataset-specific skeletal representations, with models trained separately for benchmarks with different joint layouts. We investigate whether image diffusion architectures can model 3D human motion through a common image-compatible representation that accommodates heterogeneous skeletal layouts while preserving motion-specific kinematic structure. To this end, we organize root-centered joint trajectories into topology-informed joint--time images and model global root dynamics through a complementary latent stream. A motion autoencoder conditions local-motion decoding on the root latent, while a text-conditioned Scalable Interpolant Transformer (SiT) jointly generates both latent streams, with supervision on decoded 3D joint positions further constraining generation in motion space. In addition to dataset-specific models, we train a single motion autoencoder on HumanML3D and KIT-ML, followed by a single text-conditioned SiT shared across both datasets, preserving their respective skeletal definitions without skeleton retargeting to a common joint layout. Experiments on HumanML3D and KIT-ML show that our dataset-specific models achieve state-of-the-art performance, while shared training yields further gains on both benchmarks, demonstrating the benefits of shared modeling across heterogeneous skeletal layouts.

items.title: InfraWorld: Motion-Aware World Modeling for Roadside 4D Occupancy Forecasting
items.content: arXiv:2610.14544v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Roadside 4D occupancy forecasting predicts future semantic occupancy in a fixed infrastructure coordinate system. Roadside scenes are globally structured yet locally evolving, requiring comprehensive scene-level context while precisely modeling sparse localized motion. However, existing forecasting paradigms struggle to tackle both requirements. To address this limitation, we propose InfraWorld, a world model formulating roadside occupancy forecasting as selective state evolution. InfraWorld maintains a dense BEV state for the complete scene and persistent motion queries for moving regions, assigning complementary states to global context and local dynamics. Specifically, we propose Dynamic Query Initiation (DQI) to initialize queries in regions supported by motion in the observed history. During rollout, the dense state is updated through Long--Short Temporal Fusion (LST), which combines short-term adjacent-frame continuity with long-term motion trends to preserve stable context while capturing scene evolution. Motion-Aware Query Injection (MAQI) then refines the queries and injects confidence-weighted query information into corresponding BEV tokens, enabling targeted dynamic updates without perturbing global context. Together, InfraWorld concentrates predictive capacity on evolving traffic regions. Extensive experiments on the InfraOcc and Occ3D--nus datasets demonstrate that InfraWorld achieves state-of-the-art performance for roadside 4D occupancy forecasting while retaining its effectiveness under ego-centric settings. Code will be released.

items.title: CAST: Real-Time Motion Capture for Any Skeleton Topology
items.content: arXiv:2610.14856v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper studies the problem of recovering motion from monocular video, even when the target skeleton topology differs from the subject observed in the video. Although previous methods have made efforts to resolve this problem, they remain vulnerable to joint-rotation errors that are coupled across the skeleton and can propagate along its kinematic hierarchy. To mitigate these errors, we present CAST, a topology-aware motion capture framework that combines learned local rotations with geometric correction guided by predicted global bone directions. Our observability analysis characterizes which rotational components can be constrained by outgoing bone directions. Guided by this analysis, GRACE uses reliability-gated alignment to correct composed orientations in parent-to-child order, leaving unconstrained components to the learned rotation predictor. The motion predictor and correction module are trained jointly with motion-derived supervision, using a frozen image encoder. Experiments under the TopoCap evaluation protocol show that the proposed framework improves motion recovery across different target topologies, including unseen structures. Reference-based cross-skeleton evaluation on a curated Mixamo benchmark and a user preference study further assess transfer to different target structures. A causal CAST-B variant achieves over 51 FPS on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, with timing covering image encoding and motion prediction. Code repository: https://github.com/fankewen/CAST.

items.title: UniForge3D: Joint 3D Reconstruction and Generation in a Shared Anchor-Guided Space
items.content: arXiv:2610.15357v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generating complete 3D assets from sparse, unposed images requires preserving observed geometry while completing unseen regions. Joint reconstruction and generation offers a way to address both goals: reconstruction recovers the geometry observed in the input images, while generation contributes learned shape priors. However, combining camera-relative reconstruction with canonical-space generation introduces a coordinate mismatch that makes direct geometric interaction more difficult. Moreover, conditioning each 3D location on all views without accounting for their relevance may mix useful geometric evidence with unrelated image content, hindering local detail recovery. We present UniForge3D, which jointly models reconstruction and generation in a shared anchor-guided space, resolving their coordinate mismatch. This space follows the anchor view's azimuth while keeping the object upright. The two branches exchange features bidirectionally to predict per-view point maps and a complete sparse voxel structure. We further condition point-map prediction on the generated structure to establish pixel-to-voxel correspondences and select the most informative input view for each voxel. Features from the selected views then guide detailed shape generation, helping preserve observed geometric details. Our method achieves state-of-the-art appearance and geometry results on Toys4K and GSO, generating complete 3D assets with improved fidelity. Project webpage: https://xishuxishu.github.io/uniforge3d-project/

It conditions each 3D location on relevant views to preserve observed geometry while completing unseen regions.

items.title: Frozen History: When Temporal Losses Stop Accumulation in Learned Real-Time Supersampling
items.content: arXiv:2610.15752v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Learned real-time supersampling accumulates jittered low-resolution samples along motion vectors. Many methods use a temporal consistency loss to reduce flicker. We show that with accurate registration, this loss can suppress accumulation: on static content, the network copies its warped history at almost no temporal cost. Camera jitter in motion vectors raises this cost and can hide the effect. We identify four registration errors that training can conceal: jitter-carrying motion vectors, one motion field for both resolution lattices, jittered depth, and an unregistered skip path. A model-free oracle shows that correct registration makes freezing two orders of magnitude cheaper on static pixels. Controlled training shows that registration reverses the temporal weight's effect on PSNR. Under exact registration, increasing the weight reduces pixel variance at the expense of accuracy and perceived quality, with a 0.7 to 0.9 dB loss on static frames at weight 0.25. This reversal recurs across three network families and two scales; the loss also reduces accuracy on unjittered STSS data. With a small temporal weight and a normalised sample accumulator, a plain registered network improves the best published QRISP PSNR by 0.34 to 0.62 dB at $\times$2, $\times$3 and $\times$4 upscaling to 1080p. At $\times$2, its static pixel standard deviation is one quarter that of DLSS 2. Without retraining, it outperforms classical temporal upsampling by at least 4.4 dB on Arm's jittered Bistro capture. Our most accurate $\times$4 model runs in 2.03 ms per 1080p frame on an H200. Code: https://github.com/CV-AC/Frozen_history

items.summary: This paper shows that temporal consistency losses in learned real-time supersampling can paradoxically suppress sample accumulation: with accurate registration the network copies its warped history instead of accumulating jittered samples. items.title: Meaningful Moments: A Corpus of VLM-Derived Temporal Importance Labels for Video Action Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2610.16009v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Not every moment in a video is equally useful for recognizing an action. A few decisive moments often carry the evidence: the instant an object moves, the peak of a dive, or one object placed on another. Existing video datasets rarely provide large-scale, action-conditioned labels for which short segments carry that evidence. This work asks whether vision-language models can identify meaningful moments at scale and whether those labels improve action recognition.We introduce Meaningful Moments (MM), a corpus of about 4.58 million VLM-generated per-segment importance scores for nearly 500,000 class-labeled videos spanning Something-Something v2 (SSv2), Kinetics-400 (K400), and Diving-48 across 622 action classes. We freeze the action classifier and vary only temporal sampling. An alpha-parameterized comparison of importance-led selection against an importance-inverted control separates gains from the VLM signal from gains caused by variable-density sampling alone. Across all three datasets, VLM-derived importance is informative: at the hard-cut endpoint, keeping VLM-important segments outperforms keeping VLM-designated filler. Usefulness depends on class structure. On Diving-48, importance-led fast-forwarding preserves full-video recognition while the inverted control collapses by roughly 30 percentage points. On K400, hard-cut selection beats uniform sampling by 1.45 percentage points, rising to 2.05 under threshold selection. On SSv2, the labels carry signal but do not recover full-video performance. Direct scoring matches greedy removal within its noise floor at roughly 25 times fewer oracle calls, and a four-VLM cross-oracle study shows consistent downstream trends. We release the importance labels and evaluation protocol under CC-BY-4.0; SSv2 class strings remain under CC-BY-NC-4.0.

The goal is to identify which short video segments carry decisive evidence for recognizing an action and to test whether these labels improve video action recognition. It matters because most video datasets lack action-conditioned temporal importance labels, and VLMs could make such labeling scalable.

Using frozen VLMs to derive importance scores is a pragmatic approach, though the reliance on VLM-generated labels rather than human ground truth introduces potential noise and circularity concerns. Utility is likely strongest for temporal localization and efficient video recognition research rather than a fundamental methodological advance.

items.title: EgoAlign: Situated 3D Understanding without Situation Descriptions
items.content: arXiv:2610.16176v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Situated 3D Question Answering requires models to interpret a 3D scene relative to an agent's pose. Existing methods commonly convey that pose through a natural-language situation description, which may be unavailable or costly to obtain in real-world deployments. While some methods additionally incorporate numerical pose, we find that randomly shuffling the agent pose causes little performance degradation, indicating limited functional dependence on the numerical pose. To address this gap, we introduce EgoAlign, a simple 3D language model that represents a scene in an agent-centric coordinate frame, together with a dedicated egocentric alignment stage comprising four complementary tasks: object category recognition, egocentric direction prediction, metric distance estimation, and spatial relation prediction. This stage teaches the model to consistently interpret scene geometry relative to the agent's pose before task-specific fine-tuning. EgoAlign achieves the strongest performance on SQA3D, Real-3DQA, and MSQA among compared methods while remaining highly efficient. More importantly, removing textual situation descriptions yields comparable or better downstream performance, whereas shuffling EgoAlign's numerical pose causes substantial degradation. These results show that EgoAlign establishes agent-centric spatial context directly from numerical pose without requiring textual situation descriptions.

It adds an egocentric alignment stage with four complementary tasks including object recognition and direction prediction.

items.title: Anomaly-Guided Observation and Two-Level Semantic Feedback for Training-Free Video Anomaly Analysis
items.content: arXiv:2610.16324v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Training-free language-based video anomaly detection (VAD) uses frozen vision--language models (VLMs) and large language models (LLMs) to localize abnormal events without task-specific model-weight optimization. Existing approaches increasingly exploit broader temporal and semantic context, yet generic context does not necessarily foreground abnormal events or specify how video-level semantics should modify local anomaly scores. We introduce a training-free semantic feedback framework that uses VAD-guided active observation for video anomaly understanding (VAU) and returns the resulting anomaly-focused description to refine temporal detection. Starting from an upstream anomaly-score curve, we adapt reasoning-based iterative frame selection: high-score regions seed the observations, and anomaly scores together with VLM relevance assessments guide subsequent temporal exploration. A frozen video-language model generates a single open-ended anomaly description from the selected frames. The description is returned through two complementary feedback levels: video-level feedback determines whether the score distribution should be suppressed, preserved, or sharpened, with selective visual rechecking, while local feedback retrieves event-related windows and promotes scores only after target-local visual verification. All model weights remain frozen, and feedback is applied once without regenerating the description. On the HIVAU video-summary evaluations of UCF-Crime and XD-Violence, VAD-guided observation improves GPT-rated reasonability, detail, and consistency over the matched CLIP-guided variant. For VAD, semantic feedback improves the re-evaluated upstream detector from 84.36% to 86.25% AUC on UCF-Crime and from 68.07% to 72.58% AP on XD-Violence, where the final AUC is 91.74%.
items.author: Hangil Park, Seungheon Kim, Tae-Kyun Kim
items.summary: Introduces a training-free semantic feedback framework where anomaly-score-guided active observation drives reasoning-based iterative frame selection, and anomaly-focused descriptions generated by VLMs and LLMs are fed back to refine temporal detection. This closes the loop between anomaly understanding and localization without any task-specific training.

However, it shares authors and topic with another paper in this batch, and training-free pipelines building on frozen VLMs are becoming a crowded direction, tempering novelty.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.16324v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training-free language-based video anomaly detection (VAD) uses frozen vision--language models (VLMs) and large language models (LLMs) to localize abnormal events without task-specific model-weight optimization. Existing approaches increasingly exploit broader temporal and semantic context, yet generic context does not necessarily foreground abnormal events or specify how video-level semantics should modify local anomaly scores. We introduce a training-free semantic feedback framework that uses VAD-guided active observation for video anomaly understanding (VAU) and returns the resulting anomaly-focused description to refine temporal detection. Starting from an upstream anomaly-score curve, we adapt reasoning-based iterative frame selection: high-score regions seed the observations, and anomaly scores together with VLM relevance assessments guide subsequent temporal exploration. A frozen video-language model generates a single open-ended anomaly description from the selected frames. The description is returned through two complementary feedback levels: video-level feedback determines whether the score distribution should be suppressed, preserved, or sharpened, with selective visual rechecking, while local feedback retrieves event-related windows and promotes scores only after target-local visual verification. All model weights remain frozen, and feedback is applied once without regenerating the description. On the HIVAU video-summary evaluations of UCF-Crime and XD-Violence, VAD-guided observation improves GPT-rated reasonability, detail, and consistency over the matched CLIP-guided variant. For VAD, semantic feedback improves the re-evaluated upstream detector from 84.36% to 86.25% AUC on UCF-Crime and from 68.07% to 72.58% AP on XD-Violence, where the final AUC is 91.74%.

items.title: MiMaAlign: Hierarchical Micro-Macro Alignment for Physically Plausible Video Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.16482v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) diffusion models have made remarkable progress in generating high-fidelity visuals, yet their outputs still often exhibit physically implausible phenomena, including discontinuous dynamics and implausible event interactions. Existing representation alignment methods mainly transfer generic video features or short-range motion cues, treating physical plausibility as a single-level representation problem. To address this issue, we propose MiMaAlign, a hierarchical micro-macro alignment framework that transfers complementary dynamics-oriented and event-oriented knowledge into different abstraction depths of a pretrained video diffusion model. Specifically, micro-level continuous dynamics alignment imposes constraints by aligning diffusion features with a continuous-time motion representation learned by a Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE), while macro-level event-commonsense alignment provides representations of object interactions and event semantics through an instruction-prompted vision-language model (VLM). With training-only auxiliary objectives, we align the complementary supervision from the two teachers with shallower and deeper generator features, respectively, enabling the generator to internalize the corresponding physical priors. Empirical evaluations show that, on CogVideoX-2B, MiMaAlign achieves a relative improvement of up to 21.0% in the Physical Commonsense (PC) score on the VideoPhy benchmark over the baseline, and also delivers substantial gains on the highly challenging VideoPhy2 benchmark, while maintaining general video quality on VBench and being supported by blind user comparisons.

items.reasoning: Physical plausibility in video generation is a recognized unsolved weakness of current T2V models, and the hierarchical micro-macro decomposition is a reasonable and distinguishable approach among many representation-alignment proposals. Impact hinges on convincing empirical gains over strong baselines like the latest commercial and open video models.

items.title: NoduleFlow: Automatic 3D Lung Nodule Detection and Segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2610.16548v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Low dose Computed Tomography (CT) is the standard imaging modality for lung cancer screening. On CT scans, lung cancer typically manifests as pulmonary nodules, whose manual identification is time-consuming and prone to observer variability, image quality limitations, and suboptimal reading conditions. Moreover, subtle temporal changes are often difficult to quantify reliably in CT scans from the same patient across follow-up examinations. Deep learning-based approaches for the automatic detection and segmentation of lung nodules have demonstrated improved accuracy and efficiency. However, most existing approaches provide only coarse region-of-interest localisation, rely on prior lesion annotations or human supervision, or treat detection and segmentation as separate tasks. In this work, we present NoduleFlow, a framework for lung nodule detection, classification, and segmentation directly from series of CT volumes. Our proposal consists of four interconnected modules and operates in an automated manner at inference time, without requiring prior lesion annotations, manual initialisation, or region-of-interest pre-selection. We further investigate whether nodule localization benefits from the propagation of candidate regions across follow-up scans through inter-scan registration fields, as opposed to conventional independent per-scan analysis. The generalisability of the framework is systematically evaluated across four independent datasets. The results underscore the potential of automated pipelines for lung nodule analysis in screening and diagnostic settings.

items.summary: NoduleFlow addresses automatic 3D detection and segmentation of lung nodules in low-dose CT screening, aiming to go beyond coarse region-of-interest localization and reduce dependence on prior lesion annotations. It treats detection and segmentation jointly to improve accuracy and efficiency in follow-up monitoring of subtle temporal changes.

items.title: Brain2Face: A Study on the Relation of EEG Signals and Spatio-temporal Head Avatars
items.content: arXiv:2610.17356v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Driving digital head avatars is classically done by hand-crafted artist design or by image-based facial performance capture. In this work, we ask whether spatio-temporal tracking of the humans's head geometry and appearance can be performed solely from brain signals, i.e., Electroencephalography (EEG). Since prior work mostly focused on activity and emotion recognition, this task is relatively unexplored without even having publicly available high-quality datasets and benchmarks. Thus, we contribute a dataset featuring paired EEG and human head geometry as well as appearance annotations. We synchronize 64-channel EEG with per-frame expression latent codes of a personalized Gaussian head avatar. Second, we introduce a baseline to the task of expression recovery of a head avatar from EEG signals. To this end, we propose a dedicated EEG-to-expression model that takes a temporal sequence of EEG signals as input and regresses the latent expression parameters of the 3D Gaussian head avatar. Lastly, we validate our capture and algorithmic design choices through a benchmark protocol that we introduce to this task. We believe this work paves the way towards better understanding of the relation between EEG signals and facial surface as well as appearance changes.

items.title: Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Scene Reconstruction: Methods, Systems, and Trade-offs
items.content: arXiv:2610.17513v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) allows for high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis. Since its inception in 2023, its explicit and highly configurable scene representation has been extended toward sparse-view generation, dynamic reconstruction, efficiency and compression, streaming, and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). Although Gaussian Splatting can provide real-time rendering, rendering an existing representation is distinct from constructing, updating, or maintaining the scene itself. In this survey, we synthesize current literature, categorize them and provide a connection of current approaches and tools towards an end-to-end pipeline. Explicitly, we categorize GS scene reconstruction into five overlapping families: single-shot generation, dynamic representations, efficiency and compression, streaming and immersive systems, and Gaussian Splatting SLAM. We distinguish render-only throughput from task-specific scene generation, update, tracking, mapping, and optimization costs, and combine controlled sparse-view benchmarking with native evaluations to identify cross-family quality, latency, memory, and update-cost trade-offs.

items.title: ScenePercept: Scenario-Conditioned Perceptual Assessment of Real-World User-Generated Content Images
items.content: arXiv:2610.17661v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The rapid development of mobile imaging and social platforms has led to explosive growth in user-generated content images, making their systematic and comprehensive perceptual assessment increasingly important. Existing image perception benchmarks are typically task-oriented, curating specific scenarios for quality or aesthetic assessment and applying a uniform perceptual criterion across diverse scenarios. This limits their ability to capture the scene diversity and perceptual complexity of real-world UGC images. To address these limitations, we introduce ScenePercept-Bench, a benchmark designed to reflect the distribution of real-world UGC images, comprising 23,100 images across 21 categories and 105 fine-grained scenes. To account for the influence of scene context on human perception, we design a hierarchical, scene-aware annotation protocol, covering visual quality, aesthetic perception, and scene semantics, with 15 attributes in total. Each image is annotated with an overall score, 15 attribute-level scores, and structured explanatory reasoning. Building on this benchmark, we further introduce Scenario-Conditioned Perceptual Alignment, a training framework that tackles the heterogeneity of perceptual criteria across scenarios. SCPA jointly optimizes absolute score prediction, preference ranking, and cross-scenario calibration, preserving the model general perceptual assessment ability while encouraging it to explore and adapt perceptual criteria across different scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SCPA achieves state-of-the-art performance in UGC image perception and generalizes effectively to established IQA and IAA benchmarks.

items.title: PUGS: Physics-Guided Uncertainty Modeling for Underwater Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting
items.content: arXiv:2610.17936v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides an efficient framework for dynamic scene reconstruction. Most existing approaches model scene dynamics with deterministic deformation fields, assuming each Gaussian follows a distinct geometric trajectory over time. This assumption breaks down underwater, where light scattering, refraction, marine snow and low visibility create substantial physical ambiguity in captured images. We present PUGS, a physics-guided uncertainty model for underwater dynamic 3DGS. PUGS learns inherent uncertainty induced by underwater image formation and leverages it as a physical signal for dynamic scene modeling. Rather than estimating a single deterministic displacement, it parameterizes each Gaussian's motion as a probability distribution with expected deformation and physical uncertainty. We adopt stochastic deformation optimization to sample Gaussian trajectories via local reparameterization, exploring multiple physically plausible solutions during training. We further propose uncertainty stochastic annealing and a dual-path self-consistency distillation objective, converting stochastic exploration to deterministic reconstruction while preserving temporal coherence. Extensive experiments on underwater dynamic datasets and physics-aware benchmarks demonstrate superior rendering quality, temporal consistency and reconstruction robustness. Our method achieves 1.16 dB PSNR gain over the strongest baseline on UVEB and 3.99 dB on DRUVA.

items.title: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Zero-Shot Human-Object Interaction
items.content: arXiv:2610.18161v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong zero-shot reasoning across diverse domains, but their potential for Human-Object Interaction (HOI) remains unexplored. Unlike traditional HOI approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets and fixed interaction taxonomies, MLLMs offer flexible reasoning, making them well-suited for dynamic, real-world scenarios. In this work, we present the first systematic study of MLLMs for HOI recognition and detection within a pipeline that combines an external object detector for entity localization with zero-shot multimodal reasoning for interaction understanding. We introduce a benchmark framework for principled zero-shot evaluation, consisting of (i) a unified taxonomy of zero-shot prompting strategies, and (ii) a methodology that transforms token-level logits into interaction scores, enabling fair comparison with specialized HOI models under standard metrics. To support prompt-based evaluation, we additionally construct new question-answer annotations for standard HOI datasets, transforming them into a format suitable for MLLMs. Building on this, we propose two visual prompting strategies, namely Objects as Context and Black Other Objects, that guide MLLMs to target objects while preserving scene context. Experiments on HICO, HICO-DET, and V-COCO demonstrate state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, achieving 53.50 mAP on HICO and 23.69 mAP on HICO-DET. Overall, our work provides a principled benchmarking framework for MLLMs in HOI, opening the door to new models and datasets and enabling flexible open-world interaction understanding.

items.title: Recasting DiT for Extreme Image Compression with Hierarchical Visual Priors
items.content: arXiv:2610.18607v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Pretrained diffusion models provide powerful generative priors for extreme image compression, but their stochastic, iterative generation processes are not designed to decode compressed representations directly. We present PrismCodec, which recasts a pretrained Diffusion Transformer (DiT) as a bitstream-grounded one-step generative decoder. PrismCodec uses the decoded representation in two complementary roles: a projected codec state defines the starting state for generation, while hierarchical visual priors derived from the same decoded latent provide semantic and structural guidance. To bridge the gap between stochastic, iterative generation and deterministic one-step decoding, we develop a progressive adaptation strategy. We first learn codec-conditioned transport from a noisy neighborhood centered on the codec state, distill it into a one-step mapping, and finally anneal the source perturbation to zero during end-to-end optimization. The resulting decoder reconstructs deterministically from the received representation without additional conditioning bits. Across Kodak, CLIC, and DIV2K, PrismCodec consistently improves rate-perception performance over prior generative codecs, achieving BD-rate reductions of 70-75% in LPIPS and 75-81% in DISTS over StableCodec. Code will be released upon acceptance.

items.title: Temporal Diffusion Bridge Model for Vessel Extraction Using Physics-informed Synthetic Data
items.content: arXiv:2610.14105v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Accurate artery extraction from X-ray coronary angiography (XCA) is essential for coronary artery disease diagnosis and intervention. However, low vessel visibility, respiratory and cardiac motion, and limited annotations challenge existing methods. Moreover, most deep learning approaches produce binary vessel masks without preserving clinically relevant intra-arterial contrast information. We propose a Temporal Diffusion Bridge Model (TDBM) that formulates vessel extraction as image translation and learns from physics-informed synthetic data without manual vessel annotations. A physics-based XCA synthesis engine generates diverse, perfectly aligned pairs of contrast-enhanced and contrast-free images. Using these pairs, TDBM learns cross-domain mappings to recover high-fidelity vessel information. Temporal conditioning incorporates adjacent frames to improve consistency, while a vessel-aware contrastive loss exploits background-invariant synthetic pairs to enhance vascular discrimination. We evaluate TDBM on two XCA vessel segmentation datasets and conduct a reader study using two real-patient XCA sequence datasets. Zero-shot segmentation is further assessed on retinal imaging and fluorescence microscopy datasets. Results demonstrate that TDBM consistently outperforms existing methods and generalizes effectively across imaging modalities. Code and trained weights will be available at: https://github.com/Advanced-AI-in-Medicine-and-Physics-Lab/TDBM

items.summary: The authors propose a Temporal Diffusion Bridge Model that formulates coronary artery extraction from X-ray angiography as image translation, trained entirely on physics-informed synthetic data without manual vessel annotations. A physics-based synthesis engine generates perfectly aligned contrast-enhanced and contrast-free image pairs, and the model preserves intra-arterial contrast information rather than producing binary masks. This matters clinically for coronary artery disease diagnosis and avoids costly annotation.

However, low vessel visibility, respiratory and cardiac motion, and limited annotations challenge existing methods. Moreover, most deep learning approaches produce binary vessel masks without preserving clinically relevant intra-arterial contrast information. We propose a Temporal Diffusion Bridge Model (TDBM) that formulates vessel extraction as image translation and learns from physics-informed synthetic data without manual vessel annotations. A physics-based XCA synthesis engine generates diverse, perfectly aligned pairs of contrast-enhanced and contrast-free images. Using these pairs, TDBM learns cross-domain mappings to recover high-fidelity vessel information. Temporal conditioning incorporates adjacent frames to improve consistency, while a vessel-aware contrastive loss exploits background-invariant synthetic pairs to enhance vascular discrimination. We evaluate TDBM on two XCA vessel segmentation datasets and conduct a reader study using two real-patient XCA sequence datasets. Zero-shot segmentation is further assessed on retinal imaging and fluorescence microscopy datasets. Results demonstrate that TDBM consistently outperforms existing methods and generalizes effectively across imaging modalities. Code and trained weights will be available at: https://github.com/Advanced-AI-in-Medicine-and-Physics-Lab/TDBM

items.title: Federated Coreset Subsampling for Distributed Memory Banks
items.content: arXiv:2610.16425v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In real-world scenarios, industrial processes can span multiple factories and goods are often produced at multiple sites, leading to a shared yet non-identical distribution of data across locations. To address this, we propose two federated approaches for i) combining existing coresets (Double Subsampling) and ii) creating new coresets (Federated Subsampling) in a distributed anomaly detection setting. In particular, we adapt the memory bank based PatchCore algorithm to a federated setting, resulting in increased cold-start performance, resilience to domain- and sensor-shift, and resilience to unreliable actor participation, a common problem in classical, network based federated learning strategies.
items.author: Jason Witzemann, Daniel Pr\"oll, Sebastian Hegenbart
items.summary: This work adapts the PatchCore memory-bank anomaly detection algorithm to federated settings spanning multiple factories with non-identical data distributions. It proposes two approaches, Double Subsampling for combining existing coresets and Federated Subsampling for creating new ones, improving cold-start performance and robustness to domain shift and unreliable participant availability. It is relevant to practical industrial deployment of anomaly detection across sites.
items.reasoning: Addresses a practical federated learning problem with sensible coreset-based solutions and attention to realistic constraints like flaky actors. Novelty is incremental but the industrial relevance and evaluation of robustness to unreliable participation add value.

items.title: Composable Dynamics for Cooperative Humanoids: A RoboCompiler Extension
items.content: arXiv:2610.14237v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Physically connected humanoids need consistent dynamics for internal actuator loops, inter-robot forces, and changing ground supports. We extend RoboCompiler with member-wise dynamics assembly, compiling reduced dynamics from rigid bodies, moving actuator parts, and reflected rotor inertias. Compiled body Jacobians and analytic constraint curvature yield an explicit Coriolis factor satisfying the power identity for floating-base quasi-velocities. A two-level reduction retains reusable robot models while composing their supports and hand connections; local inertial updates have rank at most six, and prescribed-acceleration constraint wrenches are affine in actuator efforts. These interfaces support actuator-aware tracking, coupled force allocation, payload updates, and support-mode switching for five hand-linked humanoids. Across 264 feasible states in eight humanoid configurations, normalised acceleration discrepancies remain within $1.6\!\times\!10^{-10}$ against a hard-constraint reference and $1.4\!\times\!10^{-10}$ against a compiler-independent reference; MuJoCo simulations achieve 0.73~mm root-mean-square (RMS) pelvis error in the ring dance and complete side steps through 20 support-mode changes.
items.author: Mehdi Heydari Shahna, Jouni Mattila
items.summary: This paper extends the RoboCompiler framework to handle the dynamics of physically connected humanoid robots, including internal actuator loops, inter-robot forces, and changing ground supports. It introduces member-wise dynamics assembly, analytic constraint curvature for Coriolis factorization satisfying the power identity, and a two-level reduction that reuses individual robot models while composing their physical connections. This matters for building principled, efficient control software for cooperative humanoid teams rather than ad-hoc per-robot solutions.
items.reasoning: Solid theoretical robotics contribution with clean formal properties (rank-bounded local updates, affine constraint wrenches), but it is an incremental extension of the authors' own RoboCompiler toolchain rather than a field-opening result. Impact is mostly within the dynamics-compilation and humanoid control niche, and validation scope is unclear from the abstract.

items.title: Successful but Unsafe: An Analytical Benchmark for Revealing Collisions in Vision-and-Language Navigation
items.content: arXiv:2610.14682v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) agents are typically evaluated by whether they reach a target and how efficiently they follow an instructed route, yet these metrics provide little information about collision behavior. Moreover, continuous VLN evaluation commonly uses a sliding regime, where an agent can slide along obstacles after a collision, potentially masking the effect of unsafe actions on navigation performance. We introduce VLN-Safe, a benchmark for analyzing collision safety under two complementary evaluation regimes: sliding, reflecting common VLN evaluation practice, and blocking, where collision-inducing actions prevent forward motion and more directly expose their consequences. Across six published agents on R2R-CE, 38.5-56.8% of successful episodes contain contact under sliding, while switching to blocking decreases success rate by 11.7-36.1 percentage points. We further analyze signals for anticipating imminent collisions and find that depth geometry and recent movement history are more informative than policy-derived signals, while safe alternatives near the policy's preferred action are rarely available. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a training-free collision guard that vetoes risky forward actions, executes an escape maneuver, and returns control to the original policy. Under blocking, the guard reduces collision steps by 62-98% and improves success rate by 6.9-29.3 percentage points across five recurrent, topological, and vision-language-action agents. Under sliding, it leaves success rate unchanged while raising the share of collision-free successes by 4.1-12.4 points. These results reveal a substantial gap between task success and collision-safe navigation and show that lightweight collision-aware intervention can improve both safety and navigation performance.
items.author: Hieu D. Pham, Quoc-An Luong, Dung D. Le
items.summary: VLN-Safe is a benchmark revealing that vision-and-language navigation agents collide frequently even when standard success metrics look good, evaluating under both sliding regimes (which mask collisions) and blocking regimes that expose their consequences. Across six published agents on R2R-CE, a substantial fraction of apparently successful episodes involve collisions. This highlights a safety blind spot in prevailing VLN evaluation.
items.reasoning: A useful evaluation-driven contribution that exposes a real flaw in standard VLN metrics with a well-designed dual-regime benchmark; safety-aware evaluation for embodied agents is increasingly important, though the scope is limited to one benchmark environment and analysis rather than a fix.

items.title: Training-Free Multi-Agent Cooperative Embodied Search from Uncertain Vision-Language Priors
items.content: arXiv:2610.15038v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Real-world Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to act under partial observability, where map structure, semantic cues, and target locations may be incomplete or incorrectly inferred by foundation models. This paper presents a lightweight, training-free, and uncertainty-aware framework for cooperative multi-agent multi-target search in mapless environments. Instead of learning an end-to-end navigation policy, the framework separates high-level semantic reasoning from low-level execution through a scalable graph-optimization backbone. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) serve only as hypothesis generators, proposing semantic zones, target-location cues, and possible navigable connections. These outputs are treated as uncertain priors and further refined using online observations and graph-context evidence. Cooperative navigation is then formulated as a rolling-horizon multi-agent mixed-integer linear program with a lexicographic objective that first maximizes target-directed reward and then reduces travel distance, uncertain-edge use, and repeated visits. Experiments derived from 100 Matterport3D test cases show that the proposed framework improves target coverage and search efficiency over representative baseline methods, while shared information and joint planning enable more balanced workloads across agents. By operating on an abstract graph without relying on embodiment-specific policy parameters, the framework scales across varying numbers of agents and targets, generalizes to unseen environments, and accommodates different perception modules and low-level controllers without task-specific retraining.

The contribution is somewhat incremental, combining known components (MLLM priors, graph optimization), and no major-lab backing strengthens expected impact only moderately.

items.title: nanoflann: A Header-Only KD-Tree Library for Exact Nearest-Neighbor Search on Compile-Time Product Manifolds
items.content: arXiv:2610.15215v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Nearest-neighbor (NN) search underlies countless robotics algorithms, but many state spaces are not Euclidean: orientations live on $SO(2)$ or $SO(3)$ and poses on $SE(2)$ or $SE(3)$, and a Euclidean KD-tree on their raw coordinates returns wrong neighbors. We present a header-only, dependency-free C++ KD-tree library for exact NN search on user-defined product manifolds declared at compile time: the space is composed from base manifolds ($\mathbb{R}^n$, $SO(2)$, $SO(3)$, $S^n$; products $SE(2)$, $SE(3)$, tori) with a single type alias, and the library synthesizes a metric whose pruning is provably admissible, wrap-aware for circular coordinates and double-cover-aware for unit quaternions. Experiments confirm exactness (recall $1.0$ vs an exhaustive scan under the same product metric), where the Euclidean-on-raw shortcut collapses to recall $\approx 0.5^{m}$ for $m$ rotation blocks, with up to three orders of magnitude speedup over brute force. We further contribute an incremental, self-balancing single-tree index for points under heavy churn (e.g. sliding-window LiDAR maps) or $SE(3)$ trajectories: bounded memory and faster updates than prior work, with an optional asynchronous tail-latency-bounding mode. The implementation is open source: https://github.com/jlblancoc/nanoflann
items.author: Jos\'e Luis Blanco-Claraco
items.summary: This paper introduces a header-only, dependency-free C++ library for exact nearest-neighbor search on non-Euclidean manifolds such as SO(2), SO(3), SE(2), and SE(3), which are common in robotics but handled incorrectly by standard Euclidean KD-trees. Users compose state spaces from base manifolds via a compile-time type alias, and the library synthesizes provably admissible, wrap-aware and double-cover-aware metrics for correct pruning, with experiments confirming exact recall.
items.reasoning: Solid systems and algorithms contribution addressing a real, well-known pitfall in robotics (Euclidean KD-trees on manifold-valued states returning wrong neighbors). The theoretical guarantees on admissible pruning and the practical, dependency-free design add value, but it is an incremental library extension of existing nanoflann work rather than a novel modeling or learning breakthrough, limiting broader AI impact.
