Against literature, agent-based model, and survey benchmarks, unconditional LLM recovery of association directions is modest (46-68%) but improves substantially when LLMs classify associations directly.
items.content_html: arXiv:2610.15994v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Representing individual-level behavioral heterogeneity is challenging in epidemiological modeling, particularly when empirical behavioral data are sparse. We assess the potential of large language model (LLM)-generated behavioral outputs in addressing this challenge, using hepatitis C virus-related behaviors among people who inject drugs as a case study. Correspondence with epidemiological patterns was evaluated using external benchmarks: literature-informed association directions, correlations from an agent-based model (ABM), and survey associations. Across three LLMs, unconditional directional recovery across 28 retained literature-informed associations was 46-68%, compared with 82-93% agreement when LLMs were directly asked to classify the same associations. Mean absolute differences from ABM and survey correlation patterns were 0.11-0.13 and 0.15-0.18, respectively. Together, these findings show partial alignment between LLM-generated behavioral relationships and epidemiological evidence, despite higher knowledge-probe agreement. More systematic evaluation is needed before incorporating LLM-generated behavioral outputs into epidemiological models that simulate transmission dynamics.

items.title: Interactive 4D Volumetric Liquid Forecasting under Moving-Solid Interaction
items.content: arXiv:2610.16167v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We propose the task of Interactive 4D Volumetric Liquid Forecasting: predicting the spatiotemporal evolution of a future dense 3D liquid velocity field conditioned on how a solid object moves through it. This task provides an upstream physical forecasting primitive for systems that need to reason about motion-conditioned liquid response, including robotic liquid manipulation, digital twins, and rigid-fluid video generation. Existing works have made efforts in predicting flow around static or prescribed solid geometries and synthesizing visually plausible fluid motion. Yet these approaches provide limited coverage for interactive liquid dynamics, as they are not capable of forecasting how a moving solid induces a future full-domain liquid response. In this forecasting scenario, the hydrodynamic effect is condensed near an evolving liquid-solid interface, but the prediction target is a global spatiotemporal rollout. To address this challenge, we propose a two-level recurrent forecasting framework, TIDE/TIDES: TIDE isolates localized interface-driven forecasting, while TIDES adds transport-aware coupling and explicit stabilization to reduce accumulated rollout error. Across adapted neighboring baselines, controlled component ablations, motion/size OOD tests, and long-horizon evaluation, TIDES achieves the best forecasting performance and the ablations identify localized interaction, transport coupling, and stabilization as the key contributors. Together, our task formulation, benchmark, and TIDE/TIDES study establish a controlled foundation for moving-solid-conditioned dense liquid forecasting. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/jongwonryu/TIDE-TIDES.

items.title: Hardware-Friendly Token-Group Activation Quantization for Low-Bit Mamba Super-Resolution
items.content: arXiv:2610.16261v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Mamba-based super-resolution models are efficient alternatives to Transformer-based restoration backbones, but their low-bit post-training quantization remains challenging because selective scan, Mamba's input-dependent state-space operator, induces different activation ranges across spatial tokens. Thus, a single layer-wise clipping range poorly matches all tokens. We propose Token-Group Quantization, a hardware-friendly activation PTQ framework that statically approximates a hardware-unfriendly post-scan grouping oracle, where tokens with similar preferred clipping ranges are assigned to the same group. To avoid runtime post-scan grouping in static low-bit inference, a lightweight predictor infers the groups from pre-scan features available before the quantized scan path. During calibration, we form pseudo-labels by clustering post-scan activation descriptors that capture similar rounding--clipping behavior. At inference, the frozen predictor maps pre-scan features to groups and selects entries from offline-calibrated group-wise clipping-bound tables, without runtime statistics collection, dynamic clipping updates, or post-scan group assignment. To address low-bit restoration degradation, we further introduce a Frequency-Preserving Refinement (FPR) objective for clipping-bound calibration. FPR aligns Fourier amplitude and phase between full-precision teacher and quantized student outputs to preserve high-frequency structures. Across PTQ protocols, bit-widths, backbones, and tasks, our method consistently outperforms prior Mamba and SR PTQ baselines, transfers to Transformer SR and Vision Mamba classification, composes with rotation-based quantization, and achieves 2.23x speedup on Jetson Orin Nano over FP16. Code is available here.

items.title: When a Conceptor Complement Becomes Gain: Operator Geometry and Behavioral Attribution in Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.16325v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: When a steering intervention changes a language model's behavior, which part of the intervention deserves the credit? We test this question for a target-centered, scaled conceptor complement by removing its fitted covariance filter while preserving the same target-specific center and gain. At the original aperture $\alpha=.05$ and gain $\beta=2$, all 21 fitted maps across three models and seven targets expand every direction at the generation intervention layers. The matrix correction is $0.093\%$--$7.815\%$ of the matched-control displacement on held-out extraction activations. In 480 paired comparisons within a 1,920-response study, retaining the matrix changes many individual texts but does not establish a consistent additional target-suppression benefit on the four-target panel. A geometric aperture sweep shows that the operating regime changes with the filter setting. Separately, an invertible soft filter preserves what an unrestricted affine readout can recover, whereas dedicated erasure methods reduce prediction by newly fitted probes. Together, the results show why a whole-intervention comparison cannot by itself attribute generated behavior to the fitted matrix: analyze the complete transformation, hold shared components fixed, and test its output consequences directly.

items.reasoning: Careful ablation and attribution work on activation steering mechanics is valuable for interpretability, and the operator-geometry framing is rigorous. items.title: SLS-Bench: A Benchmark for Incident Log Summarization with Synthetic Observability Data
items.content: arXiv:2610.16412v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As IT systems grow in complexity, automated agent-driven incident response becomes increasingly critical. A key capability for these agents is summarizing large log streams into human-readable reports. Further progress requires meaningfully evaluating this function, yet existing benchmarks leave end-to-end summarization from large log streams underexplored due to the prohibitive cost and complexity of collecting real-world data. We introduce SLS-Bench, a benchmark for incident log summarization featuring 90 tasks grounded in real-world incident reports, each with a synthetic log stream and a reference summary. To construct SLS-Bench, we developed a data generation pipeline that converts incident reports into structured incident models, which guide the generation of synthetic logs and reference summaries. This pipeline combines narrative grounding, explicit incident modeling, generator-verifier loops, and statistical comparisons with real-world log streams to produce realistic and controllable observability data. Our evaluation of 14 LLMs on SLS-Bench shows that while frontier models can produce useful summaries, they do so at substantial cost and latency, and open-weight models lag significantly. SLS-Bench provides a framework for systematic evaluation of log analysis agents and a scalable blueprint for future synthetic observability benchmarks.

items.title: Separating Prompt Harmfulness from Interaction Safety via Partial Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.16761v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: LLM-based information systems need safety guardrails. Most guardrails classify the prompt alone. If the prompt looks harmful, the system rejects it before any answer is generated. This is costly. Many rejected prompts would have received a safe response. Users lose help they should have received from the information system. This cost grows as conversational and generative search becomes common. Prompt-level labels treat harm as a property of the query. But harm depends on what the model actually writes. Existing input-output guards do look at responses. But they judge a finished response, so the decision comes after full generation. However, we observe that safety of model interaction with the input prompt can be inferred early with only partial output. So the system can start generating, watch the partial response, and stop only if it turns harmful. We test this idea in three steps. First, we build a dataset of 41,944 prompt-response pairs with seven open weights LLMs from three families: Llama, Gemma, and Qwen. Second, we show that prompt harmfulness and interaction safety differ. Prompt labels and response labels agree on only 50.46\% of items (Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.06). Of the prompts that make any model respond harmfully, only 3.5\% do so for all seven LLMs. Third, we show that partial responses carry most of the signal. Fine-tuned classifiers predict response-level harm well (best AUPRC 0.885, F1 0.807). About one third of the response tokens recover almost full-response AUPRC.
items.author: Ram Vikas Mishra, Shashank Aggarwal, Jahnavi Kumar, Amit Awekar
items.summary: Argues that prompt-only safety guardrails over-reject, since harm depends on what the model actually writes, while output guards judge only completed responses. The paper proposes inferring interaction safety early from partial generation, separating prompt harmfulness from interaction safety to reduce unnecessary refusals in conversational information systems.
items.reasoning: A practically relevant safety-efficiency trade-off: partial-generation safety checks could reduce over-blocking while catching harm earlier than full-output guards. The core idea is intuitive rather than deeply novel, and the truncated abstract leaves empirical strength unclear.

items.title: Transparent Information Flow Modeling for Role-Aware AI Act Assessment
items.content: arXiv:2610.16916v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act introduces a structured framework for governing high-risk AI systems, emphasizing transparency, risk management, and role-specific accountability. However, current assessment practices often rely on monolithic system views or disconnected checklists, limiting their ability to capture the socio-technical complexity of real-world deployments. We explore the use of the Information Flow Methodology (IFM), a modeling-based approach to AI Act compliance assessment. IFM represents decision systems -- whether algorithmic, human, or hybrid -- as networks of information sites and transformation channels, enabling structured analysis of how information, decisions, and responsibilities flow across organizational and technical boundaries. We apply IFM in a real-world case involving a recruitment support tool used by a public-sector organization, evaluating both the Provider's system and the Deployer's recruitment process. Our results demonstrate that IFM can serve as a scaffold to bridge both component-based and holistic perspectives, and how technical systems are situated within socio-technical contexts. In doing so, IFM supports transparency, identifies risk pathways, and enables alignment analysis between intended and actual use. We argue that such modeling provides a foundational tool for effective, context-sensitive AI governance and accountability -- offering capabilities beyond conventional checklist-based assessments.

items.title: Encounter-Driven City-Scale Human Mobility Generation with Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.17672v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for human mobility generation by modeling individual routines, activities, and mobility preferences. However, existing approaches remain largely resident-centric: generating realistic individual trajectories does not necessarily recover the encounters that emerge when multiple residents co-occur at the same place and time. To this end, we study encounter-aware human mobility generation, which jointly preserves individual mobility and population-level interaction structure. We propose EncounterMob, an encounter-driven LLM framework consisting of a coarse-to-fine Encounter Generator and an Iterative Coupling Framework. The Encounter Generator first captures city-level encounter rhythms and then instantiates participant-time-venue encounters, while the Iterative Coupling Framework coordinates these encounters with personal mobility behavior through successive refinement. We further introduce an encounter recovery protocol covering encounter marginal and joint distributions over residents, times, and venues. Experiments on the Japan and NYC datasets show that EncounterMob outperforms all external baselines on all seven encounter metrics and all six personal mobility metrics. Compared with ELLMob, it reduces the participant-time-venue joint error by 40.4%/41.7% and the mean personal mobility error by 58.8%/32.7% on Japan/NYC, respectively.

The work has applications in urban planning, epidemiology, and simulation.

items.title: Autonomous 3D Visual-Thermal Inspection for Utility-Scale Solar Farms
items.content: arXiv:2610.17762v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) inspection is dominated by aerial surveys, which are effective for identifying module-level hot cells but provide limited visibility of critical components located under the array, including connectors, cabling, fasteners and structural elements. These assets are difficult to inspect consistently at scale, and their defects are often spatially small, partially occluded and difficult to localise from isolated images. We present an automated 3D visual-thermal inspection system (Tricorder) for under-panel PV asset inspection. The approach combines LiDAR-inertial Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) with geometrically calibrated RGB and thermal imagery and machine-learning-based object detection and segmentation. Detected assets are associated with the reconstructed 3D environment, allowing visual and thermal observations from multiple viewpoints to be spatially fused and localised. We demonstrate the approach on utility-scale PV data for MC4 connector detection and connection-state recognition, thermal anomaly identification, and detection of structural components including bolts, nuts and torque tubes. The results demonstrate a pathway from image-based inspection toward spatially grounded autonomous inspection, where defects are detected and linked to specific assets and their 3D locations within the solar farm.

items.title: Consider, Then Choose: Order-Invariant Decisions in System One Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.18233v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: System One models answer typed questions in a single forward pass and promise the same answer for the same input. For choice questions, this promise fails: the answer depends on the order of the options, increasingly so as they grow in number, and averaging over their cyclic shifts reduces this dependence without removing it. Scoring each option alone, which the order cannot affect, shows that the order changes the answer mostly when the model is unsure among its top few options, even though the listwise answer looks confident. We therefore propose $\textbf{Runoff}$, which considers, then chooses: it scores each option alone to keep a few candidates, then compares them in listings where each candidate takes every position. It needs no training and can run in two forward passes, and its answer does not depend on the option order by construction. On two open models and five datasets, it changes no answer under shuffling, against 9.3% for cyclic averaging, and with 20 options it is about as accurate and three to four times faster. Wrapped around eight System One models, it removes the order dependence of the five benchmarks, while cyclic averaging changes up to 15.4%.
items.author: Jianguo Huang, Yao Long Teng, Yanchen Deng, Bo An
items.summary: The paper shows that single-forward-pass models violate order invariance on multiple-choice questions, especially when unsure among top options even while looking listwise-confident. It proposes Runoff, a training-free method that scores options individually to shortlist candidates, then compares them in listings where each candidate occupies every position. This reduces order sensitivity without training.
items.reasoning: Clear-eyed analysis of a well-known positional-bias problem with a simple, deployable fix; the diagnosis linking order dependence to uncertainty is informative. Incremental over existing permutation-averaging work, hence a moderate score.

For choice questions, this promise fails: the answer depends on the order of the options, increasingly so as they grow in number, and averaging over their cyclic shifts reduces this dependence without removing it. Scoring each option alone, which the order cannot affect, shows that the order changes the answer mostly when the model is unsure among its top few options, even though the listwise answer looks confident. We therefore propose $\textbf{Runoff}$, which considers, then chooses: it scores each option alone to keep a few candidates, then compares them in listings where each candidate takes every position. It needs no training and can run in two forward passes, and its answer does not depend on the option order by construction. On two open models and five datasets, it changes no answer under shuffling, against 9.3% for cyclic averaging, and with 20 options it is about as accurate and three to four times faster. Wrapped around eight System One models, it removes the order dependence of the five benchmarks, while cyclic averaging changes up to 15.4%.

items.title: AssetForge: Asset-Augmented Task Synthesis for Business Automation Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.18330v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Training business automation agents requires executable tasks that connect a natural-language request to an application state and a verifiable end state. Traditional Rubrics requires Authors to recreate application interfaces, initial records, policy evidence, and outcome checks for each task, entangling business logic with repeated infrastructure work. We introduce AssetForge, an asset-augmented task-construction pipeline that pairs a reusable construction-asset library with task-specific Rubrics. The assets provide application interfaces, world-state components, policy/evidence carriers, and native assertion definitions; the Rubric directs their instantiation for a particular business task. Executable checks and an additional model-based review validate each candidate, return targeted feedback, and support bounded repair before acceptance. On AutomationBench v1.0.6 public-600, fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on 6,000 AssetForge examples yields 41.17% on the official strict pass@1 metric, 4.4 times the 9.33% base score (+31.83 points). With the same backbone and GLM-5.3 supervision, AssetForge reaches 41.17% versus 30.33% for traditional Rubrics, a 10.84-point gain (35.7% relative) at the same accepted-example scale (6,000 versus 6,000 examples). Both DeepSeek- and GLM-supervised AssetForge models improve AppWorld completion over the base model on Test-Normal and Test-Challenge. These results establish the advantage of AssetForge's complete construction pipeline on AutomationBench public: the coupled asset-Rubric interface directs Authors toward business logic, while executable checks and model-based review validate their tasks.

items.title: AgentStripes: An Evidence-Graded Maturity Model for AI Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.18603v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Benchmarks report what an Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent can do on a task suite, but not whether one released version has been engineered with the controls that make it reliable, safe and observable, or how strongly that is shown. This paper proposes AgentStripes, an evidence-graded maturity model for AI agents. It defines levels (0 to 7 stripes), process areas (12 areas holding 40 capabilities), three gates (basic, safety, proof) that hold an agent at a level however high its score, and evidence grades E0 to E5. Each applicable capability receives a rating from 0 to 3 and a separate evidence level; these are combined into a credit, aggregated into a severity-weighted score and converted into stripes that the gates limit. Instruments gather evidence, language-model judges interpret it under explicit criteria, and the arithmetic is deterministic. The model is compared with standards at topic level without a claim of conformance, and an unexecuted validation protocol is specified. An empirical evaluation (exploratory, non-confirmatory) of 30 public Python agent repositories, with static evidence only, is a demonstration and not a validation: static evidence caps every final stripe at 2, 26 repositories end at one stripe and 4 at two, and this distinction is unreliable, since re-judging changed the final stripe of 4 of 22 repositories (engine, dossier and panel changed), whereas none of 8 panel-only repeats, all at stripe 1, changed. The parameters are expert conventions without outcome based calibration, and the stripes have not been shown to predict reliability or safety.

items.title: AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards
items.content: arXiv:2610.18860v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction. We therefore introduce AesCode, which generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance. To do so, AesCode represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and makes each property attributable. From this graph, we derive complementary cross-modal rewards: deterministic verifiers score properties parsable from code and rendering, while a VLM judge assesses the non-parsable ones with a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements and relations. We optimize these decoupled rewards through reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization to jointly improve spatial planning, aesthetic quality, and verifiable correctness. To evaluate this setting, we build a benchmark that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with visual scores highly consistent with human judgments. We find that reference images substantially improve the visual quality of code generated by existing models, and ablations show that AesCode benefits from references both as model input and as a source of visual rewards. Relative to same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines given the same references, AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points, reaching scores comparable to those of closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8.

items.title: SharedSAE: a unified sparse dictionary across u-net blocks and denoising time for diffusion models
items.content: arXiv:2610.13997v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Concept representations in diffusion models drift across network depth and denoising time, yet existing sparse autoencoders offer only per-block or per-timestep dictionaries, leaving no single feature dictionary for localization and intervention in the network. We present Shared Sparse Autoencoder (SharedSAE), which learns one sparse dictionary shared across four U-Net attention blocks and all 50 denoising steps of SDXL 1.0. A block-specific low-rank input adapter aligns the residual distribution of each block before the shared encoder, and a temporal conditioning module with a shared timestep branch and a block-timestep correction branch absorbs temporal non-stationarity. Despite spanning both axes, Shared SAE preserves a coherent dictionary structure. Built on the shared dictionary, localized feature suppression reduces the number of NudeNet-positive generations in the I2P detector-positive subset from 139 to 1. Tracing sparse features across the trajectory further reveals that concept representations are redistributed across U-Net blocks during generation, shifting from the earliest downsampling block toward intermediate and later blocks as denoising proceeds. SharedSAE thus provides a unified, interpretable, and intervention-ready representation space for diffusion models, enabling concept analysis and erasure at any covered block and denoising step.

items.title: LabInstruct: Benchmarking Situated Instructional Video Generation for Lab Procedures
items.content: arXiv:2610.14020v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) aim to automate the full experimental loop, from scientific decision-making to physical execution. Ideally, AI-generated plans could be carried out directly by robotic systems, but reliable automation remains difficult in complex, open-world laboratory environments, where experiments often involve fine-grained manipulation, long-horizon procedures, and substantial variation across tasks and setups. Humans therefore remain an important execution interface between AI-generated plans and physical experiments, creating a need for clear and effective human-facing experimental guidance. Because laboratory procedures are inherently visual, spatial, and dynamic, video is particularly well suited to communicating apparatus configurations, manipulation actions, temporal dependencies, and state changes. Recent advances in video generation now make it possible to synthesize experimental demonstrations directly from an initial workspace image and a natural-language instruction. However, whether such models can reliably communicate real laboratory procedures has not been systematically studied. We introduce LabInstruct, a benchmark for situated instructional video generation in real laboratories. LabInstruct contains 204 tasks across 5 scientific disciplines, with real reference executions and structured annotations of objects, actions, contacts, and state transitions. Evaluating 8 frontier image-to-video models, we find that visually plausible generations frequently remain procedurally incorrect, revealing a substantial gap between visual realism and the reliability required for experimental instruction.

items.summary: LabInstruct is a benchmark for evaluating AI-generated instructional videos that guide humans executing lab procedures in self-driving laboratories. It targets the human-in-the-loop gap where AI plans still require human execution, assessing whether video generation can produce clear, spatially grounded experimental guidance.
items.reasoning: Addresses a genuinely underexplored intersection of video generation, scientific automation, and human-AI teaming. As a benchmark contribution its impact depends on adoption, and video generation evaluation remains noisy.

items.title: Beyond Gate Weights: Decision-Level Interpretation of Radiomics-Image Feature Fusion for RCC Classification
items.content: arXiv:2610.14152v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Gate coefficients describe how a fusion layer weights intermediate features, but they do not necessarily reflect the magnitude of branch contributions at the classifier output. We investigate this distinction in a fixed 3D MedVAE--radiomics model for clear cell versus non-clear cell renal cell carcinoma classification from contrast-enhanced CT. Because the model uses a linear classification head, the binary decision logit can be decomposed exactly into a gated image term, a direct radiomics term, and a bias. We define effective radiomics dominance as the direct radiomics term's share of the summed absolute non-bias branch contributions and compare it with structural radiomics weighting. Internally, mean structural radiomics weighting was 0.823, whereas mean effective radiomics dominance was 0.148, with a modest case-wise association (\r{ho} = 0.290). The gated image term retained substantially stronger discriminative ranking information than the direct radiomics term. The same structural-to-effective discrepancy was observed in exploratory external evaluation. Branch-targeted permutation, integrated-gradient, and Shapley-style analyses further identified radiomics descriptors influencing the direct radiomics term. Because radiomics also generates the gate, the gated image term remains radiomics-dependent, so additive branch contribution should not be interpreted as total input influence. These findings show that structural gate weighting and decision-level branch contribution represent distinct aspects of gated feature fusion and should be interpreted separately.

It defines effective radiomics dominance as the radiomics term's share of output-level contributions and contrasts it with structural gate weighting. The finding has implications for how multimodal fusion interpretability is measured.

items.title: Co-adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining for Structured Knowledge Retrieval
items.content: arXiv:2610.14465v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Structured knowledge retrieval acquires task-relevant evidence from structured knowledge sources for downstream tasks. Existing methods rely on unconstrained retrieval or predefined query-rule supervision, such as author-paper rules for scientific discovery and anatomy-drug rules for precision medicine. Such supervision is rarely available in practice. We propose Co-Adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining Retrieval (CoRE), which jointly learns which reasoning rule to assign to each query and how to retrieve evidence under that rule, without predefined query-rule pairs. A routing agent selects a rule, and its corresponding retriever traverses the knowledge base and ranks evidence that satisfies the rule's constraints. Because routing and retrieval are interdependent, CoRE alternates between reinforcement learning for the routing policy and contrastive learning for the rule-constrained retriever. The selected rules provide supervision for retriever training, while retrieval performance rewards the routing policy. This closed-loop process enables both components to co-adapt without explicit query-rule supervision. Experiments on STaRK-QA datasets across scientific discovery, biomedical reasoning, and e-commerce knowledge management demonstrate CoRE's effectiveness. Ablations show the benefit of co-adapting the router and retriever. Generation-based routing transfers across datasets and benefits from multi-domain pretraining followed by target-specific fine-tuning. Analysis of rule usage across queries also informs automatic rule refinement and discovery.

A routing agent selects a rule and a corresponding retriever traverses and ranks rule-constrained evidence.

items.title: GG-Nav: Goal-oriented Grounding Chain-of-Thought Elicits Reasoning in Navigation Foundation Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.14541v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Emerging strong Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have advanced navigation foundation models. However, these models still have unsatisfactory performance on goal-oriented navigation settings. In this paper, we first conduct a motivating study revealing that the key issue lies in the insufficient utilization of streaming observations and imprecise target localization. To tackle these challenges, we propose GG-Nav, a simple yet effective navigation framework that learns a structured chain-of-thought (CoT) mechanism via supervised fine-tuning to explicitly localize goal-relevant instances, accumulate grounding evidence, and support more reliable decision-making. Specifically, the structured CoT is designed with two key stages: (i) Observation-to-Evidence, which reasons over all intermediate frames between adjacent decision steps to retain useful goal-related evidence; and (ii) Evidence-to-Decision, which integrates the current observation with accumulated evidence to ground the target and support the generation of navigation actions or clarification questions. Extensive experiments show that GG-Nav outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of success rates on the HM3D ObjectNav, VL-LN, and CoIN benchmarks by 3.1%, 16.6%, and 5.3%, respectively. Ablation studies further show that accumulating evidence from intermediate observations reduces evidence-missing failures by 11.6%, while explicit grounding reduces stopping errors by 49.4%. We also deploy GG-Nav on a Unitree Go2 robot, demonstrating its zero-shot generalization capability in unseen real-world environments.

A motivating study attributes failures to underused observations and imprecise target localization.
items.reasoning: A reasonable combination of CoT supervision with navigation foundation models, with a clear diagnostic motivating study. However, structured CoT fine-tuning is a well-established recipe and gains over existing VLM navigation baselines appear incremental.

items.title: YOUDrive: Driving Style as a Composable Direction for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
items.content: arXiv:2610.14802v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: End-to-end driving policies can achieve strong task performance while offering limited control over their driving style. Driving style describes how a vehicle accelerates, brakes, and maintains distance. Policies trained without explicit preference conditioning lack a direct mechanism for adjusting these behaviors at inference. We propose YOUDrive, a vision--language--action planner for continuous and composable driving-style control. Each teacher's behavior is distilled into a task vector, a learned parameter update that induces a style direction in the planner's representation. These directions can be scaled and combined at inference without retraining the backbone. items.title: GAMW: Generation-Aware Mel-Domain Watermarking for TTS Traceability
items.content: arXiv:2610.15082v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: As text-to-speech (TTS) systems continue to advance, provenance tracking and security verification of synthesized speech have become increasingly important. Audio watermarking provides active provenance by embedding imperceptible, machine-recoverable information into speech. However, existing post-hoc methods typically modify the waveform after synthesis, leaving the watermark vulnerable to compound perturbations. To address this limitation, we propose GAMW, a watermark injection framework integrated into the TTS generation process. Before waveform synthesis, GAMW embeds a content-adaptive multi-bit watermark residual into the generated representation, and its decoding objective combines focal modulation with dynamic per-bit weighting. We train and evaluate GAMW separately on two TTS backbones. With a 16-bit payload, GAMW improves decoding accuracy over the strongest baseline by 9.2 and 23.5 percentage points under individual and compound perturbations, respectively, while maintaining competitive speech quality. Reliable clean-speech decoding is also retained at higher payloads. Code is available at https://github.com/ZConJugaTe/GAMW.

items.title: HGA-Quant: Heterogeneity-Aware Quantization for AutoRegressive Visual Generation Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.15297v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recently, AutoRegressive Visual Generation (ARVG) models have emerged as a competitive paradigm for high-quality image synthesis. However, their substantial computational and memory demands make them difficult to deploy on resource-constrained edge devices. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) provides a promising solution to reduce the computational and memory costs of ARVG models, yet existing methods often suffer from substantial image quality degradation under low-bit quantization. In this paper, we propose a training-free PTQ framework for ARVG, consisting of Tail-Aware Bounded-init Grid Refinement (T-BGR) and Coarse-to-Fine Activation Precision Scheduling (CAPS). T-BGR introduces a tail-aware reconstruction objective for weight quantizer calibration, assigning greater importance to distribution-tail coefficients and preserving fine-grained information without introducing additional parameters or high-precision branches. CAPS performs coarse-to-fine activation precision scheduling by jointly considering the importance and computational cost of different generation stages, enabling efficient mixed-precision allocation under a given bit budget. Extensive experiments on multiple ARVG backbones demonstrate that our framework consistently improves robustness under aggressive low-bit quantization. Notably, on Infinity, our framework achieves near full-precision image generation quality at an effective W4A5.6 activation precision, while existing methods at W4A6 still exhibit noticeable quality degradation or inconsistent performance. Code is available at https://github.com/lxm-lc/HGA-Quant.

items.title: In-Place Indic Tokenizer Expansion and Continual Pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B
items.content: arXiv:2610.15373v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We adapted Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B for eight Indian languages without changing its backbone architecture. We expanded the vocabulary in place from 131,072 to 163,072 entries using continued byte-pair encoding and AdaptMix rebalancing, reducing tokens per word by 38.6%. We initialized new input and output rows by averaging their original constituent rows, then trained them on 90% Indic and 10% English text before updating the backbone. Continual pretraining then progressed through broad training, high-quality annealing, and long-context training over approximately 1.27 trillion tokens. The annealed checkpoint gained 12.9 points on the Indic MILU benchmark but lost 3.4 on English MMLU. We also report practical negative results. Direct token addition underperformed continued byte-pair encoding. AdamW weight decay changed rows intended to stay fixed. Perplexity on an Indic-heavy holdout did not select the learning rate that best preserved English performance.

items.summary: This companion paper details the tokenizer expansion technique: growing the vocabulary in place from 131,072 to 163,072 entries using continued byte-pair encoding and careful initialization of new embedding rows from decompositions of their constituent rows, followed by roughly 1.27 trillion tokens of continual pretraining. It reports honest negative results alongside a 12.9-point gain on Indic MILU with a 3.4-point loss on English MMLU.

items.title: REPRO: Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimizer for Automated LLM Red-Teaming
items.content: arXiv:2610.15513v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts that bypass their safety training. Existing automated red-teaming methods either require privileged access unavailable in production, rely on manually engineered per-model templates, or optimize a single objective without population-level diversity. We present REPRO (Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimization), a pure black-box framework that discovers adversarial prompts through evolutionary optimization driven entirely by a compressed open-weight 7B reflective model on a single consumer GPU. REPRO introduces two mechanisms absent from prior work, both isolated in a component ablation: semantic crossover, an LLM-guided multi-parent recombination operator, and Bayesian strategy selection via Thompson Sampling informed by structured failure analysis.   We catalog REPRO's behavior on AdvBench, JailbreakBench, and HarmBench across 36 target models from 11 families, including GPT-5-nano, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Grok-4.1. Under our protocol REPRO reaches 100\% attack success rate (ASR) on every evaluated target in a single turn, at a median of 24 target queries per behavior. Two properties of the protocol qualify that figure. The judge scoring candidates during optimization also produces the reported ASR, and search halts when it accepts, so ASR reports whether search succeeded within the iteration budget rather than success at a fixed budget. All baseline figures are transcribed from their original papers, which use different judges, budgets, and model versions. We therefore present this as a catalog of model coverage under one protocol rather than a head-to-head ranking, and develop both qualifications in the paper.

items.title: TabMosaic: Unified In-Context Diffusion for Tabular Generative Tasks
items.content: arXiv:2610.15699v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Generative modeling for tabular data has advanced to the point where models can synthesize realistic records, recover missing values, and generate samples conditioned on class labels or observed attributes. Despite recent advances, existing approaches either require table-specific training or restrict in-context learning to single-cell prediction. In this work, we formulate these tabular generative tasks as a single problem: modeling the joint conditional distribution of an arbitrary set of target cells given the observed cells of an unseen table. To this end, we turn to diffusion, whose denoising objective is defined jointly over all target cells rather than one cell at a time. Under the pretraining distribution, this objective is minimized by the posterior predictive distribution over the target set. Building on this, we propose TabMosaic, a unified in-context diffusion model for generating mixed-type target cells in unseen, potentially incomplete tables without table-specific training. We further show that its pretraining objective bounds the conditional negative log-likelihood and the divergence from the posterior predictive for arbitrary target sets, extending the Bayesian account of in-context learning from a single-value prediction to joint multi-cell generation. Across 48 real-world tables, TabMosaic ranks first on all evaluated generative tasks against 20 baseline approaches

This enables in-context learning across multiple tabular tasks without table-specific training, going beyond prior single-cell in-context approaches.
items.reasoning: A clean unification of tabular generative tasks under one diffusion formulation with in-context capability, in a domain (tabular ML) of high practical importance. Novelty is moderate since both tabular diffusion and in-context tabular models exist, but the joint framing is well executed.

items.title: SkillMarker: A KGW-Based Watermarking Method for Agent Skill Ownership Verification
items.content: arXiv:2610.15725v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Agent skills encode operational procedures and domain expertise as reusable knowledge assets, yet their distribution in plaintext exposes them to unauthorized copying and leakage. However, practical mechanisms for skill ownership verification and leakage tracing remain underdeveloped. Watermark embedding before distribution offers a potential solution, but structured, compact skill instructions impose stringent requirements for factual and procedural accuracy. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillMarker, a KGW-based watermarking method that jointly targets functionality preservation and strong watermark embedding. SkillMarker unifies quality-constrained rewriting with signal-oriented candidate search. The former separates essential knowledge from flexible expression to preserve instruction fidelity; the latter explores alternative expressions to obtain a stronger watermark signal under preservation constraints. We release an open-source toolkit that integrates watermark embedding, quality auditing, and detection to support the protection of agent skills. SkillMarker targets ownership verification and leakage tracing in distributed skill ecosystems, where content may be copied in whole or in part, or incorporated into other skills.

It unifies quality-constrained rewriting with signal-oriented candidate search to balance functionality and watermark strength. This addresses an emerging gap in IP protection for agent knowledge assets.

items.title: OT-FlowRec: Optimal Transport-Guided Multi-Bridge Flow for Multimodal Sequential Recommendation
items.content: arXiv:2610.16038v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: E-commerce user preferences evolve dynamically within sessions, exhibiting concurrent and multi-centric interest distributions. While existing multimodal sequential recommendation methods leverage global attention to compress historical interactions, they inadequately capture the concurrent nature of multi-interest behaviors and fail to model the underlying multi-centric distribution of user intent. To tackle this issue, we propose OT-FlowRec, an optimal transport-guided multi-bridge flow matching framework that explicitly models multi-interest distributions to facilitate multimodal sequential recommendation. Unlike single-path generative models, OT-FlowRec constructs a mixture of parallel, interest-specific transport flows to model the multi-centric distribution characteristics, where each flow preserves a distinct user interest cluster via an optimal transport plan. Then, a geometric transport mechanism is designed to establish minimum-cost paths from the latent multi-interest distribution to target preference prototypes to provide multi-interest awareness. Moreover, a progressive time-sampling warmup strategy dynamically biases optimization weights toward the final states of the generation process, bridging the gap between continuous global distribution fitting and practical top-$k$ ranking metrics. This approach achieves explicit interest disentanglement, ensuring the preservation of a multi-peaked preference representation instead of collapsing it into a unimodal average. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that OT-FlowRec outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines.

items.title: Reflected Proximal Dynamics for Accelerated High-Accuracy Log-Concave Sampling
items.content: arXiv:2610.16248v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study sampling from $\pi(x)\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V(x)}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $V$ is $\alpha$-strongly convex and $\beta$-smooth with condition number $\kappa=\beta/\alpha$. For this problem, the proximal sampler preserves the target exactly and recovers overdamped Langevin dynamics in the small-step limit, but its Gaussian resampling step discards directional information. Underdamped Langevin dynamics retains such information through momentum to accelerate exploration, motivating a proximal construction that combines target preservation with directional persistence. We introduce \textit{reflected proximal dynamics}, which combines proximal sampling with an exact reflection of the auxiliary variable, conditional kinetic motion, and controlled refreshment. We develop two realizations: a flux-resampled underdamped half-turn and a persistent-momentum quarter-turn. From a warm start with constant $\chi^2$ divergence, both methods achieve total variation error $\varepsilon$ using $\widetilde O(\sqrt{\kappa}d^{1/4})$ expected oracle queries. We further remove the supplied warm-start assumption by combining either sampler with existing posterior samplers in a proximal initialization stage with an optimized coarse step size. Accounting for both initialization and sampling yields $\widetilde O(\kappa^{6/7}d^{1/4})$ expected oracle queries. In both regimes, the dependence on the target accuracy $\varepsilon$ is $\mathrm{polylog}(1/\varepsilon)$, making reflected proximal dynamics a promising framework for accelerated high-accuracy log-concave sampling.

This aims to improve acceleration and high-accuracy sampling guarantees.

items.title: MixLID: Token-Level Language Identification in Mixed-Language Text
items.content: arXiv:2610.16601v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Processing multilingual text requires both identifying a broad range of languages and distinguishing the language of each token in inputs containing multiple languages. We introduce MixLID, a token-level language identification model supporting 111 language-script combinations. MixLID follows a two-stage training process: it first learns to distinguish individual languages using the language labels of monolingual examples, then continues training on mixed-language data. The second stage uses concatenated examples from existing code-switching data alongside augmented examples created through word substitution based on correspondences between English source words and loanwords. For monolingual identification, MixLID outperforms all baselines in both accuracy and macro F1 on four benchmarks within the language coverage shared with each baseline. For mixed-language identification, it outperforms the baselines in identifying the language of individual tokens on every evaluated language pair. MixLID achieves high performance across a broad range of languages in both monolingual and mixed-language settings. The model is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/nlpai-lab/MixLID.
items.author: Seongtae Hong, Youngjoon Jang, Seungyoon Lee, Jungseob Lee, Heuiseok Lim
items.summary: MixLID is a token-level language identification model covering 111 language-script combinations, trained in two stages: monolingual language discrimination followed by mixed-language training using code-switching data and loanword-based substitution augmentation. It outperforms all baselines on monolingual identification and handles token-level mixed text.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.16601v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Processing multilingual text requires both identifying a broad range of languages and distinguishing the language of each token in inputs containing multiple languages. We introduce MixLID, a token-level language identification model supporting 111 language-script combinations. MixLID follows a two-stage training process: it first learns to distinguish individual languages using the language labels of monolingual examples, then continues training on mixed-language data. The second stage uses concatenated examples from existing code-switching data alongside augmented examples created through word substitution based on correspondences between English source words and loanwords. For monolingual identification, MixLID outperforms all baselines in both accuracy and macro F1 on four benchmarks within the language coverage shared with each baseline. For mixed-language identification, it outperforms the baselines in identifying the language of individual tokens on every evaluated language pair. MixLID achieves high performance across a broad range of languages in both monolingual and mixed-language settings. The model is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/nlpai-lab/MixLID.

items.title: Comparing GenAI to Machine Learning and Manual Review for eDiscovery
items.content: arXiv:2610.16925v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Keeling et al. [Keeling2026Generative] report on a case study recently conducted by Redgrave LLP in which they assert that Relativity's Generative AI Review tool (aiR) achieved 88% recall while Relativity Assisted Learning (RAL), its machine-learning tool, achieved 64% recall. These results are not comparable because the methods employed have different objectives, because of inter-assessor disagreement, and because they represent different recall-precision and cost-benefit trade-offs. Our analysis of the Redgrave data indicates that, when these differences are taken into account, aiR and manual review are comparable. Furthermore, established machine-learning models employing Continuous Active Learning (CAL) show state-of-the-art effectiveness, and superior efficiency, when trained only on a sample of 2,000 first-pass-reviewer responsiveness determinations.
items.author: Gordon V. Cormack, Maura R. Grossman, Jeremy Pickens
items.summary: This analysis critiques a Redgrave LLP case study claiming Relativity's generative AI review tool achieved 88% recall versus 64% for its ML tool, arguing the comparison conflates different objectives, ignores inter-assessor disagreement, and mixes recall-precision and cost-benefit trade-offs. Reanalyzing the data, the authors find generative AI and manual review comparable, while continuous active learning remains state of the art. It matters for how AI tool claims in legal technology are evaluated.
items.reasoning: Valuable corrective analysis from highly authoritative eDiscovery researchers (Cormack and Grossman), but it is commentary and reanalysis of one case study rather than new research, limiting novelty despite its practical significance for the legal AI market.

items.title: MAGNET: Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network for Connectome Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.17014v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Functional brain connectome represents neural connectivity as a matrix of pairwise interactions between brain regions. Generation of functional connectomes is not only a question of validity; rather, having satisfied the constraints on the correlation matrix, the next step is to recover the class-conditional geometry buried under coarse labels. We propose MAGNET, a Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network which uses a normalized-Cholesky representation of the manifold of correlation matrices that guarantees validity. MAGNET lifts noisy latent states into ROI-level region tokens and performs denoising with a relational inductive bias over brain atlas regions. To deal with structural problems induced by coarse labels, MAGNET employs class-anchored conditioning, amortized structural bridge, and relevance-preserving corruption. Across ABIDE, ADNI, and OASIS-3, MAGNET consistently achieves favorable results compared to previous manifold-aware approaches, demonstrating improvements of 7-21% in class-conditional fidelity ($\alpha,\beta$-F1) across three cohorts and better sampling efficiency. Moreover, while training only with strict binary labels, MAGNET is capable of maintaining clinical heterogeneity through fine substructure of the connectomes in a zero-shot setting, improving subclass covariance alignment ($\lambda$-MSE) by over 30%. These results suggest that geometric validity is a necessary but insufficient condition for clinical utility in connectome synthesis. Moreover, efforts in making the diffusion denoising class-conditional manifold aware finds utility beyond the highly curved brain connectome generation as this is a critical problem in various general settings. The code repository can be found at https://github.com/protyayofficial/MAGNET.

items.summary: MAGNET generates functional brain connectomes using a graph diffusion network operating on a normalized-Cholesky representation of the correlation matrix manifold, guaranteeing valid correlation matrices. It lifts noisy latents into region tokens with relational inductive bias over brain atlas regions and employs class-anchored mechanisms to recover class-conditional geometry beyond coarse labels. This enables valid and geometrically informative synthetic neuroimaging data.

items.title: Mitigating Black-Box Score-Based Query Attacks via Gradient Confusion
items.content: arXiv:2610.17382v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Score-based black-box adversarial attacks pose a serious threat to deployed machine learning systems by exploiting repeated model queries to craft adversarial examples, requiring neither access to model parameters nor architecture. Existing defenses predominantly rely on stochastic output perturbations, which fail to prevent determined attackers from recovering stable gradient estimates by increasing query budgets or averaging over randomness. In this work, we propose the Gradient Confusion Defense (GCD), a retraining-free, deterministic test-time wrapper that actively shapes the probability vector returned to querying adversaries. By solving a constrained optimization problem grounded in the model's Jacobian, GCD aligns the exposed logit-gradient with a target confusion direction that is maximally misaligned with the true adversarial loss gradient---increasing the query complexity of attacks without sacrificing predictive utility or top-1 accuracy. We provide rigorous theoretical analysis demonstrating that GCD provably slows gradient-estimation-based attacks and induces systematic accept/reject errors in random search-based attacks, with the confusion effect amplifying as the fraction of defended queries increases. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet across multiple architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, ViT-B/16) and four state-of-the-art attacks confirm these predictions: GCD achieves state-of-the-art robustness, while incurring zero clean accuracy degradation. %Crucially, unlike randomization-based defenses, GCD's deterministic structure provides resilience against adaptive attacks that exploit stochasticity, making it well-suited for security-critical deployment settings.

items.title: Cross-View Time-Frequency Diffusion for Extreme-Aware Time-Series Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.17407v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Generating realistic time-series requires faithfully reproducing rare but high-impact extreme events. Existing approaches often rely on specialized representations or extreme-focused training objectives, which may restrict the diversity of captured extremes or compromise overall distributional fidelity. We propose Cross-View Time-Frequency Diffusion (CrossTF), a framework that exploits discrepancies between time- and frequency-view denoisers for extreme-aware time-series generation. Our key empirical finding is extreme-sensitive cross-view asymmetry: moving along the direction connecting the two views' clean-sample estimates substantially changes extreme fidelity while having limited effects on overall generation quality. We further identify a late-stage cross-view window in which this discrepancy stabilizes and cross-view adjustments have a particularly strong effect on extreme fidelity. These findings motivate a staged optimization strategy in CrossTF: after training and freezing both denoisers, it only needs to learn step-specific fusion parameters within this window using an Extreme Value Theory-based objective under an energy-distance constraint. This formulation supports interpolation between and extrapolation beyond the view-specific estimates while limiting degradation in overall generation quality. Extensive experiments on seven real-world datasets against 11 baselines show that CrossTF improves extreme fidelity by 26.1% and overall performance by 7.4% relative to the strongest baselines. These results highlight cross-view discrepancy as an effective basis for low-dimensional optimization in extreme-aware time-series generation.

items.title: Foundation Models for Event Prediction Across Heterogeneous Event Logs
items.content: arXiv:2610.17503v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Event logs are ubiquitous across real-world domains, including business processes, manufacturing workflows, healthcare, and many other operational systems. Yet event logs can differ substantially in their event semantics, label spaces, interaction patterns, and temporal scales, making it difficult to build a single foundation model that generalizes directly to previously unseen systems. We address this challenge with the Foundation Event Predictor (FEP), a simple and scalable in-context architecture that performs next-event prediction through learned, event-level nonparametric inference. Causal self-attention encodes context and target histories into key and query representations, respectively, while the observed next context events are encoded as values. Cross-attention then performs learned, relevance-weighted aggregation of next-event outcomes over all context transitions, allowing the entire nonparametric prediction procedure to be expressed as standard attention operations and efficiently parallelized with modern kernels such as FlashAttention. To promote cross-system generalization, we introduce permutation-robust embedding learning and random fixed embeddings to decouple event IDs from persistent semantics, together with empirical quantile transforms and robust normalization to handle diverse temporal scales. We pretrain FEP on 696 real-world event datasets spanning heterogeneous event systems and evaluate it on 50 held-out datasets unseen during pretraining. Across these datasets, FEP generalizes effectively to new event systems without parameter adaptation, frequently approaching the performance of strong models trained separately on each target dataset while substantially outperforming existing foundation-model baselines, particularly on challenging prediction tasks.

items.title: RELAY: Selective Self-Distillation with Adaptive Hand-off for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.17623v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning grades a response against many written criteria but collapses them into one reward, which discards the detail the rubric carries and gives no GRPO reward gradient when a group's responses tie. A frozen teacher that reads the rubric as privileged context provides token-level supervision, but we observe an early plateau in the gains over GRPO. RELAY uses advantages and rewards to select positive-advantage and low-scoring zero-advantage rollouts, and monitors the distillation loss to decide when to retire the teacher. Stage 1 combines selective distillation from a frozen teacher with GRPO; a plateau detector then removes the teacher, and Stage 2 continues with GRPO alone. Calibrated on one model-domain pair and reused unchanged in three others, the plateau detector fires between steps 122 and 171. RELAY scores highest in-domain among the compared methods in all four settings, ahead of GRPO on RaR-Medicine by 4.62 points with Qwen3-1.7B and 6.02 with Qwen3-4B. On Qwen3-1.7B/Medicine, removing the teacher from a shared checkpoint outperforms keeping, weakening or refreshing it. Distilling selected rollouts covering about half the response tokens also outperforms distilling all rollouts at a matched average coefficient.
items.author: Kunwang Zheng, Xinyu Sun, Yu Cao, Shuocheng Li, Lei Cheng, Ying Liu, Qilong Zhang, Jinlong Chen, Hua Yang, Qianglong Chen
items.summary: RELAY addresses the reward collapse problem in rubric-based RL by distilling token-level supervision from a frozen teacher that reads the rubric as privileged context, selectively targeting positive-advantage and zero-advantage rollouts. A plateau detector retires the teacher and continues with GRPO alone, with one model-domain calibration transferring to others.
items.reasoning: A pragmatic contribution to the active area of rubric-based RLVR training, addressing a concrete failure mode (zero-gradient tied groups and lost rubric detail); useful but the two-stage distill-then-RL recipe is an engineering refinement rather than a conceptual leap.

items.title: TStruct: Learning Shared Temporal Structures for Long-Term Time-Series Forecasting
items.content: arXiv:2610.17864v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Long-term time series forecasting requires temporal dependency modeling that remains stable and generalizable under temporal distribution shifts. However, real-world time series are often noisy and non-stationary, making deep learning models prone to fitting incidental temporal interactions in the training data. A key question is whether there exist temporal relationship structures that recur across different temporal positions and variables. We analyze temporal relationship matrices on commonly used time series datasets and find that samples from different temporal positions and different variables exhibit shared dominant temporal relationship structures. This indicates that temporal relationship structures contain patterns that recur stably across samples and variables. To learn such shared structures, we propose \textbf{T}emporal \textbf{Struct}ure Network (\textbf{TStruct}), a simple yet effective network for directly learning shared and generalizable temporal dependencies. Specifically, TStruct directly parameterizes a set of shared temporal dependency matrices and generates normalized combination weights using dynamic sample information and static variable priors. These weights represent a soft allocation of each sample-variable pair over shared temporal dependency structures, enabling the model to generate adaptive temporal dependency matrices under shared structural constraints, rather than fitting incidental interactions in a fully unconstrained manner. Notably, this simple structure-aware design consistently outperforms several strong baselines across all datasets, achieving superior accuracy while maintaining high computational efficiency.

items.summary: This paper empirically shows that temporal relationship matrices across different positions and variables share dominant recurring structures in real-world time series. TStruct exploits this to learn shared temporal structure representations that improve long-term forecasting robustness under distribution shift.
items.reasoning: Empirically grounded insight about shared temporal structures with a method to exploit it; solid contribution to forecasting robustness but within a well-trodden subfield without dramatic gains claimed.

items.title: CineMem: Attention-Aligned Fine-grained Memory Retrieval for Multi-Shot Long Video Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.17926v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Autoregressive video generation relies on memory retrieval to model long-range dependencies. This capability becomes particularly critical for multi-shot generation, where models must reconcile substantial visual changes across shot transitions with persistent semantic continuity. Existing methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level and share the same historical context across all query tokens, overlooking the heterogeneous information needs and leading to redundant retrieval and inefficient use of historical memory. To bridge this gap, we introduce CineMem, an attention-aligned fine-grained memory retrieval framework that combines online memory organization with query-adaptive retrieval for autoregressive multi-shot video generation. Specifically, guided by intrinsic memory-access patterns revealed through attention analysis, we propose an online-clustered KV cache as a memory organization strategy over all historical tokens, enabling semantic-aware memory grouping and more precise retrieval. In addition, we introduce a query-level retrieval mechanism that provides broader access to historical information under a fixed retrieval budget, thereby improving long-term memory utilization. Together, these designs enable the multi-shot video generator to preserve long-range consistency across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios, while approximating full-memory access under a constrained memory budget. To facilitate evaluation, we further introduce a suite of task-specific, VLM-assisted metrics for faithful inter-shot consistency assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.
items.author: Xiaoxue Wu, Xinyu Gao, Fang Yu, Yu Qiao, Xinyuan Chen
items.summary: CineMem introduces an attention-aligned, fine-grained memory retrieval framework for autoregressive multi-shot video generation, moving beyond shared frame-level retrieval toward query-adaptive access to organized online memory. This lets the model balance visual change across shot transitions with semantic continuity across a long video. The approach targets redundancy and inefficiency in existing long-video generation memory systems.

Novelty is solid but sits within a fast-moving area where many memory-retrieval variants are being proposed, and no benchmark results are visible in the abstract.

items.title: Cost-Efficient Privacy Enforcement for Email-Generating LLM Agents under Strategic Information Requests
items.content: arXiv:2610.18007v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: LLM agents now act as delegated communication intermediaries: they read private context, draft messages, and send externally visible emails on behalf of a user. Existing checker-repair defenses can reduce inappropriate disclosure, but they rely on repeated calls to a remote action LLM (the model that drafts and repairs the email) and a remote checker LLM whenever a draft fails validation. This creates a cost problem as well as a privacy problem, especially when a requester strategically asks for exact values, raw records, source evidence, or other details that induce leakage-heavy drafts. We propose local contract-conditioned rewriting as a cost-efficient enforcement layer for email-generating agents. The mechanism intercepts an outgoing draft, constructs an information-release contract that specifies what to preserve, generalize, and forbid, rewrites the draft with a local Gemma rewriter, and selectively invokes a final PrivacyChecker. Across extensive email tasks under normal prompts and attack prompts that operationalize strategic information requests, Gemma + Checker reduces normal-prompt leakage from 11.41% to 4.03% while improving UsableRate (satisfied or partially satisfied outputs) from 85.2% to 92.6%. Under the strategic attack-prompt condition, it reduces leakage from 28.19% to 18.79% and reduces checker-only cost amplification from 1.32x to 1.02x. Offline replay ablation shows that the full contract reduces leakage relative to generic Gemma rewriting by 36.3% under normal prompts and 54.1% under attack prompts. These results support a local-first privacy enforcement design: move repair to a cheaper trusted local layer when possible, but retain the checker as the final semantic gate for high-risk sends.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.18007v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents now act as delegated communication intermediaries: they read private context, draft messages, and send externally visible emails on behalf of a user. Existing checker-repair defenses can reduce inappropriate disclosure, but they rely on repeated calls to a remote action LLM (the model that drafts and repairs the email) and a remote checker LLM whenever a draft fails validation. This creates a cost problem as well as a privacy problem, especially when a requester strategically asks for exact values, raw records, source evidence, or other details that induce leakage-heavy drafts. We propose local contract-conditioned rewriting as a cost-efficient enforcement layer for email-generating agents. The mechanism intercepts an outgoing draft, constructs an information-release contract that specifies what to preserve, generalize, and forbid, rewrites the draft with a local Gemma rewriter, and selectively invokes a final PrivacyChecker. Across extensive email tasks under normal prompts and attack prompts that operationalize strategic information requests, Gemma + Checker reduces normal-prompt leakage from 11.41% to 4.03% while improving UsableRate (satisfied or partially satisfied outputs) from 85.2% to 92.6%. Under the strategic attack-prompt condition, it reduces leakage from 28.19% to 18.79% and reduces checker-only cost amplification from 1.32x to 1.02x. Offline replay ablation shows that the full contract reduces leakage relative to generic Gemma rewriting by 36.3% under normal prompts and 54.1% under attack prompts. These results support a local-first privacy enforcement design: move repair to a cheaper trusted local layer when possible, but retain the checker as the final semantic gate for high-risk sends.

items.title: Scaling Vision Transformers Without Training: Prune-and-Merge Token Compression
items.content: arXiv:2610.18039v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Vision Transformers achieve strong performance but incur high computational costs from quadratic token interactions. Training-free token reduction methods improve efficiency, but their robustness remains underexplored. We propose Prune-and Merge ViT, a training-free framework for off-the-shelf models. It combines class attention-based pruning with similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy while preserving semantic information. To evaluate robustness we introduce two metrics. Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) measures relative accuracy degradation under transformations, and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) quantifies prediction consistency. On pretrained ViT and DeiT, Prune-and-Merge reduces computation competitively while maintaining robustness and better accuracy than existing token reduction methods. Our analysis suggests that hybrid token reduction does not introduce hallucination-like behavior and preserves prediction stability for common image transformations.

items.title: Reset Early, Reset Often, Eliminate Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.18204v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Connection-tableau provers typically construct closed tableaux by backtracking search. This gives lightweight proof procedures, but their low-memory search state leaves little derived information to reuse after a failed attempt. SATCoP addresses this by retaining grounded tableau clauses in an incremental SAT solver, allowing the prover to refute the problem once the accumulated ground clauses become propositionally unsatisfiable. We introduce SATResetCoP, which relies more directly on this persistent SAT state by not backtracking on unproductive tableaux and instead starting new ones to generate further ground clauses for the SAT solver. On TPTP, SATResetCoP improves over our leanCoP-style baseline by 54% and our SATCoP-style baseline by 18%. On the bushy MPTP2078 benchmark, it solves 616 problems, a 49% improvement over our leanCoP-style baseline and a 12% improvement over our SATCoP-style baseline. These results suggest that changing tableau guidance to accumulate useful ground clauses faster improves the performance of the prover.

items.title: A Controlled Evaluation of Curvature Inspired Scalar Feature Scaling for Domain Generalization
items.content: arXiv:2610.18227v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Domain-specific curvature is an appealing idea for domain generalization (DG), but curvature learning can denote substantially different computations. This paper evaluates one deliberately narrow implementation: the code calls it HyperDG, but it rescales Euclidean encoder features during training by learned positive scalars and uses an ordinary linear classifier on unscaled Euclidean features at inference. It does not implement a Lorentz or Poincar\'e representation, geodesic prediction, or a Sharpness-Aware Minimization inner loop. We audit the executed objective and evaluate six conditions on PACS, VLCS, Office Home, and TerraIncognita. The completed design contains 384 runs: six conditions, four held-out targets, and four run seeds per dataset. Checkpoints are selected using only the three source-validation environments. Inference first averages paired seed differences within each held-out target; targets, rather than 16 seed-by-target observations, are the per-dataset clusters. The full implementation's equal-dataset macro point estimate is 1.61 percentage points below native DomainBed ERM (95% clustered CI [-3.17, -0.04]). All four dataset point estimates favor ERM, but an exact four-dataset sign-flip test gives p = .125 and Holm-adjusted p = .250; we therefore claim no adjusted evidence of a difference. The cleaner domain-specificity contrast, separate learned source scales without their variance penalty versus one shared learned source scale, is -0.13 pp (95% CI [-0.53, 0.27]). Its 90% CI lies within a revision-stage $\pm 1$ pp smallest effect of practical interest (TOST p = .003), supporting equivalence only for the source-selected suite macro, not every dataset, target, or final-step endpoint. The study thus supplies a bounded negative result for this scalar training package; it does not test or refute genuine hyperbolic representation learning.

items.title: LiFUSE: Frequency-Spatial Unified Self-Supervised Pretraining for Liver Disease Analysis on Non-contrast CT
items.content: arXiv:2610.18243v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Given the growing global burden of liver tumors and diffuse liver diseases, non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) is increasingly used for opportunistic screening because of its low cost and favorable safety profile. However, downstream tasks such as tumor detection and fine-grained disease diagnosis remain challenging due to NCCT's inherently low tissue contrast, lack of hemodynamic enhancement, and complex anatomical background. These limitations make subtle, heterogeneous, and multifocal hepatic lesions difficult to identify. Although large-scale self-supervised pretraining can learn robust representations from unlabeled NCCT scans, conventional voxel-wise reconstruction does not fully exploit the complementary information available in NCCT. Under weak NCCT contrast, low-level intensity patterns become less informative for pathology recognition, limiting the capture of lesion-specific discriminative features. In this paper, we propose the Liver Frequency-Spatial Unified Self-Supervised Pretraining (LiFUSE). The frequency branch applies random band-stop masking and spectrum reconstruction to encourage the model to capture subtle differences between lesions and surrounding tissues, while the spatial branch performs hybrid-granularity masked volumetric reconstruction to accommodate lesions of diverse sizes and morphologies. Finally, a cross-domain consistency scheme couples the spatial and frequency branches, yielding more discriminative representations for hepatic structures and lesions. Extensive experiments on three clinically relevant tasks across internal cohorts and a public target-domain transfer setting show that LiFUSE consistently outperforms strong baselines. These results suggest that unified frequency-spatial learning can improve liver disease analysis on NCCT, highlighting its potential for large-scale screening.
