items.title: Perception Beyond the Visible: Incompleteness-Aware Scene Understanding for Robot Autonomy
items.content: arXiv:2610.18670v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reliable robot autonomy requires reasoning about the world from partial and noisy observations. However, many perception systems model only visible scene regions, rely on fixed semantic categories, and assume reliable sensor measurements. These assumptions break under occlusion, novel object encounters, and sensor degradation. In this paper, I present a research vision for incompleteness-aware scene understanding. I organize this vision around three fundamental challenges: incomplete evidence, incomplete knowledge, and incomplete sensor reliability. I discuss my research contributions toward addressing these challenges through amodal perception, semantic occupancy forecasting, open-world scene understanding, label-efficient learning, and uncertainty-guided multi-modal fusion. Building on these contributions, I outline future research directions toward belief-centric 4D scene representations. These representations aim to jointly model geometry, semantics, motion, and uncertainty. I also discuss active sensing and safe adaptation strategies that allow robots to reduce uncertainty through interaction. The goal is to develop calibrated and actionable scene representations that support reliable autonomy in dynamic, open-world environments.

items.title: Assessing the Marginal Utility of Exocentric Head Views in UMI-Style Large-FoV Wrist-Camera Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2610.14075v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-view perception is often treated as a safe design choice for robot manipulation: if one camera is useful, more cameras should be better. We revisit that assumption in tabletop bimanual manipulation by comparing policies trained with two large-field-of-view (FoV) wrist cameras against policies that additionally receive a head view, using controlled-variable experiments on a real bimanual platform. Across three tabletop tasks, adding a head view does not consistently improve task completion or execution quality: when the wrist cameras already observe the objects, grippers, and goal regions, wrist-only policies form a strong baseline. Restricting the wrist-camera FoV increases the potential value of a head view, but performance improves most reliably when the added view supplies concentrated, task-relevant information: region-of-interest (ROI) cropping yields more consistent head-view gains than the uncropped image, which is dominated by background and task-irrelevant regions. The data-scaling results further suggest an interaction between FoV and demonstration count: wide observations improve coverage but may require more data to stabilize, and they may reach a higher performance ceiling once enough demonstrations are available. These results suggest that camera design should be framed as a task-relevance and information-density problem rather than as a simple count of input views.

items.title: CoPlanVLM: Coordinated Path Planning for a Robot Team using Vision Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.14341v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present CoPlanVLM, which uses a Vision Language Model (VLM) to translate a single natural-language instruction and image into coordinated paths for a team of two robots. While VLMs offer a flexible, natural-language interface for commanding robot teams, their weak spatial reasoning has greatly limited VLM-based path planning. CoPlanVLM improves the VLM's spatial reasoning and path planning abilities through three components: (1) an image overlay marking both free space and obstacles, (2) task classification that selects the most appropriate low-level planner and reasoning prompt for each instruction, and (3) task-specific chain-of-thought reasoning that prompts the VLM to identify key objects, allocate roles, and verify routes are collision-free before committing to a plan. Together, these components enable the team to complete complex coordinated maneuvers requiring both robots and divide large tasks between robots to increase efficiency. CoPlanVLM also supports detailed maneuvers involving specific routes, loops, and coverage of large areas, as well as tasks requiring directional reasoning such as north/south or left/right. We validate CoPlanVLM in both Gazebo simulation and on physical Turtlebot 4 hardware. CoPlanVLM attains an average success rate of 84.4% compared to 50.0% for the closest baseline. On trials where both methods succeed, CoPlanVLM's paths are 27% shorter on average. Project code is available at https://github.com/AICPS/CoPlanVLM.

This demonstrates a practical pattern for wrapping general-purpose VLMs into reliable multi-robot planning pipelines.

items.title: PC7 Model: Dynamics of Expanding and Contracting Soft Robots using Piece-wise Constant 7D Deformation Based on Similarity Transformation Group
items.content: arXiv:2610.14586v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper proposes a novel soft robot model named piece-wise constant 7D deformation (PC7) model that can represent expanding and contracting deformation of, for example, artificial muscle actuator. In the proposed model, we newly define the 7D deformation vector based on SIM(3) - 3D similarity transformation group - whereas a 6D deformation vector was defined for Cosserat rod based on SE(3) - the special Euclid group - in the piece-wise constant strain (PCS) model proposed in the previous study. The additional dimension of the 7D deformation vector represents expanding and contracting deformation, which comes from the scaling parameter in SIM(3). Common mathematical properties between SE(3) and SIM(3) allow us to directly extend the kinematics and dynamics of the PCS model to those of the PC7 model. In particular, we derive the dynamical equation of the PC7 model based on Euler-Poincare equation in a mathematically precise manner. We validate the proposed model through dynamical simulations assuming a thin cylinder structure or McKibben-type artificial muscle actuator.

items.summary: This paper introduces the PC7 model, a soft robot deformation model that extends the piece-wise constant strain (PCS) framework from SE(3) to SIM(3), adding a seventh scaling dimension to capture expansion and contraction of actuators like artificial muscles. The shared mathematical structure between the two Lie groups allows direct extension of existing kinematic and dynamic tools. This is a principled geometric contribution relevant to soft robot simulation and control.

items.title: CAG-WAM: Causal Action-Gain World Action Models for Robot Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2610.14720v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) combine action generation with future prediction, allowing predicted futures to support action evaluation and robot decision making. However, the future associated with a candidate action may contain action-induced and environment-driven changes. Directly evaluating the predicted future may not fully characterize the future change associated with the candidate action. For example, a candidate action that worsens a favorable environmental future may still yield a favorable outcome, while one that improves an unfavorable environmental future may still yield an unfavorable outcome. To analyze this issue, we formulate a Structural Causal Model (SCM) for action evaluation in WAMs. The SCM formalizes how action-induced and environment-driven changes jointly shape future evaluation, and reveals a backdoor path through which environmental evolution can also affect the future evaluation associated with a candidate action. Intervention and backdoor adjustment account for this path, providing a causal basis for characterizing the future change associated with each candidate action. Based on this analysis, we propose Causal Action-Gain World Action Model (CAG-WAM). For each candidate action, CAG-WAM predicts an action-conditioned future and an environmental future under the same current observation, and defines their evaluation difference as causal action gain (CAG) for characterizing the future change associated with the candidate action. During training, we incorporate CAG into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to guide robot policy learning. During inference, we evaluate the initial action with CAG and, when needed, revise it using predicted future information. Experiments on multiple benchmarks support the effectiveness of CAG-WAM.

items.summary: This work formulates a structural causal model for evaluating candidate actions in World Action Models, separating action-induced changes from environment-driven changes in predicted futures. The insight is that directly scoring a predicted future can misjudge an action when environmental trends dominate, and the proposed causal action-gain formulation corrects this. It improves action evaluation for model-based robot manipulation.

items.title: Embodiment-Aware Inference-Time Search for Human Reaction Selection in Humanoid Retargeting
items.content: arXiv:2610.15274v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Training humanoid robots to learn human behaviors requires expensive data collection, and human-robot interaction data can be even more difficult and costly to collect. Training a specialized reaction model for each humanoid embodiment can also be time-consuming and resource-intensive. Human-to-humanoid motion retargeting provides a more scalable alternative, allowing human-human reaction data to serve as a common motion representation for different humanoid embodiments. However, due to morphological and kinematic differences between humans and humanoid robots, a reaction preferred in human motion space may not be the most suitable one for execution on a particular robot embodiment.   In this work, we propose an inference-time reaction search framework that leverages stochastic sampling from a generative reaction model and jointly considers reaction quality and humanoid embodiment feasibility. Given the observed interaction, our framework generates multiple plausible reaction candidates. Each candidate is retargeted to the target humanoid and evaluated using complementary interaction and embodiment-specific feasibility criteria, allowing candidate selection under the physical constraints of the target embodiment. Since the reaction generator remains frozen, the framework can adapt to different humanoid embodiments at inference time without retraining. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework maintains overall human reaction quality while improving the feasibility of retargeted humanoid reactions across different embodiments. The proposed pipeline improves humanoid retargeting feasibility by 1.61%. Moreover, human-space and G1 best-candidate selections disagree in 78.98% of samples, demonstrating substantial embodiment dependence. Code will be released.

Because a reaction preferred in human motion space may not suit a specific robot morphology, the method searches for embodiment-appropriate reactions at inference rather than training a specialized model per robot.

Its novelty is moderate since retargeting and inference-time selection both exist, and validation breadth is unclear from the abstract, but the direction is promising for the humanoid ecosystem.

items.title: LERR-Nav: Learning to Coordinate Exploration, Recovery, and Reminiscing for Object Navigation
items.content: arXiv:2610.15362v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Object Navigation in unseen environments remains a fundamental challenge in embodied AI, as it requires agents to generalize visual and spatial reasoning to novel layouts. While recent advances in large language model (LLM) and vision-language model (VLM) have enhanced semantic mapping, spatial memory, and waypoint selecting for navigation, successful navigation requires more than selecting the next promising waypoint. A robot must also recognize stalled progress, escape unproductive behaviors, and revisit overlooked target cues. Addressing these challenges requires both specialized navigation strategies and a high-level policy that coordinates their execution. Motivated by the analysis of failed navigation episodes, we propose LERR-Nav, an object navigation framework that coordinates exploration, recovery, and reminiscing through a learned high-level policy. The framework comprises four complementary navigation strategies: value-function-guided exploration, LLM-guided exploration, recovery from stalled or repetitive behavior, and memory-guided reminiscing. To support history-aware coordination, we maintain the execution memory that preserves textual summaries of all strategy executions alongside a sliding window of map sequences. To learn the coordination policy, we initialize a high-level vision-language agent from Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and train it through a two-stage curriculum. The first stage uses map-centric supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to establish spatial grounding. The second stage performs SFT on variable-length navigation segments to learn which navigation strategy to invoke next based on current maps and the hybrid execution memory. Experiments on HM3D and MP3D demonstrate state-of-the-art navigation performance, while ablation studies validate the contributions of individual components.

The approach is motivated by an analysis of failed navigation episodes, aiming to make embodied agents more robust to unproductive behaviors.

items.title: Learning Safety-Constrained Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation for Lunar Surface Operations
items.content: arXiv:2610.15486v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robotic systems for lunar surface operations must act autonomously and preserve their own integrity in an environment where failures are unrecoverable and continuous supervision is impossible. This paper presents a Constrained Reinforcement Learning framework for quadrupedal mobile manipulators that learns a single whole-body policy for tracking a 6D end-effector pose specified in task space, with operational limits enforced during learning through a constrained learning mechanism. We introduce a reward formulation in which the transition between locomotion and manipulation emerges from the reward geometry rather than from an explicit gating mechanism, a stability term derived from the Gravito-Inertial Inclination Margin and motivated by the reduced-gravity dynamics of the lunar surface, and a design rule for reward regularization that follows from the multiplicative structure of the termination-based objective. The framework is evaluated in a lunar-analog simulation spanning three terrain morphologies at five difficulty levels under lunar gravity, with regolith contact properties calibrated to the JSC-1a simulant and varied from loose to dense. The learned policy attains mean position and orientation errors of 3.22 cm and 6.83 deg. under nominal conditions, retains this precision across regolith densities and over the operationally representative range of terrain difficulty, and reduces soft-constraint violation time by up to an order of magnitude relative to an unconstrained baseline while incurring no hard-constraint violations.

items.title: Model-Based Trailer-Sway Suppression for Autonomous Passenger Vehicles
items.content: arXiv:2610.15747v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Trailer sway is a persistent contributor to severe crashes among light passenger vehicles towing trailers, yet it remains largely unaddressed by the autonomous vehicle systems now entering this new era of automation. Improper cargo placement rearward of the trailer axle reduces, and can invert, the tongue load transmitted through the hitch. The resulting loss of vertical load at the tow vehicle's rear axle diminishes the lateral tire force available there and degrades yaw stability of the coupled system, admitting a divergent lateral oscillation of the trailer known as trailer sway. Under adverse combinations of speed and loading, this oscillation can progress to jackknifing, in which the articulation angle diverges rapidly and directional control is lost. This work develops a linear state-space model of the yaw-plane dynamics of a light vehicle-trailer combination, parameterized to expose tongue load as an explicit stability-determining quantity. From this model a linear quadratic regulator is synthesized to suppress articulation-angle divergence. Because consumer trailers carry no sensors, the two trailer states the controller needs, trailer yaw rate and articulation angle, are estimated by a Kalman filter from measurements taken only on the tow vehicle. The controller is then implemented and evaluated in a MuJoCo multibody simulation across a range of longitudinal speeds and tongue-load conditions, including the negative-tongue-load regime. Results show a significant decrease in trailer oscillation when controlling a given vehicle's steering with an LQR using tow-vehicle IMU and LiDAR data. These findings indicate that LQR controlled anti-sway systems are a viable control method for future autonomous vehicles.
items.author: Alec McFadyen, Pablo Covarrubias De La Torre, Connor McGovern

It fills a genuine safety gap as automation extends to towing scenarios.

items.title: Constrained Differentiable Policy Learning for Safe Quadrotor Navigation
items.content: arXiv:2610.16119v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Differentiable simulation enables efficient policy optimization through analytic gradients, yet safety is commonly incorporated as a weighted penalty, requiring manual tuning of the trade-off between task performance and constraint satisfaction. We instead formulate obstacle avoidance as an explicit constraint and train quadrotor policies using primal--dual gradient descent--ascent through a differentiable simulator. We introduce two key components to enable effective constrained training. First, we propose a bounded clearance-based constraint function that provides informative gradients around the safety boundary while preventing large violations from destabilizing primal--dual optimization. Second, we introduce log-mean-exp (LME) aggregation to smoothly emphasize critical per-step safety violations across a trajectory and training batch within a single constraint governed by one dual variable. Together, these components enable the desired safety level to be specified directly while balancing constraint satisfaction and task completion. We theoretically prove that the proposed optimization with differentiable simulation converges to feasible policy under mild assumptions. Experiments demonstrate improved safety--performance trade-offs over fixed-penalty and existing policy-learning baselines, as well as generalization to denser out-of-distribution environments. Finally, the learned policy transfers zero-shot to Gazebo/PX4 and a physical quadrotor without additional fine-tuning.

items.title: DeTac: Dual-branch Decoupling of Texture and Force Signals in Vision-Based Tactile Sensors
items.content: arXiv:2610.16463v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-based tactile sensors enable fine-grained perception for dexterous robotic manipulation, but current marker-based designs tightly couple surface texture and contact force signals within a single observation. Existing data-driven decoupling methods rely on serial mask-based inpainting, which suffers from mask-sizing dilemmas caused by physical indentation effects, error retention, and lack of real paired data for supervision. To address these challenges, we propose DeTac, a novel dual-branch generative framework that concurrently extracts clean shading and marker images from a single mixed tactile image. DeTac leverages full-image synthesis to naturally bypass mask dependency and introduces a cross-branch synergistic optimization that enables mutual supervision, effectively preventing error retention. Furthermore, we construct a strictly aligned, real-world paired tactile dataset using custom hardware to provide high-quality supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DeTac achieves state-of-the-art decoupling accuracy, significantly facilitating downstream surface reconstruction and force estimation tasks while exhibiting cross-sensor generalization.

This enables finer-grained perception for dexterous manipulation.
items.reasoning: Tactile sensing signal decoupling is a real problem for dexterous manipulation, and the dual-branch generative approach with cross-branch optimization is a reasonable methodological advance over mask-based inpainting. Novelty is solid but niche; impact is bounded by the specific sensor-modality community unless the technique generalizes.

items.title: LiDAR-based Humanoid Navigation in Dynamic, Non-Convex Environments via Spatio-Temporal Safe Corridors
items.content: arXiv:2610.17232v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Navigating humanoid robots through dynamic, non-convex environments requires tightly coupling onboard perception with footstep planning and dynamic locomotion control. Existing methods frequently discard complex free space through simplified convex obstacle bounds and fail to account for real-time dynamic occupancy predictions. This paper presents a real-time framework for humanoid navigation that directly constructs spatio-temporal safe corridors from LiDAR-based particle representations and couples them with Linear Inverted Pendulum (LIP)-based planning and Whole Body Control (WBC) to enable navigation around and within moving non-convex structures without restrictive geometric assumptions. Simulations on the Digit humanoid yield a 96% success rate in navigating around and inside moving non-convex obstacles in a 24 by 24 m^2 arena. Ablation studies confirm that the proposed iterative polytope generation significantly outperforms single-iteration baselines in narrow corridors, while evaluations demonstrate robustness to clutter, sensor noise, control delays, and force perturbations.

The system navigates around and within moving non-convex structures, demonstrated in simulation on the Digit humanoid with a 96% success rate. It integrates onboard perception, dynamic occupancy prediction, and dynamic locomotion control.
items.reasoning: Technically coherent integration of perception, corridor planning, and WBC for humanoids in dynamic environments, with strong simulation numbers. However, results are simulation-only on a single platform and the corridor-planning machinery is an evolution of existing safe-corridor methods. Solid systems work without a headline advance.

items.title: ATOM: Abstract Transition and Option Modeling - Experience-Informed Hierarchical Navigation
items.content: arXiv:2610.17555v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We propose ATOM (Abstract Transition and Option Modeling), a hierarchical navigation framework that combines higher-level graph planning with reusable lower-level option policies for efficient repeated navigation in large-scale 3D environments represented by hierarchical structures such as 3D scene graphs (3DSGs). ATOM operates on a hierarchical graph representation, implemented using, for instance, the Rooms and Places layers of a 3DSG, where each directed abstract transition is associated with a navigation option. For each transition, ATOM computes and stores a reusable option policy along with its state-dependent cost-to-go. Across repeated navigation tasks, ATOM maintains a smoothed empirical distribution over option initiation states and uses it to progressively refine the corresponding abstract transition cost. Ablation studies show that ATOM reduces cumulative repeated-planning time by 97.5% relative to a monolithic MDP baseline while maintaining trajectories within approximately 7% of a Global Places A* shortest-path reference. Experience-informed refinement further reduces abstract transition-cost estimation error by 10.3%. Physical experiments validate ATOM on an F1Tenth vehicle, successfully completing all five navigation queries with 43% of inter-region option executions reusing previously generated solutions.

items.reasoning: A thoughtful combination of symbolic hierarchical planning and learned options with an experience-accumulation mechanism, targeting realistic repeated-navigation settings. Novelty is moderate since hierarchical RL and 3DSG navigation are active areas, but the reusable-transition-policy design is a useful contribution.

items.title: Physics-Aware Object-Centric SE(3) Forecasting for Real-Time Proactive Dynamic Grasping
items.content: arXiv:2610.17843v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Proactive dynamic grasping requires robots to predict the future state at which physical contact will occur, rather than reacting to the currently observed object pose. But what future must the robot predict, and at what level of abstraction? We argue that contact-relevant rigid-body state in SE(3) is a compact task-sufficient abstraction for this problem: it directly determines where and when the robot should establish contact, without requiring visually complete future scenes. This insight leads to a lightweight object-centric forecast-then-select framework that predicts future rigid-body trajectories from short pose histories and uses a reachability-aware interception selector to choose feasible contact states under kinematic and timing constraints. Trained with randomized physics simulation over primitive shapes, the forecaster transfers to real objects once their metric geometry and SE(3) state histories are recovered. Experiments across simulation and real-world dynamic grasping tasks show that our framework improves the average success rate from \(24.5\%\) to \(62.0\%\) in simulation, and from \(15.3\%\) to \(67.3\%\) in real-world catching, conveyor, and turntable interception. The SE(3) forecaster runs in \(15\,\mathrm{ms}\), orders of magnitude faster than dense visual future prediction, enabling real-time contact decision making. Our results suggest that effective proactive grasping does not require imagining the entire future scene. Instead, predicting the compact physical future that determines contact provides an effective and practical abstraction for real-time dynamic grasping.

items.title: RESTA: Time-Scaling Augmentation for Data-Efficient Robot Imitation Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.18163v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robot manipulation policies trained through imitation learning commonly rely on costly demonstrations recorded in one task direction and at one temporal resolution. We propose Reversal and Stride-based Trajectory Augmentation (RESTA), which exploits time-scaling data augmentation to improve data efficiency through trajectory reversal and temporal resampling. Trajectory-reversal augmentation reverses and relabels demonstrations between paired tasks with opposite objectives, reusing recorded rollouts without additional environment interaction. Because contact-rich manipulation is not exactly reversible, we treat reversal as an approximate paired-task prior rather than a physical symmetry. Temporal-stride augmentation varies observation and action sampling strides and conditions the policy on the resulting offsets, enabling fixed or randomized temporal schedules. Experiments across 16 paired bimanual manipulation tasks show that trajectory reversal is particularly effective in the low-data regime and that temporal-stride augmentation improves success under randomized temporal schedules. With 25 and 50 independently collected demonstrations per task, RESTA achieves 78.4% and 85.2% average success, respectively, matching or exceeding baselines trained with twice as many demonstrations (77.3% and 85.4%). These results show that RESTA can improve data efficiency in robot imitation learning.
items.author: Yunpeng Jiang, Jianshu Hu, Han Fang, Zhiyuan Guan, Paul Weng, Yutong Ban
items.summary: RESTA improves data efficiency in imitation learning by exploiting time-scaling augmentations: trajectory reversal with relabeling between paired tasks with opposite objectives, and temporal-stride resampling of demonstrations. The authors treat reversal as an approximate paired-task prior rather than a strict physical symmetry, which is a realistic framing for contact-rich manipulation.
items.reasoning: A practical and low-cost augmentation recipe that extracts more value from existing demonstration data; the idea is intuitive but the honest treatment of non-reversibility and empirical data-efficiency gains make it a useful contribution to the imitation learning toolkit.

items.title: Reach-Avoid Certificates for Contact-based Stochastic Hybrid Systems
items.content: arXiv:2610.17308v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This work studies certified reach-avoid control of stochastic hybrid systems in which a stochastic differential equation governs continuous flow and a controlled stochastic kernel governs guard-triggered resets. The input appears only in the reset kernel, where it determines the post-jump distribution. Certificates for such systems have so far assumed spontaneous or controller-chosen jump times, a finite horizon, or discrete-time dynamics; we certify, over the infinite horizon, that the target is reached before the unsafe set with at least a prescribed probability. First, we introduce reach-avoid contact certificates, whose flow and jump conditions are imposed only on a sublevel corridor, and prove that any such certificate with a compatible reset policy meets the specification; a pointwise safety filter extends this guarantee from verification to control by constraining arbitrary nominal controllers. Next, we prove that executions are non-Zeno and bound the expected settling time and reset count. We frame certificate search as a linear program over any twice-differentiable dictionary followed by independent verification. We illustrate our approach via comparisons where the certified region is a subset covering 93.6\% of the ground truth and where our certificate-based safety filter reaches the goal while reducing collisions from 68 to zero across 200 episodes of a dribbling ball problem.

Unlike prior certificates requiring spontaneous or controller-chosen jump times or finite horizons, these certificates guarantee, over an infinite horizon, that the target is reached before the unsafe set with a prescribed probability. Conditions are imposed only on a sublevel corridor, easing computation.

items.title: Prior-Informed Generalizable Low-Rank Representation Learning via Regularized Adversarial Reweighting
items.content: arXiv:2610.14414v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Modern learning problems increasingly leverage data from heterogeneous sources to improve robustness and generalizability under distribution shift, often with high-dimensional parameters admitting low-rank structure. Existing group distributionally robust optimization (group-DRO) approaches optimize against adverse source mixtures, but extending this principle to low-rank matrix estimation with a broad class of losses leads to a challenging nonconvex-concave problem for which methods and theory remain limited. We propose Prior-Informed generalizable Low-rank representation Learning via Adversarial Reweighting (PILLAR), which smooths the group-DRO objective by regularizing adversarial source weights toward a user-specified reference distribution while learning a shared low-rank representation. By tempering extreme adversarial reweighting, PILLAR improves estimation stability and reduces the potential conservativeness of group-DRO. Using Burer-Monteiro factorization, we optimize the nonconvex-concave objective by bifactored gradient descent with mirror ascent. We establish linear convergence to a statistical neighborhood of the population saddle point and derive an error bound that separates low-rank estimation from adversarial reweighting. We further show that PILLAR improves on vanilla group DRO when the latter's excess conservativeness dominates source heterogeneity and prior misspecification. Simulations and an electronic health record study of suicide-attempt risk demonstrate improved worst-source and transported predictive accuracy.

items.title: When are safe Pareto improvements individually rational?
items.content:
(Soft prerequisites: A high-level model of AI bargaining and Taboo “equilibrium”: Less confused frames for research on AI bargaining.)

Section II.1 of CLR’s safe Pareto improvements (SPI) agenda briefly reviews the challenges for making SPIs individually rational. Here, I’ll flesh out these challenges, taking renegotiation SPIs as a running example. The ideas here overlap a lot with DiGiovanni et al. (2024) and its distillation. But this post will hopefully be more accessible, and will consider bargaining problems with non-simultaneous commitments. I’ll also revisit some controversial arguments made in those previous writings.

My aim is to precisely yet informally answer: “Why might an agent expect opting out of SPIs to have better consequences? What are the mechanisms leading them to expect this?” The high-level mechanisms I’ll discuss apply to a variety of SPIs, not just renegotiation, though the details importantly differ between different SPIs. I’m not confident that this list of mechanisms is exhaustive. Rather, the point is to show that at least these obstacles need to be overcome in order for SPIs to be individually rational.

See Appendix I for a table of this post’s notation, and Appendix II for how the analysis maps onto the agenda’s breakdown of “Risks 1-3”.

items.title: How to Build a Benchmark That Actually Measures Taste
items.content: arXiv:2610.14707v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Expert-aligned "taste" benchmarks should reward craft judgment, not the ability to game the test. We introduce TasteBench, a pairwise good-vs-bad benchmark across visual, brand, book, and tech items under a frozen rubric with expert-only gold (panel n>=3; percent agreement >=0.60 primary gate; weak engagement labels train/analysis-only), together with a control protocol that separates craft judgment from test-gaming. Applying the protocol to a Round-1 pilot (primary_human_expert; three biological human experts; n=250 pairs) surfaces and quantifies three validity threats: two construction artifacts that inflate the trivial-baseline layer, and a difficulty ceiling that inflates every score. (1) Position: the preferred item is slot A with probability 0.956, so an always_item_a policy scores 0.956 (fair chance 0.5). (2) Lexical leakage: a filename token cue scores 0.912. (3) Difficulty ceiling: craft domains show near-ceiling human agreement (book/brand/tech 1.0), and even under A/B randomization (eval_assignment_seed7; gold_side_A ~0.47) all five VLM cards reach 1.0 on craft, with only visual separating (~0.84-0.91; a post-hoc hard subset, n=107, leaves craft at 1.0). The protocol (expert-only gold, a weak-label firewall, side randomization at construction, filename scrubbing, and hard filters) makes each artifact measurable and, for the two construction artifacts, correctable; we release a reference eval harness and a side-randomization tool, and show the tool removes the position skew (0.916 to 0.495/0.505). The result is a calibrated view of what the benchmark does and does not yet measure: position and leakage are fixable, whereas the craft-domain ceiling is a pair-difficulty limit that Round-2 must address. We do not evaluate engagement, era/circle conditioning, or calibration here, and we claim no general taste SOTA.

Its control protocol separates craft judgment from test-gaming and surfaces validity threats including positional artifacts and a difficulty ceiling that inflate scores.
items.reasoning: Interesting methodological contribution to measuring subjective judgment robustly, with useful lessons about benchmark gaming; pilot scale (250 pairs) and subjective domain limit general impact.

items.title: MARL-BattleGrounds: A Novel JAX-native Benchmark for Heterogeneous and Competitive Multi-agent RL
items.content: arXiv:2610.14883v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present MARL-BattleGrounds (MARL-BGs), an easy-to-use JAX-native benchmark for heterogeneous and competitive multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), designed to be sample-efficient, computationally efficient, and researcher-centric. MARL benchmarks are typically simple and efficient, like SMAX, where winning reduces to unit micromanagement, or rich and costly, like Dota 2. MARL-BGs fills this missing middle. Its first mode, Team Deathmatch, is a simultaneous turn-based game between two teams of five heterogeneous agents. The five classes have distinct basic, passive, and ultimate abilities designed to synergize with allies and counter enemies. Our 52 hand-designed maps with diverse obstacles include a 12-map curriculum and ten held-out validation and test maps. MARL-BGs provides two canonical evaluation modes. First, eight endgame scenarios form a hard generalization challenge: each asks a team to win an unseen, nearly lost position against a strong reactive controller within 5-10 ticks. Second, a monthly round-robin tournament retrains each submission on equal compute, plays it against every member of the current "Big Nine" field, and publishes the Elo results on the official leaderboard. All entrants are publicly released as downloadable opponents. MARL-BGs records 11,192 metrics per game in 28 topics. We also include three strong scripted opponents, an analytical replay viewer, and off-the-shelf tools for self-play, cross-play, curriculum learning, and zero-shot coordination evaluation. We even provide an API for LLM-based agents and use it to evaluate Qwen3.5-9B against our strongest policy. In our BattleClient, humans can play alongside or against any mix of policies, enabling human-AI evaluation. We benchmark MARL-BGs with six additional deep MARL baselines, which we release. On one RTX 5090 with 1,024 parallel games, the simulator runs 50,000 5v5 game steps per second.

items.title: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery
items.content: arXiv:2610.14959v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks to discover executable expressions that capture predictive market signals in a vast, noisy search space. Recent LLM-based approaches use prompting, iterative search, or seed-factor evolution, leaving direct factor construction through policy learning less explored. To address this, we introduce AlphaRLM, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors from financial literature without input factor expressions. AlphaRLM incorporates Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO), which conditions factor construction on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, providing semantic priors for exploration. It further aligns the generation policy with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Extensive experiments on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 show that AlphaRLM outperforms strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return. Notably, the 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance, highlighting the promise of literature-conditioned, market-aligned factor generation.

It moves beyond prompting and evolutionary search toward direct policy learning for formulaic alpha mining.
items.reasoning: Combining RL-trained LLMs with literature grounding for quantitative finance factor discovery is a credible and potentially valuable application, though backtesting-based evaluation in finance raises overfitting concerns and the work sits in a niche domain with many prior LLM-alpha efforts.

items.title: Single-step Retrosynthesis via Reinforcement Learning from Forward Feedback
items.content: arXiv:2610.15141v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Single-step retrosynthesis is a one-to-many inverse problem, yet most models are trained and evaluated against a single recorded reactant set. Reference-based training gives no explicit positive signal for unrecorded alternatives, and exact-match evaluation rejects non-matching predictions regardless of chemical plausibility. We propose Retrosynthesis via Reinforcement Learning from Forward Feedback (RetroRLFF), which optimizes reactant generation using both reference agreement and forward consistency with the target product. Starting from a supervised decoder-only Transformer, RetroRLFF generates complete reactant candidates and uses a frozen forward reaction model to predict products. A sequence-level reward combines reference agreement and forward consistency while penalizing invalid outputs. Direct Advantage-Based Policy Optimization updates the policy without human preference annotations or a preference-trained reward model. On USPTO-50K, RetroRLFF outperforms all 14 baselines in candidate-level round-trip accuracy at k = 1, 3, 5, and 10. With approximately 50 million parameters, it achieves 90.1% top-1 round-trip accuracy, exceeding R-SMILES, the strongest competing baseline on this metric, by 8.5 percentage points. Compared with its supervised policy, round-trip accuracy increases from 83.1% to 90.1%, while exact-match accuracy is maintained at 57.9% versus 57.5%. In an anonymized expert assessment of 131 randomly selected test cases, organic synthesis experts prefer RetroRLFF over EditRetro in 67.9% of comparisons. These results support forward feedback as a training signal for improving forward consistency while retaining top-1 reference recovery. Expert assessment provides complementary evidence of synthetic feasibility on the selected cases, although neither forward consistency nor expert preference establishes experimental feasibility.

items.title: ScreenASR-Bench: A Tiered Benchmark for Speech Recognition with Visual Context
items.content: arXiv:2610.16260v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Current ASR models perform well on general benchmarks but still struggle with acoustically ambiguous words. Visual context can aid recognition in screen-based scenarios, yet existing benchmarks provide limited insight into the benefits of different types of visual evidence. To address this gap, we introduce ScreenASR-Bench , a tiered benchmark with three progressively challenging levels: Explicit Textual Evidence (ETE), based on direct on-screen text; Explicit Visual Evidence (EVE), using visible content rather than on-screen text; and Implicit Semantic Evidence (ISE), requiring scene-level inference. Extensive experiments on ASR models, Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) and Omni models show that incorporating visual context substantially improves recall over the audio-only setting across all three model families. The gains are largest for ETE and smallest for ISE, indicating that models leverage direct visual evidence more effectively than indirect semantic cues. To facilitate future research on visually grounded speech recognition, we publicly release ScreenASR-Bench.

items.title: ChronoScribe: Semantic-Numerical Specialization for Instruction-Driven Time Series Forecasting
items.content: arXiv:2610.16345v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent advances in instruction-driven time series forecasting highlight a fundamental tension: systems must simultaneously master natural-language instruction following and precise numerical prediction. Current approaches often force a compromise. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret unstructured requests but may be inaccurate when asked to produce forecast values directly, whereas time series foundation models (TSFMs) provide numerical forecasts but typically require structured inputs specifying the target series, context window, and horizon. We present ChronoScribe, which applies semantic-numerical specialization to this workflow. A LoRA-adapted LLM proposes an execution path and context length; deterministic rules resolve the executable configuration. On the specialist path, a frozen TSFM produces quantile trajectories for the task-specified horizon. Deterministic trajectory summaries condition the response, while the LLM neither generates nor revises predicted values. We evaluate a Qwen3.5-9B--Chronos-2 implementation across 23 evaluation dimensions and 30 public datasets against eleven proprietary direct LLMs and three open TSFMs. ChronoScribe has the lowest error on sMAPE, MASE, WAPE, RMSE, and MAE among all evaluated systems, including fixed-context controls. Across these metrics, even the lowest direct-LLM error remains 2.0--2.7 times the corresponding ChronoScribe error. At the system level, ChronoScribe achieves a Task-Level Score (TLS) of 65.5, 10.6 points above the strongest direct-LLM baseline. The results support ChronoScribe's division of labor, in which the LLM handles interpretation, configuration, and communication while the TSFM handles numerical forecasting.

This specialization avoids forcing a single system to be both instruction-following and numerically precise.
items.reasoning: A clean division-of-labor design for a practical forecasting workflow, leveraging existing LLMs and TSFMs rather than novel modeling. The routing idea is sensible but modest in research novelty, and evaluation details are not visible in the abstract.

items.title: Output Discipline Sets the Floor: A Falsification-Guided, Model-Agnostic Agent Protocol for Auditable Hypothesis-Driven Decision Making
items.content: arXiv:2610.18298v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: What binds large language models on auditable, hypothesis-driven decision tasks, where every candidate can be checked against the evidence? On the public TCMEval-SDT benchmark for Traditional Chinese Medicine syndrome differentiation (200 cases), the binding constraint is output discipline and reasoning structure, not model capability alone: two years of model scaling move zero-shot scores by only -0.03 to +0.08, while output-discipline failures (non-terminating reasoning, format non-compliance, large run-to-run spread) persist even in frontier models. We test this with a model-agnostic agent framework formalizing decision making as a five-stage closed loop, enforced by a candidate x evidence matrix falsification protocol: every candidate is judged against every evidence item, at least half of the candidates must be falsified before a conclusion is licensed, and survivors are emitted in a machine-verifiable single-line format. Across five base models, the effect is sign-conditional on zero-shot output discipline: it rescues models whose discipline fails (DeepSeek-V4-Flash: +0.267/+0.271, entirely termination rescue), reduces a high-variance model's run-to-run standard deviation from 0.218 to 0.007 (Kimi K3), and significantly costs already-disciplined models (-0.087 to -0.120 on budget-matched Qwen3-4B/32B). Ablations attribute the cost to the candidate-bounded format layer and show the effect is independent of injected knowledge content (protocol-knowledge decoupling). The protocol also transfers to misinformation-robust mathematical reasoning, detecting injected false premises at 89.8% recall with a 6.8% false-positive rate (MCC 0.54; a flag-everything baseline scores 0) and restoring accuracy to the no-misinformation ceiling. Where zero-shot output discipline is weak, the reasoning protocol sets the floor; base-model capability always sets the ceiling.

items.title: Selective Knowledge Control for Continual GUI Agent Learning over Application Streams
items.content: arXiv:2609.06530v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Continual learning is a crucial capability for Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents to adapt to evolving applications while retaining knowledge acquired from previous applications. Such application streams pose a challenging knowledge modeling problem: new applications often share underlying knowledge with past ones, yet also introduce specific knowledge that must not interfere with historical knowledge. In this paper, we propose activation-conditioned selective knowledge control, a lightweight method that achieves selective knowledge retention via neuron-level gradient manipulation. Our method maintains a compact historical knowledge state to protect highly activated MLP neurons that preserve previous knowledge. When a new application arrives, it performs real-time gradient surgery conditioned on forward activation. Concretely, the protected neurons are categorized into two types: unactivated neurons holding specific knowledge, whose gradients are truncated to prevent interference; and activated neurons holding shared knowledge, whose gradients are orthogonally projected to preserve stability while enabling adaptation. After each application stage, newly identified critical neurons are merged into the historical state for future learning. Empirical evaluations on multi-app sequential benchmark demonstrate that our method effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting on prior applications while sustaining robust adaptation to new ones.

items.title: RealityBench: Simulated Environments to Evaluate a Vision Language Model's Ability to Document Human Physical Work
items.content: arXiv:2610.14397v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Augmenting worker capabilities in the physical world through guidance has been a decades-long goal for AI agents. One key supporting capability is to understand what the worker is doing, seeing through the human's camera or smart glasses, and assist them in documentation. Despite advances in vision language models, their capabilities in these settings remain uncertain and are challenging to benchmark because most physical work data is proprietary, and involves too much variability to study in a principled manner. Unlike structured settings such as kitchens and warehouses that have predictable lighting, geometry, and objects, field-facing tasks such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair are unconstrained and high variance. Here, we model real-world physical work in Blender across eleven environments, incorporating variants in both image acceptability and documentation. The acceptability task asks whether a particular view would be suitable proof-of-work and documentation asks whether an agent can understand the task-relevant state of the environment from that view. Across 26 vision-language models, we find that top models largely solve documentation when the answer is text in frame, but are weak at reading measurements and at judging small parts and spatial relations, such as whether a tape measure leans. Acceptability is harder to pin down because human raters disagree with each other. Measured against a scorer that agrees with the raters' majority about as often as a single rater does, the best models cannot be distinguished from a single non-author rater, at a cost within the range of a human pass. In the three environments where we can trace acceptability errors, most wrong rejections come from misreading the scene rather than the requirement. On the three documentation questions for which we have real images, model rankings on rendered frames transfer to real images.
items.author: Andrew Perrault (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA), Anmol Takiar (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA), Dominik Wienecki (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA), Arnab Nandi (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA)

It measures documentation and task-understanding capabilities of current models.

items.title: Scale, Drivers, and Limits of Representational Alignment Across Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.14476v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Comparing large language models can reveal shared representational structure and systematic differences between them. However, aggregate similarity measures can obscure how agreement varies across geometric scales and which linguistic properties support it. We introduce two complementary methods to resolve where models agree and what supports that agreement. Standard representational similarity analysis (RSA) summarizes similarity across all stimulus pairs, potentially obscuring differences in alignment between nearby and distant inputs. Neighborhood-Weighted RSA (NW-RSA) addresses this limitation by weighting stimulus pairs according to their proximity in representational space, placing alignment from local neighborhoods to global geometry on a common scale. Counterfactual RSA (CF-RSA) tests which linguistic properties support alignment by comparing intact representations in one model with representations under controlled linguistic perturbations in another. Across diverse language models, we find strong agreement in coarse representational geometry but substantial divergence in local neighborhoods. Alignment is observed both across broadly sampled natural text and within linguistic equivalence classes that preserve particular aspects of meaning or structure. Counterfactual analyses reveal selective sensitivity: changes to logical scope reduce alignment substantially more than the tested changes to hierarchical syntax, event roles, or discourse structure. Alignment also decreases when sentence structure or lexical meaning is disrupted in word lists and jabberwocky sentences, suggesting that the regularities of natural language support stronger convergence. These findings refine claims of representational universality by showing that strong overall similarity need not imply agreement in how models represent finer linguistic distinctions.

items.title: Fitting Every Hint Is Not Enough: Premature Floods in Recurrent Algorithmic Reasoners
items.content: arXiv:2610.14982v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recurrent algorithmic reasoners are trained with per-step hints on small graphs and run for many more steps on large ones. On breadth-first search in SALSA-CLRS, we find that a reasoner can reproduce every training hint and still fail on deep graphs: after some exact steps, it declares nodes reached before the search gets there. We call this a premature flood and trace two routes to it. In our GRU processor with a degree input, the flood is carried in the hidden state and set off when that input is in the tail of the training distribution. Setting the input higher at inference brings the flood sooner, and none of the six flooding models counts steps. Without the input, summing the neighbors' states instead of averaging them also breaks the processor. In the benchmark's own GIN and PGN, trained with its code, some seeds instead flood from a fixed step, on sparse and dense graphs alike. Clamping the degree input or adding 200 dense training graphs removes every failure of the GRU processor. Detaching the state between steps avoids the flood in that processor (0 of 23 seeds, against 6 under full backpropagation) but not with sums or a residual update, and two published remedies leave floods. None of the benchmark's test sets is both deep and dense, but its deepest one shows the second route: on its Delaunay graphs at 1,600 nodes, one GIN seed floods from step 18. We therefore recommend auditing the range of every input and aggregate, which catches the first route, and testing on deep graphs, which catches both.

items.title: When Does Compensating Inherited Quantization Error Help? Mean-Square Guarantees for Layer-Wise Quantization and Their Limits
items.content: arXiv:2610.16020v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Layer-wise post-training quantization methods let each layer compensate for the quantization error inherited from earlier layers. We ask under what assumptions such compensation guarantees a network output error no larger than without it. For linear networks of any depth, with the required calibration Gram matrices invertible, if the rounding error of each layer has zero conditional mean and a deterministic second-moment map common to both schemes, as under subtractive dither on an unbounded grid, then compensation with strengths in $[0,1]$ fixed in advance gives a mean-square output error no larger than no compensation, each scheme being followed along its own trajectory. The exact gain separates error removed directly from reduced excitation of later rounding noise. Outside this setting the comparison can fail. With rectified linear activations it fails for two independent reasons: noise changes activation states, and, even when no state changes, the correction moves error from samples on which a unit is inactive to samples on which it is active. With stable activations, commutators between the calibration projection and the activation patterns bound the excess. With a bounded codebook, even unique exact layer-wise minimizers with no overload can give a larger output error. For fixed rounding errors it already fails for two scalar linear layers, refuting a published universal guarantee. An exact residual identity gives the necessary and sufficient condition on a common layer input. All these comparisons hold the calibration input fixed. On two 8B models at 4 bits, fixed half-strength compensation beat uncompensated rounding in every model, text and draw tested, yet no rule for choosing the strength beat a layer-wise rule consistently, and lowering the full-network loss on the data used to choose did not reliably lower it on new text.

For linear networks, with invertible calibration Gram matrices and zero-conditional-mean rounding errors (e.g., subtractive dither), fixed-strength compensation yields mean-square error no larger than the uncompensated scheme. It precisely characterizes when the technique helps and its limits.

items.title: pi-Net: Empirical Latent Representations for Differentiable Physics Heads in Data-Scarce Systems
items.content: arXiv:2610.16504v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Developing reliable predictive models for multi-physics systems often forces a compromise between computationally demanding physical simulators and data-hungry, opaque machine learning (ML) algorithms. While incorporating dimensional analysis into directed computation graphs offers a structurally sound alternative to explicitly solving partial differential equations (PDEs), such formulations typically yield underdetermined systems that act as imperfect simulators. We introduce pi-Net, a physics-informed latent variable model that resolves these imperfect simulators. The hybrid pi-Net architecture consists of an encoder that maps inputs into physically normalized latent space, which are then decoded into final predictions by a differentiable physics head. Evaluated on a real-world, data-scarce Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW) case study, the framework achieves an R2 of 0.864 with only 60 experimental samples. The results demonstrate that pi-Net significantly outperforms purely data-driven baselines in data-scarce regimes while providing causal, process-level explainability.

It targets multi-physics prediction where full simulators are expensive and pure ML is data-hungry and opaque.
items.reasoning: A reasonable hybrid physics-ML contribution in the scientific machine learning space, with sensible handling of data-scarce regimes. The approach is somewhat incremental relative to existing physics-informed and UDE literature, and the abstract leaves empirical scope unclear.

items.title: SarcasTraps: Effect of Sarcasm on Turkish Hate Speech Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.16957v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Standard hate speech detection datasets often emphasize explicit harmful language, but directed harm can also be expressed indirectly, without clearly hateful wording. Sarcasm is one such form of indirect expression, as it can convey harmful intent through mock praise, exaggeration, humor, or apparent politeness. In this paper, we introduce SarcasTraps, a targeted external test set for analyzing the effect of sarcasm on Turkish hate speech detection. SarcasTraps contains 479 entries annotated along two dimensions: hate speech and sarcasm. We train classifiers using BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa on two existing Turkish hate speech datasets and evaluate them on SarcasTraps, using it strictly as an external test set. We also evaluate GPT-4.1 and Llama-3.3-70B in a zero-shot setting on SarcasTraps. Results show that sarcasm substantially affects hate speech detection. Fine-tuned encoder models lose recall on sarcastic hate, while zero-shot LLMs maintain higher recall but suffer substantial precision drops on sarcastic examples. These findings show that both fine-tuned hate speech detectors and zero-shot LLMs struggle when sarcasm is involved, and SarcasTraps provides quantitative evidence of this challenge through a targeted Turkish test set. Due to the presence of sensitive and hateful language, SarcasTraps will be shared upon request for academic research purposes. Warning: This paper has examples from the dataset which contains offensive and hateful content towards groups of people.
items.author: Niyazi Ahmet Metin, Dilara Kek\"ull\"uo\u{g}lu
items.summary: SarcasTraps is a 479-entry Turkish external test set annotated for hate speech and sarcasm, used to show that sarcasm — harmful intent conveyed through mock praise or apparent politeness — degrades hate speech detection by fine-tuned BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa classifiers and by large models including GPT-4.1. It matters because indirect harm evades detectors trained on explicitly hateful wording, and non-English languages are under-tested.
items.reasoning: Focused, useful resource for a real failure mode in an underrepresented language, and inclusion of commercial LLM baselines adds relevance. Small test set and localized scope limit general impact.

items.title: SonicWorld: Source-Centric Latent Dynamics for Spatial Audio Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.17131v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Dynamic spatial audio reasoning requires a model to associate changing acoustic observations with the correct source and recover its spatial state at a queried time or interval, a challenge intensified by overlapping speech and source motion. To study this problem, we introduce Sonic-Bench, comprising 2.8K first-order Ambisonics clips and 28.8K target-specific question-answer pairs across 480 simulated indoor scenes. The benchmark covers localization, distance estimation, and motion reasoning in single- and dual-source settings. We further propose SonicWorld, which integrates physical, learned acoustic, and semantic features into persistent source states through learned transitions and recurrent updates, and projects them into an Omni LLM for spatial reasoning. Compared with Spatial-Omni on the Sonic-Bench test split, SonicWorld improves direction accuracy from 31.98% to 34.69% and reduces azimuth error from 57.22{\deg} to 48.01{\deg}. In zero-shot transfer to Spatial LibriSpeech, SonicWorld retains strong localization performance, achieving 73.98% direction accuracy and 19.29{\deg} azimuth error, compared with 27.14% and 70.74{\deg} for Spatial-Omni.
items.author: Chenlong Wei, Hanling Wang, Mingjin Lou, Yufan Shi, Yandong Sun, Sheldon Yu, Xiaohui Zhu, Xiaobo Jin, Yiwei Wang

To study this problem, we introduce Sonic-Bench, comprising 2.8K first-order Ambisonics clips and 28.8K target-specific question-answer pairs across 480 simulated indoor scenes. The benchmark covers localization, distance estimation, and motion reasoning in single- and dual-source settings. We further propose SonicWorld, which integrates physical, learned acoustic, and semantic features into persistent source states through learned transitions and recurrent updates, and projects them into an Omni LLM for spatial reasoning. Compared with Spatial-Omni on the Sonic-Bench test split, SonicWorld improves direction accuracy from 31.98% to 34.69% and reduces azimuth error from 57.22{\deg} to 48.01{\deg}. In zero-shot transfer to Spatial LibriSpeech, SonicWorld retains strong localization performance, achieving 73.98% direction accuracy and 19.29{\deg} azimuth error, compared with 27.14% and 70.74{\deg} for Spatial-Omni.

items.title: HASTE: Hierarchical and Attribute-aware Supervision for Generative Recommendation
items.content: arXiv:2610.17368v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Generative recommendation models have shown promising results by representing items as semantic IDs and generating these IDs autoregressively. We introduce an approach showing that explicitly incorporating hierarchical and attribute-level supervision into generative recommendation can simultaneously improve training efficiency and long-tail recommendation performance. Existing approaches typically optimize semantic ID prediction with a standard causal cross-entropy objective, which does not explicitly exploit the hierarchical structure of semantic IDs and can require substantial training to learn effective item representations. Moreover, data-sparse tail items often suffer from poor representations due to limited supervision, resulting in weaker long-tail recommendation performance. We address these challenges with HASTE (Hierarchical and Attribute-aware Supervision for generaTive rEcommendation), a unified training framework that introduces hierarchical and attribute-specific supervision. HASTE's Hierarchical Loss explicitly exploits the multi-level structure of semantic IDs, providing supervision at each level of the item hierarchy and substantially accelerating training convergence. Its Attribute-Specific Losses encourage the model to preserve fine-grained item attributes, leveraging the language model's inherent semantic knowledge to improve representations and recommendations for tail items. We extensively evaluate HASTE on a fashion recommendation benchmark and across multiple domains of the Amazon dataset. HASTE improves recommendation performance across datasets and item-frequency regimes. Notably, the Hierarchical Loss achieves approximately 2x faster convergence than the standard causal cross-entropy objective, substantially improving training efficiency while maintaining strong recommendation quality.

items.title: Dissociating Answerability from Extraction in LLM Question Answering over Radiology Reports
items.content: arXiv:2610.17576v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Answering questions from radiology reports involves two decisions: whether the report contains an answer and which span gives it. A false answer presents an unsupported claim as fact; an over-abstention hides what the report says. Yet RadQA results are reported as a single F1 that merges both. We propose an evaluation method that separates them, reporting false-answer and over-abstention rates beside F1 and splitting F1 changes into extraction and answerability terms. We apply it to 13 LLMs on the RadQA test set, zero-shot and with three cumulative demonstration sets, the last adding an unanswerable example. Models with similar F1 differed more than twofold in false-answer rate. The unanswerable example changed when models answered, not how well they extracted: 12 of 13 models abstained more often, and three-quarters of the answers they withdrew had F1 $\geq$ 0.5. Within models, false answers showed no clear association with extraction quality, but acting on the decision itself helped: keeping an answer only when enough other models also answered lowered the zero-shot false-answer rate by 4 points without a detectable F1 change. Because the two decisions can change independently, we suggest radiology QA evaluations report them separately, not through F1 alone.

items.title: Dynamic K-Head: Difficulty-Supervised Budget Selection for Continuous Latent Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.17679v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) improves reasoning but incurs substantial autoregressive rationale cost. Continuous CoT moves intermediate computation into recurrent hidden states, yet typically uses a fixed number of updates even though the best budget varies across questions and accuracy need not improve monotonically with $K$. We introduce Dynamic K-Head, a question-conditioned, pre-rollout budget selector. It is jointly trained with the reasoner under selected budgets, using difficulty supervision based on scores assigned from the question alone. We also show that latent-update count can misrepresent end-to-end cost because a short latent rollout can shift computation into a longer explicit continuation. We therefore count latent updates, implementation-specific special tokens, and all decoded text. Instantiated with CoDI on Llama 3.2 1B and GSM8K, Dynamic K-Head reaches 54.44% exact-match accuracy at 12.03 average reasoning/output tokens, compared with 52.31% at 15.21 tokens for fixed-$K=6$ CoDI---a 2.12-point gain with 20.9% lower token cost. Across three out-of-distribution arithmetic datasets, it reduces cost by 19.3--25.7% while improving accuracy by 0.30--2.22 points. These results demonstrate that difficulty-supervised budget selection can improve both accuracy and efficiency, while stable budget selection remains a central challenge.

items.title: FASHION-RQ: Mining Hierarchical Semantic Structure for Automated Evaluation of Fashion Retrieval
items.content: arXiv:2610.17841v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Evaluating fashion retrieval systems remains challenging due to the limited availability of benchmarks that capture the fine-grained, open-ended queries encountered in real-world search and recommendation. Existing benchmarks often rely on manual curation, predefined taxonomies, or synthetic prompts, limiting scalability and semantic coverage. We introduce FASHION-RQ: Mining Hierarchical Semantic Structure for Automated Evaluation of Fashion Retrieval, an automated framework that derives user-type queries and relevance sets directly from catalog structure. Our key insight is that hierarchical discrete representations learned by Residual Quantized Variational Autoencoders (RQ-VAE) organize products into semantically coherent clusters at progressively finer granularities. We leverage this structure to construct FASHION-RQBENCH, a scalable benchmark without manual query annotation or predefined taxonomies. We propose four complementary tasks for evaluating ranking, relevance classification, fine-grained sibling discrimination, and paraphrase robustness, alongside query- and attribute-level relevance metrics. Experiments across recent retrieval models demonstrate that FASHION-RQBENCH differentiates model capabilities across query types and attributes. A human study further shows that benchmark queries achieve comparable naturalness and higher intent clarity than real user queries, supporting their validity for real-world evaluation. The code and FASHION-RQBENCH dataset will be publicly released upon acceptance.

items.title: GLST: Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Memory Decomposition Framework for Online Chained-Goal Navigation
items.content: arXiv:2610.17927v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Autonomous navigation in real-world environments often requires long-horizon operation under partial observability and evolving goals. Existing mapless navigation approaches predominantly assume fixed goals throughout an episode, limiting applicability to practical scenarios where goals change online during execution. We study online chained-goal navigation, where goals evolve through existing-goal redirection or new-goal emergence without explicit transition signals. Under this setting, we find navigation may require either continued exploration or strategic revisitation, creating conflicting memory requirements. We propose Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Belief Learning (GLST), a memory-decomposition framework that separates latent beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations for long-horizon reasoning. We further introduce goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation under evolving goals. Extensive experiments in simulation across diverse terrains demonstrate improved chained-goal navigation performance over baselines. Real-robot experiments using the Spot quadruped further validate our memory decomposition framework.

The author list includes well-known robotics researchers (Tomlin, Pavone, Sastry), lending credibility.

items.title: Lightweight but Linguistically Fair? Quantisation Robustness across Bavarian, German, and English
items.content: arXiv:2610.18343v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Post-training quantisation reduces the memory cost of large language models, but it remains unclear whether compression preserves language skills of regional varieties as reliably as their standard-language counterparts. We study this question for Bavarian, Standard German, and English using BAVGROUND, a multiple-choice benchmark, where 206 source questions are aligned across all three languages. Across 14 open-weight 7B--10B instruction models, we compare BF16 with 8-bit GPTQ and two 4-bit settings, GPTQ and AWQ. Eight-bit GPTQ remains close to BF16 and largely preserves the relative behaviour of the three languages, while 4-bit quantisation was found to be much less stable. The two 4-bit methods reduce average accuracy by about 1.4--1.5 percentage points and change 11.9--16.0% of BF16 decisions, with changes concentrated on examples where the BF16 model is already uncertain. This instability does not translate into a consistent Bavarian disadvantage. Although Bavarian, a low-resource dialect, has lower baseline accuracy than German and English, the language most affected at 4 bits varies across models and quantisation methods. Calibration further shapes these cross-language effects: the relative Bavarian--German effect changes with calibration language, while changing the calibration source has little average effect on GPTQ-4 but can affect AWQ-4 much more strongly. Free-form evaluation on five models further shows that 4-bit compression can degrade generated responses even in settings where multiple-choice accuracy changes only modestly, while 8-bit GPTQ remains comparatively stable. Overall, our results show that quantisation robustness for regional language varieties depends on the model, quantisation method, calibration data, and evaluation setting, and cannot be measured by aggregate multilingual accuracy alone.

The fairness question of whether compression disproportionately harms low-resource varieties is directly addressed.

items.title: Task-evoked eye movements as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults
items.content: arXiv:2610.18494v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Objective digital measures of depression severity could complement conventional symptom assessments and facilitate more timely clinical evaluation. Here, we investigated whether task-evoked eye movements provide interpretable behavioral markers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults. In this single-center, cross-sectional study, 155 participants aged 14--20 years completed emotional-spatial free-viewing and memory-guided recall tasks and were stratified by 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores. We examined 19 prespecified eye-movement features across six task-informed domains using covariate-adjusted ordinal-trend models. Greater depression severity was associated with lower gaze-allocation entropy (standardized $\beta=-0.599$), fewer inter-area switches ($\beta=-0.526$), longer first target-entry latency ($\beta=0.572$), and lower target dwell proportion ($\beta=-0.678$; all false-discovery-rate-adjusted $q<0.001$). Emotion-specific attentional-bias measures were not associated with severity, whereas associations involving fixation dispersion weakened after adjustment for anxiety symptoms. In a complementary machine-learning analysis incorporating 44 candidate eye-movement features and demographic covariates, a three-stage cascade classifier achieved the highest four-class stratification performance (accuracy, 0.665; macro-F1, 0.670; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.869), outperforming single-stage and two-stage approaches. Together, these findings identify altered visual exploration and memory-guided gaze control as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity, rather than generalized negative attentional bias. These results support further prospective evaluation of task-evoked eye tracking as a complementary approach for timely severity assessment and clinical decision support.

items.title: Variance Fingerprints: Component-Wise Identification of Content Factors by Augmentation Design
items.content: arXiv:2610.14260v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Augmentation-based self-supervised learning can recover the content shared across views without separating its underlying factors into individual coordinates. We ask whether augmentations can be designed to make those factors identifiable. Our approach allows content factors to fluctuate across augmented views while preserving their mean for each source instance. Each instance receives a fixed, recorded set of augmentation strengths that controls how much its factors fluctuate. When factors respond differently to changes in these strengths, their patterns of variation provide information that distinguishes them. Under suitable decoder and support assumptions, we prove that these differences identify individual factors in a conditional Gaussian model, up to permutation, scaling, and translation. We then develop a learner that uses the recorded strengths to estimate these patterns jointly across instances, enabling learning from few views per instance. Synthetic experiments demonstrate near-perfect factor recovery through nonlinear mixing. Controlled dSprites experiments show improved coordinate alignment using augmentations that target known factors, even without telling the learner which augmentation corresponds to which representation coordinate. These results suggest a route to component identification in self-supervised learning: augmentation design can supply identifying information beyond shared content alone.
items.author: D. Hudson Smith
items.summary: The paper asks whether augmentation design in self-supervised learning can make individual content factors identifiable, assigning each instance a fixed recorded set of augmentation strengths so that differing factor responses yield distinguishing variation patterns. Under decoder and support assumptions, the authors prove factor identifiability in a conditional Gaussian setting. It advances theory on when SSL recovers disentangled factors rather than an entangled content subspace.

items.title: DEFT: Disentanglement-Enhanced Fine-Tuning for EEG Foundation Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.14497v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: EEG foundation models (EFMs) have improved EEG representation learning by transferring knowledge from large-scale multi-subject pretraining to downstream tasks. However, their pretrained embeddings often retain substantial subject-related variation, placing an additional burden on the downstream classifier, especially in cross-subject settings. To address this issue, we propose Disentangled EFM Fine-Tuning (DEFT), a plug-and-play adapter for EFM fine-tuning. DEFT encourages branch disentanglement of pretrained tokens into task-oriented content and subject-consistent style, then performs downstream prediction from the content branch.
