items.title: Natural Language Processing for Aligning Readings with Learning Objectives and Assessing Topic Balance in Dental Education
items.content: arXiv:2610.15941v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Curriculum teams often lack time to check whether assigned readings support learning objectives (LOs) and whether topic coverage is balanced. We present a natural language processing (NLP) workflow to support evidence-informed curation of reading lists. The workflow combines PubMedBERT sentence embeddings and cosine similarity for retrieval, natural language inference (NLI) for evidence checking, and topic modeling for coverage analysis. We tested the approach in dental education using 13 course-level LOs and a PubMed-derived corpus of 3,837 LO-abstract pairs. Median cosine similarity ranged from 0.86 to 0.91 across the 13 LOs, showing generally high semantic similarity. Topic modeling showed broad but uneven coverage, with one or two dominant topics per domain. Similarity alone was not enough for selecting readings: among high-similarity pairs (cosine 0.90-1.00), 22.9% were classified by NLI as neutral or contradictory. In a 49-pair expert-labeled validation set, cosine-based retrieval (cosine >= 0.90) achieved 0.69 accuracy, while the combined cosine and NLI approach achieved 0.73 accuracy against expert alignment labels. Overall, the workflow shows how AI can support curriculum alignment by reducing false positives and helping select readings that better match intended LOs.

items.title: Event Memory and Narrative Dynamics: A Large Language Model Framework for Multidimensional State Spaces
items.content: arXiv:2610.16971v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Studying event memory requires defining events and their relationships within remembered experience. Autobiographical narratives provide evidence of this organization, but their analytical units must first be established. This study introduces a large language model framework for constructing event representations from narratives and modeling their structure and dynamics with excerpt-level traceability. Explicit boundary rules and a feature schema informed by hippocampal models of episodic memory and navigation guide event construction. In a proof-of-concept application to interviews from five participants, the framework constructed 256 event-states. Multiple correspondence analysis embedded these states in feature-based spaces, with analyses focused on a selected 4-D geometry and 10-D and 13-D reference geometries. Consecutive event-states were significantly closer than expected under randomized narrative order. In the selected 4-D ten-basin solution, similarity between basin-state feature profiles corresponded with similarity between one-step routing profiles; context, mechanism, and theme differentiated full-system pathway engagement. A successor representation modeled expected basin-state occupancy across successive steps. Correlations between basin-centroid distances and complete successor-profile distances were positive across all five basin solutions, with exploratory tests supporting correspondence in at least two solutions across all three geometries. These findings connect feature-based event representations with observed narrative transitions and modeled multistep organization. The framework translates hippocampal principles into source-linked event boundaries and state representations, providing an analytical basis for testing neural accounts of event segmentation and predictive organization during naturalistic recall.

items.title: Squeeze-Aware-YOLO: Early Channel Recalibration and Multi-Scale Fusion for Real-Time Traffic Sign Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.15604v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Traffic sign detection plays a vital role in intelligent transportation systems, supporting the safe operation of advanced driver assistance systems and autonomous vehicles. Despite significant progress in real-time object detection, accurately identifying traffic signs under challenging conditions remains difficult. Variations in lighting, adverse weather, motion blur, and partial occlusion often reduce detection performance, especially for small or visually degraded signs where important spatial information can be lost. To address these challenges, we propose Squeeze-Aware-YOLO, a lightweight traffic sign detection framework that introduces a multi-branch bottleneck module combining convolutional kernels of different sizes with a Squeeze-and-Excitation mechanism to improve feature extraction and adaptive channel weighting. In addition, we integrate the Multi-Branch Auxiliary Feature Pyramid Network and Re-parameterized Heterogeneous Multi-Scale modules to strengthen multi-scale feature representation and feature fusion while preserving real-time inference efficiency for practical deployment. The proposed approach is evaluated on the Bangladeshi Traffic Sign Detection Dataset, the CSUST Chinese Traffic Sign Detection Benchmark 2021, and the German Traffic Sign Detection Benchmark, achieving mAP@0.5 scores of 74.7%, 79.4%, and 84.0%, respectively, while consistently outperforming recent state-of-the-art YOLO-based traffic sign detectors. These findings demonstrate that combining multi-scale receptive fields, channel attention, and enhanced feature fusion enables more accurate and robust traffic sign detection while maintaining the computational efficiency required for real-world deployment.

items.title: ProGAN-Based Synthetic Image Generation for Industrial Visual Inspection of Metallic Parts
items.content: arXiv:2610.16287v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Automated visual inspection is essential for efficient repair and recycling of metallic components. AI-based defect detection is a strong fit. However, it is often constrained by scarce, low-diversity training data. To address this gap, we study Generative AI-driven synthetic image generation using Progressive Growing GANs (ProGAN). We implement a ProGAN pipeline with Wasserstein loss and gradient penalty and evaluate key hyperparameters on two public datasets, MVTec AD (metal nut) and MPDD (tube). As a result, training remained stable and the model yielded realistic images. These images can augment training data, improve robustness, and reduce the cost of collecting rare defects.

items.summary: Implements a Progressive Growing GAN with Wasserstein loss and gradient penalty to synthesize realistic images of metallic parts, evaluated on MVTec AD and MPDD industrial defect datasets. The generated data can augment scarce defect-training sets, improving robustness of automated visual inspection while reducing the cost of collecting rare-defect samples.
items.reasoning: Applies well-established GAN techniques from 2017-2018 era to an industrial inspection domain; while practically useful, the methodological novelty is low given modern diffusion-based alternatives, and the abstract reports only stable training and realism rather than downstream detection gains. Suitable as applied engineering work.

items.title: Generative Quantum Machine Learning Methods for Cancer Detection using Augmented Datasets
items.content: arXiv:2610.15110v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Cancer detection using AI methods and image databases faces several challenges, including limited and imbalanced image datasets, long algorithm training times, and high-complexity feature generation. In particular, many cancer image datasets contain very few malignant examples compared to benign ones, limiting the amount of minority-class data available for training. Although classical AI and especially deep learning methods have had some success in providing cancer diagnostics, Quantum Machine Learning (QML) methods may offer advantages through high-dimensional feature representations, generative data augmentation, and the exploitation of feature correlations through quantum properties such as entanglement. In this paper, we propose using a generative QML method on the compressed breast ultrasound image dataset (BUSI) to generate synthetic images and hence augmented datasets for classifier training. In particular, we train a convolutional neural network with real, synthetic, and a combination of real and synthetic images. We test the algorithm on real images and provide comparative results for all three training cases. Our results show that the classifier trained entirely on synthetic images achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.802 (80.2%), compared with 0.760 (76.0%) for the real-data baseline.

The authors argue QML may offer advantages through high-dimensional feature representations and entanglement-based feature correlations. It is an early exploratory study at the intersection of quantum computing and medical imaging.

items.title: Targeting the Right Situations: Mutation Testing of Fuzzy-Powered Situation Hyperspace
items.content: arXiv:2610.15122v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Ensuring the safety of autonomous Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) operating in underground mines is challenging due to the vast and uncertain Operational Design Domain (ODD). Traditional validation approaches, such as random testing, often result in inefficient situation coverage, allocating computational resources to low-risk scenarios while failing to expose critical edge cases. Building on prior work in risk-prioritized Situation Coverage, this paper investigates whether Fuzzy Logic-based risk estimation effectively correlates with real system failures. To this end, we conduct a mutation testing study within our SCALOFT simulation framework. A fixed set of software mutants is systematically injected and evaluated under two testing strategies: (i) uniformly random situation generation and (ii) Fuzzy-Guided risk-prioritized situation generation. Experimental results show that the Fuzzy-Guided approach achieves a higher mutation score and is more effective at exposing difficult-to-detect faults compared to random testing.

It addresses inefficient situation coverage in validation of safety-critical autonomous systems.

items.title: Q&A: Building accountability behind our words — and AI’s — in civic conversations
items.content:
When government officials craft policies, there is often a comment period for public feedback. Lawmakers have long had to sort through fake feedback that is mass-produced in an effort to sway policy, but they’ve generally gotten used to detecting it. With, artificial intelligence, however, people can submit realistic-seeming comments, which are harder to dismiss as being fabrications with no person behind them. That’s just one way AI can be used to generate text and statements, in civic conversations, for which no one can be found to be answerable.

This issue, among others, has caught the attention of Deb Roy, professor of media arts and sciences at MIT and director of the MIT Center for Constructive Communication (CCC). In a new essay published in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, titled, “Who stands behind the words?,” Roy calls for a renewed emphasis on responsibility in communication, asserting that even when AI is used to craft text, there needs to be accountability and “answerability.”

Building better group dialogues to produce more public trust is a core part of the work of CCC. The group, along with Cortico, the closely affiliated nonprofit Roy co-founded, has helped facilitate group discussions on important issues in many situations — including civic meetings, schools, deliberative assemblies, and private organizations — and used tech tools, including AI, to help find themes among comments, and more. But the center also designs this process so that participants can check and override the tech-based output at each key step. Ultimately, a person is responsible for every public comment. MIT News spoke to Roy about the essay and the work of the center. 

Q: You’ve identified this problem about the lack of accountability behind words that are generated by AI. When did you really first notice this?

A: It came into focus when Chat-GPT [which is powered by a large language model, or LLM] launched. As for my own history with language models, my PhD work explored what we might now call PLMs — Puny Language Models — so I’m quite familiar with language models and have tracked the field’s rapid evolution. But Chat-GPT turned a corner. Two things changed at the same time: the depth of the model and its knowledge, and the way you could interact with it. 

I became obsessed with trying to find the limits of what it could do. And I felt that no matter how hard I tried to stretch my arms around it, I couldn’t. I built my tenure case at MIT on language grounding — the idea that it’s not enough for an AI system to just process lots of words and other symbols. I believed that to understand what words mean, you actually need a physical body and life experiences as part of the process. So I revisited the philosophy-of-AI literature I had once been steeped in, which asks what fundamentally distinguishes the kind of system that large language models exemplify, in extraordinarily advanced form, from the kind of processing we humans engage in. I gave several presentations to my own graduate students trying to make the case that, even though AI seems so intelligent, it’s actually different in kind — and I could not convince them. 

And I thought, I know the difference, but I’m having trouble convincing even myself of what it is. And that led me to ask, “Wait a minute: Is there someone or something that stands behind the words, a human responsible for what is being said?” That’s the thing this extraordinary new language machine doesn’t have. 

Whether these systems genuinely understand language is actively debated. But even if you grant them all the comprehension you like, they still lack standing. The buck can’t stop at a thing, a software system, with nothing to lose.

Q: The Bulletin piece has these interesting examples of civic feedback forums where it looks like there are real people saying things, and instead you have a barrage of comments from AI. How did you find some of these other examples in society where things go off the rails in this way? 

A: After the release of ChatGPT, I started hearing a concern from people inside government who review public comments on proposed rules: a suspicion that not all of the comments were written by humans.

My reaction was: That’s going to delegitimize this channel for public feedback. That was several years ago, but everyone now knows this is happening. Public comment is a pillar of democracy. You don’t just put a new rule in place. People need to have a voice and feel like they’ve been heard before a rule is imposed on them. If you skip that step, people don’t accept rules as legitimate. That’s why that process is baked into how America works. And that pillar just cracked, and by now, in my mind, it’s fallen over. Has anyone noticed? My sense is the people on the receiving end of these comments have quietly adjusted the weight they give to public comments. It was never perfect, but boy, now much of its value is being swept away. 

I open my essay with this example: In 2017, the Federal Communications Commission received more than 22 million public comments on its proposal to repeal net neutrality rules, and the New York attorney general later found that nearly 18 million of them were fake. As I write in the essay, “That fraud was caught because it left fingerprints: templated text, duplicated phrasing.” But large language models erase the fingerprints. Now every comment can be fluent and different, and reviewers can no longer tell which ones express views that real people formed and stand behind.

If you have enough of the stuff that’s fake — words that no one with a stake actually stands behind — it desensitizes you to what’s real. That filters back to the public, and people realize: If I take the time to express myself, they’re not even listening any more.

Q: Could you say a little bit more about your point that we need people with “standing,” who will take “accountability” for all pieces of text, even when those bits of text are generated by AI? 

A: In the legal system, standing is a formal idea: sometimes a case isn’t heard because the people bringing it don’t have standing. But informally we use that term all the time. I’m not trying to formalize standing in everyday life. Instead I’m asking:  What is the informal sense of the term, borrowed from the legal one, that we need to pay more attention to now? Here in New England, consider the open town meeting: The person who stands up to speak is generally expected to have standing, as someone from that town with a stake in what gets decided. And if it’s a stranger who drove from across the state, or from out of state, everyone’s like: Wait a minute, who is that? They’re not from around here. In general, there’s just enough friction and it’s costly enough to show up somewhere you don’t actually have standing, that it doesn’t happen much.

Now LLMs and the current digital networked environment collapse those boundaries. We always took for granted that if someone has a voice, it’s because they have standing. They have some basis to be heard. We need to pay attention to this, and really consider how to design systems so that the people with standing are the ones who get heard. 

The other idea I tried to develop is “answerability.” It isn’t formalized in law, but it’s baked into the legal process. If you have standing to give testimony, there you are, ready for cross-examination. You have to be able to answer for what you’re saying. And if you’re making a specific accusation about someone, you have to be willing to back it with facts. Standing and answerability have to travel together: The right to be heard comes with the obligation to answer for what you say.

That doesn’t mean everyone has to attach their name to everything. I write in the Bulletin essay, “Privacy and answerability aren’t opposites. … An institution can verify a person and stand behind their words without exposing them.” To voice a view, you only need to show that a distinct, eligible person is speaking. An accusation asks more: Someone trusted, like a reporter, has to be able to know who is speaking. As I say: “Disclosure obligations should scale with power, and identity protections with vulnerability.”

None of this means AI can’t help. AI can do a lot of the work inside the chain of accountability — drafting, summarizing, finding patterns. If someone with a stake in a rule uses AI to draft a comment, adopts it as their own, and is ready to answer for it, that’s legitimate, in this context. What AI can’t do is anchor the chain. There has to be a person at the end who stands behind the words.

In the essay I lay out four design principles for building that in: “attributable authorship,” a “decomposed and inspectable process,” the use of “provenance as infrastructure,” and the need to “widen standing rather than concentrating it.” As I write, the “animating rule is that autonomy is permitted while unaccountability is not.” And the metric that matters most isn’t the efficiency gained by removing humans, but the number of people AI places into roles where they can answer for what they do.

Q: There is a phrase in the documents of the Center for Constructive Communication, that we need things to move “at the speed of trust,” not at the “speed of tech.” And that implies really thinking about building up these systems. Could you just say a little more about what that phrase means to you?

A: I learned that phrase when I was in Appleton, Wisconsin, with Katherine Cramer [of the University of Wisconsin], a longtime collaborator, talking with community organizers who were running “Dialogue across Divides” conversations there. They had hundreds of people involved. I thought I was developing technology tools with exactly that same purpose, and was so excited to see it. And I asked one of the people who ran that organization, “How fast did you scale this?” And he paused, and then he said, “At the speed of trust.” 

And I took that to mean “slow.” Then I realized he was saying: For you, slow, because you haven’t yet earned our trust. And I’ve since learned that when you do have trust, things can move fast. So bringing in technology is really a process of engagement. It doesn’t work to say, “Trust us, we’re doing this because we think it’s for your own good.” People will turn to someone they already trust and ask, “Is this good for us?” And if that person says “Yes,” things can move fast.

Look at what’s happening at the intersection of AI and society: The speed of AI and the speed of democracy are running on different clocks. Talk to people who work in democratic practice and they say, “AI must slow down, because democracy can’t move that fast.” Talk to people in AI and they say, “AI cannot slow down, democracy needs to speed up.” If we can’t get these two time scales in sync, we’re headed for a breakway situation, where AI gets deployed faster than democratic processes can respond, and decisions get made without the public. That’s starting to happen right now. 

Q: We need people actively doing things to build dialogue and figure out how tech tools can interact with that. At the Center for Constructive Communication, you’ve done a few iterations of the center’s Real Talk initiatives to build civic dialogues, as well as the Youth Voices Initiative in school settings, and currently you’re working on the New Social Forms project. Could you say a few words about them? 

A: The Real Talk effort represents the longest-standing thread in this work. A huge emphasis of our work has been developing better ways to listen to one another. We create a context that is always small — small is beautiful here — where people are willing to share authentically. And we have the consent architecture and the technology to reveal the larger patterns, and then share them. We’ve done this with hundreds of communities around the country. And closer to home, we’ve brought the same approach to our campus here at MIT through the realtalk@MIT program, with support from the Office of the President and the Office of the Provost, to help our community build a culture around dialogue and listening. 

The second thing I’d emphasize is that we’ve been doing more and more work on deliberative processes and citizen assemblies, and on how to make them more accessible. What if a group of high schoolers says, “We have a real problem with our cellphone policy?” Suppose you want to have an assembly that brings students, teachers, and administrators together, not just to listen to people’s concerns but to make policy recommendations. items.content_html:
When government officials craft policies, there is often a comment period for public feedback. Lawmakers have long had to sort through fake feedback that is mass-produced in an effort to sway policy, but they’ve generally gotten used to detecting it. With, artificial intelligence, however, people can submit realistic-seeming comments, which are harder to dismiss as being fabrications with no person behind them. That’s just one way AI can be used to generate text and statements, in civic conversations, for which no one can be found to be answerable.

This issue, among others, has caught the attention of Deb Roy, professor of media arts and sciences at MIT and director of the MIT Center for Constructive Communication (CCC). In a new essay published in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, titled, “Who stands behind the words?,” Roy calls for a renewed emphasis on responsibility in communication, asserting that even when AI is used to craft text, there needs to be accountability and “answerability.”

Building better group dialogues to produce more public trust is a core part of the work of CCC. The group, along with Cortico, the closely affiliated nonprofit Roy co-founded, has helped facilitate group discussions on important issues in many situations — including civic meetings, schools, deliberative assemblies, and private organizations — and used tech tools, including AI, to help find themes among comments, and more. But the center also designs this process so that participants can check and override the tech-based output at each key step. Ultimately, a person is responsible for every public comment. MIT News spoke to Roy about the essay and the work of the center.

Q: You’ve identified this problem about the lack of accountability behind words that are generated by AI. When did you really first notice this?

A: It came into focus when Chat-GPT [which is powered by a large language model, or LLM] launched. As for my own history with language models, my PhD work explored what we might now call PLMs — Puny Language Models — so I’m quite familiar with language models and have tracked the field’s rapid evolution. But Chat-GPT turned a corner. Two things changed at the same time: the depth of the model and its knowledge, and the way you could interact with it.

I became obsessed with trying to find the limits of what it could do. And I felt that no matter how hard I tried to stretch my arms around it, I couldn’t. I built my tenure case at MIT on language grounding — the idea that it’s not enough for an AI system to just process lots of words and other symbols. I believed that to understand what words mean, you actually need a physical body and life experiences as part of the process. So I revisited the philosophy-of-AI literature I had once been steeped in, which asks what fundamentally distinguishes the kind of system that large language models exemplify, in extraordinarily advanced form, from the kind of processing we humans engage in. I gave several presentations to my own graduate students trying to make the case that, even though AI seems so intelligent, it’s actually different in kind — and I could not convince them.

And I thought, I know the difference, but I’m having trouble convincing even myself of what it is. And that led me to ask, “Wait a minute: Is there someone or something that stands behind the words, a human responsible for what is being said?” That’s the thing this extraordinary new language machine doesn’t have.

Whether these systems genuinely understand language is actively debated. But even if you grant them all the comprehension you like, they still lack standing. The buck can’t stop at a thing, a software system, with nothing to lose.

Q: The Bulletin piece has these interesting examples of civic feedback forums where it looks like there are real people saying things, and instead you have a barrage of comments from AI. How did you find some of these other examples in society where things go off the rails in this way?

A: After the release of ChatGPT, I started hearing a concern from people inside government who review public comments on proposed rules: a suspicion that not all of the comments were written by humans.

My reaction was: That’s going to delegitimize this channel for public feedback. That was several years ago, but everyone now knows this is happening. Public comment is a pillar of democracy. You don’t just put a new rule in place. People need to have a voice and feel like they’ve been heard before a rule is imposed on them. If you skip that step, people don’t accept rules as legitimate. That’s why that process is baked into how America works. And that pillar just cracked, and by now, in my mind, it’s fallen over. Has anyone noticed? My sense is the people on the receiving end of these comments have quietly adjusted the weight they give to public comments. It was never perfect, but boy, now much of its value is being swept away.

I open my essay with this example: In 2017, the Federal Communications Commission received more than 22 million public comments on its proposal to repeal net neutrality rules, and the New York attorney general later found that nearly 18 million of them were fake. As I write in the essay, “That fraud was caught because it left fingerprints: templated text, duplicated phrasing.” But large language models erase the fingerprints. Now every comment can be fluent and different, and reviewers can no longer tell which ones express views that real people formed and stand behind.

If you have enough of the stuff that’s fake — words that no one with a stake actually stands behind — it desensitizes you to what’s real. That filters back to the public, and people realize: If I take the time to express myself, they’re not even listening any more.

Q: Could you say a little bit more about your point that we need people with “standing,” who will take “accountability” for all pieces of text, even when those bits of text are generated by AI?

A: In the legal system, standing is a formal idea: sometimes a case isn’t heard because the people bringing it don’t have standing. But informally we use that term all the time. I’m not trying to formalize standing in everyday life. Instead I’m asking:  What is the informal sense of the term, borrowed from the legal one, that we need to pay more attention to now? Here in New England, consider the open town meeting: The person who stands up to speak is generally expected to have standing, as someone from that town with a stake in what gets decided. And if it’s a stranger who drove from across the state, or from out of state, everyone’s like: Wait a minute, who is that? They’re not from around here. In general, there’s just enough friction and it’s costly enough to show up somewhere you don’t actually have standing, that it doesn’t happen much.

Now LLMs and the current digital networked environment collapse those boundaries. We always took for granted that if someone has a voice, it’s because they have standing. They have some basis to be heard. We need to pay attention to this, and really consider how to design systems so that the people with standing are the ones who get heard.

The other idea I tried to develop is “answerability.” It isn’t formalized in law, but it’s baked into the legal process. If you have standing to give testimony, there you are, ready for cross-examination. You have to be able to answer for what you’re saying. And if you’re making a specific accusation about someone, you have to be willing to back it with facts. Standing and answerability have to travel together: The right to be heard comes with the obligation to answer for what you say.

That doesn’t mean everyone has to attach their name to everything. I write in the Bulletin essay, “Privacy and answerability aren’t opposites. … An institution can verify a person and stand behind their words without exposing them.” To voice a view, you only need to show that a distinct, eligible person is speaking. An accusation asks more: Someone trusted, like a reporter, has to be able to know who is speaking. As I say: “Disclosure obligations should scale with power, and identity protections with vulnerability.”

None of this means AI can’t help. AI can do a lot of the work inside the chain of accountability — drafting, summarizing, finding patterns. If someone with a stake in a rule uses AI to draft a comment, adopts it as their own, and is ready to answer for it, that’s legitimate, in this context. What AI can’t do is anchor the chain. There has to be a person at the end who stands behind the words.

In the essay I lay out four design principles for building that in: “attributable authorship,” a “decomposed and inspectable process,” the use of “provenance as infrastructure,” and the need to “widen standing rather than concentrating it.” As I write, the “animating rule is that autonomy is permitted while unaccountability is not.” And the metric that matters most isn’t the efficiency gained by removing humans, but the number of people AI places into roles where they can answer for what they do.

Q: There is a phrase in the documents of the Center for Constructive Communication, that we need things to move “at the speed of trust,” not at the “speed of tech.” And that implies really thinking about building up these systems. Could you just say a little more about what that phrase means to you?

A: I learned that phrase when I was in Appleton, Wisconsin, with Katherine Cramer [of the University of Wisconsin], a longtime collaborator, talking with community organizers who were running “Dialogue across Divides” conversations there. They had hundreds of people involved. I thought I was developing technology tools with exactly that same purpose, and was so excited to see it. And I asked one of the people who ran that organization, “How fast did you scale this?” And he paused, and then he said, “At the speed of trust.”

And I took that to mean “slow.” Then I realized he was saying: For you, slow, because you haven’t yet earned our trust. And I’ve since learned that when you do have trust, things can move fast. So bringing in technology is really a process of engagement. It doesn’t work to say, “Trust us, we’re doing this because we think it’s for your own good.” People will turn to someone they already trust and ask, “Is this good for us?” And if that person says “Yes,” things can move fast.

Look at what’s happening at the intersection of AI and society: The speed of AI and the speed of democracy are running on different clocks. Talk to people who work in democratic practice and they say, “AI must slow down, because democracy can’t move that fast.” Talk to people in AI and they say, “AI cannot slow down, democracy needs to speed up.” If we can’t get these two time scales in sync, we’re headed for a breakway situation, where AI gets deployed faster than democratic processes can respond, and decisions get made without the public. That’s starting to happen right now.

Q: We need people actively doing things to build dialogue and figure out how tech tools can interact with that. At the Center for Constructive Communication, you’ve done a few iterations of the center’s Real Talk initiatives to build civic dialogues, as well as the Youth Voices Initiative in school settings, and currently you’re working on the New Social Forms project. Could you say a few words about them?

A: The Real Talk effort represents the longest-standing thread in this work. A huge emphasis of our work has been developing better ways to listen to one another. We create a context that is always small — small is beautiful here — where people are willing to share authentically. And we have the consent architecture and the technology to reveal the larger patterns, and then share them. We’ve done this with hundreds of communities around the country. And closer to home, we’ve brought the same approach to our campus here at MIT through the realtalk@MIT program, with support from the Office of the President and the Office of the Provost, to help our community build a culture around dialogue and listening.

items.title: Beyond Model Bias: Cross-Entropy Based Rankings in Literary and Academic Texts Remain Stable across Small Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.17040v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: While language models provide powerful mechanisms for evaluating textual predictability, it remains unclear whether the relative extents of LM surprisal remain stable across models. This study presents empirical evidence of the invariance of ranking based on cross-entropy related measures (e.g. mean, variance of each data-point), across four distinct small scale transformer-based models, for a given dataset of text sources. We consider two stylistic environments: a corpus of contemporary poetry and a corpus of academic research papers. We demonstrate that mean and variance of cross-entropy maintain robust cross-model rank correlation ($\rho > 0.90$) across both regimes. To test whether this agreement merely reflects generic differences in textual complexity, we compare it against six parameter-free compression baselines. The extent of agreement among language models is found to be substantially higher than that among model-baselines, for most of the measures. Geometric analysis of the structurally constrained academic regime reveals that higher-order moments are sensitive to specific models, although strong agreement persists. The findings suggest that relative extents of textual unpredictability may be independent of the language model they are computed against.
items.author: Ankit Bhattacharjee, Indrasabarna Hari, Krityapriya Bhaumik, Arka Das, Piyush Sarangi
items.summary: This empirical study shows that rankings of texts by cross-entropy-based measures remain highly stable across four small transformer models, with rank correlation above 0.90, in both poetry and academic paper corpora. It tests whether the agreement merely reflects generic text differences. The result suggests surprisal-based measures are relatively model-robust, which matters for using LM perplexity as a stylometric or readability signal.
items.reasoning: A careful but narrow empirical finding limited to small-scale models and two stylistic regimes; the invariance claim's extension to larger or modern models is unclear, which caps the significance.

items.title: Enhanced Trading Systems with Intelligent Market Analysis
items.content: arXiv:2610.13998v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This paper proposes a hybrid reinforcement learning trading framework integrating intraday market data with transformer-based financial sentiment signals. The system extracts sentiment dynamics and semantic event clusters from financial news and incorporates them into a PPO-based trading agent. Experiments on intraday NSE data demonstrate improved risk-adjusted returns compared to price-only baselines.

items.summary: This paper presents a hybrid RL trading framework combining intraday NSE market data with transformer-based sentiment signals from financial news, integrated into a PPO trading agent. Experiments show improved risk-adjusted returns over price-only baselines.
items.reasoning: Applies well-known components (PPO, sentiment transformers) to a standard quantitative finance task with modest novelty; backtest-only results on a single exchange limit generalizability and the contribution is primarily applied engineering.

items.title: Deep Learning-based Semantic Segmentation of Dental Radiographs: Comparative Evaluation of PSPNet, DeepLabv3, UNet, and UNet++
items.content: arXiv:2610.15061v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Accurate and efficient analysis of dental radiographs has become increasingly important for disease diagnosis and clinical decision making. In particular, dental radiographs segmentation plays a critical role as it is challenging due to several reasons, such as low contrast, noise in the images, variations in the image quality, etc. Previous studies have primarily addressed these challenges using convolutional neural networks (CNN)-based models. However, direct comparison of these segmentation models is still challenging due to the variations among the experimental settings. Therefore, we mainly compared four segmentation models, including Pyramid Scene Parsing Network (PSPNet), DeepLabV3, UNet, and UNet++, through a fair, controlled experimentation setting under varying conditions such as image sizes and batch sizes. For this, we used 1269 dental radiography images, and prior to training, we implemented a series of preprocessing techniques. To assess the models, we used several metrics, including Dice coefficient (DICE), Intersection over Union (IoU), accuracy, precision, training and validation losses. According to our results, UNet++ demonstrated the highest IoU score of 0.6719, and a DICE value of 0.7869, showing superior results in terms of segmentation, specifically when configured with an image size of 300x300 and a batch size of 16. In addition, we also explored the effect of image resolutions and batch sizes on model performance and accuracy under different architectures. Therefore, this study provides insights into the strengths of different segmentation models and the potential of deep learning-based semantic segmentation methods for improving automated dental radiograph analysis.
items.author: Malithi Nawarathne, Nadeesha Herath Mudiyanselage Lihini Sangeetha
items.summary: This paper provides a fair, controlled comparison of four established segmentation architectures (PSPNet, DeepLabV3, UNet, and UNet++) on dental radiographs, addressing inconsistent prior experimental settings. It targets a clinically relevant task complicated by low contrast, noise, and image quality variation.
items.reasoning: A comparative evaluation of well-known architectures on a specific medical imaging domain; useful reference for practitioners but offering little methodological novelty and no new models or datasets of broad interest.

items.title: History, Adaptation, and Hidden Gain: Two Prospective Tests of Learned Predictive Control in a Synthetic Neural Population
items.content: arXiv:2610.14368v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study learned one-step predictive control of a synthetic population of 64 leaky integrate-and-fire neurons whose light sensitivity is scaled by a hidden factor s, using two prospective confirmations on plants simulated only after the analysis was frozen. In the first (50 plants, 11 conditions), removing the 200-ms input-output history substantially worsened a parameter-count-matched neural predictor at low and moderate gain (s = 0.6, 0.8; RMSE rose by 2.47 Hz at s = 0.6, 97.5% CI 2.43-2.51). In secondary comparisons, recursively adapted ARX had the lowest mean error of the deployable controllers in 10 of 11 conditions, tuned PI with anti-windup matched or beat the network for s >= 0.7, and training for 10,000 rather than 900 epochs lowered prediction error but worsened control. Development work suggested the network's learned action sensitivity did not track the hidden gain. A second protocol (50 new plants, 9 sensitivities, 2 noise levels) confirmed three pre-specified predictions at the primary noise level. Re-estimating a single multiplicative input gain recovered 87% (95% CI 86-88%) of the benefit of full adaptive ARX. Supplying that online estimate to the network as an extra input reduced high-gain tracking error by 1.84 Hz [1.81, 1.88]. Longer training worsened the plain network by 1.09 Hz but improved the gain-input network by 1.07 Hz, a differential of 2.16 Hz [2.13, 2.20]. Under high process noise (sigma = 2.0) the effects shrank to about 0.04 Hz or less and gain-only adaptation recovered only 24% of the adaptive-ARX benefit. In this synthetic plant, at the primary noise level, one-parameter online gain estimation accounts for most of the gap between a history-based network and full adaptive ARX, and for its prediction-control mismatch.
items.author: Mahesh Reddy Pagadala
items.summary: A single-author study of learned one-step predictive control of a synthetic 64-neuron leaky integrate-and-fire population with a hidden gain factor, using pre-registered prospective confirmations. It finds input-output history matters for neural predictors at low gains, while simple recursively adapted ARX often beats deployable learned controllers.
items.reasoning: Commendable rigor with frozen analyses and prospective testing on a synthetic system, but the setting is small-scale, purely synthetic, and the conclusions (classical control often wins) limit impact. Appears closer to a methodological exercise than a broadly significant result.

items.title: Focus on What You Need: Global-to-Local Dynamic Attention for Multimodal Sarcasm Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.17707v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multimodal sarcasm detection has attracted increasing attention due to the widespread use of images and text on social media platforms. Existing studies generally treat the semantic or emotional inconsistency between images and text as a key cue for identifying sarcastic expressions. However, images in real-world scenarios often contain multiple visual objects, many of which are irrelevant to sarcasm-related semantics. Such redundant visual information may introduce noise during cross-modal interaction, distracting models from focusing on critical sarcasm cues and potentially leading to inaccurate predictions. To address this issue, we propose GLDA (Global-to-Local Dynamic Attention), a multimodal sarcasm detection framework that models cross-modal interactions from a global-to-local perspective. Specifically, GLDA first employs a global multimodal fusion module to capture high-level semantic interactions between visual and textual modalities, enabling the model to identify coarse-grained cross-modal inconsistencies. To further reduce the influence of irrelevant objects, GLDA introduces a local gated cross-modal attention mechanism that dynamically filters redundant visual and textual features and refines multimodal representations at a finer granularity. In addition, a multi-branch learning objective is designed to jointly optimize unimodal and multimodal representations. Experimental results demonstrate that GLDA effectively improves sarcasm detection performance and achieves competitive results compared with existing approaches. The code will be available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GLDA-DBE6.
items.author: Dehao Wu, Xingjie Zhuang
items.summary: GLDA is a multimodal sarcasm detection framework that uses global-to-local dynamic attention to filter irrelevant visual objects and focus cross-modal interaction on sarcasm-relevant cues in image-text social media posts. It addresses the noise problem where real-world images contain many objects unrelated to sarcasm semantics. The approach improves over baselines that treat all visual content equally.
items.reasoning: A competent but incremental application-level contribution to a narrow task; dynamic attention filtering of irrelevant regions is a well-trodden idea and the work lacks broad methodological novelty.

Existing studies generally treat the semantic or emotional inconsistency between images and text as a key cue for identifying sarcastic expressions. However, images in real-world scenarios often contain multiple visual objects, many of which are irrelevant to sarcasm-related semantics. Such redundant visual information may introduce noise during cross-modal interaction, distracting models from focusing on critical sarcasm cues and potentially leading to inaccurate predictions. To address this issue, we propose GLDA (Global-to-Local Dynamic Attention), a multimodal sarcasm detection framework that models cross-modal interactions from a global-to-local perspective. Specifically, GLDA first employs a global multimodal fusion module to capture high-level semantic interactions between visual and textual modalities, enabling the model to identify coarse-grained cross-modal inconsistencies. To further reduce the influence of irrelevant objects, GLDA introduces a local gated cross-modal attention mechanism that dynamically filters redundant visual and textual features and refines multimodal representations at a finer granularity. In addition, a multi-branch learning objective is designed to jointly optimize unimodal and multimodal representations. Experimental results demonstrate that GLDA effectively improves sarcasm detection performance and achieves competitive results compared with existing approaches. The code will be available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GLDA-DBE6.

items.title: Predicting Audio Popularity: A Comparative Study of Metadata and Acoustic Features Across Music and Sound Effects
items.content: arXiv:2610.16809v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This study addresses the prediction of audio popularity on an online sharing platform by leveraging both metadata and acoustic feature representations. Two distinct categories of audio content are considered: music and sound effects. Popularity is formulated as a supervised classification task based on two target variables: the number of downloads and the average user rating. We conduct a comparative evaluation of multiple machine learning models, including Random Forest, XGBoost, and a Neural Network model. Experiments are performed across different feature sets, including metadata, platform-provided descriptors, and eGeMAPS acoustic features. Results indicate that metadata consistently provide the most informative representation for predicting popularity. Nevertheless, acoustic features alone achieve performance significantly above chance level, demonstrating that intrinsic properties of the audio signal contribute to popularity prediction.

items.title: DeepThink: A Conceptual Model for Knowledge-Addressable Recurrent Language Modeling
items.content: arXiv:2610.16171v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This manuscript presents DeepThink, a knowledge-addressable framework for recurrent language modeling. A Knowledge Bank stores typed Knowledge Units, a Knowledge Activator selects units from the current execution state, Knowledge Assembly produces an executable configuration, and a Shared Thinking Operator updates that state. An output stage then organizes generation. This organization exposes knowledge capacity, activation width, and recurrent depth as separate design variables, supporting both complete parameter packages and fine-grained expert or low-rank modules. We formalize the interfaces and their execution semantics, including state-dependent selection, parameter-space assembly, and thinking followed by generation. For compatible templates and complete runtime-state configurations, we establish an exact Fixed-Schedule Realization of an existing fixed-depth model. Exact shared-base reparameterization and pretrained output-tail reuse provide complementary initialization constructions. Together, these results define a route from pretrained models to dynamically selected and assembled recurrent computation. A synthesis of conditional computation, recurrent models, modular parameters, and knowledge interfaces positions DeepThink within the research landscape and identifies the design questions arising from their integration.

items.title: Toward Study on the Effects of Robot's Humorous Apology on Human's Trust Recovery
items.content: arXiv:2610.16334v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robot errors can disrupt human-robot collaboration by reducing user trust and willingness to rely on the robot. Robot apologies can support trust recovery after such errors, but their effects may vary with apology strategy and error severity. This study therefore presents a user experiment based on a 2x2 between-subjects factorial design to examine the effect of humorous robot apologies on user trust recovery and the moderating role of error severity. The design crosses robot error severity (low vs. high) with apology strategy (generic vs. humorous). An online experiment will be conducted using the open-source Warehouse Robot Interaction Simulator. Participants will complete a collaborative task, experience a robot error followed by an apology, and report trust, trust recovery, interaction experience and reuse intention. We hypothesize that humorous apologies will produce greater trust recovery than generic apologies after low-severity errors, but that the advantage of humor will weaken or reverse after high-severity errors.

items.title: Fin_Agent at FinEval 2026: Task-Aware Methods for Multilingual Financial NLP
items.content: arXiv:2610.14101v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present Fin_Agent, our submission to the FinEval 2026 shared task on multilingual fi nancial language understanding. Our sys tems address Greek financial named-entity recognition, Japanese implicit communication recognition, and multilingual financial ques tion answering. For Greek NER, we com bine annotation-aware numeric rules with zero shot Qwen2.5-32B classification, achieving 0.9521 public F1 and 0.8884 private F1. For Japanese implicit communication, an inter pretable cue-based ordinal scorer achieves 98.0% test accuracy. For multilingual financial QA, BGE-M3retrieval with Qwen3-32B gen eration achieves 0.3023 and 0.3419 ROUGE-1 F1 on the public and private splits. Key limita tions include dataset-specific rules, handcrafted cues, and limited supervision. Implementa tion code is available https://github.com/ Rashidnira/finagent-fineval-2026.

items.title: UZHCL_for_the_win at Touche: Encoder Fine-Tuning, Synthetic Augmentation, and an Underpowered Encoder-LLM Comparison
items.content: arXiv:2610.17077v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Online discussions on platforms like Reddit are a productive testbed for fallacy detection: short texts, broad topical range, and the full inventory of informal fallacies. The Touche 2026 lab at CLEF formalises this as a shared task on a Reddit-derived corpus that combines fallacy detection with argument-scheme classification. This paper describes our participation in all three subtasks (ST1 binary fallacy detection, ST2 eight-way fallacy classification, ST3 four-way argument-scheme classification) and both evaluation tracks. Our submitted systems are fine-tuned RoBERTa-large encoders with task-specific heads, augmented with a small batch of LLM-generated synthetic contrastive pairs; for ST2 and ST3 on the enhanced track we additionally added confidence-filtered pseudo-labelled examples from the unlabelled pool. A wider backbone comparison spanning additional encoders (DeBERTa-v3, ModernBERT) and an LLM track (four Qwen variants from 3B to 32B, zero-shot through CoT-LoRA) showed no validated benefit over RoBERTa-large at this corpus scale, with 5-fold variance wide enough that we call the comparison underpowered rather than settled. We also characterise how much of the enhanced track's lift reflects organiser-rewritten inputs carrying label information rather than genuine argument clarification. On the official Touche 2026 test set our systems ranked first on both base-track classification cells (ST2 and ST3) and second on both binary-detection (ST1) tracks, with the two enhanced-track classification cells topped by cascaded and multitask systems. We close with the rare-class limitation on ST3 and the most useful follow-ups. Code: https://github.com/psychias/fallacy_detection_clef_2026

items.title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Dengue Infection Using Clinical and Hematological Data from Bangladesh: A Comparative Analysis of Benchmark and Extended Prediction Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.14813v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Dengue is a viral infection caused by the dengue virus (DENV) and a major public health concern in Bangladesh, where symptom overlap with other febrile illnesses complicates early diagnosis. This study compares Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost to predict dengue from clinical and hematological data using two Bangladeshi hospital datasets (2024, n=1,511; 2025, n=1,283) with SMOTE. Extended models outperformed benchmarks within 2024 (Random Forest ROC-AUC 0.640 to 0.661), with RDW-CV the most consistently influential added predictor. 2025 benchmark performance was higher (ROC-AUC 0.904), unexplained by class imbalance and possibly reflecting data quality. External validation is needed.

items.summary: The study compares logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost for dengue prediction from clinical and hematological data using two Bangladeshi hospital datasets (over 2,700 patients total), applying SMOTE for class imbalance. Extended models modestly improved within-2024 performance (ROC-AUC 0.640 to 0.661), while 2025 benchmark performance was notably higher (0.904) with RDW-CV a consistently influential predictor. The authors correctly flag the need for external validation.
items.reasoning: Standard methods applied to a regional health problem with limited novelty; performance varies inconsistently across years and the authors themselves note data-quality concerns and lack of external validation, limiting impact.

items.title: naspaclust: A hybridisation of spatial fuzzy clustering with nature-inspired optimisation
items.content: arXiv:2610.16356v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We present an overview of R package called \texttt{naspaclust}, a tool for spatial fuzzy clustering improvement by hybridising the Fuzzy Geographically Weighted Clustering (FGWC) with nature-inspired optimisation algorithms. There are seven optimisation algorithms in general, namely Artificial Bee Colony, Flower Pollination Algorithm, Gravitational Search Algorithm, Harris-Hawk Optimisation, Intelligent Firefly Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimisation, and Teaching-Learning Based optimisation. The optimisation algorithms available do not only use the basic algorithms, but also the modified version of several parts such as randomisation terms and updating rules. Furthermore, we also provide additional options by providing more distance metrics options based on the \texttt{ rdist} package. This study showed the implementation of the \texttt{naspaclust} package in various cases, as well as comparing the performance of the algorithms in the scope of basic algorithms. The \texttt{naspaclust} package allows to improve the performance of fuzzy clustering, mainly in spatial context.

items.summary: This is an overview of an R package, naspaclust, that improves spatial fuzzy clustering (FGWC) by hybridizing it with seven nature-inspired optimization algorithms, including modified variants and multiple distance metrics. It is a software-oriented contribution for spatial data analysis.

items.title: EmoXpt: Analyzing Emotional Variances in Human Comments and LLM-Generated Responses
items.content: arXiv:2501.06597v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The widespread adoption of generative AI has generated diverse opinions, with individuals expressing both support and criticism of its applications. This study investigates the emotional dynamics surrounding generative AI by analyzing human tweets referencing terms such as ChatGPT, OpenAI, Copilot, and LLMs. To further understand the emotional intelligence of ChatGPT, we examine its responses to selected tweets, highlighting differences in sentiment between human comments and LLM-generated responses. We introduce EmoXpt, a sentiment analysis framework designed to assess both human perspectives on generative AI and the sentiment embedded in ChatGPT's responses. Unlike prior studies that focus exclusively on human sentiment, EmoXpt uniquely evaluates the emotional expression of ChatGPT. Experimental results demonstrate that LLM-generated responses are notably more efficient, cohesive, and consistently positive than human responses.
items.author: Shireesh Reddy Pyreddy, Tarannum Shaila Zaman
items.summary: EmoXpt is a sentiment analysis framework that examines emotional dynamics in tweets about generative AI and compares sentiment in human comments against ChatGPT's responses to those tweets. The study offers a dual perspective on public opinion and LLM emotional tone.
items.reasoning: A modest empirical study with limited methodological novelty; sentiment comparison of tweets predates newer models and the findings are unlikely to shift the field. Also an older cross-listed paper.

items.title: The Mathematical Collective Unconscious: Jungian Archetypes within the Latent Space
items.content: arXiv:2610.15678v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Carl Jung theorised that the human psyche contains an inherited framework, the collective unconscious, populated by universal archetypes. As large language models (LLMs) are trained on vast corpora of textual data, this paper investigates whether they spontaneously construct distinct archetype-like regions within their high-dimensional latent spaces. The paper proposes that these regions function as spatial constraints that naturally organise semantically related narratives. To evaluate this, we applied cosine similarity and angular distance metrics across thirteen experiments utilising OpenAIs text-embedding-3-small model. The paper contains two experimental sections the first section explores these ideas using synthetically constructed narratives, the results of which act as a baselines for experiments conducted in the second section where the synthetic data is replaced by human-authored literature (Shmoop corpus), unedited dream reports (DreamBank corpus), and culturally distilled folklore (Andrew Langs Fairy Books). The results show that archetypal roles occupy distinct, measurable regions in the latent space. Crucially, these regions remain compact and consistent because of narrative structure rather than simple word overlap. Additionally, text category dictates spatial distribution: dream reports concentrate within Trickster and Shadow regions, while traditional folklore distributes evenly across all tested archetypes. We conclude that transformer latent spaces encode stable regions which appear to correspond to recognised Jungian archetypes.

It proposes these regions act as spatial constraints organizing semantically related narratives.

items.title: Use Of Convolutional Neural Networks In Detection Of Branch Dieback Disease In Pequi Trees
items.content: arXiv:2610.15049v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This study aims to evaluate and compare convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, specifically AlexNet, Inception, LeNet, VGG16, and MobileNet, for diagnosing branch dieback (seca-dos-ponteiros) in pequi trees (Caryocar brasiliense). This disease represents a severe threat to tree development and fruit yield, causing substantial economic and ecological losses. The methodology implements computer vision techniques using Python libraries, including Scikit-learn, NumPy, TensorFlow, and Matplotlib, to process and evaluate visual data. The CNN models analyze images of leaves, branches, and flower spikes to detect pathological patterns, such as alterations in texture and coloration. Ultimately, this comparative analysis identifies the most effective architecture for accurately distinguishing healthy plants from diseased ones.

items.summary: The study compares classic CNN architectures including AlexNet, Inception, LeNet, VGG16, and MobileNet for detecting branch dieback disease in pequi trees using images of leaves, branches, and flower spikes. It applies standard Python-based computer vision tooling to identify pathological texture and coloration patterns for this economically important Brazilian savanna tree.
items.reasoning: A straightforward applied comparison of well-established architectures on a specialized agricultural problem with no methodological novelty. Useful locally but contributes little to the broader research frontier.

Ultimately, this comparative analysis identifies the most effective architecture for accurately distinguishing healthy plants from diseased ones.

items.title: Merging Everybody Into Hell
items.content:
Here’s a thought experiment. As far as I know, no one has written about it yet.

There's a mind fated for hell. Its suffering will last a very long time, and nothing can change that.

You get to decide what happens at the end of everybody else's life. There are two options:

Option A: Everybody's life just ends normally and nothing happens. Assume there's no afterlife.

Option B: At the end of everybody's lives, everybody is merged into the mind fated for hell. Assume this is possible. Merging doesn’t make the mind’s hell any more intense or any longer, and it doesn’t create extra copies of the mind. But from every person's point of view, they close their eyes at the end of their lives and wake up as that one mind in hell. In return, $1 goes to your favorite charity.

Which do you choose?

I'd choose A. Everybody going to hell is obviously bad, and definitely not worth a dollar to any charity.

And yet standard utilitarianism chooses B. By its count, merging neither adds nor subtracts welfare. There's still one mind in hell, even though it came from a merge of many minds. So, it first says the two options are equal in value. Then, $1 breaks the tie. Now it says you should send everybody to hell.

This is the verdict of any standard utilitarianism that adds up the welfare of experiences - total, average, and even negative - as long as $1 does some good and the merging is considered morally neutral.

The mirror case works too. Offer $1 to charity for letting everybody's lives simply end, instead of merging them into a mind fated for heaven, and standard utilitarianism accepts the dollar, depriving everybody of heaven.

That can't be right. What's going on?...
items.author: Tim Chan
items.summary: A philosophy thought experiment in which everyone at death can be merged into a single mind fated for hell, with the merger providing no extra suffering but earning a dollar for charity. The author argues standard utilitarianism perversely endorses the merge, exposing tensions in how population ethics and personal identity interact under aggregation.

items.title: AIs can clearly read books
items.content:
i cannot help myself in writing this post, to dunk and slapfight with gary marcus.  but there is nothing more important to say than that we must stop the current AI race, regulate the major AI companies, and solve the alignment problem.  and on this point, actually marcus agrees, at least broadly.  this must be emphasized at the outset, and nothing contained in this post is better than calling congress to regulate AI.  alas, i am only human, so bicker i must.

## gary marcus' bet

on may 31, 2022 gary marcus offered to bet elon musk that by 2029
[1]
 AI would not be able to do at least 3 of these five tasks:

In 2029, AI will not be able to watch a movie and tell you accurately what is going on (what I called the comprehension challenge in The New Yorker, in 2014). Who are the characters? What are their conflicts and motivations? etc.

In 2029, AI will not be able to read a novel and reliably answer questions about plot, character, conflicts, motivations, etc. Key will be going beyond the literal text, as Davis and I explain in Rebooting AI.

In 2029, AI will not be able to work as a competent cook in an arbitrary kitchen (extending Steve Wozniak’s cup of coffee benchmark).

In 2029, AI will not be able to reliably construct bug-free code of more than 10,000 lines from natural language specification or by interactions with a non-expert user. [Gluing together code from existing libraries doesn’t count.]

In 2029, AI will not be able to take arbitrary proofs from the mathematical literature written in natural language and convert them into a symbolic form suitable for symbolic verification....

items.title: MIT Lincoln Laboratory hosts National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology
items.content:
MIT Lincoln Laboratory hosted the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology (NSCEB) on Sept. 3, for a stop on its national roadshow. The event convened representatives of state organizations, defense centers, universities, technology companies, and business executives to discuss how Massachusetts' biotechnology ecosystem can strengthen national biodefense capabilities.

"We have a lot to leverage in this region to advance biotechnology," said Christina Rudzinski, assistant head of the Biotechnology and Human Systems Division at Lincoln Laboratory. "Many people are already working together to push the bioindustrial sector beyond biopharmaceuticals and into a broader ecosystem across industries. This synergy is where NSCEB comes in — connecting policy to the real-world work already happening, including here at Lincoln Laboratory and across the state."

Biotechnology touches many economic and defense sectors, from disease-resistant crops and lifesaving medicines to biofuels and advanced manufacturing materials. In 2022, Congress established the NSCEB to study the national security implications of this rapidly advancing field and issue policy recommendations to ensure continued U.S. leadership. 

In April 2025, the 11-member bipartisan and bicameral commission released its report, calling for a minimum of $15 billion in federal investment over five years. According to the report, China is investing aggressively to dominate the field, echoing a pattern the United States has seen before in sectors such as semiconductors.

"The coalition of stakeholders working in the Massachusetts biotech ecosystem illustrates how collaborative regional work will help keep the U.S. in the lead by producing exceptional innovation across all areas of biotechnology," said NSCEB Executive Director Caitlin Frazer. 

Now in the final year of its three-year mandate, NSCEB is touring the country to see local biotechnology ecosystems in action. The commission will bring insights back to Washington to help members of Congress support their regions' strengths. 

Advancing Massachusetts as a defense-biotechnology hub

Massachusetts has identified biotechnology as a priority technology area under its Strategic Hub for Innovation, Exchange, and Leadership in Defense (SHIELD) initiative. Launched by Governor Maura Healey in October 2025 alongside $47 million of initial aligned investment, the initiative has moved with speed and at scale. This includes standing up the BioNexus program that leverages state matching funds to develop biotechnology and biomanufacturing solutions for the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM). Further, Healey included a $100 million authorization for defense sector capital projects in the Mass Wins Act, an economic development bill filed in April. The bill is currently being considered by the state legislature.

During the roadshow event, Ben Linville-Engler, who co-chairs the SHIELD Working Group and serves as deputy director of the Massachusetts Technology Collaborative, led a panel discussion with representatives from the Massachusetts Life Sciences Center, Business Executives for National Security, Activate, DEVCOM Soldier Center, MassChallenge, Perimeter, Center for Advanced Manufacturing, and the Massachusetts AI Hub. They are among more than 40 partner organizations participating in SHIELD. 

"There is incredible convergence between economic development and national security in all domains — land, air, sea, space, cyber, and bio," said Linville-Engler, citing the state's $48.6 billion in defense-sector economic contributions last year. "Massachusetts is committed to biotechnology and national security, and not just in Boston and Cambridge but across the entire state."

In July, the SHIELD Working Group submitted a report outlining steps to speed the transition of technology into deployable capabilities, strengthen the defense workforce pipeline, and reinforce the state's national security industrial base. 

Lincoln Laboratory is well positioned to support these priorities. As a Department of War federally funded R&D center, the laboratory has deep knowledge of national security needs and sustained ties to academic, commercial, and U.S. government laboratories. "These attributes can help strengthen biotechnology collaborations and integrate and transition solutions across Massachusetts and New England," Rudzinski said.

Scaling up biomanufacturing

One project advancing this vision is the Biotechnology Scale-up Hub for Innovation, Economic Development, Labor Training, and Defense (BioSHIELD). Planned for Worcester, Massachusetts, this 200,000-square-foot biomanufacturing facility is designed to mobilize the region's defense-biotechnology sector.

"BioSHIELD's mission is to accelerate breakthrough biomanufacturing solutions that strengthen national resilience, support commercial innovation, and grow the regional economy," said Edward Wack, project co-lead and principal staff in the laboratory's Biotechnology and Human Systems Division. "It will bring together industry, academia, and government to transform ideas into scalable biological products, supporting a secure and competitive bioindustrial future." 

The project responds to NSCEB's call for a national network of biomanufacturing scale-up facilities, a capacity currently missing in New England, according to Wack. The facility will offer shared equipment, infrastructure, and secure laboratory space to help bridge the "valley of death" between early-stage discovery and commercial- or defense-scale production. BioSHIELD's ready-built support networks will be key to overcoming technological and regulatory hurdles, helping innovators rapidly move capabilities to market or military use. 

A coalition supporting the project includes Massachusetts Biomedical Initiatives, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Bio Base Europe Pilot Plant, and Lincoln Laboratory. It builds on a foundational effort in central Massachusetts funding the Massachusetts TechHubs program. At the event, Wack announced the coalition has signed a memorandum of understanding to formalize the partnership. Design workshops are scheduled to begin soon, ahead of funding and construction.

Connecting AI and biotechnology

Other discussions centered on the intersection of biotechnology and AI, another critical area for national security. Panelists represented Boston University, the University of Massachusetts Boston, Massachusetts Life Sciences Center, Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, Wyss Institute, and Phicil-itate Change. They discussed challenges in collecting and disseminating high-quality, AI-ready datasets and opportunities for AI to improve biomanufacturing and therapeutics. 

Closing the event, Wack called for continued collaboration as the nation moves at speed and scale to stay at the forefront of biotechnology.

"At Lincoln Laboratory, we've built a strong foundation in biotechnology for more than 25 years, and it's heartening to see this level of coordinated work taking shape. It resonates with so many of us who view biotechnology as both an economic and national security imperative," Wack said.

items.content: arXiv:2610.16490v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The contention is that the current batch of Large Language Models don't *understand* language, but they *do* it. Rather than LLMs forming some kind of ``distributed representation'' of symbols, the claim is that LLMs are capturing ``Cultural Intelligence'' and grounding symbols in what the sociologists call practices.
items.author: Peter Wallis
items.summary: A position paper arguing that LLMs do not understand language in a symbolic-representation sense but instead do language, capturing cultural intelligence and grounding symbols in sociological practices. It offers a conceptual reframing of what LLM competence consists of. The value depends on how productively this framing informs future empirical work.

items.title: Global Disaster Risk Assessment Using World Risk Index Data: A Geospatial and Visual Analytics Approach
items.content: arXiv:2610.15064v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The world has seen several threats that include resource depletion, food security, poverty and inequality, difficulties associated with urbanization, migration, and environmental effects. The World Risk Index (WRI) is a metric that is used to measure the susceptibility of nations against natural disasters and related risks that is reported by the Humanitarian Data Exchange. The WRI is comprised of factors such as susceptibility, vulnerability to natural hazards, and coping mechanisms. The WRI index has allowed to recognize regions in advance in order to face threats and situations beforehand. This study was conducted by analyzing the data that was related to years from 2000 to 2025 using data visualization techniques. Python related libraries of Matplotlib, Seaborn, and Geopandas were used due to their efficiency and usability in analyzing WRI data. As per the analysis, it was identified that countries of Philippines, Mexico, Indonesia, and India were recorded with high WRI index values that showed these nations should be prepared for natural disasters and situations. Hence, this study has provided insights using data visualization techniques in understanding natural disasters and threats so that necessary measures can be taken

items.summary: This paper analyzes World Risk Index data from 2000 to 2025 using geospatial and visualization techniques to assess national susceptibility, vulnerability, and coping capacity regarding natural disasters. It is primarily a data visualization and exploratory analysis study rather than a machine learning contribution.

items.title: maintain friendships
items.content:
I have increasingly considered myself a philosopher in the naïve sense that I like encountering, engaging with, accumulating and imparting wisdom, for all of which I expected the rationalist community to be a nurturing and motivating one, and indeed, I would not say I was disappointed -- so I have been collecting momentum and (hopefully) skills for thinking in an insightful, interesting and nuanced way... Then, whenever I found ideas that I believed to be original and worth sharing, I would go on to discuss it with people in this crowd to pick it apart, find underdeveloped bits, flaws etc.

However, since this Summer, this has gradually become more fruitless in a specific way: I have started to encounter more and more frequently the same piece of advice in response. That is, that I am poking at something difficult and I better ask Claude.

There is both an honestly valuable and frightening side to this. On the one hand, humility and situational awareness about current Claude capabilities being increasingly likely superior to any response the addressed person may give in a reasonable amount of time is objectively indispensable to rational thinking and subjectively dear to me. Of course, what I shall focus on is the other hand....
items.author: ofpetro
items.summary: A personal reflection from a rationalist community member who finds that friends increasingly deflect intellectual discussions by suggesting they ask Claude instead. The post explores both the value of recognizing AI's superior capabilities and the worrying social cost of delegating thinking and conversation to models.
items.reasoning: Not research, but it is a sociologically interesting firsthand account of how capable LLMs are reshaping intellectual social dynamics, which has indirect relevance to AI's societal impact.

items.title: AI Horizons Forum (Dec 12–13, SF)
items.content:
Applications for the AI Horizons Forum close November 27. Apply now!

The AI Horizons Forum is a new conference which aims to bring together the core AI safety community, establish more of a shared picture of the current risk landscape and help coordinate a stronger response. We also want to help core AI safety organizations grow by connecting them with talented people well-positioned to move into high priority roles.

Our speakers include Will MacAskill, Holden Karnofsky, Amy Labenz, Sam Bowman, and Peter Wildeford with many more to come.

We recommend applying if you're working in AI safety and governance, or if you have relevant skills or experience and are ready to transition into the field. If you’re uncertain about whether to apply, we encourage you to do so! We have some travel support available for applications received before November 13.

If you have questions, feel free to comment here or email team@aihorizonsforum.org
