items.title: Launching the Hong Kong AI Safety Hub (HASH), a new home for AI safety work in Hong Kong
items.content:
We’re excited to announce that AI Safety Hong Kong is relaunching as the Hong Kong AI Safety Hub (HASH). As part of this move, all our branding will transition from AISHK to HASH.

As the community of people working directly on AI safety in Hong Kong grows, the best way to leverage that is to set up our in-person hub. Hong Kong sits in one of the most important regions for the global trajectory of AI, one the AI safety field has so far neglected. There have been a growing number of voices calling for more local AI safety hubs. We agree, and we’re building one.

Read on: https://hkaisafetyhub.substack.com/p/launching-the-hong-kong-ai-safety

items.title: Against (some of) rationality
items.content:
TL;DR: Before fighting a bias, ask yourself why it's there.

Epistemic status: Uncertain

At first, it seems almost self evident that if something feels more “rational”, it’s better. However, in reality, this heuristic leads to a lot of incorrect actions. A classic example is a someone thinking revenge is irrational, and suppressing his wish to take revenge. This will probably harm him, as people will be less reluctant to take actions that would get others to take revenge.

Some of the sequences are posts along the lines of “Here is an example of a bias: When one group of people are asked to estimate P(A) and another group are asked to estimate P(something that can only happen if A is true), people in the first group sometimes predictably give a lower probability than the second. Therefore, people are irrational.” 

However, I think this is somewhat closer to bounded rationality. People use heuristics that work most of the time, and you can find experiments to show that people sometimes make choices that aren't the best choice, but it's much harder to figure out which end of the rope to pull or if there is even irrationality at all.

The claim I am trying to make here is that snuffing out biases is a Chesterton's fence situation. Often, we may think we found a proof of irrationality (e.g. the revenge example) but in reality the mechanism behind the supposed irrationality is there for a good reason.

I am not suggesting that we just say "oh, there's a bias, probably there for the best". What I am suggesting is instead of thinking "here is a failure mode in our rationality, we should avoid this", we should aim for "here is a failure mode. It's there because of X. X is bad, therefore we should avoid this failure mode"

items.title: Chess without opening theory
items.content:
Try the game.

In chess, things get tedious when your Elo rating plateaus and you reach the point where you need to study openings. So, what if there were an easier introductory game? However, chess has standardized engines, and there didn't seem to be anything I could do there. Developing a new game seemed interesting. Adopting standard chess conventions were easy starting point. It took about a week, including the time spent going for walks with the session running.

items.title: Book Review: The Receipt Horizon by Joel Borgen
items.content:
When author Joel Borgen—in an act of eagle-eyed marketing marksmanship—contacted me as an "unusually plausible reader" for his debut novel, I grudgingly had to agree. Deploying a little tasteful and well-deserved flattery and then suggesting that

hard SF, AI governance, and violins [...] superintelligence, emulated minds, identity and continuity, and civilization-scale consent

might be relevant to my interests, he had me dead to rights. I stepped into the baited trap eyes-open, expecting to have, at best, a mildly bad time.

Instead I discovered a book that instantly found a place on my bookshelf of favourite speculative SF novels.

## Summary (no spoilers)

From Amazon:

Elara Lindholm has spent years testing the seams of a life that feels too perfect to be fully her own.

When she is selected for the Fulcrum Institute, she steps behind that calm into a world of uploaded minds, hidden governance, carefully managed history, and the Steward: the superintelligent system that ended a devastating AI war and now holds the postwar order in place.

The Receipt Horizon is a post-AGI hard science fiction novel about emulated minds, civilizational consent, and the cost of disagreeing with a system that saved the world.

So, yes, it's hard-SF, but the thing we're getting hardest about isn't the usual rocket engines or space wars or ML architectures themselves, so much as the semi-ambiguous web of institutional structures that now govern and control living humans and Ems (emulated humans) alike. It's a kind of limited-information thriller about acting under profound uncertainty as the opaque and mysterious moral and legal machinery of governing Utopia reveals itself slowly through the eyes of an entry-level participant who cannot stop testing boundaries and picking at stitches, waiting all the while to be crushed....

items.title: Today I Killed; Tomorrow I Will Kill Again
items.content:
When must we kill them? Now. Later. Continuously. Infinitely.

A very specific trigger warning: Noah Smith, if you ever see this, please do proceed with caution.

Based on a true story.

A favorite pastime of mine is wandering about in nature’s splendor. The whole experience is delightful: The planning, the topo maps, the gear setup, the drive, the type II hedonism of light, voluntary suffering at an oxygen-deprived altitude. The locomoting while chatting with friends, or solitarily listening to a podcast. The sheer adventure of exploring the Earth. Fun for the whole internal family of experiencing and remembering selves. My ancestors studied hunting and gathering and then agricultural science so that I might have liberty to study an approximation of hunting and gathering. And it’s a great way to stay in shape.

So there I was at the edge of civilization when it all happened, on approach to the trailhead to climb a mountain. Driving my still-quite-new, designed-overseas-but-made-in-America, symmetrical all-wheel drive, turbocharged, off-roading family station wagon (practical and a blast to drive). Digesting my favorite fast food breakfast—a superstimulus of sweet and savory delight, and purchased at a heavy discount. Drinking my favorite artificially sweetened mountain beverage (zero, not diet). Listening to one of my favorite podcasts. Wearing my new, limited-edition desert boots of ethically sourced exotic leather, designed by hippy shoemakers across the ocean, and made in a different country across the other ocean to take advantage of market efficiencies.

Peak human experience really. Brought to me by globalism.

The weather was perfect. There was just a bit more pavement, passing some cabins by, and then a few dusty miles up the canyon. What a great day. All my problems were behind me for the moment....

items.title: Feierabend
items.content:
Epistemic status: n=1, an ongoing experiment, describing a practice rather than a result.

AI use: Claude fact-checked the links and the etymology, found the labour-law and etymology sources, wrote the footnotes, and proofread grammar and phrasing. The text is mine.

Feierabend (German, literally "celebration evening"): "done with the work for the day" or "free time after work".

Germans have an interesting concept called Feierabend, which I have been exploring recently.

Currently I don't have fixed working hours and, as I like to joke, I work both never and always. It is a weird thing, but on the one hand I don't have to work at any point in time, on the other hand I might be working at weird times (like Christmas evening). Another huge disadvantage for me is that it is hard to detach from work, since you could be working right now.[1]And the worst part of the experience, which actually forced me to explore the Feierabend approach, is when I don't feel like working (e.g. tired or not feeling well), but then I feel guilty that I should be working and end up not fully enjoying my free time without being productive either. It is like a half-baked state in which I am not doing anything productive (e.g. scrolling), but I am also not doing the most enjoyable thing I could be doing right now, since I feel guilty that I am supposed to be working now.

Germans seem to have this idea that once you are done with work, it is over and you can just enjoy yourself - i.e. the boundary between work and not-work is very well defined, sharp, and intentionally preserved. E.g. German working-time law requires 11 uninterrupted hours of non-work time at the end of the working day.[2]

In a sense this reminds me of "work hard, play hard" (but this one is more about intensity in both parts, not the separation between them) and Working yourself ragged is not a virtue.[3]...

items.title: Sleep puzzle system
items.content:
Here’s an obscure life hack.

If (like me) you:

- Don’t like going to bed, due to it conflicting with keeping on doing things
- When in bed, wish you had something more engaging and enjoyable to do instead of just lying there waiting—for instance, playing a very compelling computer game until you get tired
- Do not in fact reliably get tired from playing a very compelling computer game
- Like puzzles

..then a solution that has worked surprisingly well for me before (and I wrote about previously) is having hard math puzzles handy to think about as I go to sleep. Somehow thinking about math at the bounds of my limited ability to imagine does make me sleepy. And is also quite compelling.

I haven’t done this for a while, I think due to disorganization and losing track of the puzzles I had, and not having a great source of new ones. But I have recently reinstated this in a nice format.

I think ideally you want this to involve no preparation at all at bed time, and no going on your computer. So you want a nice supply of the right kind of puzzles in a physical place near your bed. So I sorted through puzzles and found a bunch of good-looking ones, printed them out, cut them up, folded them into pleasing parcels, and put them in my ex-housemate’s ex-teapot. Now if I’m ready for bed, I can draw a tiny package, and open something actually fun and helpful to think about in bed.
